News.title: Trump says ‘big, beautiful agreement’ on Ukraine ‘might involve ALL of Europe’ after Putin envoy meets at White House
News.content:
Next

DONALD Trump has declared there is going to be “a big, beautiful agreement” on Ukraine which “might involve all of Europe”.

The US president made the shock remark while hosting Vladimir Putin‘s envoy and Ukrainian officials at a rare, face-to-face event in the White House.



However, he stopped short of giving further details on how any proposed deal would bring an end to the conflict, which is now in its fifth year.

Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev and Ukrainian representatives attended the event in recognition of first lady Melania Trump’s role in brokering a six-day ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky.



Speaking from the Oval Office, Trump said he had met with Dmitriev, but not the Ukrainian officials.

The president declined to give details of the discussions, but indicated the war, triggered by Russia’s 2022 invasion, was close to being settled.

He said: “There’s going to be an agreement. It’s going to be a big agreement, and it’s going to involve more than Ukraine.

“It’s going to involve more than Ukraine, and I could even say it might involve all of Europe.



“It’s going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone’s going to be thrilled.”

Trump has been pressuring Volodymyr Zelensky and his government to reach a peace deal with Moscow.

Following the crushing electoral defeats in this week’s midterms, which saw the Republicans lose control of Congress, the president is now even more likely to be seeking a settlement, which he can hold up as a win.



There has been growing discomfort among allies at the shift by Washington towards Moscow over its conflict with Kyiv.

This has seen Trump waive sanctions against the Kremlin, decline to blame Russia for starting the war and call for Zelensky to be replaced, portraying him as an obstacle to peace.

The UK Government has been a staunch supporter of Ukraine in the face of Russian aggression.

At the recent G20 meeting in Atlanta, Georgia, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband stressed the need “to secure just and lasting peace in Ukraine”.

Meanwhile, hundreds of British troops and RAF jets are due to take part in a major multinational wargame in Poland to prepare for potential peace in Ukraine.



The UK and France will jointly lead Exercise Koalicja, involving 2,800 military forces from 11 nations, aimed at ensuring Nato forces are ready to provide Ukraine with security guarantees once the conflict is over.

Running from November 9 to 22, it will be the first major military exercise conducted by the Multinational Force Ukraine (MNF-U), the military arm of the Coalition of the Willing.

Speaking at the White House event on Thursday, Slovenian-born Mrs Trump urged both sides in the conflict to choose “humanity over war” ahead of talks next week.

She said: “We must use the courage we brought to Oleshky to find common ground through a shared concern for the suffering of innocent people.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

She added: “What matters is not the modesty of this beginning but the determination to turn into something extraordinary.”



Both the Russian and Ukrainian delegations presented her with gifts.

News.title: Desperate search for missing pensioner, 69, who vanished walking his dog 4 days ago as cops share ‘distinctive dog lead’
News.content:
FIND ANTHONY Desperate search for missing pensioner, 69, who vanished walking his dog 4 days ago as cops share ‘distinctive dog lead’







Next

A FRANTIC search for a pensioner who vanished while walking his dog continues as cops release an image of a “distinctive” dog lead.

Anthony, 69, was last spotted near the Royal Oak Pub in Radcliffe, Manchester, on Sunday.



His dog was discovered several hours later, near the High Ainsworth Road junction and Bury and Bolton Road.

Search teams have been desperately trying to locate him since, with multiple units now involved.



This includes an underwater search team who are operating near Anthony’s home.

The pensioner was seen wearing a blue puffer coat and jeans.

Cops have released CCTV images of his last sighting, as well as a picture of the dog lead they believe he was using the day he disappeared.

Detective Inspector Steven Horton said: “We are becoming increasingly concerned for Anthony’s welfare and officers are working alongside our partners, including Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service, as we continue our search.

“We believe Anthony could have walked onto a canal path behind the Royal Oak pub on Sunday and we’re urging anyone who knows the surrounding area, or regularly uses the route, to remain vigilant and get in touch with us with any information.

“We are also releasing an image of the lead we believe Anthony was using to walk his dog when he went missing.



“This lead has not been found and anyone who comes across it, or thinks they have seen it, is being encouraged to call us on 101 or report online.

“While underwater search teams are involved in this operation, the hypothesis that Anthony could have entered water is just one line of enquiry that we are currently exploring.

“Our priority is bringing Anthony home to his family who we are supporting during this particularly distressing time.”

Cops are urging anyone with information that could assist the investigation to come forward.

News.title: Incredible moment hero veteran takes down shirtless gunman who ‘fatally shot woman at bank office over £1,850 debt’
News.content:
Next

THIS is the dramatic moment a hero Marine veteran takes down a shirtless gunman who stormed a banking office and shot a woman dead.

Jacob Pearson, 35, drove from Orlando to a massive CitiBank campus in Tampa in a rage after receiving a court summons for a £1,850 debt.



Shocking footage shows Pearson ram his car through the office complex’s gates and into the courtyard, narrowly missing a man sitting at a table.

He can be seen exiting the vehicle armed with a rifle, shooting Leanne Selman, 41 – the first Citibank employee he could find – three times.





After his rifle malfunctions, Pearson goes back to the car, retrieves a handgun and executes Leanne as she tries to crawl away.

The harrowing CCTV footage continues with Pearson storming the facility’s cafeteria and prowling the corridors in search of more victims.



Citibank security guard, John Fraley, can meanwhile be seen taking up a tactical position in the men’s bathroom.

As Pearson rounds the corner, the former Marine unloads five bullets into him.

The shirtless gunman is then seen keeling over as a mask covers his face.

Emergency services rushed to the scene at around midday yesterday, where Leanne was pronounced dead.



Pearson was taken to hospital, where he was pronounced dead at 1.12pm.

Before carrying out the shooting, Pearson had written a threatening message to the attorney’s office contracted for collection by Citibank.

It read: “Unless you want me to go over there with my AR- 15, my bulletproof vest, and my insanity, you MFing cancel this court case.

“Do you understand me? There are only an hour and three minutes away, so the last thing you want to do is F with me.”



Police said that Pearson, a married dad of a 7-year-old child with no criminal record, left home without telling his family soon after making the threat.

The attorney’s office relayed the threat to Citibank’s head of security, a retired Secret Service agent, who in turn warned Orlando police.

“Would you guys mind going out there and doing a welfare check on this individual?” he asked cops, according to Hillsborough County Sheriff Chad Chronister.

“This certainly doesn’t sound like something any sane person would say.”

But by the time officers arrived at Pearson’s home, he was already en route to the Citibank complex, where 3,200 employees were working.



The security chief had also contacted the Hillsborough County Sheriff’s Office, who sent detectives to the bank’s Tampa headquarters.

They heard gunshots ring out just as they were arriving at the scene shortly after noon.

Pearson was stopped in his tracks by Fraley, who was described as a “highly trained Marine Corps veteran” working as a security officer and vice president of operations on the CitiBank security team.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Of the shooter, Chronister said: “He was there, intent on one purpose, and that purpose was to hunt any human being he could find and kill.

“Because of the heroic actions of this CitiBank security officer, vice president of operations, his reign of terror ended before it even began.”

News.title: Newborn baby remains found inside toilet tank at restaurant in Philippines after waitress ‘heard infant crying’
News.content:
TRAGIC DISCOVERY Newborn baby remains found inside toilet tank at restaurant in Philippines after waitress ‘heard infant crying’







Next

A NEWBORN baby has been discovered dead inside a toilet tank at a restaurant after an employee heard faint cries.

Horrified staff at an eatery in the Philippines found the abandoned infant, who is believed to have drowned, prompting a desperate search for the person responsible.

A waitress reportedly heard muffled sounds resembling the cry of a baby inside the restroom in Nagcarlan on Wednesday, the Manila Bulletin reports.

By the time she investigated and eventually removed the ceramic lid of the toilet water tank she found the small body submerged in water.





Tragically the newborn showed no signs of life.

The worker frantically alerted restaurant management who reported the incident to the police.

Police and officials launched an investigation into the incident and later turned over the body to a funeral parlour.

Just two days prior to the tragic find, the remains of another fetus were reportedly found in a shoebox among a pile of rubbish in Manila.



The Council for the Welfare of Children condemned the two acts which they said completely disregarded the children’s dignity.

They urged authorities to ensure proper handling of the remains and accountability once the facts have been established.

The remains of the fetus, found on Monday, were found in the box wrapped in plastic mixed in with roadside rubbish in Quezon City, according to the council.

A person collecting recyclable materials found the box and alerted a nearby resident, who notified the authorities.



Executive Director Undersecretary Angelo Tapales said: “The circumstances surrounding these discoveries are deeply disturbing.

“No child’s life or dignity should ever be treated with disregard, and the discovery of fetal and infant remains in places where they were left calls for serious attention and a thorough investigation.

“We must establish the truth, ensure accountability where warranted, and strengthen the support systems that can help prevent such incidents.”

The council emphasised the need for accessible health, social welfare and psychosocial services for individuals and families facing difficult circumstances, including information on where to seek assistance.

In another similarly horrific incident in August, a baby was found dead inside a suitcase in Athens.



Six people found at the property – including a pregnant 15-year-old girl – were taken to a police station for questioning after the grim discovery in Kypseli.

Cops were called to the address by the property owner after he alleged that the family had failed to pay rent and were using drugs.

Inside the property, police found a Greek man, 43, his German wife, 38, and their two sons, aged 12 and nine.

They also discovered a 15-year-old girl and a 26-year-old Afghan man, who said he was the girl’s partner.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

During a search of the suitcases, officers found the body of a dead baby inside a glass container.



The baby had ten knife wounds in its back, believed to be inflicted by a criminal act, said news outlet GreekReporter.

News.title: How Trump may have blown a hole in Burnham’s desire to give ‘breathing space’ to hard-pressed Brits
News.content:
Next

HAS Donald Trump blown a big hole on Andy Burnham’s desire to give “breathing space” to hard-pressed Brits?

Well, that’s how it looked as I sat at the Bank of England yesterday as interest rates were hiked for the first time in three years.



Bank chiefs are desperate to control inflation and bring it back to its 2 per cent target.

But it looks like we could be waiting quite a while as households and business struggle with a major costs squeeze with the Iran war energy price shock.



It’s currently at 3.5 per cent and could hit 5 per cent next year.

To help contain inflation, rates went up yesterday from 3.75 per cent to 4 per cent.

Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey says it’s more likely than not a second hike is on the cards if energy prices go back to where they were before this week’s dip.

The long and short of it is that the Middle East conflict needs to be resolved and energy prices need to come down.

There are inflationary pressures in the pipeline and a further hike in December or February could well happen.

All this at a time when average energy bills for households will hit £2,150 in January.



Andy Burnham and Chancellor John Healey wanted to offer this breathing space and they acted quickly when getting in office.

Action on capping bus fares and VAT off energy bills were small measures but it showed those living in Downing Street were attempting to help out.

But with the public finances so tight the government can only do so much to help out.

The £100 for 20 million homes this winter will only go so far when bills land on the doormat.

Britain has called on the US President to bring an end to the hostilities to help the inflation fight.



Maybe the shocking results for the Republicans in the mid-term elections will help him decide to change course in the region.

But for the time being, the pain is going to get worse before it gets any better.

News.title: Italian chef sacked after refusing to put pineapple on pizza calling it ‘an insult to his culture’
News.content:
CRUST ISSUES Italian chef sacked after refusing to put pineapple on pizza calling it ‘an insult to his culture’







Next

AN ITALIAN chef has been sacked after refusing to put pineapple on pizza, claiming it was an insult to his culture.

Pizza-purist, Davide Tamburella, was let go from the now shuttered La Costa restaurant in Brisbane, Australia, following a string of complaints concerning his behaviour.



Among them was his refusal to top a batch of pizzas with the controversial topping at a function earlier this year.

The details have recently come to light after the chef went to Australia’s Fair Work Commission claiming he had been unfairly dismissed.



On Tuesday, when handing down their decision, the body noted that Tamburella’s refusal to put pineapple on the pizzas was because “he considers, as an Italian, that putting pineapple on a pizza is an insult to his culture”.

Despite this, he lost his unfair dismissal claim on the grounds that the application had been filed too late, according to the ruling.



The commission also noted it was the third time in four years that Tamburella had rejected the topping.

Tamburella had previously requested his boss to “check how important it is for Italians not to put pineapple on a pizza”.

The body also noted that various concerns were raised about Tamburella’s use of foul language, his communication style and “escalation of frustration in the workplace”.

Also detailed in the ruling was an incident at work in April this year where Tamburella fractured bones in his right hand when he struck a metal hand rail.



Prior to his sacking, Tamburella had been hoping the restaurant would sponsor a visa which would grant him permanent residents.

But the restaurant ended the sponsorship process when he was let go, the tribunal heard.

On the chef’s LinkedIn profile, he describes himself as someone who, throughout his career, has focused on “delivering exceptional food” and “improving business performance”.

Three months ago he posted a “letter for chefs” with the theme “respecting the ingredients”.

The LinkedIn profile states he now works at another Brisbane restaurant where pineapple is not on its menu, the BBC reports.



It comes as a wicked waitress was charged after she spiked tourists’ food with bleach in a sickening act of revenge on the Costa Del Sol.

Holidaymakers had a lucky escape after the worker doused the dessert area of the buffet with toxic bleach.

After learning the Benalmadena resort wouldn’t renew her waitress contract, the woman hatched the vengeful plan to sabotage the venue.

But she was thwarted when she was spotted pouring a glass of bleach directly onto a tray containing yogurt, pineapple and watermelon, foods that were ready for consumption by the guests of the hotel.

The woman was arrested and later handed a one year suspended sentence for her toxic-food-tampering crimes.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Subsequent tests on the food were later confirmed to have been tainted with bleach, according to cops.

The prosecution said she acted with the “clear intention of harming the hotel through food poisoning.”

News.title: Huge fire erupts at takeaway restaurant as 70 firefighters battle inferno as man jumps from building to escape flames
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

BLAZE BATTLE Huge fire erupts at takeaway restaurant as 70 firefighters battle inferno as man jumps from building to escape flames







Next

A RAGING fire has broken out at a takeaway restaurant with 70 firefighters tackling the inferno as one man jumped from the first floor of the building.

Emergency services rushed to Seven Sisters Road in Finsbury Park, London, at around 3.52pm this afternoon.

The blaze had broken out at ground floor restaurant Shish Shash, causing damage to a second floor flat as well as the roof.

Around eight people were evacuated from the premises.





One man was seen jumping from the first floor to escape the flames.

He suffered only minor injuries from the fall and was taken to hospital for treatment.

Ten fire engines and around 70 firefighters attended the scene.

Onlookers reported seeing flames billowing from the rooftop as fire engines blasted it with water jets.



Pictures show people gathering outside the restaurant on the brightly-lit street as smoke escapes through windows.

Station Commander Adam Lawson was at the scene, he said: “Local residents were advised to keep their windows and doors closed.

“There was very heavy traffic and motorists and pedestrians should avoid the area.

“The Seven Sisters Road is closed between Holloway Road and Finsbury Park station.”



The cause of the fire is currently unknown but is now under control, the London Fire Brigade said.

The closure of the Seven Sisters road caused major congestion in the area and led to multiple bus diversions.

Motorists and pedestrians were advised to avoid the area in an update issued this evening.

News.title: Labour’s tax hikes force Betfred to pull sponsorship of British Classics horseracing events
News.content:
Next

LABOUR’S new betting tax hikes have forced Betfred to pull sponsorship of the British Classics horseracing events.

The industry giant blamed the “sad” decision on John Healey’s increase to Machine Games Duty in last week’s Budget.



The Chancellor raised the levy from 20 to 25 per cent to fund cost of living handouts for 20 million families.

But the company has warned of even greater job cuts on top of those already expected because of a raid by Rachel Reeves last year.



A Betfred spokesperson said: “Following successive tax rises for the betting industry – and in particular the increase to machine games duty at the most recent budget – it is with great sadness that we have taken the difficult decision not to proceed with a three-year renewal of our sponsorship of the British Classics.

“It is not a decision we wanted to make, but the cumulative cost of government policy has left us with no choice.”

The British Classics include the Guineas Stakes at Newmarket, the Epsom Derby and the St Leger Stakes at Doncaster.

The Sun’s Save Our Bets campaign has been warning of the devastating impacts on livelihoods as a result of tax rises.

Sector analysis showed that the Machine Game Duty hike could see 9,000 people laid off and almost 1,000 betting shops shut.

The industry was already absorbing £1.7billion in tax hikes from Ms Reeves’ Budget unleashed in 2026



Betting giant Flutter has already said it will make 1,400 people redundant following Labour’s devastating tax raid on the industry.

The home to brands such as Paddy Power and Sky Bet will cut around 15 per cent of its workforce.

News.title: Met chief warns policing 'heading for failure' without reform
News.content:
The head of the Metropolitan Police is to warn that policing in England and Wales is "heading for failure" without urgent reform.

In a speech on Friday, Sir Mark Rowley will call for the system to change, arguing it is unable to cope with the sophistication of modern criminals.

He is proposing eight to 10 regional police forces, supported by hundreds of local policing commands and a new National Police Service, in what would be the biggest overhaul since the 1960s.

The changes would replace the 43-force structure with three tiers: local teams dealing with neighbourhood issues, regional forces sharing specialist resources and a National Police Service tackling the most serious crimes.

Sir Mark says organised crime groups, fraud networks, cyber-criminals and those involved in online child abuse increasingly operate across regional and international borders, while police forces remain organised around local areas.

He will warn that the current system is struggling to keep pace with these threats, saying: "We have 43 overstretched forces trying to do too much, with too little."

He believes merging forces would reduce duplication, arguing this could free up thousands of roles to be redirected towards front line policing.

His proposals follow a consultation launched by Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood in January. This included plans for a National Police Service to tackle the most complex crimes and a possible merger of the 43 forces into fewer, larger forces.

However some rural police and crime commissioners have described the plans as "political manoeuvring" by larger forces to "load the dice in their favour".

The Association of Police and Crime Commissioners (APCC) has also questioned whether merging forces is the best way to improve policing.

It said: "The case for modernisation and a National Police Service is clear. The case for reducing 43 forces to nine regional 'mega-forces' is not."

A Home Office spokesperson defended the plans, saying: "Our current model of policing has not changed since the 1960s and is no longer fit for purpose."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has not yet commented.

Sir Mark has also highlighted the financial pressures facing policing, asserting that spending on policing had fallen from about 0.9% of GDP to 0.7% since 2010.

He says years of underinvestment have left forces relying on ageing technology, while officers are increasingly diverted from neighbourhood policing to deal with other demands, including mental health and social care.

He will also point to falling police performance, saying positive outcomes nationally are now less than half the level they were 12 years ago, while public confidence has fallen by 9%.

News.title: Russell Brand is being investigated over two new rape complaints, police say
News.content:
Warning: Details of rape and sexual assault

Russell Brand is being investigated over rape allegations made by two more women, it can now be reported.

The disgraced comedian has been found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault by a jury of eight men and four women at Southwark Crown Court, following a three-week trial.

More victims are likely to come forward following his conviction, the detective who led the police investigation has said.

Det Supt Andy Furphy, from the Metropolitan Police, said he hoped other women would gain "courage" and "confidence" from the guilty verdicts.

Brand was found not guilty of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

News.title: Firms told to publish salaries in job adverts ahead of new law
News.content:
The Cabinet Office launched a consultation into pay and reducing discrimination in the summer, and the government said there had been "overwhelming support" for greater transparency, with 94% of respondents backing the move.

"Whether you're a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it," Burnham said.

The government said the move was part of attempts to reduce the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - ahead of the final report of the Milburn Review into youth inactivity, which is due in the coming weeks.

Publishing salary details upfront could "expose unjustified differences in pay, give workers greater confidence to challenge discrimination and prevent disagreements over pay escalating into disputes".

The proposals are similar to measures being introduced in the European Union., external

Employers in Europe will have to disclose the initial pay or range for new roles, which must either be included in a published job advert or shared before an interview.

According to data from UK jobs website Adzuna, external, 51% of the adverts on its site in September had salary information, but the proportion has been falling in recent years.

Adzuna co-founder Andrew Hunter said being open about pay "should be the norm, not the exception".

He added that employers who put a salary on a job advert "attract more applicants, and better-suited ones".

News.title: Thatcher's Right to Buy split my estate. Now its days could be numbered
News.content:
Growing up in a council flat in the 1980s and 1990s, my mum would often point out homes that tenants had bought from the council. You could usually tell just from looking. A plain wooden door had been replaced with something fancier. New windows had appeared. Sometimes there was a porch or pillars outside the front door.

Those houses were bought under the Right to Buy scheme - arguably the most consequential housing policy of my lifetime. It was introduced in 1980, three years before I was born, when Margaret Thatcher's government gave council tenants in England the legal right to purchase their homes at a discounted price.

Supporters welcomed the chance for working-class families to own their own home and build wealth. Critics argue it hollowed out the country's stock of social housing and contributed to today's housing crisis.

Some of my neighbours "made a killing" from the policy, in the words of my mum. One bought an almost identical flat to ours in 1989 for Â£21,200, after receiving a discount of Â£18,800. Eight years later it sold for Â£54,500. Five years after that it changed hands again for Â£143,000. (Notably, the person who made the most money from that flat wasn't the original council tenant - it was the people who bought it afterwards.)

News.title: Police car set alight in Glasgow amid Bonfire Night trouble
News.content:
Seven people have been arrested during Bonfire Night disorder in parts of Scotland, police say.

A police officer and an ambulance staff member sustained minor injuries when they were attacked with fireworks while responding to a report of an injured man in Glasgow, according to Police Scotland.

A police vehicle was set alight and seriously damaged during the incident in the Greenside Street area, and a 16-year-old boy was arrested.

Police and members of the public were also targeted with fireworks in several areas of Edinburgh.

Fire service personnel came under attack in a number of towns while responding to calls but none were hurt and no serious damage was caused to fire engines.

"Police officers, ambulance staff and firefighters are there to protect communities â not be the target of violence," Chief Superintendent David Robertson said.

"I want to make it clear that thorough investigations will now take place to identify those responsible and bring them to justice."

He added that the policing operation covering the Halloween and Bonfire Night had been "one of the most complex and demanding deployments in recent memory involving the largest number of officers" since the visit of US President Donald Trump last year.

However, there had been a "reduction in serious incidents requiring... specialist resources" compared with the same period last year, he added.

News.title: King relishes 'politically charged' deployments, Palace aide says
News.content:
The King relishes the "tough parts" of his role and will continue to be used in "politically charged situations", a senior palace aide said at the end of the King's tour of the Caribbean.

Over the past nine days, the King visited the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda and has been used as "a great secret weapon", the aide said.

Questions over whether the UK should apologise and pay reparations for its role in the transatlantic slave trade were a theme of the visit.

"I think what we're seeing is a very clear pattern emerging of the government asking the King to head into quite politically charged situations, quite challenging situations," the aide said.

"We have to tread quite a careful line sometimes between government policy and the King's role."

The leadership of all three countries visited on the Caribbean tour wanted reparatory justice.

"I would say, in the round, this has been a complex visit. It's been challenging. It's been exhausting," the aide said. "But the takeaway is that it's been very successful and I think the King has demonstrated his statecraft both by word and deed."

Most of the King's visits outside the UK have seen him draw on some delicate diplomatic skills on behalf of his government.

In the US, he used his speech to Congress to remind President Donald Trump of the UK's value as an ally.

A year earlier he made a flying visit to Canada to welcome new Prime Minister Mark Carney as the latter faced an onslaught of threats and insults from Trump.

Visits to Germany and France in the early part of the King's reign were designed to establish new UK alliances post-Brexit.

"The King is not just King for the easy parts of the job, but the tough parts of the job, too," said the aide.

"In fact, that's probably the part of the job that he relishes most, whether that's leading on the environment, whether it's renewing and refreshing and reinvigorating relationships with nations where there have been some complex political issues at play, that is what he lives and breathes for."

News.title: Andrew received up to £2,000 per month from sub-letting, watchdog reports
News.content:
But it emerged that as a tenant he had been intermittently sub-letting three cottages that were part of the property, which was thought to be for staff and at a below market rate, with Mountbatten-Windsor keeping the income.

The Crown Estate had told MPs that it did not have any oversight over how much Mountbatten-Windsor charged - and sub-letting was allowed as part of his lease.

But the MPs have recommended that in future the default position for such Crown Estate properties should be that such sub-letting should be banned, unless there was a specific exemption.

The Public Accounts Committee report also confirms what has happened since Mountbatten-Windsor's departure from Royal Lodge.

There was a payment of about Â£300,000 due to him for his early surrender of his lease, but because of "dilapidations" in the state of the building, there was a repair bill of Â£1.8m.

That meant the Crown Estate was owed Â£1.5m, which King Charles paid on his brother's behalf.

The watchdog's report also highlighted concerns about the level of rent being charged to non-working royals who had been given accommodation in three royal properties.

That was believed to be Mountbatten-Windsor's daughters, Princess Beatrice and Princess Eugenie, and Prince and Princess Michael of Kent.

A National Audit Office report had revealed earlier this year that Princess Beatrice and Princess Eugenie do not pay anything themselves for their accommodation in St James's Palace and Kensington Palace respectively.

The King pays their rent to the Royal Household from his own private income.

But the group of MPs were concerned about whether the level of rent on such properties for non-working royals was based on up-to-date valuations and recommended a more consistent approach to ensure value for money.

There was criticism too for the Crown Estate concentrating too much of its urban property portfolio in London and the south east of England, with MPs calling for more of a regional spread.

There were also warnings about how the Crown Estate's administration costs had increased significantly, at a time when MPs noted government budgets were under pressure.

The report said administration costs had risen by 129% since 2020-21 and that the chief executive, Dan Labbad's salary had risen by 106% over that time. In 2025-26 his pay package was worth Â£2.3m.

In response, a Crown Estate spokeswoman said: "The Public Accounts Committee report is an important part of our accountability to Parliament. We are considering its findings and recommendations and will respond to the Committee in due course."

News.content:
More than 20 aircraft across Europe have been targeted by bomb threats. It's the second time this week, which the UK has called a "malicious hoax".

BBC Verify has been analysing the messages sent by an aircraft to find out what happens when a flight receives a bomb hoax - as Thomas Copeland explains.

News.title: Home Office investigating after BBC catches lawyer offering to make fines go away
News.content:
The Home Office has launched an investigation after a solicitor was secretly filmed by the BBC explaining how he could make a Â£45,000 illegal-working fine go away.

Mohammad Alias Yousaf - also known as Alias - made the claim to an undercover reporter, who was posing as a mini-mart owner facing a fine for employing an illegal worker.

The Solicitors Regulation Authority has said it will also examine the BBC's findings to see whether there has been misconduct by solicitors or law firms.

The Bradford-based solicitor told his potential client he could avoid paying the fine if he was able to find someone overseas prepared to declare themselves the owner of the mini-mart.

Yousaf has denied ever providing such advice to anyone, or giving false information to the Home Office.

The BBC's wider investigation also revealed at least Â£150m is currently owed to the government in uncollected illegal-working fines, according to Home Office figures exclusively obtained by the BBC.

In response, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood ordered a review of the way such fines are issued and collected.

Mahmood said she wanted to thank the BBC "for exposing those who undermine our rules".

"Illegal working undermines honest employers, undercuts local wages, and fuels organised immigration crime," she added.

The Home Office said it would be investigating the allegations to see whether there had been a breach of immigration rules.

Senior politicians have since called UK immigration enforcement "weak" and a "laughing stock".

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp has called for Yousaf to be "struck off as a solicitor", while shadow justice minister Nick Timothy has written to the head of the regulator for solicitors to take "urgent action, and stop Mr Yousaf practising as a solicitor".

Philp said: "Shabana Mahmood likes to boast about how many fines are issued, but now it turns out most just get ignored. No wonder we have a borders crisis with enforcement turning into a laughing stock."

A spokesman for the Solicitors Regulation Authority said: "We will be considering this information to see if there are any issues arising which we need to look into further."

The BBC also heard from a law enforcement whistleblower who, speaking anonymously, revealed it was a struggle to identify the real owners of businesses caught with illegal workers.

She said she had seen immigration fine notices, "some worth Â£40,000, stuffed in a box" on a mini-mart counter.

"I've said to owners 'I see you've got a fine, are you going to pay it?' And they just laugh in my face, throw the fine back in a box and say 'it's got nothing to do with me'."

News.title: Could the earliest weakening of the polar vortex on record bring UK snow?
News.content:
High above the Arctic, powerful winds usually circle the North Pole each winter, helping trap some of the coldest air on Earth.

But this circulation, known as the polar vortex, has weakened and shifted position in recent days.

While such disruptions can occur during winter, scientists say an event this early in November is unprecedented in modern observations.

Similar disruptions in past years have sometimes been followed by colder weather affecting parts of Europe and North America.

However, as this is happening so early in the season, there are few historical examples to compare with and it could throw current winter forecasts into even more uncertainty.

News.title: Interest rates hiked to 4% in first increase in over three years
News.content:
Interest rates have risen for the first time in more than three years and the Bank of England has signalled a further increase is likely unless the US-Iran war is resolved.

Rates rose to 4% from 3.75% in a bid to curb inflation mainly driven by the conflict's impact on global oil prices.

Andrew Bailey, the Bank's governor, said the decision "shouldn't be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes", but warned "unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase".

The higher level will increase the cost of borrowing for things such as mortgages, loans and credit cards, but will also lead to higher returns on savings.

The Bank's rate-setting committee all backed increasing interest rates, with eight out of nine voting in favour of the rise to 4%. One member wanted an even bigger increase to 4.25%.

Bailey said the hike was warranted due to higher energy prices and pointed to what happens in the Middle East as the main factor in future decisions.

"Put simply, it requires real progress towards settling the conflict in the Middle East," the governor said.

Bailey said he could "see the argument" for a further rate hike, before taking a "more conditional approach" dependent on the path of energy prices and inflation in the coming months.

However, the views of members on the rate-setting committee differed on the path forward.

Clare Lombardelli agreed there was "likely to be a case for a further increase in rates in the near term", while Megan Greene went further, suggesting "additional hikes" might be likely depending on how inflation impacted wages, prices and the jobs market.

However, Alan Taylor said the rate rise was a "a risk-management 'one-for-now' insurance hike".

News.title: Married at First Sight UK cancelled after BBC revealed rape allegations
News.content:
Married at First Sight UK will not return, Channel 4 has said, following a BBC investigation into the hit reality TV show.

The Channel 4 show was plunged into crisis earlier this year, after Panorama revealed rape allegations from two female cast members on the show, while a third woman alleged a non-consensual sex act. The men involved have denied all the allegations against them.

A review was commissioned by Channel 4 shortly after the BBC first contacted the broadcaster, with details of the allegations we had heard.

On Thursday, the completed review recommended extra safeguards on the show. But Channel 4 said the programme had "run its course" and apologised to the women involved in the investigation.

The broadcaster's chief executive Priya Dogra said she was "very sorry for the distress those women have clearly felt", adding that the show's budget would be reinvested in "distinctive new programming".

The Panorama investigation in May, in which three women made allegations about the men they were partnered with - claims the men deny, made the following allegations:

One woman said her onscreen husband raped her and threatened her with an acid attack.

A second woman told both Channel 4 and CPL, before broadcast, about being allegedly raped by her onscreen husband. Her episodes were still aired.

A third woman - Shona Manderson, the only woman who was identified - accused her onscreen husband of sexual misconduct.

All three women accused the show of not doing enough to protect them.

Lawyers for CPL, the independent production company that makes the UK version of the show, previously said its welfare system is "gold standard" and industry-leading, and that it acted appropriately in all these cases.

Channel 4 had initially told Panorama that all the allegations were "wholly uncorroborated".

Dame Caroline Dinenage MP, chair of the House of Commons culture and media committee, said the decision to axe the show "makes sense" given the review's findings and the "seriousness of the allegations".

"Reality TV contestants have often been treated as a commodity, with duty of care a slogan rather than a genuine principle. Everyone involved in producing and regulating reality TV must now learn and act," she added.

A spokesman for Ofcom said the broadcast regulator would "carefully consider the reports published today as we move to strengthen our guidance for broadcasters".

"We are clear that broadcasters have a duty of care towards members of the public who participate in their programmes."

News.title: Henry Nowak’s killer has minimum term increased to 25 years by Court of Appeal
News.content:
A man jailed for life for murdering Henry Nowak has had his minimum prison term increased to 25 years by the Court of Appeal.

Vickrum Digwa was serving a minimum of 21 years for stabbing 18-year-old student Nowak with a large dagger in Belmont Road, Southampton, on 3 December 2025.

The Attorney General referred the case to the Court of Appeal on the grounds it was "unduly lenient", while Digwa also challenged his jail term as "manifestly excessive".

The Lady Chief Justice quashed the sentence, ruling the original term "did not adequately reflect the overall seriousness of the murder".

Digwa, who was also refused permission to appeal, told police Henry had attacked and racially abused him, which led to Henry, from Chafford Hundred in Essex, being handcuffed as he lay dying.

The trial judge later found Digwa's accusations of racism to be a lie. Then 22, he was jailed for life at Southampton Crown Court in June.

News.title: UK doctor infected with Ebola being treated at London hospital
News.content:
A British doctor who tested positive for Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo has been flown back to the UK.

The man, who has not been identified, landed at RAF Northolt before being transported to a specialist infectious diseases unit at the Royal Free Hospital in north London.

It is the first confirmed case of a UK national contracting Ebola during the most recent outbreak of the rare but deadly virus in DR Congo, which has so far led to more than 5,000 deaths.

Dr Renu Bindra, deputy director of the All Hazards Public Health Response team at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), said there are "well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this" and the risk to the public remains low.

News.title: Farage says he is worried Trump will step up Iran war after midterm 'disaster'
News.content:
Nigel Farage has said he fears Donald Trump will "aggressively" continue his war with Iran after his "disaster" in the US midterm elections.

The Reform UK leader said the US president was still a friend, but accused him of having "broke a promise" to the American electorate by launching the war.

The war in Iran, which the US began in February 2026, weighed heavily in the midterm election results earlier this week in which the Democrats swept Trump's Republicans out of power in Congress.

Farage, who had initially urged people to support the war, said that following the election results he worried Trump would respond with more strikes on Iran.

Asked how he thinks President Trump will respond, Farage told broadcasters on Thursday: "I suppose I worry that the president will continue aggressively attacking Iran.

"That worries me because that would have even more serious implications for the price of oil, for inflation, for the whole western world".

He acknowledged he had initially supported the war but stressed he "never supported endless war".

Asked if the war was a mistake, he said: "There's no question about it."

The US president had "always kept his promises," added Farage, but "in this case, he said no more foreign wars and here we are in month eight of a war with no sign of ending."

"That and the resulting fuel prices are what in the end has done the damage."

Trump said on Tuesday that the poor results for Republican congressional candidates were partly due to the war and the related surge in oil prices.

But he insisted he did not regret launching a joint attack with Israel on Iran.

News.title: More Mandelson papers set to be published before Christmas
News.content:
The government is preparing to publish more documents about the appointment of Lord Mandelson as US ambassador.

Batches of papers were published in March and June - but others were withheld because they were part of a Metropolitan Police investigation.

The Cabinet Office has now said a number of extra documents will be published, likely before Christmas. Some will still be withheld at the request of the Met.

Cat Little, permanent secretary at the Cabinet Office, said that some of the documents could "now be published without prejudicing their investigation".

The Met Police had launched an investigation over allegations that, while he was serving as a government minister, Lord Mandelson had passed on market-sensitive government information to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Writing to the chair of Parliament's Intelligence and Security Committee, Little said: "The Cabinet Office is now beginning the process to prepare these documents so that they may be laid before the House in response to the humble address motion as soon as possible."

She said the documents would be reviewed and in some instances may need to be redacted "for the purposes of avoiding prejudice to national security or international relations".

The process is expected to be completed before Parliament rises for the Christmas recess on 17 December.

Lord Mandelson was arrested on 23 February on suspicion of misconduct in public office.

He has repeatedly let it be known that he believes he has not acted criminally, did not act for personal gain and is cooperating with the police.

"Our investigation into alleged misconduct in public office is ongoing," the Met Police said in a statement.

The lifelong Labour politician became the British ambassador to the US in February 2025, but was sacked in September after Downing Street said new information about the extent of his relationship with Epstein had emerged.

After his sacking, the government - then led by Sir Keir Starmer - was heavily criticised for giving Lord Mandelson the job and in February MPs voted to force the government to publish papers relating to his appointment.

Mike Wood, shadow Cabinet Office minister, said: "We still haven't got to the bottom of the Mandelson scandal.

"Labour did their utmost to hold this information back and it was only released because of the Conservatives humble address."

News.title: Thailand bans academic textbook citing national security
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Thailand has banned an academic textbook on the country, citing national security concerns.

The editor of the textbook has claimed that the ban is linked to chapters examining the monarchy and its role in Thai politics.

The second edition of the Routledge Handbook of Contemporary Thailand, published in English in August, was edited by Pavin Chachavalpongpun, a Thai academic and outspoken critic of the monarchy who is based in Japan.

The revised edition includes discussions of the monarchy in the 21st century and the authorities’ use of Section 112 of Thailand’s Criminal Code, commonly known as the lese majeste law.

The book’s first edition, published in 2019, was not prohibited.

Mr Pavin told AFP that the latest edition was updated to “reflect changes in Thai politics” following the youth-led pro-democracy demonstrations of 2020, during which protesters made unprecedented demands for reforms to the monarchy and military.

An order signed by National Police Chief Samran Nualma and issued on Wednesday said the publication contained articles that “adversely affect national security and might cause unrest in the country”.

The order also stated that its contents “affect the security of the kingdom, public order or the good morals of the people”, authorising police to confiscate and destroy copies of the book.

open image in gallery File. Maha Vajiralongkorn Rama X King of the Kingdom of Thailand on his arrival before a meeting with the President of the French Republic and his wife and the Queen of the Kingdom of Thailand at the Elysee Presidential Palace in Paris France on June 29, 2026. ( AFP/Getty )

Importing or distributing the publication could result in a prison sentence of up to three years, a fine of 60,000 baht or both.

Mr Pavin has said that the subjects covered in the revised edition were the reason for the ban, as the textbook is “packed with material on the monarchy”.

“Topics like this are why they decided to ban it,” he was quoted as saying by CNA. “Thailand’s democracy is backsliding, and book bans are a clear indicator of that.”

In a Facebook post, Mr Pavin thanked the Royal Thai Police for drawing attention to the book, suggesting that the restrictions could have the opposite of their intended effect.

“In the era of social media and the internet, a ban like this doesn’t work,” he wrote. “People might just skip the hard copy and get an ebook.”

In a separate post, he added that “after the ban, the publisher gets money, I get money, Thai people are more aware. It’s a win-win all around”.

This is not the first time authorities have prohibited a publication by Mr Pavin. In 2023, his book Rama X: The Thai Monarchy under King Vajiralongkorn, published by Yale University Southeast Asia Studies, was banned under a similar order.

A police statement at the time said the book’s cover and contents reflected “the attitude of the author, deemed insulting to the Thai monarchy, and threatened the peace and good morality of the people”.

Mr Pavin, 55, previously worked for Thailand’s ministry of foreign affairs for 16 years before pursuing an academic career.

He has lived in exile in Kyoto since the 2014 military coup, after refusing to comply with a summons issued by the junta. His passport was subsequently revoked and an arrest warrant issued, according to The Bangkok Post.

He has also faced legal action over his involvement in the Facebook group Royalist Marketplace, known in Thai as Talad Luang, which discusses the monarchy and proposals for political reform.

Thai Lawyers for Human Rights said in August this year that he was among three people facing lese majeste charges linked to posts in the group.

Thailand’s lese majeste legislation protects the royal family from insults, defamation or threats. Those convicted can receive prison sentences ranging from three to 15 years for each offence.

News.title: South Korea apologises for government manual classifying homosexuality as juvenile delinquency
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

South Korea has pledged to revise a government-affiliated youth counselling manual that classified homosexuality as a form of juvenile delinquency, placing it alongside sexual violence, theft and drug-related problems.

The Ministry of Gender Equality and Family announced the decision on Wednesday, apologising after the classification prompted criticism from human rights organisations and LGBT+ advocates.

“We regret that the classification of content concerning sexual minorities as a type of delinquency-related problem in the manual has caused discomfort and concern to sexual minority youth and those involved,” the ministry said in a statement.

The manual was published by the Korea Youth Counselling and Welfare Institute, an organisation affiliated with the ministry, and distributed to specialists known as “youth companions”. They work with young people considered at risk, providing counselling and connecting them with welfare, healthcare and education services.

The wording was first included in the manual's third revised edition, published in December 2019, and remained in its fourth edition, released in December 2025.

LGBTQ supporters participate in the Seoul Queer Culture Festival on 13 June 2026 in Seoul ( Getty )

The classification came to light on Monday after it was reported by South Korean media.

On Wednesday, human rights organisations, led by a support centre for LGBTQ+ young people, issued a joint statement demanding that the government correct the manual.

The institute attributed the wording to an error by the team responsible for writing the manual, saying it had been carried over from older reference material.

The ministry said it would immediately remove the problematic classification and undertake a broader review of the manual in consultation with counselling experts. It also pledged to strengthen human rights training for youth companions and staff at youth counselling and welfare centres.

The government further promised to improve guidelines and support systems for youth shelters to ensure that young people are not refused admission or disadvantaged because of their sexual orientation or gender identity.

The ministry pointed to changes made in August to a separate human rights protection manual for youth shelter staff, following feedback from LGBTQ+ support organisations and other groups.

The revised guidance explicitly prohibits shelters from refusing admission or treating young people unfavourably because of their sexual orientation or gender identity. It also requires staff to document the reasons for restricting admission or asking a resident to leave, and to ensure such decisions are not influenced by an individual's personal characteristics.

Where young people experience difficulties adjusting to shelter life, staff are instructed to consider counselling, mediation and improvements to living conditions before resorting to discharge.

“Based on feedback gathered last December from groups supporting sexual minorities and others, we revised the youth human rights protection manual for youth shelter staff in August,” a ministry official said. “We will work to ensure that all young people can receive counselling and protection without discrimination.”

The controversy comes against the backdrop of longstanding international medical recognition that homosexuality is not a mental disorder.

The World Health Organization's International Classification of Diseases, approved in 1990, does not regard sexual orientation by itself as a disorder. The revised classification came into force for health services in 1994.

News.title: Closing arguments expected in trial of ex-cop accused of killing Sandra Birchmore
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Closing arguments are expected Friday in the trial of a former Massachusetts police officer accused of killing a pregnant woman to keep her from revealing that they had been in a sexual relationship that began when she was 15.

Federal prosecutors say Matthew Farwell killed Sandra Birchmore, 23, and tried to stage her death as a suicide in 2021 after learning she was pregnant with what he thought was his child. At the time, Farwell was a married detective with the Stoughton Police Department, where Birchmore had participated in a youth program as a child.

Lawyers for Farwell, who is now 40, acknowledge he had an extramarital relationship with Birchmore. But they say he didn't kill her and didn't have sex with her until she was an adult.

The trial has unfolded in federal court in Boston, partly because local prosecutors never brought criminal charges.

Local police and investigators from the Massachusetts State Police, some with personal connections to Farwell, quickly concluded Birchmore's death was a suicide after she was found slumped on her apartment floor with a strap around her neck.

The state’s medical examiner, relying partly on information from police, also initially ruled that Birchmore died by suicide. The office has since changed the official cause of death to “undetermined.”

But Birchmore's friends and family never believed the teacher's aide had killed herself.

She had told dozens of friends about her pregnancy and, according to prosecutors, was thrilled to start her next chapter as a single mom. She had booked a maternity shoot, was searching for a venue for her baby shower and considering baby names. A stroller, still in the box, was found in her apartment along with an ultrasound photo pinned to her refrigerator.

The FBI began looking into Birchmore’s death in 2023, partly at the urging of a former deputy chief at the Stoughton Police Department who had led an internal affairs investigation into Farwell and several other officers accused of misconduct.

As they dug into the case, federal investigators concluded the local probe was rushed and compromised. Farwell was interviewed for just 15 minutes in a parking lot, they said. Investigators didn’t take notes, examine him for injuries or sample his DNA. Police did look at Farwell’s phone, but only after he had deleted texts with Birchmore.

Farwell’s twin brother, Billy Farwell, testified that the lead investigator — a longtime family friend — told him he wanted the case closed and needed the investigation like he needed a “bullet in the head.”

The FBI investigation uncovered about 40,000 texts between Farwell and Birchmore, including some in which they reminisced about having sex when she was 15 — too young to consent under Massachusetts law.

The text exchanges also showed how their relationship grew contentious as Birchmore pressed Farwell to get her pregnant — and threatened to tell his wife about their relationship if he didn’t. After she learned of her pregnancy in late 2020, texts showed they argued over what role, if any, Farwell would play in the child's life.

At the trial, a digital forensics expert testified that Birchmore’s phone stopped moving at 9:40 p.m. on Feb. 1, 2021 — three minutes before the lobby security camera recorded Farwell leaving her building on the night of her death.

An expert hired by prosecutors, Dr. William Smock, testified that Birchmore’s injuries indicated she was strangled with a duffel bag strap and that she struggled before dying.

The defense countered with their own expert, Dr. Thomas Andrew, the former chief medical examiner in New Hampshire, who said the evidence pointed to hanging. He dismissed Smock's determination that it was a homicide.

Farwell’s lawyers say he went to Birchmore’s apartment to break up with her, not kill her. They say Birchmore was broke and alone when she became pregnant, and took her own life.

A paternity test later revealed that a different man was the father of Birchmore's unborn child.

Farwell's legal team also leaned heavily on Birchmore's mental health challenges and attempted to show she was at risk of suicide. She began taking psychiatric medication at age 6, they said, attempted suicide as a teenager and wrote several times about suicide in her journals.

News.title: What to know about Pope Leo XIV's trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Pope Leo XIV is returning home to the continent where he spent two decades as a missionary priest and learned to be a pastor, visiting Uruguay, Argentina and his second homeland of Peru.

The Nov. 6-17 trip marks the longest and farthest of his papacy and is coming just three weeks after Leo underwent surgery Oct. 13 to remove a cancerous tumor from his right lung. Doctors nevertheless gave him the green light to make the trip.

Latin America still is home to around 40% of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics, but the Catholic proportion of the region’s population has shrunk in recent year s and the decreases are especially notable in the countries Leo will visit.

Uruguay: Nov. 6-8

The trip begins in Uruguay, whose secular identity and separation of church and state are so deeply entrenched that Christmas is officially “Family Day” and Holy Week is “Tourism Week.”

According to Vatican statistics, nearly 77% of Uruguay’s 3.5 million people are baptized Catholics. But more than half of all Uruguayans identify as religiously unaffiliated — the highest portion in Latin America – and only a fraction of those who identify as Catholic actually go to Mass regularly.

Leo’s itinerary includes a stop at a parish in Casavalle, a poor neighborhood on the outskirts of Montevideo plagued by drug trafficking and gang violence. The church works with national and municipal authorities on support initiatives, including housing construction and addiction recovery programs.

Leo will also celebrate Mass in Paysandú, some 375 kilometers (230 miles) from the capital and chosen because of its accessibility to those living north of the Río Negro, a river that crosses the country, and proximity to the Argentine city of Colón.

The visit begins with a welcome ceremony at the Plaza Independencia in the center of Montevideo, a symbol of Uruguay’s national identity and history. The plaza features a monument to independence hero José Gervasio Artigas.

But most significantly, Leo will mark an important Catholic feast day Nov. 8, which commemorates the Virgin of the Thirty-three, the patron of Uruguay and an icon deeply rooted in the country’s history and patriotism.

According to tradition, 33 independence patriots acquired the small, wooden Guaraní statue and had it with them when independence was declared from the Brazilian empire in the Uruguayan city of Florida on Aug. 25, 1825. It was to the virgin that the insurgents entrusted their faith.

By celebrating the feast day, paying homage to Artigas and celebrating Uruguay’s independence, Leo is expected to emphasize that Uruguay’s secular nationhood is intrinsically connected to its Catholic heritage. The goal is to suggest that there is still a place for faith today in even the most secular of countries.

Argentina: Nov. 8-11

Pope Francis’ refusal to return home to Argentina during his pontificate, and his polarizing tenure as both archbishop and pope, left a conflicted legacy that will dog Leo’s visit. But the American pope will formally honor his predecessor when he visits Buenos Aires’ cathedral and in a more symbolic way when he visits the federal prison where then-Cardinal Jorge Mario Bergoglio ministered to inmates.

In the capital, Leo will also meet with libertarian President Javier Milei, who once called Francis “the representative of evil on Earth.” Milei later apologized.

Milei’s sweeping spending cuts, though, have strained relations with Argentine church leaders, who have criticized his government for cuts to disability funding and for putting economic orthodoxy ahead of the needs of the poor.

That flashpoint will be on display when Leo visits the Don Orione care home in Claypole, south of Buenos Aires, a Catholic institution that houses more than 400 people with disabilities. The institution has reported facing extreme economic problems due to the spending cuts, outdated rates, inflation, and state payment delays.

Leo will also hear of economic woes when he meets with business leaders, trade unions, workers and social representatives at the Argentine Catholic University. Union leaders have said they intend to brief him on the crisis, including rising unemployment, poverty, and the erosion of household purchasing power.

According to official data, poverty in Argentina reached 32.3% of the population during the first half of 2026, representing about 15 million people.

Another possible flashpoint between Milei and Leo could come over artificial intelligence. Milei, a Trump ally, has courted AI investment and data centers with promises of limited regulation, while Leo has warned about the threats to humanity and the environment of the AI race and called for strict, internationally policed safeguards on its development.

Leo will celebrate his first Mass in Argentina at Buenos Aires’ Monumento de los Españoles, where St. John Paul II led prayers for peace on June 12, 1982, during Argentina’s war with Britain over the Falkland Islands. John Paul, who also came in 1987, was the first and last pope to visit.

When Francis was elected, around 71% of Argentina’s population identified as Catholic, according to the Pew Research Center. That percentage has fallen to 58% in 2024.

And yet this year, in a prelude to Leo’s visit and despite persistent rain, a record of more than 2.8 million people took part in the annual pilgrimage south of Buenos Aires to the Basilica de Nuestra Señora de Luján, Argentina’s patron.

Peru: Nov. 11-16

The highlight of Leo’s trip will certainly be his return to Peru and especially his diocese of Chiclayo, including the sprawling midsize city in northern Peru near the Pacific Coast. Leo will celebrate Mass in all his old stomping grounds including the mountain village of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba.

Leo spent two decades ministering in Peru as a missionary priest and then bishop, and has credited the place and its people with shaping his view of the church and being a shepherd.

Because he knows the country so well, his speeches will be closely watched, especially one he'll deliver from the square in front of Lima's cathedral “on the challenges and hopes for the future of the Peruvian people.”

Peru, a nation of 34 million people, is beset by multiple challenges: the climate chaos of El Niño, violent crime, poverty and inequality. In 2025, 25.7% of the Peruvian population was living in monetary poverty.

Conservative President Keiko Fujimori came to power in July on promises of restoring order to a nation plagued by extortion and homicides. Illegal gold mining and the cultivation of coca leaves, the raw material used to produce cocaine, are affecting Indigenous peoples especially.

Leo will meet with popular groups in Cusco, in the Peruvian Andes, and will honor Peru's Indigenous peoples by travelling to Pucallpa, in Peru's Amazon to celebrate Mass.

Cusco was the capital of the Inca empire, an important city of Spanish colonial rule and today remains an important cultural destination, including the nearby ruins at Machu Picchu. He’ll celebrate Mass and pray in Cusco’s main square, where in 1781 the Indigenous hero Túpac Amaru II was killed following the most significant rebellion against the Spanish during the colonial era.

Huge crowds are expected to turn out to welcome Leo home, even though Peru has seen Catholicism fall in recent years. According to Pew, the Catholic population was at 76% in 2013-2014, but now stands at around 67%.
