World.title: Higher copper prices present opportunity for restructured government ministries
World.content:
Ministry of Information and Media Director Spokesperson, Henry Kapata, says the World Bank’s projection that copper prices will average US$13,000 per tonne in 2027 presents an opportunity for Zambia.

Mr Kapata says the World Bank’s projection also puts the country’s production ambitions into perspective.

He says with a target of producing 3 million metric tonnes of copper annually by 2031, Zambia must expand its mining capacity, secure reliable electricity and strengthen its ability to turn mineral wealth into jobs, exports and revenue.

Mr Kapata has told the media business news that the World Bank has raised its 2027 copper price forecast by 18 per cent, reflecting expectations of sustained demand

driven by electricity networks, electric vehicles, data centres and other technologies.

Mr Kapata says Copper prices are projected to average US$13,200 per tonne in 2026 before settling at around US$13,000 per tonne in 2027.

For the Republic of Zambia, these projections come at an important time as President Hakainde Hichilema moves to restructure Government ministries to strengthen the implementation of national development priorities.

Mr Kapata noted that the restructuring creates an opportunity for more focused institutions to drive key sectors of the economy.

“The newly established Ministry of Electricity, Ministry of Petroleum, Ministry of Trade and Exports, and Ministry of Industry provide a more defined institutional framework for addressing some of the challenges affecting production, energy security, trade and industrial development, “he said.

Mr Kapata stated that the connection between copper production and electricity is particularly important.

He says achieving annual copper production of 3 million metric tonnes will require substantial investment in mining operations, processing facilities and supporting infrastructure saying these activities depend on reliable and affordable electricity.

Mr Kapata added that the creation of a dedicated Ministry of Electricity therefore provides an opportunity to give greater attention to power generation, transmission, distribution and regional electricity trade.

” As electricity generation expands towards the Government’s 10,000-megawatt target, the country will be better positioned to support mining and industrial activity while also exploring opportunities to export surplus power to regional markets,” says Mr Kapata.

Mr Kapata further stated that electricity can therefore, become an important economic sector in its own right, supporting domestic production, attracting investment and generating export earnings.

He explained that the benefits of higher copper prices also extend beyond the mining sector, increased global demand and favorable prices provide an opportunity to expand mineral production, strengthen exploration and develop local processing capacity.

World.title: ZAPD distributes wheelchairs in Kapiri mposhi
World.content:
The Zambia Agency for Persons Living with Disabilities (ZAPD), through Destiny Center for Children with Autism, has distributed over 12 wheelchairs to children living with autism in Kapiri Mposhi District.

Destiny Center Coordinator, Aku Sakala highlighted the impact of the initiative, saying the gesture is in an effort to foster inclusivity and empower children with special needs.

“The wheelchairs were distributed last week to our clients in Kapiri Mposhi District as part of our ongoing efforts to support children with special needs,” Ms Sakala said.

And Destiny Center has launched a registration exercise for children with autism in Serenje and Luano Districts of Central Province to ensure more children access vital mobility aids.

“We are currently registering children with autism in Serenje and Luano so that they too can benefit from this initiative,” Ms Sakala explained.

She added that despite the progress, the organization faces logistical challenges in delivering wheelchairs to outlying districts.

“We need support from well-wishers to help us find transport to ferry the wheelchairs to Serenje and Luano Districts. We are also calling upon the government and other Non-Governmental Organizations (NGO) to support this project so that inclusivity in society is enhanced,” she said.

She emphasized that the latest donation is a testament to Destiny Center’s dedication to uplifting children with special needs across Central Province.

Ms Sakala stated that by providing them with the gift of mobility, the centre is helping to ensure that every child, regardless of their physical condition, has the opportunity to participate fully in their community and pursue their dreams.

World.title: Serenje Council urged to prevent unplanned settlements
World.content:
Central Province Planning Authority Chairperson, Keith Katazo has urged Serenje Town Council to be proactive in physical planning to prevent the emergence of unplanned settlements.

Mr Katazo, says the district is expanding rapidly due to increased mining activities, hence the need for the local authority to plan ahead and curtail unplanned settlements.

He said this during a courtesy call on Serenje Town Council Chairperson, Patrick Munshya at his office.

Mr Katazo said the Provincial Planning Authority would not allow local authorities to permit unplanned developments and later incur additional costs trying to re-plan them.

“If we wait for people to start having unplanned settlements, it will be costly, but if you curtail it by planning ahead for the people, it will be cheaper,” Mr Katazo said.

He further called on the council to work closely with the Provincial Planning Authority to ensure development projects in the district were properly planned.

Mr Katazo also urged the local authority to equip officers in the planning department with adequate transport to enable them to conduct regular field inspections and effectively monitor developmental activities.

He further emphasised the need for the council to ensure that buildings meet the required standards while strengthening the capacity of staff in the planning department to enhance service delivery.

Meanwhile, Serenje Town Council Chairperson, Patrick Munshya, said the council was ready to collaborate with the Provincial Planning Authority to ensure the district is properly planned.

And Serenje District Commissioner, Ellen Mibenge, speaking when the Provincial Planning Authority delegation paid a courtesy call on her, expressed concern over chiefdom boundary disputes in the district.

During the delegation’s tour of the Mailo Solar Plant, one of the projects approved by the Provincial Planning Authority, Mr Katazo expressed satisfaction with the progress made in implementing the project.

World.title: MRC Seeks strong mining Regulation as it plots2027–2031 Strategic Plan
World.content:
The Minerals Regulation Commission (MRC) has called for strengthened regulatory oversight, transparency, accountability and stakeholder collaboration to enhance the governance and management of Zambia’s mineral resources.

The Commission says its inaugural Strategic Plan for 2027–2031 will provide a clear roadmap for strengthening mineral regulation, improving service delivery and ensuring that the country’s mineral wealth contributes meaningfully to sustainable national development.

MRC Director General, Tom Hara, said this during a stakeholder engagement and consultation meeting on the draft Strategic Plan in Lusaka, which brought together representatives of Government institutions, mining companies, civil society organisations, cooperating partners, academia and other stakeholders.

Dr Hara said the development of the Strategic Plan comes at a critical time when Zambia is pursuing an ambitious target of increasing copper production to three million metric tonnes annually by 2031.

He emphasised that achieving this target requires a predictable regulatory environment, responsible investment, effective mineral rights administration, environmental protection and strict compliance with regulatory requirements.

Dr Hara said the Commission was committed to building a credible regulator that commands public confidence, earns the respect of the mining industry and provides effective oversight in the national interest.

“The success of this Strategic Plan will depend on collective responsibility and sustained collaboration,” he said.

He stressed that the consultation was not merely intended to present a document for endorsement but to solicit practical contributions that would ensure the final Strategic Plan reflects the realities and expectations of the mining sector.

Dr Hara identified transparency, responsiveness and collaboration as the guiding principles of the Commission’s strategic direction, emphasising the importance of fair, accountable and predictable regulatory processes.

He further underscored the need for stronger partnerships with Government institutions, the mining industry, communities, environmental regulators and civil society to address challenges such as illegal mining, environmental degradation, mineral security, occupational health and safety, and the formalisation of artisanal and small-scale mining.

Meanwhile, ActionAid Zambia has urged the Mineral Regulation Commission to place human rights protection, environmental accountability, gender equality and meaningful community participation at the centre of its regulatory agenda.

ActionAid Zambia Business Development Manager, Geofrey Sizala, said the country’s mineral wealth must translate into tangible improvements in the livelihoods of ordinary citizens, particularly communities directly affected by mining activities.

Mr Sizala identified five priority areas for consideration in the Strategic Plan: business and human rights, gender equality and public disclosure, formalisation of artisanal and small-scale mining, domestic revenue mobilisation, and community participation and environmental accountability.

He urged the Commission to ensure that mining companies go beyond fulfilling licensing requirements by demonstrating responsible business conduct, protecting workers’ rights, preventing environmental pollution and addressing the concerns of affected communities.

Mr Sizala also called for improved public disclosure of gender-disaggregated information in the mining sector, including employment levels, remuneration, management positions and participation in procurement opportunities.

On artisanal and small-scale mining, he advocated for accessible licensing processes, affordable financing, improved occupational health and safety, responsible sourcing and stronger market linkages to support the formalisation of miners.

He further called for strengthened oversight of mineral production, trading and exports through collaboration with institutions such as the Zambia Revenue Authority to minimise revenue leakages and ensure that the country derives fair economic benefits from its mineral resources.

Mr Sizala emphasised that mining communities must be meaningfully involved in decisions relating to mineral licensing, environmental management, regulatory monitoring and activities that affect their livelihoods.

He said the effectiveness of the Strategic Plan would ultimately depend on measurable targets, transparent reporting and accountability mechanisms that enable citizens to assess the Commission’s performance.

The MRC was established under the Minerals Regulation Commission Act No. 14 of 2024, with the mandate to regulate, monitor and safeguard the development and management of minerals in Zambia.

The stakeholder consultation is expected to validate strategic priorities, generate recommendations, identify partnership opportunities and provide a practical roadmap for finalising and implementing the 2027–2031 Strategic Plan.

The Commission remains committed to strengthening regulatory systems and ensuring that mineral resource development is undertaken responsibly, transparently and in accordance with the law, in support of Zambia’s national development aspirations.

Oxfam country focal point person, Chitimbwa Chifunda commended government for the establishment of a MRC, saying it will promote oversight in the mineral value chain.

She said the Commission is expected to streaming and enhance transparency and accountability in the mining sector.

World.title: Muchinga Province begins remembrance day preparations
World.content:
Preparations for the 2026 Remembrance Day parade are officially underway in Muchinga Province, with military personnel and cadets ramping up rehearsals ahead of the annual event scheduled for Sunday, November 8.

The parade, which honors fallen heroes who sacrificed their lives during the First and Second World Wars, is a global and national moment of solemn reflection.

A visit to the Chinsali Cenotaph this morning revealed a hive of activity, as disciplined contingents of military personnel and youth cadets perfected their drills in readiness for the commemoration.

Zambia Army Muchinga Command Staff Officer Grade One, Lieutenant Colonel Jerome Mwangala, who is also serving as the parade coordinator, confirmed the province’s full preparedness for the event.

Lt Col Mwangala highlighted the deep historical significance of the commemoration, explaining that the traditional wearing of the poppy flower serves as a poignant symbol of remembrance.

He noted that the poppy represents the resilient flowers that bloomed across the devastated battlefields and graves of fallen soldiers during the World Wars.

The commander urged the local community to bridge the gap between the barracks and civilian life by attending the ceremony in solidarity.

He said the event is not just for military personnel, but for every citizen, as we have all been affected by the sacrifices of our fallen heroes in some way,” Lt Col Mwangala said.

“Let us turn out in large numbers as citizens of this province, as Muchinga joins the rest of the world to observe this day in honor of our fallen heroes and heroines,” said Mwangala.

The Remembrance Day service in Muchinga Province is scheduled to take place this Sunday at the Chinsali Cenotaph, drawing dignitaries, veterans and residents from across the region.

World.title: Lumezi schools make progress in irrigated maize production
World.content:
Two schools selected to implement the Presidential Irrigation Initiative Programme (PIIP) in Lumezi District of Eastern Province are making steady progress in irrigated maize production.

The programme, introduced by President Hakainde Hichilema, seeks to promote year-round agricultural production, mitigate the effects of climate change and drought, and transform schools and other institutions into centres of agricultural productivity.

Lumezi Day School and Lumezi Boarding School are each cultivating one hectare of irrigated maize under the initiative, which is part of the broader Grow Zambia Agenda to increase the country’s annual maize production to 10 million metric tonnes by 2031.

Lumezi District Commissioner, Brigadier General Patrick Mtonga (Retired), has expressed satisfaction with the two schools’ commitment and dedication to the successful implementation of the programme.

Meanwhile, the Department of Agriculture in the area is providing technical support to ensure the successful implementation of the programme.

Lundazi district Senior Agricultural Officer Joris Mwale says the Schools will also receive support with the provision of inputs.

“The Department has been granted permission to provide the schools with fertiliser under the Farmer Input Support Programme (FISP), while facilitating their participation in the Sustainable Agriculture Financing Facility initiative.

Learners at the two institutions have also thanked President Hakainde Hichilema for introducing the initiative, saying it will provide them with practical agricultural skills and opportunities to venture into farming.

Masida Banda, a Form One pupil at Lumezi Day Boarding School, said the initiative will help improve the school’s resource base while equipping learners with practical farming skills.

She said the programme is giving learners hands-on experience in agriculture and preparing them to consider farming as a viable business venture in the future, rather than relying solely on white-collar employment.

And Lumezi Day School Head teacher, Innocent Lungu said the sustainability of the project remains a priority for the institution.

“The school is closely working with various government departments, including Agriculture, Water Affairs and the local authority, to ensure the continued success of the initiative,” he said.

Meanwhile, the District Education Board Secretary James Chibuye has thanked President Hakainde Hichilema for extending the Presidential Irrigation Initiative to Lumezi District.

Mr Chibuye said the project is an inspiration not only to learners but also to teachers, some of whom are now considering establishing similar agricultural ventures.

He said the Grow Zambia Agenda can only be realised when everyone takes responsibility and actively participates in food production.

World.title: ZACOSO backs fish inclusion in school meals
World.content:
The Zambian Aquaculture Cooperative Society Limited (ZACOSO) has expressed optimism over the planned integration of fish into the school feeding programme, citing opportunities to create new markets for local producers while promoting entrepreneurship among learners.

The statement follows the Government’s call for the integration of nutrient-dense aquatic foods to improve learner nutrition and strengthen local food systems.

ZACOSO General Manager, Evans Chilandani said the initiative, if implemented, would increase demand for locally produced fish by encouraging schools and other production units to venture into fish farming.

Mr Chilandani emphasised that introducing fish ponds in schools would also provide learners with practical skills in fish production, including how to rear and manage fish, equipping them with entrepreneurial knowledge they could use after completing their education.

Meanwhile, Zambia Aquaculture Alliance Cooperative Society Secretary General Ferdinand Simfukwe has called on the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock to involve small aquaculture associations and cooperatives in the proposed school fish feeding programme, stating that their participation will be key to creating reliable markets for local producers.

Mr Simfukwe said the initiative will help many small-scale fish farmers who struggle with markets.

He further urged the Ministry to bring together relevant stakeholders and establish clear mechanisms for small-scale aquaculture associations to participate and benefit from the programme, saying their inclusion would strengthen its implementation and ensure that local fish farmers are not left out.

World.title: Shiwang’andu farmers urged to expand cultivation
World.content:
Farmers in Shiwang’andu District have been challenged to increase agricultural production by taking advantage of the district’s 59,200 hectares of arable land, of which only 21,000 hectares are currently under cultivation.

District Agricultural Coordinator (DACO) Chewe Mutale said the district has vast agricultural potential which, if fully utilised, could contribute to the country’s national maize production targets by 2031.

Ms Mutale told the media in an interview that about 38,200 hectares of arable land remained available for agricultural expansion.

She disclosed that the district recorded a maize output of 27,900 metric tonnes against a target of 66,000 metric tonnes during the 2025/2026 farming season.

The DACO attributed the low adoption of good agricultural practices among farmers as one of the major challenges affecting increased agricultural production.

“Low levels of mechanisation, inadequate storage facilities and poor road infrastructure were also contributing to low productivity” she said.

Meanwhile, Shiwang’andu District Commissioner Maureen Bwembya has urged farmers to embrace modern farming practices and fully utilise the available arable land to unlock the district’s agricultural potential.

Ms Bwembya has challenged farmers and agriculture officers to work towards achieving the district’s maize production target of 82,000 metric tonnes by 2031, thereby contributing to the national target of producing 10 million metric tonnes of maize within the same period.

World.title: Magaya’s Miracle Boys seal PSL return in dramatic fashion
World.content:
YADAH FC have stormed back into the Premier Soccer League (PSL) after surviving a nerve-wracking title showdown to clinch the Pacific Storm ZIFA Eastern Region Division One championship with a game to spare.

The Walter Magaya-bankrolled outfit sealed their promotion in dramatic fashion on Wednesday afternoon, edging Masvingo United 2-1 in a pulsating encounter at Heart Stadium to send their supporters into wild celebrations.

It was a victory that carried the weight of an entire season, as the Harare-based side fought tooth and nail to secure their place among Zimbabwe’s football elite.

World.title: Tobacco hectarage rises 28%
World.content:
Land allocated to tobacco production this season has increased by 28% from last year, with more than 22 000 hectares already under the golden leaf.

The growth reflects a strong start to the production season, with irrigation accounting for the bulk of the planted area as growers seek to cushion their crops against anticipated dry conditions.

Latest Agricultural Development Advisory Services (ADAS) weekly figures show that 22 918 hectares had been planted by October 30, up from 17 867 hectares recorded during the same period last year.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: End of an era: Ronaldo hangs Portugal boots after camp walkout and suspension
World.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo has retired from international football, ending a 23-year Portugal career that produced a European title, two Nations League crowns and records that may never be broken.

Portuguese newspaper O Jogo reported that his decision was irreversible and that the Nations League match against Wales was his last for Portugal.

The end comes on the back of a bitter dispute with coach Jorge Jesus.

World.title: Pay regularisation fee to council or face demolition, Harare warns illegal settlers
World.content:
HARARE City Council has warned residents illegally occupying council land to avoid third parties and pay their regularisation penalties directly to the council within 14 days to avoid demolition of their structures.

The warning came amid reports that some land barons were fleecing desperate residents of their money by purporting to represent them.

On Wednesday, the council’s head of human shelter services, Edgar Dzehonye, said affected settlers should avoid third parties but pay directly at their nearest council district offices.

World.title: PSL chairman Mupfurutsa appointed to COSAFA finance committee
World.content:
Premier Soccer League chairman Isaiah Mupfurutsa has been appointed to the COSAFA finance committee, giving Zimbabwe a voice in the financial governance of football across southern Africa.

The PSL has confirmed the development, saying Mupfurutsa’s appointment would strengthen football administration, financial governance and development across the region.

A finance committee seat gives him a say in how resources are managed and accounted for within the confederation at a time when clubs and associations across the region are working to improve their commercial and governance structures.

World.title: South Africa: Court to Rule on Zuma-Sambudla's Terrorism Charges - South African News Briefs - November 6, 2026
World.content:
press review

Court to Rule on Zuma-Sambudla's Terrorism Charges

The Durban High Court is set to rule on Duduzile Zuma-Sambudla's application to have terrorism-related charges against her withdrawn, reports EWN. The former president's daughter is accused of inciting terrorism and public violence through social media posts during the July 2021 unrest, which followed Jacob Zuma's arrest. She maintained that her posts, which included images and videos of the violence captioned "Amandla" and "We See You", were not intended to incite violence. Her lawyers have argued that the State has failed to present sufficient evidence, while the NPA maintains there are reasonable grounds for a conviction.

Severe Thunderstorm Warning Issued for Parts of KwaZulu-Natal



The South African Weather Service has issued a Level 2 warning for severe thunderstorms in parts of KwaZulu-Natal, reports SABC News. The storms are expected to bring heavy rain, damaging winds, hail and lightning, with a risk of localised flooding and infrastructure damage. Several areas, including uMlalazi, uMngeni, KwaDukuza, Mandeni, Maphumulo and Ndwedwe, are affected. Motorists have been urged to exercise caution and avoid crossing flooded bridges or travelling on roads prone to flooding.

IEC Faces Over 800 Complaints as Election Results Near Finalisation

The Electoral Commission of South Africa is working to resolve more than 800 complaints lodged by political parties as it continues to count and verify local government election results, reports EWN . Most complaints relate to allegations that party agents were prevented from observing voting and counting processes, with about 106 cases still outstanding. 18 municipalities had completed the results process. More than 23,000 result slips had been scanned and nearly 23,000 results captured. Parties have to submit objections that could affect election outcomes, delaying the final declaration of results. The IEC estimated that 15.9 million South Africans participated in the elections, although the final turnout figure is still pending.

World.title: Africa: Deadly Viruses Know No Borders, Nor Should Our Resolve to Stop Them
World.content:
Sjoerd Sjoerdsma, Dutch Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization at WHO headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland.

guest column

In this guest column for AllAfrica, the Dutch Trade and Development Minister and the head of the World Health Organization stress that addressing viral health crises anywhere protects everyone everywhere. The government of the Netherlands is committing funding both for the current Ebola crisis and flexible funding to quickly respond to new or emerging global threats.

COVID-19 may feel like a distant memory to many. But the virus claimed millions of lives around the world, including approximately 50,000 in the Netherlands. The lesson is clear: preparedness is not optional.

Preventing health crises abroad is in the interest of all countries, including the Netherlands.

Governments everywhere face competing priorities and constrained budgets. But infectious diseases do not respect national borders. In an interconnected world, health threats that emerge in one place can quickly become risks for all of us. No country can safeguard its health security alone.

That lesson is evident today in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), where a major Ebola outbreak is unfolding in a region already affected by insecurity, displacement and limited access to health services.

Already the outbreak has crossed national boundaries, underlining how quickly a health threat in one country can become a shared international concern.

Responding effectively requires rapid action, strong local leadership and international solidarity. Under the DRC Government's leadership, the World Health Organization (WHO) is working closely with the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, local authorities, communities and partners to contain the outbreak in the DRC and save lives.

Mystic Stock Photography / Shutterstock.com The MV Hondius, a cruise ship owned by the Dutch company Oceanwide Expeditions experienced a Hantavirus outbreak last year. The Netherlands and the World Health Organized collaborated to safely evacuate passengers and crew.

To support these efforts, the Netherlands is providing €7 million to WHO for the Ebola response. But responding to outbreaks requires more than emergency funding alone. It requires flexible, predictable financing that can be directed rapidly to where needs are greatest. That is why the Netherlands is also providing a new €10 million flexible contribution to WHO for future emergencies, enabling the WHO to rapidly respond to health threats while helping countries strengthen preparedness and prevent future outbreaks whenever possible. This is additional to the existing €9.6 million yearly core funding to the WHO.

No country can safeguard its health security alone.

Some may ask why the Netherlands, or any country, should invest in health emergencies far from its own borders when domestic health systems also face challenges. The answer is simple: diseases do not stop at borders. Supporting countries to detect and contain outbreaks early is not only the right thing to do. It protects local populations while reducing the risk of wider international spread. Investing in health security abroad is also an investment in health security at home.

Outbreaks are most effectively controlled at their source. Local leadership is essential. National authorities understand their communities, their health systems and the challenges they face. WHO's role is to support those efforts, coordinate international expertise and ensure that countries have access to the tools, funding and technical assistance they need.

International cooperation remains the foundation of effective health security. This year, for example, a hantavirus outbreak on a Dutch-flagged cruise ship was swiftly contained through rapid collaboration among countries and partners coordinated through WHO. During an earlier outbreak caused by the "Sudan virus" species of Ebola in Uganda, investments that helped advance an Ebola vaccine developed by the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative (IAVI) and Batavia Biosciences contributed to global preparedness efforts. These examples demonstrate that cooperation works.

Dany Bitita/WHO Two new candidate vaccines to join Ebola trial as treatment research advances.

Yet this progress cannot be taken for granted. The international health system is under growing strain, even as health threats continue to increase. Climate change is altering the distribution of infectious diseases. Europe has already seen growing concern from vector-borne diseases, including West Nile virus, while other diseases such as dengue and malaria are expanding into new regions. At the same time, funding for global health, including for WHO, is declining.

Diseases spreading to new areas amid decreased global health funding is dangerous.

This is a dangerous combination. The need for cooperation, preparedness and rapid response is growing, just as the resources required to sustain them are coming under pressure.

We therefore call on European governments to strengthen their support for global health security by increasing flexible and unearmarked contributions to WHO. Such investments enable outbreaks to be detected earlier, contained more rapidly and addressed where they begin, before they become larger regional or global crises.

No one can rule out the possibility of another pandemic. . But we can ensure that we are better prepared for the next one. Strong health systems in the DRC, and in countries everywhere, are not only vital for the local communities. They are an investment in a safer, healthier and more secure future for us all.

Sjoerd Sjoerdsma is the Dutch Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation. Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus is Director-General of the World Health Organization.

World.title: Nigeria: Atiku Vows to Appeal Court Judgement Against His Candidacy, Seeks Stay of Execution
World.content:
Atiku Abubakar says he will challenge the Federal High Court judgement invalidating his presidential nomination. At the same time, his campaign council says it will seek interim relief and disputes the ruling's legal basis.

The presidential campaign council of Atiku Abubakar says its lawyers are preparing to seek a stay of execution of Thursday's Federal High Court judgement invalidating his nomination as the African Democratic Congress (ADC) presidential candidate and nullifying the party's David Mark-led leadership.

Atiku also rejected the ruling and promised to challenge it at the Court of Appeal, insisting that his campaign would continue in Kebbi State following Wednesday's launch in Sokoto.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

In a statement issued by Phrank Shaibu, Director of Strategic Communication of the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, Atiku accused the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) of trying to use court proceedings to derail his presidential campaign.

"The timing of this judgment is no coincidence. It is part of a strategy to weaken my support in the North and frustrate a campaign whose message is resonating across the country," he said.

Atiku also disputed the portrayal of his candidacy as a Northern political project.

"My roots are in Northern Nigeria, but my candidacy belongs to all Nigerians. There is a difference between being from the North and being a candidate only for the North," he said.

Atiku interpreted the turnout at his Sokoto rally as a sign of support for his campaign's promise to make living costs more affordable.

He said the ADC's Affordable Life campaign would continue in Kebbi and other parts of the country despite the judgment.

Mr Shaibu published the statement on X after PREMIUM TIMES sought the campaign's reaction.

Justice Peter Lifu of the Federal High Court in Abuja delivered the judgment in suit FHC/ABJ/CS/1819/2025, brought by Nafiu Bala Gombe, a former ADC National Deputy Chairman (North-East).

Mr Gombe challenged the emergence of former Senate President David Mark and former Osun State Governor Rauf Aregbesola as the party's national chairman and secretary, claiming that he was entitled to succeed former chairman Ralph Nwosu.

PREMIUM TIMES reported earlier on Thursday that the court invalidated the Mark-led leadership and decisions taken under it, including the nomination of candidates for the 2027 elections.

The complete enrolled orders have not been independently examined for this report.

Why Atiku disputes the ruling

Atiku argued that Thursday's judgment conflicted with an earlier Federal High Court decision delivered by Justice Musa Liman on 2 July in suit FHC/ABJ/CS/1637/2025.

That case was brought by House of Representatives member Leke Abejide, who also challenged the process through which Messrs Mark and Aregbesola assumed office.

Atiku said Justice Liman dismissed the case after considering questions of jurisdiction, standing and the failure to exhaust internal party remedies. He maintained that the earlier ruling also resolved substantive issues in favour of the Mark-led leadership.

"Why, after that judgment, was another case filed to reopen the same dispute? This is a calculated attempt to circumvent a subsisting judgment. We will challenge this judicial manoeuvre at the Court of Appeal," he said.

The cases involved different claimants. PREMIUM TIMES has not examined both judgments to determine whether their orders conflict.

PREMIUM TIMES previously examined the ADC leadership dispute, including separate proceedings concerning the party's leadership and congresses.

Campaign council prepares stay application

In a separate statement, the ADC Presidential Campaign Council described Justice Lifu's judgment as an academic exercise that had been overtaken by events.

Its Director of Media and Publicity, Kola Ologbondiyan, said the council's legal team was taking steps to seek interim relief, including a stay of execution where legally applicable, before pursuing an appeal.

The statement did not confirm that a notice of appeal or stay application had been filed.

According to Mr Ologbondiyan, Justice Liman distinguished between a stakeholders' meeting held on 2 July 2025 and a National Executive Council meeting on 29 July 2025, at which Messrs Mark and Aregbesola emerged as national officers.

He said the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) monitored the latter meeting and maintained that the leadership transition complied with the ADC constitution.

PREMIUM TIMES has not obtained the judgment or INEC records to verify that account.

Close 

Mr Ologbondiyan also questioned the timing of Thursday's ruling, contrasting what he described as an unsuccessful APC presidential campaign launch in Kaduna with the ADC's rally in Sokoto.

Mr Ologbondiyan also alleged political interference in the proceedings but provided no evidence to substantiate the claim.

He cited an earlier ruling by Justice Lifu ordering the deregistration of the ADC and four other parties, which he said the Court of Appeal had overturned.

PREMIUM TIMES reported in June that the appellate court stayed the execution of that judgement. The reported order did not establish that the appeal had been finally determined.

That deregistration case was separate from Thursday's ADC leadership dispute.

The campaign council maintained that Messrs Mark and Aregbesola remained the ADC's legitimate national officers and urged supporters to continue campaigning.

The council did not identify any court order suspending Thursday's judgment.

The ADC's National Publicity Secretary, Bolaji Abdullahi, had earlier rejected the judgement, accusing the APC of interference and warning that the ruling could affect other candidates.

World.title: Trump's massive Arlington triumphal arch approved for construction by federal planning commission
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The National Capital Planning Commission on Thursday approved President Donald Trump's proposed triumphal arch in downtown Washington, D.C., allowing construction to move ahead.

The federal panel approved construction of the 250-foot-tall structure, which is inspired by Paris' Arc de Triomphe and intended to attract visitors crossing the Memorial Bridge from Arlington National Cemetery into the nation's capital.

The panel voted 8-4 in favor of the project following a public hearing, giving the green light for construction to begin, potentially as soon as this week, according to administration officials.

Mark Paoletta, the commission's Trump-appointed chairman, expressed support for the new structure during the panel's meeting.

SEN JIM BANKS: TRUMP’S NEW TRIUMPHAL ARCH IS A MONUMENT TO AMERICAN GREATNESS

"President Trump understands as president and a superb builder that it's important to our national identity to display who we are through grand monuments," Paoletta said.

Paoletta, who also serves as general counsel for the White House Office of Management and Budget, pointed to Trump's admiration for similar monuments around the world.

"As Trump has often remarked, the great cities around the world have arches: Paris, Rome, London," Paoletta said.

TRUMP SAYS NEW ARCH WILL ALSO DEPLOY DRONES, POSITION SNIPERS AND STORE AMMO

The proposed structure would be clad in granite and topped with three golden statues.

Trump has previously said the triumphal arch would be converted into a military complex capable of rapidly deploying large numbers of drones, with snipers positioned on the roof and plaza areas. He also said the complex would store "large quantities of sniper ammunition."

The project has drawn criticism from preservationists, lawmakers and veterans, who argue that it could disrupt views of the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

Opponents have also questioned whether the project requires congressional approval under federal law.

The National Capital Planning Commission previously approved the site and preliminary plans.

World.title: Ravens' playoff hopes hinge on Jacoby Brissett after third-stringer Joe Fagnano gets demolished by Jaguars
World.content:
It’s very rare we see moments in the NFL that feel like high school football, but Thursday night gave us that feeling in the Jacksonville Jaguars’ 33-10 trounce of the Baltimore Ravens to kick off Week 9.

The Jaguars were heavily favored going into the game, as third-string quarterback Joe Fagnano, who took over as the team’s emergency signal caller last week following the injuries to both Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley, got his first career start.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Yes, the Ravens traded for Jacoby Brissett when the Arizona Cardinals demoted him to third string earlier this week, but he wasn’t ready on a short week to take over Declan Doyle’s offense and compete.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

But, boy, does Brissett need to get right quickly if the Ravens have any hope of reaching the playoffs.

That’s the biggest takeaway from this game, because the Jaguars didn’t really need to do all too much after scoring on their opening drive of the game. It was clear Doyle was going to be creative, or as much as he possibly could, with Fagnano very green under center.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

However, Fagnano, despite being a fun story to begin a new week in the NFL, isn’t what the Ravens need after a devastating injury to the two-time MVP in Jackson and Huntley going down.

Brissett is the only saving grace for a Ravens season that almost seems at the brink of disaster even though they only fell to 4-4 on the year.

Fagnano was 10-of-18 passing for only 80 yards, as some heavy rain in Baltimore didn’t help the fact that Jacksonville was all over what the Ravens were trying to do in the first place. The ball was wet, leading to a few fumbles, while Fagnano couldn’t handle the pressure the Jaguars threw at him on his clear pass downs, leading to two interceptions.

The body language on the Baltimore sideline was clear – it wasn’t going to be their night.

Meanwhile, Trevor Lawrence and the Jaguars looked clean and poised coming off the bye week. Bhayshul Tuten, who was questionable entering the game due to injury, suited up and scored the first touchdown of the game. Then, Lawrence found Parker Washington before the end of the first half on a 50-yard catch-and-run touchdown that almost felt like a kill shot after what we witnessed with the Ravens’ offense in half.

At 17-3 to start the second half, Fagnano threw his first interception, followed by two punts, a turnover-on-downs, his second interception, and a fumble on the kickoff.

Chris Rodriguez Jr. smashed it in for a touchdown in the fourth quarter that made it 33-3, and if it weren’t for Justice Hill’s 65-yard run on the ensuing drive, Baltimore likely wouldn’t have sniffed the end zone in a game they’ll look to forget and move on to next week.

With a meeting against the lowly Los Angeles Chargers on "Monday Night Football" upcoming, Brissett has more than enough time to get acclimated.

Because for Ravens fans, that’s really the only thing to look forward to as they hope and pray his passing prowess can get them back to being a playoff team after losing their last four.

World.title: Indiana, Florida and Alabama carry out rare US triple execution day
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Indiana, Florida and Alabama each put a man to death Thursday, the second time this year that three inmates were executed in the U.S. the same day.

The first triple execution this year took place Aug. 13, when Oklahoma, Tennessee and Alabama executed inmates within hours of each other. Before Aug. 13, the last time three executions were carried out in the U.S. on the same day was Jan. 7, 2010.

On Thursday, Indiana officials put to death the first inmate of the day when it executed Jeffrey Weisheit, 50, for setting a 2010 house fire that killed his girlfriend's two children, ages 8 and 5, as the couple's relationship deteriorated. He was pronounced dead at 12:45 a.m. at the Indiana State Prison in Michigan City after receiving a lethal injection.

His attorneys sought permission for additional brain scans, arguing that his history of head injuries and mental health problems warranted further examination. Republican Gov. Mike Braun denied the request. Braun also rejected appeals to commute Weisheit's death sentence to life in prison.

INDIANA EXECUTES MAN CONVICTED OF KILLING 2 CHILDREN AS MORE US EXECUTIONS LOOM THURSDAY

Weisheit's lawyers had also raised separate concerns about Indiana's planned use of execution drugs obtained from a pharmacy facing a disciplinary hearing before the Indiana Pharmacy Board next week.

But the Indiana Department of Correction maintained it was confident in its ability to carry out the execution "humanely." After the execution, Braun said Weisheit's case had undergone repeated reviews in state and federal courts.

"These reviews have never resulted in an overturned sentence," Braun said in a statement. "Today, Weisheit's sentence has been carried out as ordered by the court."

The execution provided "long-awaited justice for Alyssa Lynch and her brother Caleb, two innocent children whose lives were stolen in an act of unspeakable cruelty," Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita said.

In Florida, Jesse Guardado, 64, was executed after confessing and pleading guilty to fatally stabbing a 75-year-old woman who had helped him find a job and housing in 2004. Guardado killed Jackie Malone inside her home before stealing her jewelry box, $80 and other items to fund his drug addiction.

Guardado was pronounced dead at 6:13 p.m. following a lethal injection at Florida State Prison near Starke.

Florida's latest execution matched last year's state record total of 19 inmates put to death in a single year.

Florida has ramped up executions after Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis signed a series of death warrants since 2025. The state's 19 executions last year was more than under any other Florida governor in a single year since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. Those executions accounted for roughly 40% of the 47 carried out nationwide in 2025.

FLORIDA PUTS 77-YEAR-OLD MAN TO DEATH FOR DEPUTY'S MURDER AS STATE CLOSES IN ON EXECUTION RECORD

The Sunshine State has also accounted for more than half of the 35 executions carried out nationwide, which includes Thursday's executions. In July, Florida executed two prisoners on the same day, the first double execution by a single state in nearly a decade.

Alabama capped off the triple execution day by putting Michael Taylor, 54, to death for the 1991 murders of an older couple who were beaten to death with a metal bar during a robbery inside their home. Authorities caught Taylor in Birmingham, about an hour away, with the victims' Cadillac.

Taylor was executed by lethal injection after a judge ruled against his attorneys' objections to the method. Taylor had previously requested execution by nitrogen gas, and his attorneys sought to preserve that choice.

His attorneys said he "knew the depth of the harm he caused" and "grieved it for the rest of his life." They also said he became a changed man while behind bars, saying, "Michael’s life was proof that God isn’t finished with any of us. Tonight we pray that both families find peace, and we deeply mourn the loss of Michael."

Death penalty opponents had urged Republican Gov. Kay Ivey to commute Taylor's sentence to life in prison, arguing that he was too young and immature at 19 to fully understand the consequences of his actions.

But the governor declined to stop the execution. Ivey issued a statement on Thursday night describing his actions as "reprehensible."

"Thirty-five years ago yesterday, Ivan and Lucille Moore kindly opened their home to Michael Taylor. Mr. Taylor repaid the Moores by beating them to death with a metal bar, all to rob them for money to buy clothing and jewelry," she said.

The victims' family thanked the state attorney general's office for bringing closure to the case but expressed disappointment for having to wait 35 years to see the death sentence carried out.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"We know that a person has the right to appeal, but there should come a time when the jury’s decision is final. For all these years, our family has had to live with the waiting, the delays, and the uncertainty," the statement read. "We have never forgotten our loved ones or what was taken from us."

The executions come amid renewed scrutiny of lethal injection procedures following a failed execution attempt in Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital and was rushed to a hospital in late September. She has since been released from the hospital and returned to prison.

Thursday's executions came on the same day California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom announced he is seeking to commute all 548 death sentences in the Golden State to life without parole, though 382 of the commutations require a recommendation from the California Supreme Court, saying he believes "state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us."

Newsom, who put a moratorium on executions in the state in 2019, said he "knew we cannot execute people in our imperfect legal system and remain true to our core values, the first among them justice and human decency."

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

World.title: MLB outfielder Anthony Santander faces backlash over Abdul El-Sayed video, Blue Jays respond
World.content:
Toronto Blue Jays outfielder Anthony Santander violated the unwritten rules of modern sports culture this week by questioning a key Democratic win, sparking an immediate backlash that sent him rushing to delete two post-midterm clips.

The first clip Santander shared featured a preacher claiming Islam is "driven by war" and that there is "no such thing as kind Muslims."

The second video raised a separate issue. It focused on Michigan's U.S. Senate race, won by Democrat Abdulrahim El-Sayed, questioning the influence of Sharia principles and how that doctrine misaligns with the U.S. Constitution.

UNEARTHED CLIP EXPOSES CLASH BETWEEN EL-SAYED AND EX-GOP RIVAL: 'MUSLIMS DEFINITELY HATE YOU'

Nobody gets a pass in American politics, and asking how a newly elected leader views the law is entirely legitimate.

Santander, a native of Margarita, Venezuela, watched political movements systematically transform his home country's legal institutions and economy.

From that perspective, questioning fundamental ideological shifts in religion and politics is second nature for someone who watched his homeland unravel.

It is also hard to imagine Santander facing anywhere near this level of pushback had the video targeted Christianity, but that selective outrage is nothing new.

But mainstream media coverage avoids the political question entirely and uses the preacher's remarks to dismiss any scrutiny of newly elected lawmakers and mock Santander for objecting.

As calls for team action grew, the Toronto Blue Jays addressed the matter without issuing an apology on Santander's behalf or handing down discipline.

Their statement read, "Baseball is for everyone, and the Blue Jays have created an inclusive experience where all fans feel welcome at our ballpark. Individual comments do not represent our organization’s values and beliefs."

The front office restated its ballpark policy, established that Santander spoke for himself, and moved on.

On the field, Santander already faces significant pressure.

After signing a five-year, $92.5 million deal before 2025, injuries limited him to 54 games. He missed the entire 2026 season following left shoulder surgery, with three years and over $57 million remaining on his contract.

His priority heading into 2027 needs to be getting healthy and producing at the plate. But the reaction to his posts shows how quickly real questions about governance get erased when an athlete delivers them without discipline.

Offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel is going to start calling plays from the booth instead of the sideline amid his unit’s tremendous struggles. The Chargers haven’t scored a touchdown on 27 straight drives, a drought spanning nine quarters.

World.title: 'The View' co-host confronts Abdul El-Sayed on his response to attack on Jewish Synagogue
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

"The View" co-host Sara Haines pressed Michigan Senator-elect Abdul-El Sayed about his response to an attack on a Jewish synagogue in the state and his delay in apologizing for his comments.

On March 12, a man drove a truck into Temple Israel in West Bloomfield Township and exchanged gunfire with security personnel before killing himself, according to authorities.

El-Sayed condemned the attack but drew criticism for subsequently saying, "Hurt people hurt people," referring to the attacker's relatives who had been killed in an Israeli airstrike in Lebanon.

ABDUL EL-SAYED HITS BACK AT ISRAEL QUESTIONS, SUGGESTS HIS NAME AND FAITH ARE BEHIND PRESS SCRUTINY

"Your response, that ‘Hurt people hurt people’ after the Temple Israel attack in Michigan in March really stuck with a lot of people," Haines said.

"And you did apologize for that. But it took you a while to. It took about five months to seemingly understand why that landed wrong with people and voters and constituents. You know, do you think that leaders have a responsibility to challenge the extremist views in their own religion, especially considering you're the first Muslim senator of the United States?" she asked.

"Yeah, well, I really appreciate that question," El-Sayed said. "And I agree with you entirely that we want to live in a world where faith is something that's used to uplift all of us, rather than to justify the worst human actions that sometimes drag us down."

He recalled having visited the temple after the attack and having been there for a bar mitzvah in his youth.

"You know, I condemned it immediately, and I wanted to offer context, but ... you know, when people are hurting, context is secondary, and I just should have stood with their pain. And I learned from that experience. And I'm not above apologizing when I make a mistake," he said.

El-Sayed continued and said he had tried to "offer context around the fact that that individual had lost a child, niece and nephew in an airstrike. And I want us to be thinking a little bit about, A, how we demonstrate our ability as leaders to stand with people's pain with no exceptions and no asterisks around them. And also be able to have an adult conversation about the ways in which actions ricochet around the world and create worse for all of us."

'THE VIEW' CO-HOSTS DEFEND EL-SAYED COMPARING HIMSELF TO JFK OVER MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD SCRUTINY

"I respect that. I just think that if that had been done anywhere near what I believed, I would be so furiously enraged that they would use the words that I have led my life with to hurt people that way," Haines said. "And that was young kids. So, I just was surprised it took a minute for you to understand that part."

"I hear you on that," El-Sayed said.

"Better late than never," co-host Joy Behar said.

Jesse Arm, a vice president at the Manhattan Institute and a pollster originally from Michigan, told Fox News Digital, "Imagine an American politician responding to Dylann Roof’s massacre of Black worshipers at Bible study by saying ‘Hurt people hurt people,’ then asking us to consider the killer’s grievances. That politician would rightly be run out of American public life."

"Why should the standard be any different when the targets are Jewish children and the attacker is an Islamist?" Arm continued. "El-Sayed’s comments were grotesque, and this interview compounds the problem. He’s still presenting his mistake as a matter of timing as though the same rationalization would have been acceptable once the victims had time to grieve. The problem wasn’t when he offered it. The problem was suggesting that events overseas somehow mitigate responsibility for trying to massacre Americans at home."

"Whatever someone has suffered, there is no justification for attacking a synagogue full of children. None," Arm wrote.

"Americans deserve leaders who can say that without pivoting to the terrorist’s pain. Our politics is in a dangerous place when that basic moral clarity becomes negotiable depending on the identities of the attacker and the intended victims," he continued.

World.title: Trump’s D.C.-area arch approved by federal planning commission as court battle looms
World.content:
The National Capital Planning Commission voted Thursday to approve President Donald Trump’s massive — and controversial — “Triumphal Arch” for Washington, with construction scheduled to begin almost immediately.

The commission, led by Trump appointees, gave the project a green light after a hearing at which scores of area residents lined up to voice their opposition to the project, which would sit in Memorial Circle between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

The motion to approve final site building plans passed 8-4, with the four votes in opposition coming from commissioners who were not appointed by Trump.

Public comment at the hearing lasted more than nine hours, which commission Chair Mark Paoletta said was “more than ever.” The comments mostly related to the impact on Arlington National Cemetery, as well as the project’s height, scale and safety.

Paoletta, who is general counsel at the Office of Management and Budget and was appointed chairman of the commission in August, said at the meeting that it was a “national disgrace” that such a memorial had not already been built. He also praised Trump’s “monumental vision,” saying it would be “the grandest arch ever built by mankind.”

The virtual meeting was interrupted for around 30 minutes during public comments by what Paoletta said was a “malicious attack” that caused the site to crash. He said it’s the “first time this has ever happened.”

Close to 130 members of the public were signed up to speak.

“We’ll have this thing done, whether it’s past midnight or not,” Paoletta said after the interruption. The vote ended in the 10 p.m. hour.

Reps. Brian Mast, R-Fla., and Andrew Clyde, R-Ga., spoke in favor of the project, while Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., whose district includes Arlington National Cemetery, expressed concern over the project and criticized the Trump administration over the approval process.

Opponents of the project, including the governments of Virginia and the District of Columbia, are seeking an emergency court order blocking the construction from moving forward, arguing the project is illegal.

They’ve already asked a judge to immediately halt any construction in a bid to head off possible legal gamesmanship by the administration, citing its earlier destruction of the East Wing of the White House to build a ballroom that includes national security measures.

“It is entirely foreseeable that, once construction begins, Defendants will argue, as they have done in other cases, that an order halting construction would irreparably harm the federal government, pose security risks, and impermissibly alter the status quo they have unilaterally created,” they said. “The Court should not allow this cynical gambit to succeed.”

Following Thursday’s vote, attorneys for the Justice Department filed a document notifying U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan, who had asked to be notified after the commission took action.

Trump has said the arch would celebrate the nation’s 250th anniversary and include a military complex with drones and snipers, which he said would be important for national security. The final plans submitted to the commission, however, did not mention drones, ammunition storage or sniper positions.

Asked about the omission at the hearing, Greg Wischer, deputy chief of staff at the Interior Department, said the current “design is capable of hosting national security functions,” but details of those functions aren’t public and have been filed under seal in the court case.

A rendering of the 250-foot arch. Harrison Design

Preservationists and military veterans first sued to block the project this year, arguing that it needed to be authorized by Congress and that the site was improper.

“Its location on Memorial Circle would situate the monument on an axis between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery, obstructing a line of sight that was designed to represent the unification of the Nation following the Civil War and that has existed for nearly a century,” they said.

Testifying at the meeting Thursday, one of the plaintiffs, Vietnam War veteran Michael Lemmon, who was U.S. ambassador to Armenia during the Clinton administration, called the planned arch “frankly blasphemous.”

The site of the planned arch is across from the Lincoln Memorial on the Potomac River. Saul Loeb / AFP via Getty

Virginia and the District of Columbia filed their own action to stop the project last week, contending it “defies at least five federal statutes,” including one that “generally limits buildings in the District to a maximum height of 130 feet.”

The 250-foot arch “would exceed that limit almost twice over.”

They also argued it would harm both D.C. and Virginia residents.

“The Arch is slated to be built on a busy traffic circle that abuts the border between the jurisdictions, at the center of a historic viewshed, in a river whose environment the District has a statutory responsibility to protect,” their suit said.

“Both the construction of the Arch and the completed monument will disrupt the operations of both jurisdictions, impair their ability to carry out their responsibilities under federal and local law, and require the expenditure of substantial resources to mitigate and address those impacts,” they added.

In court filings, the administration countered that the city and state don’t have standing to sue and that Congress gave the project the green light about a century ago, when it “authorized erecting and redesigning 166-foot-tall columns surmounted by statues — exceeding any applicable height limits — and those columns have not yet been built.”

Attorneys for the city and Virginia called those arguments “implausible” and said those columns had initially been planned to be built with the Memorial Bridge before the idea was dropped.

“As Defendants do not dispute, the Memorial Bridge Act nowhere mentions an arch,” they said.

World.title: Head of DOJ Civil Rights Division resigns after GOP midterms loss
World.content:
WASHINGTON — Harmeet Dhillon, the Republican attorney who oversaw a massive overhaul of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, submitted her resignation Thursday.

Attorney General Todd Blanche posted on X that he has accepted Dhillon’s resignation. He wrote that she “defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor” and that the DOJ “is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors.”

Dhillon posted Thursday on X that the job had been the “honor of a lifetime.”

“We ushered in the downfall of illegal DEI, we fought to protect women and girls’ sports, and so much more,” she wrote.

The departure of Dhillon, who had a long history of working as an election lawyer for the GOP, comes just two days after Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate in the midterm elections.

Under Dhillon’s leadership, the Civil Rights Division led some of the Trump administration’s most controversial legal maneuvers, including lawsuits that cited claims of discrimination at elite universities. The division declined to open a use-of-force investigation into the ICE officer who shot and killed Renee Nicole Good in Minnesota earlier this year.

Her office also filed lawsuits against 30 states and Washington, D.C., in an effort to obtain voter registration lists from the states in the months before the election, with federal judges dismissing 27 of those cases. Dhillon was a regular presence on conservative media in the run-up to Tuesday’s elections, promoting the work of the Civil Rights Division.

Dhillon is set to speak at the Donald Trump Ballroom at the Mar-a-Lago Club during the Conservative Political Action Committee’s Circle Retreat and Gala on Thursday.

Bloomberg Law first reported her resignation plans.

Dhillon’s office recently attempted to indict Cassidy Hutchinson, the former Trump administration official who testified before the House Jan. 6 committee about Trump’s actions during the Capitol siege.

Her office also brought a criminal case against former CNN journalist Don Lemon and protesters over a demonstration at a church in Minnesota under a statute historically used to protect reproductive rights facilities.

Stacey Young, the executive director of the group Justice Connection, called Dhillon “the most destructive, lawless, and hateful head of the Civil Rights Division in DOJ history,” and said in a statement that she “wielded the enormous power of the Justice Department to threaten universities, state and local officials, and election workers in spurious cases that rarely won in court.”

Dhillon “decimated” the Civil Rights Division, Young said, and called on the incoming Senate “to exercise its full advice and consent powers to ensure the next Assistant Attorney General fulfills the division’s congressional mandate to enforce all Americans’ civil rights diligently and fairly.”

Kristen Clarke, the NAACP’s general counsel and the former chief of the Civil Rights Division during the Biden administration, said Dhillon “abdicated her responsibility to enforce our nation’s federal civil rights laws and destroyed the crown jewel of the Justice Department.”

Clarke said in a statement that Dhillon “abandoned cases, purged the work force and weaponized the Division to target institutions to achieve illegitimate, partisan goals” and that the NAACP would demand that her replacement “respect the agency’s sacred mission, enforce the law fairly, and protect our civil rights.”

World.title: Brands lean into human creativity as handcrafted art becomes more of a luxury in the age of AI
World.content:
The sound of pencil putting lines to paper. The geometric shapes of a cartoon animal before it comes to life on the page.

Those were the opening shots of a teaser for Prada’s 2026 holiday campaign, which introduced a series of films made “using the anachronistic craft of hand-drawn animation,” working with longtime Disney animator John Pomeroy.

“I learned my craft with pencil and paper, old-school analog drawing with pencil and paper,” Pomeroy, who left Disney in 2003, says in the teaser video.

It’s that kind of skill that some artists say has become a greater asset than ever. In the age of widespread and accessible AI, artists say they’ve noticed more brands leaning into handcrafted art as a selling point.

In recent weeks, the luxury fashion houses Prada and Hermès touted their human-made art projects in social media campaigns — even tagging the artists behind the work to showcase their authenticity.

A still from the Prada Holiday 2026 campaign. Glen Luchford for PRADA

Alina Golovlova, a stop-motion artist in Prague, said that recently, she has felt that her work is actually “appreciated more than in previous years” as brands try to separate themselves from the AI content flooding the internet.

“In previous years, I felt like I was just some hired content creator. No one really cared to tag me or make a [collaborative post],” Golovlova said. “And I think now for brands, it becomes valuable to bring the artists together with the brand to show that they are working with real people.”

Golovlova directed a short film for Anthropologie last month, featuring a needle-felted bunny, embroidered stars and stop-motion movements — all designed and put together entirely by hand by a team of artists.

And the choice proved to be an effective marketing strategy, as support rolled in from commenters online.

“Beautiful! Love the creativity and seeing something human made and NOT AI 👏❤️,” a user wrote on Anthropologie’s post, accruing thousands of likes.

“AI = Broke, cheap, lazy,” another user posted in response to Prada’s campaign. “Art from human hands = High-end, luxurious, high quality.”

Animator Jon Densk, who worked on the hand-drawn Prada campaign under Pomeroy, said that while he suspects AI still has a way to go before it can be used successfully in animation, he has seen signs of it in commercials. Coca-Cola, he said, comes to mind as a major company that has leaned into AI for its s.

“After the first one I saw two years ago, I was like, I’m not buying Coke until they stop it. I still haven’t bought a Coke in two years,” Densk said. “So having a stance against [AI], I think, is a smart move for brands.”

Coca-Cola’s use of AI stirred some controversy, as attitudes about the technology remain divided over labor and environmental concerns, as well as fatigue over the swath of mass-produced content commonly described as “AI slop.”

Still, Densk said he wasn’t expecting the explosion of support that Prada’s hand-drawn campaign would attract online.

“I think people that see people like us who are still drawing things, and even people working in CG animation, as true craftsmen, because that stuff really does take hours and hours and hours of practicing to get to a proficient level,” Densk said.

World.title: Wisconsin reports its first measles death in decades, the third in the U.S. this week
World.content:
An infant in Wisconsin has died of measles, the state health department said Thursday — the third measles-related death reported in the U.S. this week.

It’s Wisconsin’s first measles-related death since 1990, the Health Service Department said, adding that a coroner had listed measles as the infant’s immediate cause of death.

The news came just one day after Pennsylvania’s Health Department reported another measles-associated death there — the state’s sixth this year. It said Wednesday that an unvaccinated resident in Jefferson County who tested positive for measles had died.

On Monday, New York health officials announced that a child in Lewis County had died of measles. Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a statewide disaster emergency over measles in early October.

In total, the U.S. has recorded eight measles-associated deaths this year, according to state health department data. It’s the highest measles death toll in the country since 1991.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed four of those deaths. It says it will update its count “as additional information becomes available and relevant reviews are completed.”

None of the eight people who have died were vaccinated, according to state health departments; some were ineligible because of their age or health status. Typically, the first dose of the vaccine is administered around a child’s first birthday.

Before the outbreaks in Wisconsin, New York and Pennsylvania, none of the states had recorded a measles death in more than 30 years.

Dr. Stephanie Schauer, the immunization program director at the Wisconsin health department, said some chains of transmission started with residents traveling out of state to events like funerals and weddings.

The department is recommending an early dose of the measles vaccine for infants as young as 6 months who are at increased risk of exposure. Around 500 such early doses have been administered since August, Schauer said.

Around 85% of kindergartners in Wisconsin have been vaccinated against measles — below the national average of 92%. Experts say 95% is the threshold needed to keep the population protected.

“We can actually eliminate transmission of measles in the community by getting enough people vaccinated,” said Dr. Ryan Westergaard, the state epidemiologist for communicable diseases. “We have the opportunity to take a disease that could affect everybody and essentially make it go away.”

The health department said it has sent out 2,000 additional measles vaccine doses to local health departments over the last few months.

World.content: Governor Gavin Newsom issued the broadest commutation of death sentences in modern American history. In an open letter, Newsom said he’ll reduce every death sentence in the state to life without the possibility of parole. NBC News’ Laura Jarrett has more on what happens next. Nov. 5, 2026

World.title: Muscle health is key to longevity. Here’s how to measure yours.
World.content:
Muscle health is linked to how well we fight off disease and our longevity. But healthy muscles aren’t just about the size of a bicep or how much we weigh.

An international team of kinesiologists and nutrition experts recently urged doctors to pay more attention to skeletal muscle quality and the ratio of muscle to fat as a key to “metabolic regulation, immune function and overall vitality and functioning.”

“Muscle health estimation could be as important as measuring somebody’s blood pressure,” said longevity expert Dr. Nicolaas Deutz, a professor in the Department of Kinesiology and Sport Management at Texas A&M University and a co-author of the expert review. Kinesiology is the study of physical activity and body mechanics.

Healthy muscles not only help you move safely, they’re also the body’s main storage system for blood sugar, which maintains an active metabolism and lowers inflammation in the body.

Muscle health is usually associated with muscle size in younger people, but that relationship becomes less clear as we get older, said Deutz.

In fact, mass is only a part of overall muscle health. For instance, women generally have lower overall muscle mass than men, yet their muscle health is generally comparable to men’s.

A more complete picture of muscle includes strength, balance, physical function, activity levels and the amount of fat stored within the muscle itself, said Dr. Fatima Cody Stanford, an obesity medicine physician-scientist at Mass General Brigham.

How to prevent muscle loss

There’s growing awareness of how muscle health plays a role in longevity and metabolic diseases such as Type 2 diabetes, especially in the wake of the phenomenal popularity of GLP-1 medications. Drugs such as Ozempic and Zepbound have been shown to improve blood sugar, blood pressure and cardiovascular risk, but they’re also linked to loss of both fat and lean mass, including skeletal muscles.

Stanford, who is also associate professor of medicine and pediatrics at Harvard Medical School, said people taking GLP-1s need adequate nutrition to preserve muscle function.

“As a person loses substantial body weight, the body requires less muscle to carry that weight, and reductions in fat within muscle may improve muscle quality and function,” Stanford said. “At the same time, older adults, individuals with frailty or low baseline muscle mass, and people who are losing weight rapidly warrant particularly close attention to strength, function, protein intake and resistance exercise.”

A sufficient amount of high-quality daily protein — including fish, poultry, eggs, dairy, tofu, beans, lentils, nuts and seeds — helps protect against muscle loss, Stanford said.

The U.S. dietary guidelines encourage people to prioritize protein with nutritious, minimally processed foods at every meal, recommending 1.2 to 1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight.

Staying active — working in the yard, walking or weight training — strengthens different muscle groups, Deutz said.

If lifting heavy gym weights isn’t appealing, resistance exercises can effectively preserve muscle strength and function, particularly during weight loss.

“Body-weight exercises, resistance bands, machines or supervised strength work can all be appropriate depending on the individual’s mobility, fitness level and medical history,” Stanford said.

How to measure muscle health

Muscle power is the ability to produce force quickly, and handgrip strength is one of the simplest ways to measure it.

“An often-overlooked consideration is muscle power — the ability to produce force quickly, which declines earlier and more rapidly with aging than muscle strength,” said Stephen J. Carter, associate professor in the kinesiology department at the School of Public Health — Bloomington Indiana University. “From a practical perspective, muscle power is more relevant to daily life than simply strength.”

Grip strength measures the force generated when squeezing a handheld tool called a dynamometer.

While “low” strength depends on factors like age and BMI, a large analysis of grip strength of over 20,000 older men and women defined it as less than 57 pounds for men and 35 pounds for women.

Fortunately, targeted resistance training can successfully improve the numbers.

Carter recommended resistance training, such as free weights, weight machines, resistance bands or body-weight exercises like push-ups, two to three times weekly, progressing gradually to a higher intensity to build more muscle.
