World.title: Judge blocks construction on Trump's 250-foot arch for now
World.content:
Washington — A federal judge temporarily blocked the Trump administration from beginning construction on President Trump's proposed triumphal arch late Thursday, siding — for now — with a group of Vietnam veterans and the District of Columbia and Virginia, which sued to stop the project.

U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan ruled in a brief order that the government cannot start any "construction-related activity" for 14 days, while further legal proceedings play out. She said she would explain her reasoning in a forthcoming opinion.

The ruling came shortly after the National Capital Planning Commission voted Thursday to approve plans for the 250-foot triumphal arch, giving the final go-ahead for the monument that's set to be constructed between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

The NCPC, which acts as the federal government's planning agency for the region and is stacked with Trump allies, voted 8-4 to greenlight the project after almost 9 hours of public comments from members of Congress, veterans, architects and Washington, D.C., and Virginia residents.

Chutkan's order aside, it's unclear how soon construction of the arch could start, though the Justice Department said in a court filing last month that it could begin as soon as Thursday.

In a separate filing Wednesday night, the Trump administration said that a construction company "may be — but is not necessarily — arranging off-site preparations for construction mobilization in anticipation of permit approval" at the site.

Ahead of the meeting, the NCPC's executive director, Mark Paoletta, recommended approval of the final site and building plans for the structure, which is supposed to celebrate 250 years of American independence.

Paoletta, the top lawyer at the Office of Management and Budget, heralded Mr. Trump's "historic vision" for the structure and said it would be the "grandest arch ever built by mankind."

But California Rep. Jared Huffman, the top Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, said during the hearing that the arch is "illegal" and would "disrupt the solemn connection" between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

"This arch would dishonor America, our ideals, and our laws," Huffman said during remarks to the planning commission, adding that Congress is the appropriate body for debating the proposed monument.

One Marine veteran who spoke in opposition to the proposal, Jimi Shaughnessy, said "a dominating arch with a carnival-like atmosphere of tourists, food trucks and buses is abhorrent and insulting to those who gave all and to their families."

"Instead of focusing on the issues facing military families, this administration is intent on spending taxpayer dollars to site, plan, and design a monument no one asked for, and are content with bypassing any laws or regulations that may prevent them from breaking ground," he said.

The arch itself will be 166 feet tall and topped with "three gilded figures" — a gold, winged female figure flanked by a gold flying eagle on each side — bringing its overall height to 250 feet, according to documents filed with the NCPC. The structure will sit close to Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, though the Federal Aviation Administration determined it will pose "no hazard to air navigation," with a "condition for safety lighting that includes a non-standard eternal flame and continuous floodlighting."

The arch will also feature an observation deck, and the Trump administration has estimated that it could draw between 2,000 and 22,400 visitors each day.

It's expected to take three years to build the arch, which will be located in the center of what is called Memorial Circle, across the Potomac from the Lincoln Memorial. It's unclear how much the project will cost, and who will foot the bill.

Mr. Trump said in September that his "Triumphal Arch" would be a "top grade Military Complex" and house drones and sniper ammunition. But the documents from the NCPC do not include the military usage.

Lawyers for the Justice Department declined to provide more details about the national security features in an October hearing.

The commission received more than 1,300 public comments about the project, most of which were in opposition, it said.

The NCPC's approval comes as Chutkan weighs how to act. A group of Vietnam War veterans, as well as the Commonwealth of Virginia and the city of Washington, D.C., have filed lawsuits arguing that the Trump administration is acting without congressional authorization and is not complying with the required procedures to construct the monument.

In an order Tuesday, Chutkan required the government to provide her notice within one hour of any NCPC vote and a thirty-minute notice to any preparation for construction of the arch to give her time to issue a decision on whether to block construction.

The government filed the required notices late Thursday, and Chutkan responded by issuing a temporary restraining order that blocked "construction, excavation, demolition, land-disturbance, utility installation, or roadway-closure activity, or any other construction-related activity" at the site.

In a hearing last month, Chutkan said the most important issue for her is whether the Vietnam War veterans had the legal right to sue. Earlier this year, the Supreme Court found that a group of plaintiffs who brought a similar suit to block the White House ballroom construction likely did not have legal standing to challenge the project.

In court filings, the Justice Department called the plaintiffs' motions "breathless" and urged Chutkan to follow the Supreme Court's decision in the White House ballroom case, but attorneys for the groups of plaintiffs argued that their legal arguments were different than the ballroom case and urged Chutkan to halt the arch's construction.

Two of the plaintiffs, Vietnam veterans Michael Lemmon and Shaun Byrnes, told Chutkan in a hearing last month that the arch construction would impact their experience when visiting graves at Arlington National Cemetery, and said they would be harmed by the arch's size and purpose.

In a separate suit brought in late October, Virginia and the District of Columbia sued, and the case was assigned to Chutkan, who had heard arguments the day before from the Vietnam veterans group. The state's attorneys general argued that "as soon as Defendants break ground on this project, they will inflict irreparable harm" on them because "the Arch project will inevitably snarl traffic between the jurisdictions, produce pollution and stormwater runoff in the Potomac, interfere with emergency services, and pose numerous other challenges."

World.title: Trump signs proclamation declaring Oval Office a national monument
World.content:
President Trump on Thursday signed a proclamation that he says will preserve the Oval Office and Cabinet Room as a national monument, his first official action after his party was swept aside in midterm elections on Tuesday.

But the action does not prevent future presidents from restyling the iconic office that Mr. Trump has filled to the brim with gold flourishes, nor does it prevent a successor from rolling back the proclamation itself. Mr. Trump himself has reversed national monument designations made by his predecessors.

Mr. Trump, however, described the Oval Office order in expansive terms.

"It will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape," Mr. Trump said. "We like the Oval Office, and it's a symbol, like the White House itself."

President Trump in the Oval Office of the White House on Nov. 5, 2026. Jim Lo Scalzo / EPA / Bloomberg via Getty Images

It was the third day this week that the president, a real estate mogul, delivered remarks fixated on his pet projects in Washington. On Wednesday, a day after Republicans suffered defeats in key races across the country, Mr. Trump gathered reporters to see the final beam being raised during construction of his opulent ballroom project. On Monday, he went to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool to talk about his renovation of the landmark.

The proclamation, released after Mr. Trump's remarks, says that nothing in it will "restrict the President's authority to redecorate the monument, select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security modifications that do not substantially impair the monument's historic structure or architectural character."

It orders the Interior secretary to manage the Oval Office and requires "documentation, review, and consideration of alternatives before any action that would substantially alter or demolish the monument." Mr. Trump separately said any major changes would need review from Congress, though such a requirement is not in the document's text.

"If they want to say, 'Let's not have oval anymore, let's make it square,' what happens is they have to go back to Congress and hopefully the Congress, the people in Congress, will be smart enough not to let that happen," said Mr. Trump — who notably demolished the East Wing of the White House to make room for his ballroom.

A red baseball cap with "VETO" on the front was sitting on the Resolute Desk as Mr. Trump signed the document, a not-so-subtle nod to the shifting of powers in Congress.

His effort to preserve changes at the White House comes as Democrats gear up for new scrutiny of Mr. Trump. Connecticut Sen. Richard Blumenthal, the top Democrat on the Homeland Security Committee's Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, sent a flurry of letters Thursday to known donors to Mr. Trump's ballroom, demanding that they provide information or face "alternative measures to obtain compliance."

Since returning to the White House, Mr. Trump has overseen numerous design changes to various rooms, including the Oval Office, where he has filled the wall space with portraits, a copy of the Declaration of Independence and numerous golden accents.

As he talked about his interior decorating decisions, Mr. Trump highlighted new chandeliers that he says were installed in the Cabinet Room to address "very bad lighting." His other additions to the Oval Office include numerous gold wall appliqués and gold-framed portraits.

Mr. Trump did not elaborate on precisely what he was hoping to prevent but suggested that the Oval Office might face some threat in the future. Mr. Trump himself has faced several lawsuits alleging that his Washington beautification projects were done without the necessary approval.

"If anybody ever decides to come and start knocking down walls, you call me wherever I may be," Mr. Trump said, "and I'll come back here and I'll make sure it never happens."

Late Thursday, the National Capital Planning Commission gave final approval for the president's 250-foot triumphal arch, which will be constructed between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

The NCPC, which acts as the federal government's planning agency for the region and is stacked with Trump allies, voted 8-4 to greenlight the project after almost 9 hours of public comments from members of Congress, veterans, architects and Washington, D.C., and Virginia residents.

However, a federal judge is weighing whether to temporarily block construction of the arch.

World.title: FEMA backlog causes delays in California infrastructure projects
World.content:
The Federal Emergency Management Agency is behind on approving major projects to protect Southern California totaling more than $191 million, a backlog that affects projects intended to reduce damage from floods, earthquakes, fires, and landslides, according to FEMA data.

The projects are supposed to be funded by a FEMA program called Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities — or BRIC. The Government Accountability Office has been studying the BRIC program over the last year.

"Back in March of 2025, the new administration came in, and they immediately canceled the BRIC program, and what we found is there wasn't a lot of rationale behind that," said Chris Currie, the director of the GAO's Homeland Security and Justice team. "They basically said that it was wasteful at the time. When we looked at it, though, they made that decision pretty haphazardly and quickly without really thinking through any of that."

California and 19 other states sued the federal government over the cancellation of BRIC, and in the spring of 2026, a federal judge ordered FEMA to continue the program.

Despite FEMA announcing BRIC was reinstated months ago, emergency management sources tell CBS California Investigates that FEMA has not approved any pending BRIC projects in California this year, and payments on already obligated projects are slow-moving.

A GAO report released in September says the backlog of projects nationwide totals $2.2 billion.

"Inflation happened. The cost increases happened. Labor prices increased," Currie explained. "A lot of work had to be redone. In many cases, these projects couldn't continue because they were twice as expensive as they were going to be before."

Emergency management sources in California echoed those concerns, telling CBS California Investigates that some communities in the state scrapped their BRIC projects altogether due to the delays.

California has the most projects pending of any state in the country, some first submitted in 2022, including a flood control project in San Bernardino with a price tag of $15 million.

San Bernardino County declined an interview for this story, but provided a written statement to CBS California Investigates.

"We maintain a positive and productive working relationship with FEMA and Cal OES. We received initial confirmation in April that the funding was moving forward, as evidenced by the issuance of the Final Public Notice," a county spokesperson wrote in an email to CBS California Investigates. "When the County originally applied for the grant, we factored in potential cost increases five years out, and we expect the project to remain within that allocation. The project is currently in design, and we continue to advance the work, so we are positioned to move into construction once funding is received."

Some counties with projects impacted by the delays say they've had limited communication since the BRIC program went back online this year about where their projects stand and if or when any next steps should be expected.

This is happening, as some counties waiting on BRIC funds are also waiting on reimbursements for hazard mitigation funds that FEMA promised following natural disasters in those communities. Delays with those checks are putting some rural counties in a real financial bind, sources tell CBS California Investigates.

Emergency management sources say FEMA's staff covering California projects has been significantly cut down, which could cause more delays.

Currie believes the delays could leave Californians at risk.

"The longer it takes to finish a resilience project, the greater the risk, wherever that project is," Currie said. "You have to remember, I mean, the whole purpose of these projects is to reduce risk. So, if you don't implement them, or they're not done, the risk doesn't change."

In Orange County, a BRIC grant has already funded phase one of a project to build an elevated berm and vegetated sand dunes to protect a portion of Capistrano Beach from more intense flooding.

The construction phase — the phase for which FEMA is expected to pay $9,377,094 — is scheduled to begin next year, the county says.

But with FEMA's backlogs, some experts fear phase two for projects like the one in Capistrano Beach — and others in California — could take a lot longer to move forward, and with flooding battering the coast this year, moving quickly is critical.

In October, Orange County Parks acquired an additional grant to supplement the BRIC project.

"The $2.4 million grant from the Ocean Protection Council helps to offset the County's expenses to construct the Nature Based Shoreline project, and is meant to supplement the federal BRIC funding, not replace it," a spokesperson for OC Parks wrote to CBS California Investigates in a written statement.

Some homeowners in the area are hoping for as many beach restoration projects as possible.

Asked about the delays to projects nationwide, Capistrano Beach homeowner Natalie Driessen said, "it's horrible, you know, and I don't think it's right, and it's sad."

She says the beach in front of her Capistrano Beach home has changed dramatically since she bought it three years ago. Her house is now yellow-tagged, and she's searching for answers to protect her community from further damage.

"I think we just have to be humanitarians again," Driessen said. "I think we need to be fiscally responsible, but we need to be humanitarian, and if there are funds, we need to help people."

Despite this backlog of hundreds of projects nationwide sitting unpaid, FEMA just put out a call for more applications this fall.

Rep. Pete Aguilar (D-San Bernardino) says he intends to get answers from FEMA about the delays.

"From the beginning, Donald Trump has played politics with disaster relief. He has continued to release money for projects in Republican-held states and districts while leaving billions in aid requests unanswered from California," he said in a written statement to CBS California Investigates. "Nearly two years after the devastating January 2025 wildfires that ravaged Southern California, families are still left waiting for help. Disaster aid should not depend on your zip code or political affiliation."

CBS California Investigates reached out to FEMA for a comment, but has not yet received a response.

In a letter dated September 2, 2026, Jeffrey Bobich, FEMA's executive director of financial management and systems, wrote to the GAO concurring with the GAO's recommendations.

"FEMA is exploring opportunities to streamline the BRIC sub application process and expedite project reviews, while maintaining appropriate program oversight and compliance with applicable statutory, regulatory, and policy requirements," Bobich wrote. "These efforts are intended to improve the applicant's experience, support timely award decisions, and help ensure mitigation investments are delivered efficiently to communities."

World.title: Nithya Raman ousts incumbent Karen Bass in LA mayor's race, CBS News projects
World.content:
Councilmember Nithya Raman will be Los Angeles' next mayor after defeating incumbent Karen Bass in the November general election, CBS News projects.

Raman's win comes after resounding victories for Democrats across the country on Election Day.

On Thursday night, Raman stood among supporters in the Fairfax District and pledged to restore Angelenos' "faith in City Hall."

"My goal is to earn your trust. My goal is to make sure that we're doing the work to actually have a City Hall that is capable of delivering on the promises that I made during the campaign," she said. "That is my commitment to every single person, whether you voted for me or you didn't, or you sat out this election completely. I want to make sure that we can restore your faith in City Hall."

Nithya Raman defeats incumbent Karen Bass in the Los Angeles mayoral election, CBS News projects. CBS News

Bass released a statement on Thursday morning conceding to Raman, saying she called her to congratulate her on the victory. The last time a challenger ousted a sitting LA mayor happened in 2005, when Antonio Villaraigosa defeated incumbent James Hahn.

"While this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken. I have called Councilmember Nithya Raman to congratulate her on her victory, and I have committed to ensuring a smooth and seamless transition," Bass wrote.

Bass thanked her supporters and other leaders who helped during her campaign. She added that she will continue to "ensure the promise of a better life belongs to all of us."

During her Thursday night speech, Raman thanked Bass for "her decades of service to the city" and for her work to make LA "the epitome of the American Dream."

"I know her service is something that people across America have gratitude for, and certainly every person across Los Angeles," she said. "We committed to working together on the smoothest possible transition for Angelenos. We love this city. We want to make it an incredible, incredible place."

After Bass' concession, Los Angeles Police Department Chief Jim McDonnell congratulated Raman and thanked Bass for her time in office.

"As Chief of Police, I remain committed to leading a department that delivers professional, constitutional, and compassionate policing to all Angelenos," McDonnell wrote in a statement. "By working together, we can meet the challenges ahead and continue building a safer Los Angeles for everyone."

Raman, a Democratic socialist, has been riding her momentum after pushing past Spencer Pratt in the June primary, but suffered a setback with voters a week before the election, according to the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the Los Angeles Times.

A survey released by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the LA Times shortly before the election showed Bass and Raman tied, with 40% support among likely voters.

Bass and Raman became frontrunners after the primary election when they rallied ahead of third-place candidate Pratt.

"I want to tell every single Angeleno out there, I am going to work so hard, and everyone behind me is going to work so hard to earn your trust," Raman said. "To earn the trust of everyone across this city and to make people believe in Los Angeles again."

Councilmember Nithya Raman

Raman announced her surprise bid for mayor in February after previously endorsing Bass' reelection bid.

During the primary, Raman called her campaign a "long shot" before ultimately overtaking Pratt to face Bass in the general election.

Before being elected to Los Angeles City Council in 2020, Raman served as the co-chair of the Silver Lake Neighborhood Council Homelessness Committee and co-founded a homeless advocacy nonprofit.

One of her most notable acts in office came in 2025, when she introduced a motion capping maximum annual rent increases for tenants in rent-stabilized apartments built before 1978. It eventually passed 13-2. She said she hoped to undertake similar work to help small businesses.

Mayor Karen Bass

After serving more than two decades in public office as a congresswoman and as LA's 43rd Mayor, Bass said this race will be her last campaign for office.

Bass was raised in LA with her three brothers. She began her professional career as a nurse and physician assistant, where she later founded the Community Coalition to help underserved residents of South LA battle substance abuse, poverty and crime.

She kickstarted her career in politics in 2004 as a member of the California Assembly, where she became the first Black woman to serve as Speaker of a state legislative body. She left the Assembly in 2010 to run for Congress, where she served in the House for 12 years.

Leading up to the primary election, Bass received endorsements from notable politicians including California Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Vice President Kamala Harris. Nearly a week before the November election, billionaire Rick Caruso threw his support behind his former rival in the 2022 mayoral race and vowed to vote for her in November.

"For the love of LA, I must put the past behind me because this election must be about our future," Caruso said in a post to X. "I will be casting my ballot for Mayor Karen Bass."

He also said in the video that he had concerns about Raman that were not "much about ideology, but about competence."

World.title: Wendy's rejects $1.4 billion hostile takeover bid
World.content:
Wendy's board of directors on Thursday unanimously rejected a $1.4 billion hostile takeover bid from a group of investment firms, saying the offer undervalues the restaurant chain and is not in the best interest of shareholders.

"The Independent Committee thoroughly evaluated this Proposal and unanimously concluded that it substantially undervalues Wendy's standalone prospects and long-term earnings potential," Art Winkleblack, chairman of the board, said in a statement, while also expressing confidence in CEO Bob Wright.

The takeover bid was led by asset management firm Trian Partners, founded by activist investor Nelson Peltz, along with Flynn Group LP, BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners.

The groups are offering $7.35 per share for Wendy's, whose stock traded at $7.75 before markets opened on Thursday. Wendy's confirmed it received the unsolicited offer last month and said it would create an independent board to review the proposal.

Although it remains profitable, Wendy's has faced slowing revenue growth in recent years, and its stock price has slumped nearly 14% over the last 12 months.

In its latest earnings report on Thursday, Wendy's said that U.S. same-restaurant sales fell 5.7% in the third quarter, compared to the same time last year. The chain reported $547 million in revenue, down from $549.5 million in the year-ago quarter.

Wendy's is losing traction with customers as inflation and rising beef costs force the burger chain to raise prices, the Associated Press reported last week.

The company has also struggled with operational issues, including staffing, employee training, handling drive-thru orders and marketing, Wright said during a call with Wall Street analysts in August. More broadly, he acknowledged that Wendy's must improve the quality of its food to drive business.

"Wendy's has always been known for quality, fresh, never frozen beef, hamburgers made to order, bacon cooked in our restaurants and fresh produce prepared daily," he said. "But over time, we've drifted away from some of the standards that made Wendy's distinctive. While we've maintained core practices in some areas, we've led cost and efficiency drive decisions that weaken that differentiation."

Other businesses across the fast-food industry are also struggling as inflation weighs on customers' wallets. McDonald's reported on Wednesday that it would offer a new array of affordable options next year to boost sales.

World.title: Democrats have flipped over 40 House seats. Here's the breakdown.
World.content:
Democrats won control of the House of Representatives on Tuesday by flipping more than three dozen Republican-held seats, picking up perennial swing districts and seats that were once considered deep red. The party's wins ranged from suburban areas in the northeastern United States to areas of South Texas that were once viewed as increasingly GOP-friendly.

The 2026 midterm elections were also shaken up by last year's nationwide mid-decade redistricting gambit, with Texas Republicans shifting several districts rightward at President Trump's behest, California Democrats moving districts to the left and several other states tweaking their House maps for partisan purposes. Democrats notched several wins under the new maps, while the GOP's pickups have been more limited so far.

Winners in dozens of races have yet to be projected by CBS News.

So far, 43 districts have shifted to Democrats and two have shifted to Republicans. Here's a look at the seats that swung:

Upsets

In several districts, Democrats ousted GOP lawmakers who won by double digits two years ago.

Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz of Indiana speaks at the Capitol on April 26, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite / AP

Rematches

A few Democrats won against Republicans who they'd faced before — in one case, multiple times.

Democratic Rep. Elaine Luria of Virginia speaks at a hearing on the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol, on Dec. 19, 2022. J. Scott Applewhite / AP

Northeastern Battlegrounds

Both parties invested in districts in the Northeast, including seats with a history of swinging from one party to another, and a competitive Pennsylvania seat that was held by an overperforming Republican for a decade.

Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, a Republican from Pennsylvania, speaks during a news conference at the Capitol on March 6, 2024. Tierney L. Cross / Bloomberg via Getty Images

Tight Midwestern Districts

A few Midwestern states will have dramatically different congressional delegations starting next year.

Michigan Democrat William Lawrence greets supporters at an election night event in Lansing on Nov. 3, 2026. AP Photo/Kristen Norman

Western States

Some Western cities and states elected their first Democrats to the House in years.

Montana's 1st District : Former smokejumper and union leader

: Former Utah's 1st District : Democrat Ben McAdams won the newly drawn district, which encompasses Salt Lake City and its suburbs. After a lengthy legal battle, court-ordered redistricting produced one Democratic-leaning district in the state, giving the party its best opportunity in nearly a decade to flip one of the state's four House seats.

After a lengthy legal battle, court-ordered redistricting produced one Democratic-leaning district in the state, giving the party its best opportunity in nearly a decade to flip one of the state's four House seats. Colorado's 5th District : GOP Rep. Jeff Crank lost reelection to Jessica Killin, who will be the first Democrat to ever represent the Colorado Springs-area district. Crank won by nearly 14 points in 2024, but the area has shifted left over the years.

Juan Ciscomani in this competitive district, which stretches from the Tucson-area suburbs down to the southeastern corner of the state along the U.S. Mexico border.

Sam Forstag Courtesy of Sam for Montana campaign

Texas

Republicans in the Lone Star State redrew their House maps last year with the goal of picking up as many as five seats that were held by Democrats. Ultimately, one seat flipped to the GOP, and two red districts were captured by Democrats. The shifts coincided with a slate of statewide Democratic wins in Texas, which elected its first Democratic senator and governor in decades.

Bobby Pulido, a Latin Grammy winner and Democratic candidate for Texas' 15th Congressional District, at a campaign event in Weslaco, Texas, on Oct. 25, 2026. Gabriel V. Cardenas /AFP via Getty Images

California

Voters in California approved their own redistricting plan after Texas redrew its maps, aiming at moving several California seats to the left. Democrats have picked up all five of the seats they had hoped to flip.

Republican Rep. David Valadao of California on May 12, 2022. Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images

North Carolina

A handful of House seats in North Carolina changed hands, including some upsets in places that were tilted to the GOP in redistricting a few years ago, part of a wave in the Tar Heel State as Roy Cooper decisively won the state's Senate race.

North Carolina Democratic congressional candidate Jamie Ager greets a supporter in Asheville on Oct. 31, 2026. Allison Joyce / Getty Images

World.title: Trump's arch gets a late-night green light. Will a judge stop construction?
World.content:
Trump's arch gets a late-night green light. Will a judge stop construction?

toggle caption i Tom Brenner/Getty Images

A federal panel packed with administration allies has given final approval to President Trump's proposed arch, after hearing nearly eight hours of impassioned pleas from veterans, lawmakers, residents and concerned citizens opposed to the structure.

The National Capital Planning Commission voted 8-4 to greenlight the arch, which would stand 250 feet tall on Memorial Circle, a traffic island on the bridge linking the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington National Cemetery. The Trump administration has said it could begin excavation work that same day, despite lacking authorization from Congress and an ongoing legal challenge.

A group of Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian sued the government earlier this year, arguing that an arch is unlawful without Congressional approval, which the administration has not sought. The Democratic governments of D.C. and Virginia jointly filed a similar lawsuit last weekend.

Sponsor Message

D.C. District Court Judge Tanya Chutkan consolidated the lawsuits and asked the government to notify the court within an hour of commission approval. That suggests she could issue an 11th-hour preliminary injunction to block construction, as plaintiffs have requested.

The day started with a protest on Memorial Circle, where dozens of people spoke against the arch. The grass underfoot was already marked with white paint. Lawyers for the government told the court in a midday filing that the lines were painted on Saturday by its designated construction firm, seemingly without authorization from the National Park Service.

The commission meeting began at 1 p.m. It was held virtually because of the high volume of public testimony: 131 people were signed up to speak.

Just minutes into public testimony, the livestream crashed, lengthening the meeting by about an hour until it was restored. Over the course of nearly nine hours, commissioners heard from dozens of veterans and their relatives, Democratic lawmakers, historic preservation experts and concerned citizens from D.C. and beyond.

Among their many concerns, critics said the structure would obstruct an important view, insult service members buried on the hallowed ground of nearby Arlington National Cemetery and add a layer of risk to the notoriously complicated D.C. airspace. They have questions about its legality and its cost, which the administration has not confirmed.

Many see the arch as part of Trump's unilateral effort to memorialize himself in the nation's capital — and described Democrats' midterm sweep as a referendum against it.

Sponsor Message

"Leaving aside all of the legitimate concerns and challenges about the required approvals, funding, land use, single-source bidding, and peer review, the American people spoke this past Tuesday at the ballot box," said former D.C. resident Emi Yamauchi. "They said enough vanity projects, enough corruption, enough Reflecting Pool travesties."

Only a handful of speakers offered support for the arch, including Republican Reps. Andrew Clyde of Georgia and Brian Mast of Florida, both of whom are veterans.

Much of the night's testimony was heartfelt and personal: Many speakers had family members buried — or plans for their own future burials — at Arlington National Cemetery. Several implored the commissioners not to ruin their reputations by recording their support for the arch.

"[These are] warnings about the threat your own behavior poses to your political power, your moral authority, the legacy you leave to your descendants, and your eternal souls," said Stephen Eubank, some seven hours into the public testimony.

As the night wore on, a few speakers even questioned whether the commissioners — who were not shown on screen — were even listening. Many suggested the approval was a foregone conclusion, noting the political makeup of the commission and the fact that Trump-appointed Chair Mark Paoletta and several other members had expressed their support for the arch at the start of the meeting.

The commission started deliberating just before 10 p.m. The discussion lasted less than an hour.

The commissioners who spoke first were Trump allies and appointees. They thanked the speakers for taking the time to share their views, but — in brief comments — expressed their support for moving forward. They continued to cast the arch as a tribute to the nation and those who served, despite the broad pushback from individual veterans and veterans' groups.

The Trump allies dismissed concerns that the arch would violate D.C.'s restrictions on building heights as well as federal environmental and historic preservation laws. They maintained that Congress authorized the project when it approved a pair of 166-foot columns on Memorial Circle in 1925, which were never built.

Sponsor Message

And they pointed to recent claims by Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that the monument will enhance national security — even though officials at the meeting confirmed that no such analysis or details were included in the final submission. In fact, Interior Department official Greg Wischer said "specific national security functions have been filed under seal" in court but that the National Park Service "has not been privy to any national defense preparations."

The most vocal criticism of the arch came from D.C. Council Chair Phil Mendelson, a Democrat who sits on the council. He asked questions about the arch's purpose — military and otherwise — earlier in the meeting and said, during deliberations, that he was dissatisfied with the government's contradictory answers.

"We cannot approve final site and building plans until we have the final site and building plan," Mendelson said. He introduced a motion to postpone the vote until those plans could be submitted, or until the commission's next meeting in early December. The motion failed by a vote of 4 to 8.

Vice Chair Stuart Levenbach, a Trump appointee, expressed concerns about delaying the vote because the "project proponent is under a time constraint and wants the decision today," suggesting the government wants to "commence building very quickly."

Within minutes, the commission had given the arch its green light. The Trump administration notified the court within half an hour.

Arch critics look to the courts and Congress for relief

Historic preservation groups wasted no time slamming both the process and the outcome.

Brent Leggs, the president and CEO of the National Trust for Historic Preservation, called the night's vote a "sham."

"It undermines the democratic process, violates federal statute, and insults our nation's veterans who have made the ultimate sacrifice," he said in a statement. "From the start, this Arch project has been driven by an artificial sense of urgency, while public opposition has been brushed aside."

Sponsor Message

Jimi Shaughnessy, veterans program manager for the National Parks Conservation Association, said in a statement that the organization is disappointed but not surprised. He vowed to "bring this to members of Congress, to ensure this arch is never built. Not here. Not ever."

Many Democratic lawmakers have vowed to stop — and investigate — the arch after they regain a Congressional majority in January.

Robert Weissman, the co-president of Public Citizen — the consumer rights nonprofit representing the veterans in their lawsuit — told NPR on Thursday that Congress doesn't need to act to stop the arch, since it never actively approved it. That decision, he said, will be up to the courts.

But, he added: "It would be fine if Congress takes additional measures to block construction, since we've seen this lawless administration circumvent the law and court orders so frequently."

Virginia Rep. Don Beyer has introduced a bill that would prohibit and defund the arch, and said Thursday he expects the number of co-sponsors to grow from 80 to at least 200 in the new year.

And Rep. Jared Huffman, D-Calif., the ranking Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, warned commissioners that companies and "officials working to advance a project not authorized by Congress will put themselves at legal risk."

He argued that the project violates federal environmental and historic preservation laws, which fall within the jurisdiction of the House committee he expects to soon lead.

"I urge all officials and firms involved with this illegal project to consider the legal hazards they may be facing by advancing it, because, in case you hadn't heard, we'll soon have a new Congress that takes the rule of law very seriously," Huffman said.

World.title: Fears of an AI crackdown after midterms spark $2 trillion rout in tech stocks
World.content:
Fears of an AI crackdown after midterms spark $2 trillion rout in tech stocks

toggle caption i Timothy A. Clary/AFP via Getty Images

Two days after Democrats won overwhelmingly in the national midterm elections — and in state races across the country — investors started to come to terms with the potential consequences.

Fears that an incoming Democratic Congress would crack down on AI sent the tech-heavy Nasdaq down more than 5% and wiped out more than $2 trillion in market value. The Dow Jones and S&P also sank.

The losses were a stark reversal from Wednesday, when investors had initially sent shares higher across the board, relieved that the midterms did not end with the fate of Congress undecided.

Sponsor Message

The sobering-up seen across markets on Thursday reflected investors' concern about a big signal sent by voters: They revolted against AI data centers, which many people worry will gobble up water and energy resources. Those voters supported Democrats who have vowed to push back against the proliferation of these projects.

But many AI companies — including Meta and Alphabet, the parent company of Google — need to keep building out these data centers to continue developing the technology.

The Nasdaq's decline comes after what has already been a rough year of technology shares on Wall Street, with investors starting to question whether the massive investments companies have plowed into AI will pay off anytime soon.

"There is some concern regarding AI regulation, and fears that there could be far more regulations coming to AI technology, as well as a pushback on the buildout of data centers across the country," says David Busch, chief investment officer of Trajan Wealth.

Musk companies hit hard

AI-related or AI-dependent stocks of all kinds were among the biggest decliners on Thursday, with Tesla and SpaceX — both controlled by billionaire Elon Musk — falling particularly sharply. Musk spent hundreds of millions of dollars in an unsuccessful attempt to elect more Republicans, and investors fear he and his companies could also come under Democratic scrutiny when the new Congress is seated in January.

Sponsor Message

It's not only Congress, however. Democrats who vowed to slow down AI development also won at the state level, most prominently Gina Hinojosa, who won the Texas governor's race in stunning fashion.

It's unclear whether the AI stock rout will continue — or spread beyond tech stocks. AI has become a big driver of the U.S. economy, helping it post a solid annual growth of 3.4% in the July-September quarter.

And sophisticated Wall Street investors are not the only ones who own a lot of shares in AI companies. Average Americans also own them through their retirement investment portfolios — such as 401(k)s or pension funds — leaving them also vulnerable to a prolonged AI rout.

World.title: Melania Trump touts rare agreement she brokered between Russia and Ukraine
World.content:
Melania Trump touts rare agreement she brokered between Russia and Ukraine

toggle caption i Samuel Corum/Getty Images

First lady Melania Trump hosted a rare meeting between Russian and Ukrainian officials at the White House to recognize a temporary ceasefire in southeastern Ukraine.

The six-day pause from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky comes as the administration ramps up efforts to secure an agreement to end the war in Ukraine.

"We have chosen humanity over war," the first lady said. "Undeniably, the lives of innocent people must transcend the divisions of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace."

Trump has accomplished something that has so far eluded her husband - helping broker a temporary ceasefire and bringing together representatives of the two sides in acknowledgement of the human costs of the war.

Sponsor Message

The White House sees it as a diplomatic breakthrough, but some European analysts worry the efforts can backfire.

The temporary reprieve, which expired on Sunday, enabled humanitarian aid to reach the city while allowing hundreds of residents to be evacuated.

Kirill Dmitriev, Russian President Vladimir Putin's special envoy, thanked the first lady. He said Putin personally gave the instructions to ensure the successful implementation of the ceasefire.

"On behalf of President Putin, on behalf of the people of the Russian Federation, we would like to thank first lady Melania Trump for her distinguished humanitarian role in resolving a key situation and resolving this humanitarian issue," he said.

Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets presented Melania Trump with an award for her humanitarian work. The Order of Princess Olha, 1st Class, is Ukraine's highest award for women.

"I have only one request from all Ukrainian nation," Lubinets said, "please continue doing your wonderful work and support people."

The event comes just days before the U.S. leads a new round of peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi next week.

President Trump also met with Dmitriev at the White House.

Trump told reporters that the sides were close to reaching a deal.

Sponsor Message

"It's going to be an agreement. It's going to be a big agreement, ‌and ⁠it's going to involve more than Ukraine," he said. "I could even say it might involve all of Europe. It's ⁠going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone's going to be thrilled."

Heather Conley, who worked on European issues in President George W. Bush's State Department, supports all efforts to help suffering Ukrainians, but she also said the U.S. must be careful not to normalize Russia's bad behavior.

"In this White House ceremony, we were honoring the Russians that were the cause of both the occupation of Oleshky, the starvation of Oleshky, and now we're honoring them for allowing aid to come into Oleshky," said Conley, who is now a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. "The more we create this equivalency where the Russians and the Ukrainians are equal in this crisis, it is putting this thing upside down."

World.title: How North Carolina Democrats flipped several House seats in historically GOP districts
World.content:
How North Carolina Democrats flipped several House seats in historically GOP districts

toggle caption i A.M STEWART/AFP via Getty Images

The Associated Press has called five U.S. House races in North Carolina for Democrats, all of them in districts drawn to favor Republican candidates.

Of those districts, four are flipping from Republican control.

As of Thursday, the AP had called nine of the state's 14 House seats for Democrats and none for Republicans. It's a startling result for a delegation that went into Tuesday with 10 Republicans and four Democrats.

Races called Thursday that flipped from Republican to Democratic control included:



High Point Mayor Cyril Jefferson over first-term incumbent Rep. Addison McDowell in the Triad's 6th Congressional District.

Former West Virginia State Senator Richard Ojeda over National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Rep. Richard Hudson in the 9th Congressional District.

Paul Barringer over first-term incumbent Rep. Brad Knott in the 13th Congressional District, which wraps around the Raleigh exurbs.

LaKesha Womack over first-term incumbent Rep. Tim Moore, who previously served as speaker of the N.C. House of Representatives, in the 14th Congressional District.

Sponsor Message

North Carolina's Congressional map was redrawn in 2023 to significantly favor Republican candidates, and these four districts performed that way in 2024. The 14th District was the closest in that election, with Moore winning by about 16%, while the 6th District was the least competitive, with McDowell winning by more than 38%.

One of the candidates vying to replace Hudson as NRCC chair is U.S. Rep. Brian Jack, a Georgia Republican.

He wrote in a letter to fellow House Republicans that fellow GOP lawmakers may have contributed to the challenging environment. Former Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat, won the race for North Carolina's open U.S. Senate seat by nearly 20%.

Statewide Races What the blue wave looked like in North Carolina North Carolina Blue Wave Listen · 4:17 4:17

"When Senate Republicans withdrew support from North Carolina weeks ago, they created a cascade that likely swept away many of our colleagues from that state," Jack wrote.

The AP also called northeastern North Carolina's 1st Congressional District for incumbent Democrat Rep. Don Davis on Thursday.

Loading...

That's a district legislative Republicans redrew last year in an effort to make it easier for GOP candidates to win there, pulling Republican-leaning counties from the state's 3rd Congressional District to do so.

Yet as of Thursday, Davis was leading Republican challenger Laurie Buckhout by more than 10,000 votes. That's a larger margin than he won by in 2024.

North Carolina's 3rd Congressional District is one of five in the state that remain uncalled, with incumbent Republican Greg Murphy leading Democrat Raymond Smith by just 233 votes in a district where Democrats didn't even run a candidate in 2024. That race is likely headed for a recount.

In the 5th Congressional District, Democratic challenger Chuck Hubbard is leading 11-term Republican incumbent Virginia Foxx by 99 votes — that's another race that may go to a recount.

If all of the remaining results hold, the state's congressional delegation would flip from 10 Republicans and four Democrats to 10 Democrats and four Republicans.

World.title: Paraguay's president is impeached minutes after resigning following a bank collapse
World.content:
Paraguay's president is impeached minutes after resigning following a bank collapse

toggle caption i Jorge Saenz/AP

ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay — Paraguayan President Santiago Peña announced his resignation Thursday after the collapse of a major digital bank tied to his government triggered widespread protests, froze millions of people's savings and cost him the support of his own party.

The crisis at Ueno Bank turned Peña's long-ruling Colorado Party against him, a stunning reversal for the former International Monetary Fund economist who had enjoyed the backing of the country's most powerful politicians and was welcomed in Washington just weeks ago as a key ally of the Trump administration.

Minutes after Peña's announcement, the lower house voted 78-0 to impeach him, sending the charges to the Senate. Congressional leaders were expected to accept his resignation later Thursday, clearing the way for Vice President Pedro Alliana to be sworn in without waiting for a Senate trial.

Sponsor Message

Opposition senators were still demanding a trial, arguing that allowing Peña to resign would preserve his eligibility to become a senator for life, with legal protections that could prevent his prosecution.

toggle caption i Ted Shaffrey/AP

As lawmakers debated his impeachment, Peña said in a video posted to X that he was stepping down in the interest of "the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions."

Even Peña's mentor, Colorado Party leader and former President Horacio Cartes, backed impeachment, saying the party would not side with "the plundering of public and private funds and pensioners' money." The United States Treasury sanctioned Cartes in 2023 over bribery allegations that the Trump administration lifted last year.

Peña, who until last year held a stake in a company linked to Ueno, expressed contrition. But he stopped short of accepting responsibility for the turmoil, which has left millions of depositors, retirees and workers scrambling to recoup their frozen savings and unpaid wages.

"I want to apologize to the people if I have failed them at any point," he said. "It was never my intention to betray the trust they placed in me."

The turmoil has hit Paraguay's currency. The guaraní fell nearly 4% against the U.S. dollar Thursday, bringing its losses this week to nearly 7%, according to central bank exchange-rate data.

Sponsor Message

From star lender to seized bank

Ueno Bank, which exploded from an obscure finance company to a household name in less than five years, claimed more than 60% of Paraguay's adults as customers. Many Paraguayans are left asking how a bank linked to the president could grow so rapidly in size and importance despite repeated warnings about its lending practices.

The answer lies in the uncomfortable proximity of Peña's Colorado Party to the country's regulators and business elite, a weakness that has endured even as steady economic management and rapid growth recently earned Paraguay coveted investment-grade credit ratings.

"Santiago Peña and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings," said Luis Pineda, one of the protesters marching to Congress on Wednesday. "We are fed up with 70 years of plunder."

Soon after winning its banking license in 2023, Ueno seemed to be everywhere in Paraguay. The digital lender, a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company, lured customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries, grew to more than 70 locations, sponsored Paraguay's national soccer team and plastered its name on the country's main stadium.

Government money poured into Ueno's coffers under Peña. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, president of Financiera Ueno, the predecessor to Ueno Bank, to run the central bank, the agency charged with supervising the digital lender.

As of last month, Ueno reported holding roughly $800 million in public deposits, about a quarter of its total, including money from the state pension and health fund and the operators of Paraguay's giant hydroelectric dams.

Even as retirees' savings and other public money piled up at Ueno, worries were escalating inside the central bank. In June, its inspectors found a pattern of risky lending to insiders, reported ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper. Ueno had extended large sums to companies tied to its owners, beyond what the law allows and without enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad.

Sponsor Message

As recently as last month, Peña defended Ueno and the central bank's oversight, dismissing the concerns as a smear campaign that was spooking the public.

Long lines outside branches but customers are locked out

But on Monday, it all came crashing down. Regulators investigating Ueno's loans to companies linked to its owners found poorly documented lending, the central bank said, as well as expenses the bank had wrongly counted as assets.

Once the books were corrected, Ueno's capital, the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses, fell to less than half the legal minimum. The central bank announced the lender's seizure Tuesday, beginning a process to transfer deposits and recoverable assets to other banks before liquidating what remained.

Ueno's app, cards and transfers went dark and its branches locked their doors, leaving desperate depositors lined up outside. On Wednesday, a rush to open new accounts elsewhere crashed other banks' mobile apps, fueling public panic.

Officials have appealed for calm. Under a law rushed through Congress on Wednesday, a state guarantee fund must repay stranded depositors within five business days, starting Thursday with small accounts of up to about $1,600 held by customers with no debts to Ueno. The fund insures up to about $36,000 per customer, which the central bank says will cover the full balances of an estimated 97% of clients.

On Thursday, a judge ordered six Ueno executives, including founder Miguel Vázquez and bank President Juan Manuel Gustale, jailed pending trial and two others placed under house arrest. Prosecutors have charged 27 bank officials and associates with breach of trust and attempted fraud, alleging that Ueno made large loans to related companies without adequate guarantees and diverted some of the money to other group businesses.

Gustale's lawyer pushed back on the charges, arguing that senior executives had relied on staff for lending decisions. "The president or board is not responsible for deciding who receives a particular loan," José Fernández Zacur told local media.

Sponsor Message

Protesters in the streets

Still in their Ueno uniforms, young employees burned their credit cards and cursed Peña outside the Labor Ministry on Thursday, demanding severance and unpaid wages. Peña's resignation did little to calm them. Many vowed to keep protesting until lawmakers finished impeaching him, saying his departure alone would neither bring accountability nor return their money.

"Let the impeachment process take place and let him lose his immunity," said Adolfo Villalba, one of the protesters on Thursday.

The Labor Ministry estimates the collapse has affected about 7,000 direct and indirect jobs at the bank and its related businesses.

Many saw Ueno's collapse not just as reckless banking but as a case study in official corruption. Only Venezuela ranks worse in South America on Transparency International's latest index of perceived corruption.

"This is yet another assault on honest, hard-working citizens, people whose small savings are the fruit of years of labor," said Belarmino Balbuena, one of thousands who marched on Congress in the capital, Asunción, on Wednesday.

The crowds shouted, "We want your head, Peña!" Their signs branded him "the enemy of savers" and pleaded, "Give us back our money." Riot police fired pepper spray and rubber bullets to push them back.

At the national stadium that once bore Ueno's name, the bank's logo had already been scrubbed away. Across the capital, fresh graffiti called politicians thieves.

World.title: Head of Justice Department office on Civil Rights resigns
World.content:
Head of Justice Department office on Civil Rights resigns

toggle caption i Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

The head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, Harmeet Dhillon, is out after 18 tumultuous months in charge, during which she radically reshaped the unit's mission, oversaw the mass exodus of career staff, and aggressively pursued President Trump's agenda.

Dhillon is the first senior department official to depart the Trump administration since Democrats retook control of the House and Senate in midterm elections.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, in a statement on X, announced Dhillon's resignation and thanked her for her service.

"She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor," he wrote. "The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors."

Sponsor Message

In her own statement, Dhillon said the job had been "the honor of a lifetime."

"We ushered in the downfall of illegal DEI, we fought to protect women in girls' sports, and so much more," she added.

During her tenure, Dhillon implemented dramatic changes in the Civil Rights Division, pushing out roughly 300 career attorneys, hiring inexperienced ideological allies to replace them, and using the division's enforcement powers to advance Trump's MAGA policies.

The changes marked a dramatic shift for the division, which was created some 70 years ago during the civil rights movement to end racial segregation in the U.S. For decades, it fought to protect the constitutional rights of all Americans across all aspects of life, from housing and employment to education and policing.

Dhillon, a conservative attorney and Trump loyalist, came into office with a different view. In her eyes, the division had narrowed its mission in recent decades to only protecting the rights of people of color, and she promptly shifted to aggressively pursuing conservative priorities.

"We don't just slow down the woke," she said at a Federalist Society event in 2025. "We take up the cause to achieve the executive branch's goals."

Under her leadership, the division redirected its energies to enforce Trump's executive orders, including ending the alleged radical indoctrination in schools, defending women from "gender ideology extremism," and combatting antisemitism and purported anti-Christian bias.

In the run-up to the midterm elections, the Civil Rights Division sued dozens of states demanding they turn over voter information — in furtherance of Trump's allegations of voter fraud.

Election officials pushed back, and courts tossed the department's lawsuits.

The division also accused numerous universities and law schools of discriminating against white and Asian students, and sued UCLA and Harvard for allegedly allowing antisemitism to flourish on campus.

Sponsor Message

In an email to division staff, Dhillon said she informed Trump in early October that she planned to return to private practice after the midterms, and now is the time to do so.

"I'm proud of all we've accomplished during this time to ensure our nation's civil rights laws protect every American," she wrote in the email, a copy of which was obtained by NPR. "I'm also grateful for the hard work of the dedicated employees within the Division and the rest of the Department of Justice."

For many division veterans who were highly critical of Dhillon's treatment of career staff and her enforcement goals, her departure was a welcome development.

"Harmeet Dhillon has been the most destructive, lawless, and hateful head of the Civil Rights Division in DOJ history," said Stacey Young, a former division attorney. "Dhillon wielded the enormous power of the Justice Department to threaten universities, state and local officials, and election workers in spurious cases that rarely won in court."

"Americans' civil rights don't enforce themselves. For almost 70 years, the Civil Rights Division brought to fruition the civil rights laws that Americans demanded. Dhillon decimated it," said Young, who now heads who Justice Connection, a group of department alumni that provides support to DOJ employees.

World.title: Discursive Verses: Is 'Spend Dat' the best financial indicator of America's grift economy?
World.content:
Discursive Verses: Is 'Spend Dat' the best financial indicator of America's grift economy?

toggle caption i Aaron J. Thornton/Getty Images for BET

After spending three hours counting the pores on Elizabeth Holmes' and Nathan Fielder's faces, I couldn't help but think how perfect Yung Miami's "Spend Dat" would've played over the closing credits. Whatever you feel about the veracity of the protagonist in the blockbuster doc You Can See Everything, there is no doubt about her innate ability to cop and blow money fast. She's probably about as familiar with Diddy's favorite City Girl as she is with Abbott & Costello. But a scammer of such ill repute deserves an apropos theme song. Hell, maybe we all do.

Sponsor Message

When people complain about hip-hop no longer being political, what they're really talking about is commercial rap's long-fizzled countercultural agenda. The politics of consumption and corruption however have never enjoyed a louder ringing endorsement. Like a billionaire hogging the bully pulpit. To that end, no song in 2026 comes closer to mimicking the feeling of being the violated and the violator. On its face, "Spend Dat" is a get-money flex dedicated to all the "scammers" and "booster b*****s." But behind that seductive veneer is the sadomasochistic loop of late-stage capitalism's long, punishing con. An inflation indicator like no other, it's easily our most American anthem of the year. And we're all transfixed, nodding along in unblinking commitment to the charade.

The video for "Spend Dat" feels like a throwback to the early 2000s, when making it rain in strip clubs was still obligatory signposting for selling the dream. It almost feels trite now that prediction markets allow us to place digital bets on democracy and buy-now, pay-later loans keep expanding on our freedom to fall deeper in debt. At least a good lap dance came with a tangible return on investment. Now we're all just being teased to death.

YouTube

When India.Arie echoed the public denouncement of "Spend Dat" — which included a call for Black folk to boycott the Billboard-charting song of the summer — another film, I Love Boosters, had just hit streaming. Unlike the aforementioned documentary on the blonde-haired, blue-eyed, white-collar scammer Holmes, rapper-turned-director Boots Riley's fictional narrative centered on the supposed scourge of the hood. In it, Keke Palmer plays an illegit booster, selling high-end fenced clothing out of the abandoned fast-food chicken joint she's squatting in while harboring her own fashionable aspirations. It takes an international worker-led intervention — and a sci-fi bopgun full of Marxist intentions — for her to realize the minor disruption she and her shoplifting girlfriends are causing is but a necessary cog in the ever-churning, exploitative wheel of global capitalism.

Sponsor Message

What Riley wants us all to understand, as an avowed communist who switched his weapon of choice from fronting Bay Area rap group The Coup to writing screenplays, is that we the people are hardly the problem. Even when sufferers turn into self-styled hustlers out of desperation instead of pooling their collective power. Like WEB DuBois before him, Riley calls his art propaganda. And he's equally adamant about calling art on the other end of the spectrum of propaganda, too. "When The Coup first came out they would call us a political rap group. And we'd be like, 'No,' " he said on a recent episode of Novara Media's podcast Downstream. "Don't call us that unless you're calling everybody that. Because what it then made it seem like was as if everything else was just what it is." Rather, art magnifying the status quo is not some benign representation of a fixed reality but an uncritical regurgitation of everything indoctrinated by the moneyed elite.

When the controversy surrounding "Spend Dat" reached a fever pitch earlier this summer, it came with the usual diatribe. The song was criticized for being culturally degrading. Even India.Arie caught a bunch of flak for stating the obvious when she said, "Everything you listen to see or eat is going to influence you." I don't blame anybody Black for getting in their feelings over the seemingly negative portrayals or stereotypical depiction centered in rap. But the buck doesn't stop there. It never has. "We are bound by all sorts of customs that have come down as second-hand soul clothes of white patrons," as DuBois so eloquently stated 100 years ago this month in his essay Criteria of Negro Art. "We are ashamed of sex and we lower our eyes when people will talk of it," he says, concluding with this thought: "Our worst side has been so shamelessly emphasized that we are denying we have or ever had a worst side."

Sponsor Message

YouTube

The same week "Spend Dat" went platinum, Yung Miami appeared on "The Breakfast Club" to promote the release of her solo debut, Watch Dis. When asked about the criticism the song received, she defended it as inspirational music "that builds you up to want to be somebody." Rap may have started at the bottom. But at some point the script flipped. The systems hip-hop was oriented to rebel against became the metric for its success. The victors, in this case, were found striving for the same spoils. Having finally achieved the market share and visibility we'd been denied for decades, we became centrists: a marginalized culture subsumed by the mainstream. Commercial rap made itself a useful tool of the establishment, and the perfect racially coded scapegoat.

If the American Dream really is a pyramid scheme, as commonly critiqued, all hail the original scammers who bricked up the foundation. Even with their fuzzy slave-owner math (discounting Blacks as three-fifths human) and gender restrictions on equal rights (ratified while rocking powdered wigs), the nation's so-called founders created a system even the lowest caste could be constrained and cajoled into aspiring to.

It reminds me of the funniest meme I encountered online last week: a comic strip calling cap on the promise of Black capitalism. It pictures two brothers chopping it up, with one plainly stating, "You can't buy your way out of a system that was built on selling you." Totally undeterred, the other replies back, "Well, I'm gonna try!" before invoking the Black power era's "by any means necessary" rhetoric. In the next panel, Malcolm X expresses frustration over his words being misused to validate participation in the futile American experiment.

We've been hoodwinked, indeed. Bamboozled. Led astray. Run amok and flat-out deceived like a mug.

The grift is so complete that it's almost impossible to distinguish the mark from the actual con artist. Whether it's a convicted felon hiding fraudulence behind white tears, or a ride-or-die who bossed up with the boosters and got it off the muscle. In a year when prediction markets and predatory installment loans sucked us all dry, inflation skyrocketed and tech billionaires quickened the apocalypse, an ode to America's undying hustle and flow might be the closing credits theme we all deserve.

World.title: Mark Carney's quiet revolution rests on investment and affordability
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

"Maitre chez nous" — "master in our own house" — was a rallying cry of Jean Lesage's Quiet Revolution , a period of rapid modernization and reform in Quebec in the 1960s. Mark Carney first tried it out a year and a half ago in the shadow of Donald Trump's America and a newly anglicized version — "masters of our destiny" — adorns the Carney government's second budget.

"The moment in front of us is serious," Finance Minister François Philippe-Champagne said in presenting the budget on Thursday. "The moment demands an ambitious plan to be masters of our destiny; to be maîtres chez nous."

Carney has never claimed to be a revolutionary. Champagne's suggestion earlier this week that this week's budget was about "changing Canada's growth model" is perhaps as close as the Carney government will come to declaring a rousing overthrow of the old order.

But perhaps the Carney government's second budget can be said to be another step in the prime minister's own version of a quiet revolution.

The primary front in the revolution remains that "growth model."

The single largest line item in this budget is the "productivity mega-deduction," a previously announced measure that cuts the effective tax rate on new business investment. Over the next five years it is expected to cost the federal treasury approximately $36 billion, a quarter of all new spending in the budget. Paired with a new capital-gains exemption for entrepreneurs, the government hopes the "mega-deduction" will kickstart an "investment supercycle."

Nearly $9 billion is set aside for boosting the deployment of clean electricity — the backbone of Carney's climate agenda — and there is a commitment to work with provinces to provide further financing going forward. Over $2 billion is set aside for transforming the forestry sector, and $1.7 billion for the development of critical minerals. There is money as well for the nuclear industry and building new charging infrastructure for electric vehicles.

The government will fully fund and construct the Mackenzie Valley Highway project in the Northwest Territories and support two hydro projects in the Yukon. It is moving forward with plans to privatize some of the operations of Canada's biggest airports and it will begin inviting Canadians to invest in a new sovereign wealth fund.

This is the continuation of an agenda that champions the ideas of investment and building things — a tonal and now fiscal shift away from the Trudeau era.

However much this might amount to a revolution, it is also a long-term plan that may only start to be felt in the medium term. In the meantime, the short term cries out for attention.

Wrestling with affordability

To the affordability concerns that may define this moment as much as the geopolitical upheaval, the Carney government's latest response includes enhancing both the groceries and essentials benefit (previously known as the GST benefit) and the workers benefit (an income-based tax credit), two policy changes that will particularly benefit low-income households.

Those two policies will cost $6.7 billion. A previously announced suspension of the federal gas tax is projected to cost another $2.9 billion.

The Carney government is setting a goal of eliminating homelessness over the next decade and is putting $11.2 billion over the next five years toward that goal. New funds are also being put toward affordable housing and using federal land to build more homes — a lack of new housing construction remains one of the government's most acute vulnerabilities.

WATCH | Cheers and jeers in the House as budget delivered: Cheers — and jeers — in the House as Champagne talks trust after budget release | Duration closed caption 2:00 Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne drew applause and heckling from opposition members as he spoke on Thursday, promising a federal budget that will unlock Canada's 'full growth' potential.

Though it might make fewer headlines, the budget also includes $26 billion over five years for housing, infrastructure and social supports in Indigenous communities.

Looming over all such new expenditures are the ever-lingering questions about the sustainability of the federal government's balance sheet.

Fretting about the fiscal framework

Due to higher oil prices, the federal government managed to record a lower-than-projected deficit for the last fiscal year and it has also managed to avoid projecting higher deficits for the next four years than it had in the spring. The debt-to-GDP ratio — the size of the federal debt when measured against the size of the Canadian economy — is now projected to settle in around 40 per cent, three points lower than what the Carney government predicted a year ago.

In that sense, it might vaguely claim to have held its widely drawn line on the deficit.

But the federal government still shows a deficit of $53.4 billion in 2029. And the cost of servicing the federal debt is now showing the sorts of big numbers — $78.4 billion in 2029 — that tend to attract attention.

"This budget would be better titled, 'masters of increasing debt and interest payments,'" Michael Chong, the Conservative finance critic, charged after Champagne had concluded delivering the budget. "The budget fails to establish a credible fiscal anchor to reduce the debt and balance the budget."

WATCH | Poilievre blasts Liberal budget: Poilievre blasts Liberal budget, says it will inflate cost of 'food, fuel and housing' | Duration closed caption 2:17 Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says the Liberals should have named the budget, 'mastered by debt,' saying their plan will inflate the prices of essentials and make life more unaffordable for Canadians.

The Carney government argues it has reduced the cost of government operations such that the borrowing it is doing will be put toward "capital" spending — building the sorts of things that should grow the economy. (The parliamentary budget officer has quibbled with the government's methodology.)

The cost of servicing the debt also doesn't look like a crisis when measured against the economy. As a share of GDP, the public debt charge will be 2.2 per cent in 2030. It was higher as recently as 2006. And it remains much lower than it was when Canada experienced a real fiscal crisis in the mid-1990s (when it peaked at 6.5 per cent).

In the long term, the federal government might face real fiscal questions, particularly as defence spending is projected to increase. For the moment, the Carney government is presumably hoping that economic growth will drive increased revenues.

But it also remains the case that no party in the House of Commons is really particularly interested in balancing the budget.

Can Carney's revolution show results?

The greater challenge for Carney to master is results — demonstrating that the style, direction and extent of his government's spending has been wise and productive.

"All of this borrowing isn't showing up in the numbers," Chong said. "Business capital formation has declined in five of the last six quarters. Unemployment remains a full [percentage point] above pre-pandemic highs and GDP is flatlining."

The Liberals might plead that the Canadian economy is currently beleaguered by American tariffs. And opinion polling conducted over the last year and a half would suggest that Canadians don't blame the prime minister for recent economic troubles.

It also might be fairly argued that building big things — ports, transmission lines, businesses, a new national economic growth model — takes time.

The challenge for the Carney government over the next three years — or between now and the next federal election — is to execute on its plans, demonstrate progress and find proof points that make the case that Canada is, in fact, mastering its destiny.

Revolutions may thrive on energy, spirit and purpose. But they can only be sustained by results.

World.title: Trump declares his redesigned Oval Office a national monument
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump signed a proclamation Thursday declaring the Oval Office and Cabinet room of the White House to be preserved as national monuments.

Trump said his proclamation will prevent future presidents from making major changes to the two White House rooms — which he has extensively redecorated since the start of his second term — without the approval of Congress.

"It will make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space," he told reporters in the Oval Office. "It will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people."

Even though the White House is designated a National Historic Landmark, Trump has demolished its East Wing to build a new ballroom, paved over the Rose Garden and built a concrete helipad on the South Lawn, all since his return to the presidency last year and without Congressional approval.

In a week when Trump's Republican Party suffered a dramatic smackdown in the midterm elections, this was the third day in which the president has made one of his Washington, D.C. renovation projects the central subject of his media event.

On Wednesday, he took the White House press pool to the ballroom site and put his signature on a concrete beam.

Trump has overseen a gold-tinged redecoration of the Oval Office interior. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

On Monday, the final day of the midterm campaign, he gave a speech to mark the conclusion of the problem-plagued renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

Trump's declaration of the Oval Office and Cabinet room as national monuments was his first official presidential action since the midterm loss.

'Of great interest to me'

He called the move "something that is of great interest to me, but it's of great interest to a lot of people."

As Trump signed the proclamation, a red baseball cap with "VETO" in white letters sat on his desk. The U.S. president has the power to veto legislation that falls short of a two-thirds majority in either the House or the Senate.

Trump's focus on renovations is raising questions about his political priorities, particularly in light of the drubbing the Republicans took in the midterms.
