Prior to announcing the cancellation of its connections from Newark and Houston, the airline had already withdrawn its services from Chicago and Los Angeles, thereby diminishing its presence at the Quintana Roo terminal.

Industry reports interpret the company’s “market conditions” rationale for eliminating the flights as Tulum’s lower-than-expected vacation demand.

Industry analysts cited by Aviación News blame the tourism decline on high hotel prices in the area and weaker-than-expected demand for leisure travel. Other contributing factors include the massive influx of sargassum and increased fees and other charges on foreign tourists.

The combination of factors has reportedly led airlines to reassess the profitability of their operations and shift capacity to other destinations with higher passenger volumes.

In this context, Cancún International Airport – located 130 kilometers north of Tulum – emerges as the primary beneficiary of the reorientation of supply.

In the meantime, Air Canada, WestJet, and Air Transat have announced that they will resume flights for the winter season. Viva Aerobus continues its operations at the terminal with no announced changes, and state-owned Mexicana de Aviación remains the only carrier offering an increased number of flights.

With reports from Reportur

World.title: Finance Ministry blocks accounts of former electoral institute chief and associates
World.content:
Guadalupe Taddei, former president of the National Electoral Institute (INE), and José Alfredo Hernández Casillas, a businessman whose companies received lucrative INE contracts, are reportedly among 25 people who have been added to the Finance Ministry’s Blocked Persons List.

The Finance Ministry’s Financial Intelligence Unit (UIF) announced on Wednesday that 25 individuals and 15 companies “linked to electoral suppliers” had been added to the Blocked Persons List, meaning that financial institutions must freeze their bank accounts. It didn’t name the individuals or companies.

The UIF said in a statement that their inclusion on the list came after the detection of “financial transactions that involve elements of risk and warrant review by the appropriate authorities.”

“Inclusion on the Blocked Persons List is a preventive and precautionary administrative measure and does not imply a definitive determination of liability,” the UIF said. “Individuals included on the list are entitled to defense mechanisms and the right to a hearing provided for in applicable legislation.”

The UIF’s announcement of the additions to the Blocked Persons List came nine days after Taddei resigned as INE president amid allegations of corruption. Thirty other INE officials, including 17 who worked in Taddei’s office, have also recently resigned.

During Taddei’s 2023-2026 tenure at the helm of the electoral authority, companies linked to José Alfredo Hernández Casillas and his brother Raymundo Francisco Hernández Casillas received contracts to supply electoral materials to the INE. The ex-INE president reportedly had a close personal relationship with José Alfredo, with some media outlets speculating that they were romantic partners.

The Reforma newspaper reported that José Alfredo Hernández Casillas’ companies had obtained electoral authority contracts dating back to the time that Taddei presided over the electoral organization of Sonora between 2014 and 2021. Taddei’s “closeness” to Hernández allowed the latter to obtain contracts awarded by high-ranking INE officials, Reforma reported.

In an Oct. 25 statement announcing her resignation, Taddei said she was “aware of the allegations that have circulated in the media and on social media, … including rumors, fabrications, leaks and accounts whose authenticity, context and purpose — as in all cases — must be verified and corroborated.”

“… Each allegation must be examined with evidence and through institutional channels,” she said.

Taddei, Hernández Casillas brothers reported to be on the Blocked Persons List

The newspapers La Jornada and El Universal and various other media outlets reported that Taddei and José Alfredo Hernández Casillas are among the 25 people added to the Finance Ministry’s Blocked Persons List. La Jornada cited “a source with access to the list.”

El Universal reported that Raymundo Francisco Hernández Casillas was also added to the list.

The UIF said that in light of the “elements of risk” it detected in financial transactions, it filed a complaint with the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) so that the FGR can conduct “the appropriate investigations and determine, in accordance with the law, any potential [criminal] liability.”

📢 #ComunicadoDePrensa La UIF realiza acciones preventivas sobre personas vinculadas con proveedores electorales. La Secretaría de Hacienda y Crédito Público, a través de la Unidad de Inteligencia Financiera (UIF), incorporó a la Lista de Personas Bloqueadas a 40 personas (25 físicas y 15 morales) vinculadas con proveedores electorales. https://t.co/DcPdyl2TU6 🌐 — Hacienda (@Hacienda_Mexico) November 5, 2026

The Federal Auditor’s Office has already launched its own investigation into allegations regarding the “improper use of public resources” by the INE.

At her morning press conference last Thursday, President Claudia Sheinbaum said that Taddei “betrayed the trust of the people of Mexico” by allegedly acting corruptly during her leadership of the INE.

She also asserted that “two or three” companies that received contracts to supply materials such as ballot papers and ballot boxes to the INE — i.e. companies linked to the Hernández Casillas brothers — didn’t actually produce the materials themselves but rather acted as “intermediaries.”

At the same press conference, Pablo Gómez, head of the Presidential Commission for Electoral Reform and a former UIF chief, made similar remarks.

“The companies mentioned don’t have industrial plants. … They don’t make anything. … They’re intermediaries that win contracts and buy everything or go to printers and print everything,” he said.

In light of the alleged corruption in the awarding of INE contracts to companies linked to the Hernández Casillas brothers, Sheinbaum said last Thursday that “most electoral materials” should be made by Talleres Gráficos de México, a government-run printing agency.

To that end, Sheinbaum said today that her government would present a decree next week to strengthen the agency and its governance.

The president has sought to distance her government and the ruling Morena party from Taddei, who has family links to both. Sheinbaum has said that Taddei’s resignation and the scandal engulfing the INE won’t compromise Mexico’s 2027 elections, which are scheduled to take place on June 6.

With reports from La Jornada and El Universal

World.title: Mexico’s trade surplus with the US jumped 26% in the first nine months of 2026, reaching a record US $184 billion
World.content:
The U.S. trade deficit with Mexico grew at an annual rate of 26.1% during the first three-quarters of the year, reaching a record US $184.019 billion, according to U.S. Census Bureau data cited by El Economista.

The balance resulted from a 20.7% increase in U.S. imports of Mexican products compared to the first nine months of 2025, coming in at nearly US $481.6 billion, well above the nearly US $297.6 billion in U.S. exports to Mexico, a 17.6% year-on-year increase.

Mexico’s exports to the U.S. in September (US $62.2 billion) were also a record and mark the third consecutive month that the value of goods shipped from Mexico to the U.S. surpassed US $60 billion.

Mexico accounted for the largest U.S. goods trade deficit in September (US $28.15 billion, a 40% annual increase) and set a new monthly record, although the nine-month trade deficit with Mexico was the second largest for the United States behind only Vietnam (US $190.9 billion).

While the current U.S. administration has declared that one of its priorities is to reduce its trade deficit with the world (especially China), its trade deficit with Mexico has soared due to elevated purchases of computer equipment.

Meanwhile, the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) reported this week that Mexican foreign trade increased 24.6% in the first half of the year, while also citing the expansion of manufacturing acquisitions by the United States, primarily information processing equipment, servers and electronic components for the construction of data centers and Artificial Intelligence (AI) infrastructure.

U.S. demand for AI-related goods was so significant that it explains Mexico’s entire boom in 2025 and between 75-80% of that recorded thus far in 2026, the IDB said.

Mexico’s performance is part of a regional trend as exports of goods from Latin America and the Caribbean grew above the world average in the first half of 2026, with Mexico leading the way.

According to the IDB, exports from the region rose 19.5% year-on-year from January through June, above the 14.5% increase in global trade, primarily due to increased sales of AI infrastructure equipment in the United States.

The IDB noted that Mexico accounts for 93% of regional exports of data processing equipment, servers and electronic components for the construction of data centers and was responsible for 96% of its rebound last year.

With reports from El Economista and La Jornada

World.title: Mexico in Numbers: How many people are emigrating from Mexico?
World.content:
In a previous “Mexico in Numbers” article, we reported on Intercensal Survey data that showed that almost 1.2 million foreign-born residents lived in Mexico in 2025.

Our focus today is on people who emigrated from Mexico to another country. Once again, the data comes from the 2025 Intercensal Survey results report, which was published by the national statistics agency INEGI in September. It looks at emigration from October 2020 to October 2025.

The emigrants counted by INEGI include Mexicans and people from other countries who were living in Mexico, but emigrated between October 2020 and October 2025. Migrants from many countries have spent time living in Mexico before moving on to another country, often the United States — though INEGI doesn’t specify destination countries of emigrants in the Intercensal Survey results report.

How many people emigrated from Mexico between 2020 and 2025?

INEGI reported that 1,259,978 (almost 1.26 million) people emigrated from Mexico between October 2020 and October 2025.

That number represents an increase of 56.95% compared to the preceding five-year period, during which 802,807 people emigrated from Mexico.

Former U.S. President Joe Biden was in office for most of the October 2020 to October 2025 period. Current U.S. President Donald Trump was in office for most of the preceding five-year period. Biden’s border policies were generally more permissive than those of Trump, although he imposed stricter limits on asylum late in his four-year presidency, causing illegal crossings into the U.S. to fall.

How many emigrants returned to Mexico after leaving the country?

INEGI reported that 150,752 emigrants returned to Mexico after leaving the country between October 2020 and October 2025.

That figure represents just under 12% of all people who emigrated in the five-year period.

INEGI reported that 1,022,728 (1.02 million) people had not returned to Mexico after leaving the country between October 2020 and October 2025.

That figure represents 81.2% of all people who emigrated in the period.

INEGI noted in the Intercensal Survey results report that the number of emigrants who remained abroad and the number who returned to Mexico don’t add up to the total number of emigrants in the period between October 2020 and October 2025 because there is a third “not specified” category. A total of 86,498 emigrants fall into that category.

Which states were the largest sources of emigrants?

More than half of all emigrants were living in just 10 Mexican states before leaving the country between October 2020 and October 2025. Those states are:

Guanajuato: The source of 7.5% of all emigrants between October 2020 and October 2025

Michoacán: 6.8%

Veracruz: 6.4%

Puebla: 6.2%

México state: 6.1%

Oaxaca: 5.7%

Jalisco: 5.2%

Chiapas: 4.7%

Guerrero: 4.2%

Hidalgo: 3.7%

The 10 aforementioned states provided 56.5% of all emigrants from Mexico between October 2020 and October 2025.

The five states that provided the lowest number of emigrants in the five-year period are Baja California Sur (0.3% of the total); Campeche (0.5%); Quintana Roo (0.6%); Colima (0.6%); and Tabasco (0.7%).

Men accounted for over 70% of emigrants between 2020 and 2025

INEGI reported that men accounted for 70.4% of emigrants from Mexico between October 2020 and October 2025, while women accounted for 29.6%.

Over one in five emigrants — 22.5% — were aged between 20 and 24 when they left Mexico.

After the group aged 20-24, the next largest cohorts of emigrants were those aged:

25-29: 19.5% of all emigrants

15-19: 15%

30-34: 14.1%

Thus, 71.1% of all emigrants from Mexico between October 2020 and October 2025 were aged between 15 and 34 when they left the country.

World.title: MND Local CDMX: A nighttime race, queer musical and medieval masquerade
World.content:
With Día de Muertos firmly in the rearview mirror, we have a couple of weeks before the Christmas season really kicks into high gear. But that doesn’t mean Mexico City is short on ways to keep busy in the meantime.

From a nighttime 10K run through UNAM and a musical celebration of queer identity to a medieval-inspired winter masquerade, the capital has a few quirky surprises up its sleeve this December.

Let’s get into it.

Mexico City’s Rave Run brings a nighttime 10K to UNAM

Runners looking for a different kind of nighttime outing can lace up for the Rave Run by Carrera Nocturna 2026, a 10-kilometer race taking place at the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM).

Organized by Emoción Deportiva, the event is scheduled for Saturday, Dec. 19, with the starting gun firing at 7 p.m. at Estadio Universitario in Ciudad Universitaria. The race will follow a circuit through the university campus, offering a unique opportunity to experience one of Mexico City’s most recognizable educational institutions after dark.

The competition, billed as a general 10K, is open to anyone 15 and older. Participants must complete the course within a maximum of 80 minutes, and the top three finishers in both the women’s and men’s divisions will receive awards — but don’t expect big cash prizes.

Registration is limited and costs 749 pesos, while late registration costs 849 pesos.

The entry fee includes a commemorative T-shirt, finisher’s medal, runner number, promotional item, race timing, finish-line photography, water and isotonic drinks along the course, medical assistance (hopefully that won’t be needed) and access to official results.

Date: Saturday, Dec. 19

Location: Estadio Olímpico Universitario

Cost: 749-849 pesos

For more information and to register your spot in the race, visit Emoción Deportiva.

Mexico City’s Gay Choir presents a musical journey of identity and self-actualization

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Teatros Ciudad de México (@teatroscdmx)



Mexico City’s premier queer choir, Coro Gay Ciudad de México, is gearing up for its rendition of “La Misteriosa Flama de la Reina Leona,” a coming-of-age musical journey that chronicles two characters as they navigate childhood, identity and self-acceptance.

The performance is slated to take place Tuesday, Dec. 15 at Teatro de la Ciudad Esperanza Iris in the capital’s Historic Center.

Described by the theater troupe as a “journey through shadows, memories and discoveries,” “La Misteriosa Flama de la Reina Leona” explores the search for a mysterious flame that, despite seeming lost, exists within us throughout our lives.

The production unfolds through two childhood stories: The first follows a girl trying to find her way in a world of giants, while the second centers on a boy who, while leading a parade, discovers the courage to realize the best version of himself. Together, the stories explore imagination, identity, fear and the possibility of growing up without abandoning one’s true self.

More than 100 singers and musicians bring the performance to life, allowing the power of music and storytelling to wade through the sometimes messy worlds of memory, reflection and resistance.

The performance is open to all ages, although children ages 3 and older require tickets. It’s also worth noting that Teatro de la Ciudad Esperanza Iris does not have an elevator.

Date: Tuesday, Dec. 15

Location: Donceles 36, Centro Histórico, Cuauhtémoc, 06010 Ciudad de México

Cost: 253-878 pesos

For more information or to purchase tickets, visit Ticketmaster. You can also check out the Coro Gay Choir on Instagram.

Tierra Mágica Navidad brings medieval fantasy to Mexico City

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Festival de Brujas MX (@festival_de_brujas_mx)

Our next event roundup will focus more heavily on Christmas-themed events, but for now, we’ll start with something truly unique and quirky. If your idea of Christmas involves a little more magic, a touch of medieval fantasy and perhaps a masquerade ball, Tierra Mágica Navidad might just be the event for you.

The family-friendly Christmas festival will take over Doméstico in Colonia Hipódromo on Dec. 12 and 13, transforming the venue into a fantasy-inspired celebration that blends traditional holiday festivities with the atmosphere of an enchanted medieval kingdom.

It’s like “Game of Thrones,” but Bran Stark is a young Santa and Westeros is Mexico City.

Visitors are invited to don their finest medieval or fantasy-inspired garb for a weekend of music, magical characters and festive entertainment. Don’t forget your mask, though, as one of the event’s flagship activities is a themed masquerade ball and mask competition, allowing attendees to show off their most imaginative creations.

The festivities will also include a Christmas-themed bazaar full of seasonal offerings. With its combination of holiday traditions, fantasy-inspired characters and immersive activities, Tierra Mágica Navidad sounds to us like an unusual alternative to the capital’s more traditional Christmas celebrations, and a great way to start the season.

Date: Dec. 12 and 13, 11 a.m. to 8:30 p.m.

Location: Av. Nuevo León 80, Hipódromo, Cuauhtémoc, Ciudad de México

Cost: Free

For more information and to register your free spot, visit Tierra Mágica Navidad on Boletia.

Drew Pittock serves as Mexico News Daily’s features director. He is based in Mexico City. Have an idea for a feature story or unique event in CDMX? Send an email to drew.pittock@mexiconewsdaily.com.

World.title: Navy seizes more than a tonne of cocaine off the coasts of Chiapas and Oaxaca
World.content:
The Navy seized more than a tonne of suspected cocaine in two separate operations off Mexico’s southwestern coast.

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch on Thursday confirmed on social media that the actions occurred off the coasts of Chiapas and Oaxaca, adding that one person was arrested.

According to an official statement, the operations took place during maritime patrol and surveillance in the Pacific Ocean.

In the first operation, naval personnel seized 16 packages containing approximately 629 kilograms of “a substance with characteristics similar to cocaine,” while in a second operation they located another 16 packages with around 520 kilograms.

The Navy reported that the weight of 1,149 kilograms includes the packaging and the actual weight of the narcotics will be confirmed by prosecutors.

The statement said that the economic impact for criminal groups is an estimated 273 million pesos (US $14.5 million). “Each seized shipment is a direct blow to the finances of organized crime: reducing their resources to buy weapons, corrupt and generate violence, and fewer drugs on the streets to poison our youth,” García Harfuch said.

Despite the volume of drugs confiscated, authorities reported the arrest of only one person. “The detainee was informed of his rights and placed at the disposal of the Federal Attorney General’s Office,” the statement said.

The latest operation is part of a series of actions carried out in recent months in the Pacific maritime corridor, specifically off the coasts of Chiapas, Oaxaca, Guerrero and Michoacán. Before it, more than 97 tonnes of cocaine had been seized at sea since Claudia Sheinbaum became president in October 2024.

In October, more than 1.2 tonnes of cocaine were seized and six crew members detained in international waters 366 nautical miles south of Huatulco, Oaxaca, in a joint operation with the U.S. Coast Guard.

In August, more than 4 tonnes of cocaine were seized and 13 people arrested during several Pacific operations off Oaxaca and Chiapas.

The ongoing operations are part of permanent maritime and aerial surveillance actions against international drug trafficking, one of the main issues of cooperation and tension in security matters with the United States.

With reports from Proceso, El Financiero and Aristegui Noticias

World.title: Latin America Mood Today: Paraguay’s President Quits
World.content:
The open plaza of the Memorial da América Latina in São Paulo, with its Oscar Niemeyer hand sculpture in the background. The photo shows the area, not the concert. Photo: Picturesartbr / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

Rio Times · Latin America

Key Facts Brazil Security fear after a vote: a Rio gang hijacked three buses after its boss was arrested

Mexico Violence close to the capital: cartel boss El General killed in a shootout in Naucalpan

Argentina Price fatigue: October tax revenue rose 33.7%, roughly level with inflation

Colombia Pre-strike tension: national strike set for 19 November and a rebel-held officer, María Pantoja

Chile Unsettled accounts: Codelco overstated copper output by 42,000 tonnes while a Pinochet-era agent walks free

Paraguay Institutional shock: President Peña announced his resignation over a failed bank

Latin America ended 5 November worn down by violence and shaken by institutions that wobbled, from a bank collapse in Paraguay to a counting scandal at Chile’s copper giant.

The Continent’s Mood Today

Fear of crime and doubt about institutions ran through the day. A president in Paraguay said he would quit, a drug boss died near Mexico City, and Chile learned that its flagship copper miner had counted wrongly.

Underneath sat a quieter worry about prices and fairness in Argentina and Colombia. Street fear and trust fear arrived on the same morning.

Brazil – A Winner Facing Fear in the Streets

Lula won the 25 October runoff with 51.79% of valid votes against Flávio Bolsonaro’s 48.21%. Crime is the worry closest to his voters’ homes.

On Thursday criminals in Rio de Janeiro hijacked three buses and used them as barricades after police arrested a local boss known as Pudim. Five bus lines were disrupted, and police seized three rifles.

We never share your email.

Mexico – A Boss Falls Near the Capital

Federal forces killed Édgar Aarón Vázquez Alvarado, known as El General and accused of founding the Cartel Nuevo Imperio, in a shootout in Naucalpan de Juárez on Thursday. The US Treasury had sanctioned him a year earlier.

Households have another date in mind: the Buen Fin sale, a national shopping weekend that the government expects to bring in US$12.6 billion.

Argentina – Tired of Prices

ARCA, the national tax agency, said October tax revenue rose 33.7% in a year to 21.6 trillion pesos (about US$14.0 billion). That is roughly level with prices, so the state is collecting more mainly because everything costs more.

For households, the number is a reminder of why price fatigue runs so deep. Argentines have lived through many cycles in which wages chase prices.

Colombia – Bracing for 19 November

A national strike is set for 19 November against the government’s Economic Rescue Law, a tax and spending bill. Rebels have also seized an officer, María Pantoja.

President Gustavo Petro denied claims about a sex contract, which adds personal scandal to political strain. The week feels tense before a single march has started.

Chile – Old Wounds and Copper Arithmetic

Codelco, the state copper giant, told shareholders it overstated its output by more than 42,000 tonnes across 2024 and 2025. Chair Bernardo Fontaine called the events serious.

For a country that lives on copper, a counting error at its flagship firm feels like a breach of trust. Chile also freed a Pinochet-era agent after a sentence cut, which reopens a wound that never fully closed.

Paraguay – A President Steps Down

President Santiago Peña announced his resignation in a video on Thursday, after the failure of Ueno Bank, a lender with about three million customers, turned into an impeachment fight. Congress has received his letter but had not formally accepted it at last report.

The lower house shelved an impeachment request against Vice President Pedro Alliana, who is expected to take over. The mood is bewilderment mixed with relief that a transfer looks orderly.

For a foreigner in Paraguay, daily life is unchanged, but contracts that depend on political stability deserve a second look.

Cuba – A Journalist Taken Off the Street

Cuban State Security detained the independent journalist Yoani Sánchez in Havana on Thursday. She is at least the third independent journalist detained in four days, and her newsroom says it does not know where she is.

The Shared Mood

Across the continent, 5 November felt like a day of institutions under strain: a bank that failed in Paraguay, a miner that miscounted in Chile, gangs testing the state in Rio and near Mexico City. People want governments that count honestly, keep promises and protect them from crime.

For daily market reports, see our country market reports linked below.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the mood in Latin America today?

Anxious about violence and weak institutions. A president in Paraguay announced his resignation, a Mexican cartel boss was killed and Rio faced bus hijackings.

What happened to Paraguay’s president?

Santiago Peña announced his resignation on 5 November over the failure of Ueno Bank. Congress had not formally accepted the letter at last report.

What did Codelco get wrong?

Codelco, Chile’s state copper miner, told shareholders it overstated output by more than 42,000 tonnes across 2024 and 2025.

01 A violent break in the world’s biggest market

The S&P 500 closed at 7,354, down 4.36% on the day. The Dow fell 3.44% to 51,523, and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.52% to 24,315.

The VIX rose 69.66% to 28.18. A jump of that size means investors rushed to buy insurance against further losses.

The Nasdaq fell furthest, which points to pressure on the most richly valued shares. The Dow’s smaller drop suggests older, steadier companies offered some shelter.

Gold rose 0.51% to US$4,086 an ounce, so the traditional refuge worked, but only modestly. The dollar index barely moved at 101.722, up 0.15%.

Thursday also brought central bank and data events whose results were not yet in our data at press time. The Bank of England BoE Interest Rate Decision (consensus 4%, previous 3.75%) came at 12:00 GMT, and the Euro Area S&P Global Construction PMI (consensus 44, previous 43.4) and UK S&P Global Construction PMI (consensus 46.1, previous 46.1) were published.

02 Falling yields, rising fear, and a Fed in the spotlight

The US 10-year Treasury yield fell 1.02% to 4.839% as shares tumbled. Investors usually buy government bonds when they want safety, though a yield near 4.8% is still a heavy burden for borrowers.

The main scheduled test is the October payrolls report at 13:30 GMT. Economists expect 65,000 new jobs, against 29,000 in the prior report.

Michigan consumer sentiment follows at 15:00 GMT, with a consensus of 48, unchanged from the prior reading. Traders will also watch its inflation expectations: 4.7% for one year and 3.6% for five years.

Fed officials Alberto Musalem and Michelle Bowman speak later today. Markets will listen for any sign the central bank sees this sell-off as a threat to growth.

03 What the shock means for Brazil and Latin America

Risk aversion in New York usually reaches Brazilian shares and the real within hours. Emerging markets rarely escape when the VIX spikes this sharply.

The steady dollar index limits one source of pressure on the real. Gold’s rise and lower Treasury yields also suggest this is fear, not a broad rush into the dollar.

Brazil’s central bank held the Selic, its benchmark interest rate, at 13.75% on 4 November. The next Copom meeting is on 8-9 December, the last of 2026.

A weaker Fed outlook would help Brazil, because it widens room for Copom to cut. A prolonged sell-off would instead raise the cost of foreign funding for Brazilian companies.

Oil is the other link. The US Energy Information Administration reported commercial crude stocks of 409.8 million barrels in the week to 30 October, down 0.9 million (https://www.eia.gov/petroleum/supply/weekly/).

Distillate stocks fell 3.6 million to 99.3 million barrels, a tighter signal for diesel.

Japan added a cautious note: its services PMI came in at 51.7 against a consensus of 52. That is still growth, but slightly softer than economists hoped.

We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

The S&P 500 fell 4.36% to 7,354, the Dow dropped 3.44% to 51,523 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 5.52% to 24,315.

What does the VIX at 28.18 mean?

The VIX measures expected stock-market swings. It jumped 69.66% to 28.18, which shows investors paid more for protection against further losses.

Why did the 10-year Treasury yield fall?

The yield eased to 4.839% as investors bought government bonds for safety. It remains high by recent standards.

How could this affect Brazil?

Global risk aversion tends to weigh on the real and Brazilian shares. A softer Fed outlook could eventually give Copom more room to cut the Selic, now at 13.75%.

Gold rose 0.51% to US$4,086 an ounce, a modest haven bid. The dollar index was almost unchanged at 101.722.

Times are converted from the feed to Brasília time. The jobs report is the main event, because a strong number would lift the dollar and a weak one would hand the real some relief.

Brazil’s own trade balance is the domestic anchor. A larger surplus than expected means more dollars flowing into the country, which tends to steady the currency.

Also on the calendar today are the US Unemployment Rate (consensus 4.2%, previous 4.2%), Nonfarm Payrolls Private (consensus 64,000, previous 46,000), the U-6 Unemployment Rate, a wider measure that includes part-time workers who want full-time jobs (consensus 7.6%, previous 7.6%), and Manufacturing Payrolls (consensus 5,000, previous 9,000). Source: RT economic calendar (RT).

Yesterday’s calendar held Brazil’s S&P Global Services PMI (consensus 48.7, previous 49.2) and S&P Global Composite PMI (consensus 46.9, previous 47.4); readings below 50 signal shrinking activity, and the published results were not yet in our data at press time. In the US, Initial Jobless Claims (consensus 196,000, previous 194,000), Continuing Jobless Claims (consensus 1.71 million, previous 1.701 million), the Jobless Claims 4-Week Average (consensus 196,000, previous 196,750) and Nonfarm Productivity (consensus 2.8%, previous 1.4%) were also due, with their results likewise not yet confirmed in our data.

04 Copom and the macro backdrop

The question investors are asking is not whether Copom cuts again soon, but when. The central bank says it will assess new data before deciding when to resume cuts, and the last meeting of the year ends on 9 December.

There is no August meeting left in 2026, so the next decision is in December, or the first meeting of 2027. Prediction markets, shown below, lean towards no change in December.

Inflation is the obstacle. The Focus survey of economists sees consumer prices rising 5.22% in 2026 and 4.76% in 2027, both above the target range.

The minutes of the meeting arrive on Tuesday 10 November, the central bank’s usual schedule, six days after the decision. The official statement is on the central bank’s site, https://www.bcb.gov.br, and is worth reading before the minutes land.

I found no confirmed earnings releases or ex-dividend dates for B3 today, so I will not invent a calendar. Petrobras and Vale were the most traded names on Thursday, which is where the dollar and commodity moves tend to land first.

A cheaper real helps exporters such as miners and oil producers, and hurts companies with dollar debts or imported costs.

For the Ibovespa, Thursday’s close of 166,191 is 20.5% below the 9 October peak of 209,067. For the real, the round number of 5.50 is the first line, with the 12-month high of 5.59 behind it.

Across Latin America, the pressure is shared: the Chilean peso, Mexican peso and Peruvian and Argentine stocks all weakened on Thursday. Brazil is feeling a global risk-off plus its own fiscal story.

Did Brazil cut interest rates this week?

No. Copom held the Selic, the benchmark rate, at 13.75% on 4 November, ending a run of five cuts.

When is the next Copom decision?

The next and last meeting of 2026 runs 8–9 December, with the decision on 9 December. The minutes of the November meeting come out on 10 November.

Fiscal doubts, a global sell-off in US shares and an on-hold central bank have all weighed. The real closed at 5.5051 per dollar, its weakest in at least six months.

US payrolls at 10:30 Brasília time and Brazil’s trade balance at 15:00 are the main events. The 5.50 level on the real is the line to watch.

World.title: Paraguay Pays First Ueno Bank Savers
World.content:
File photo, 2009: the Banco Central del Paraguay building in Asunción. Photo: Cmasi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

PARAGUAY · BANKING

Published Thursday, 5 November, 10:30 p.m. ET · Source: Central Bank of Paraguay communiqué, Presidency of Paraguay decree 7199

Key Facts Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Latin America story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? What happened Paraguay's central bank announced repayments for savers of Ueno, a failed digital bank, starting at 10 million guaraníes (about US$1,700).

Who qualifies Savers who owe Ueno nothing and hold an account at another bank; those under 10 million guaraníes get everything back.

Also tonight Interior Minister Enrique Riera quit, a day before the Senate resumes President Peña's impeachment trial.

What next Everyone else waits: the central bank gave no dates for the next groups.

For two days, nearly three million Paraguayans could not touch their money. On Thursday night, the central bank announced that repayment had begun.

The Central Bank of Paraguay (BCP), the country's financial regulator, announced on Thursday 5 November that it had started paying deposit-guarantee money to savers of Ueno Bank. Ueno is a digital lender the regulator took over and moved to close on Tuesday, after finding it insolvent, meaning it could not cover its debts.

The first payments cover balances of up to 10 million guaraníes, about US$1,700 at the 5 November closing rate of 5,875 guaraníes per dollar (RT market data). The same night, Interior Minister Enrique Riera resigned, a day before the Senate resumes the impeachment trial of President Santiago Peña.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Paraguay ranks 10th of 14 with 35.0 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (55); weakest: future resources (13). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Who Gets Paid First

The central bank set three conditions for this first group. A saver must hold no more than 10 million guaraníes, owe Ueno no debt, and have an account at another Paraguayan bank or financial firm to receive the money.

Savers whose total deposits stay under that line get every guaraní back. Everyone else must wait, and the BCP gave no payment date.

It said it will announce later groups as the process advances and within the time limits set by law. It also told savers to rely only on its official channels.

Download the PDF checklist

How Big Is the Safety Net?

Paraguay's deposit guarantee fund, an insurance pool for bank savers, covers up to 75 monthly minimum wages. That is 228.3 million guaraníes (about US$38,900) per saver at each institution.

So the first round is small. Ten million guaraníes is less than 5% of the cap, which means large depositors are still waiting.

The rollout was rocky. Savers reported that the central bank's lookup links failed under heavy demand.

Why Did the Interior Minister Quit?

Riera, who ran the ministry in charge of police and domestic security, resigned on Thursday night. Decree 7199 accepted his resignation and named Carlos Humberto Benítez González, until now vice minister for internal security, as acting minister.

Earlier that day Riera had delivered Peña's own resignation letter to Congress, but Congress took no decision because the joint session lost its quorum, the minimum number of members needed to vote. As we reported, Peña remains president while the Senate weighs his removal.

Riera belongs to the Colorado Party, which rules Paraguay, and now recovers his seat in the Senate. The Senate resumes the trial at 10 a.m. in Asunción on Friday 6 November (8 a.m. ET), and Peña is due to present his defence.

The charge links back to the bank failure, which we covered when the central bank chief quit and when the impeachment push began.

What It Means for US Readers

The clear winners tonight are small savers, who are first in line and recover everything. The losers for now are larger depositors with no date and no amount promised.

For US investors, the next test is Friday's Senate session, and the next signal on the bank is the central bank's announcement of the second payment group.

What Is Not Known

We do not know how many savers qualify for the first group or how much money has reached accounts. The central bank has not said when the next groups will be paid, or whether the guarantee fund holds enough for all claims.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who gets Ueno Bank money back first?

Savers with total deposits up to 10 million guaraníes (about US$1,700) who owe Ueno nothing and have an account at another bank. They receive their full balance.

When will other Ueno Bank savers be paid?

The central bank has not said. It will announce later payment groups as the process advances, within the legal time limits.

World.title: Rubio Eyes Venezuela Election in 2027
World.content:
File photo: Secretary of State Marco Rubio, official State Department portrait (public domain).

Published Thursday, Nov. 5, 9:28 p.m. ET (10:28 p.m. Caracas) · Source: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, interview remarks

Washington has floated a year for Venezuela’s return to the ballot box, and it came with a hedge. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, that elections would "ideally" be held next year, but he would not promise a vote before President Donald Trump’s term ends.

Rubio spoke in a newspaper interview at the White House. Our venezuela us tensions guide explains how the two countries got here.

Key Facts What happened: Rubio said Venezuela’s elections would "ideally" be held in 2027, without guaranteeing a date.

What comes first: A renewed Supreme Court and electoral council, a debt restructuring and security-force reforms.

The numbers: Venezuela’s debt is estimated at more than US$200 billion.

What happens next: Talks on the electoral council resume next week; court reform is targeted for mid-December.

Prediction markets: Polymarket traders put 36.5% on an election being scheduled by March 31, 2027 (9:26 p.m. ET, Nov. 5).

This story is part of our coverage of the venezuela us tensions. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: Venezuela Economy Seen Growing 6% to 7%

In plain English Venezuela is run by an acting government under Delcy Rodríguez, Nicolás Maduro’s former vice president, since the United States captured Maduro. Washington wants the courts and the election authority rebuilt first, then a vote.

Four Fixes Before Any Vote

Rubio said Venezuela must renew its Supreme Court and its electoral council, the body that organises elections. It must also advance restructuring of its debt and reform its security forces.

He said support from the security forces is essential, because that is what governing requires. In Venezuela, that puts the armed forces at the centre of any handover.

Rubio expects Washington-sponsored talks between the acting government and one sector of the opposition to produce a reformed Supreme Court by mid-December. Negotiators plan to meet next week on naming new members of the electoral council.

Under the plan, once the reforms are complete, Rodríguez should declare the presidency permanently vacant. That would open a six-month window to call elections.

His comments came a week after the Trump administration backed the road map agreed between the Venezuelan government and that opposition sector. The plan covers exactly those two bodies, the court and the electoral council.

Why Debt Is Part of the Election Story

Rubio called Venezuela’s debt, estimated at more than US$200 billion, a major obstacle to economic recovery and new investment. He said restructuring is the task of the interim authorities now, but it could well extend to an elected government.

On security cooperation, he said Washington would like, at some point, an agreement covering US troops in Venezuela. The aim, he said, is mainly legal protection for the troops, and detailed talks have not yet taken place.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, a crypto-based prediction market, traders put 36.5% on a Venezuelan presidential election being scheduled by March 31, 2027, and 8.5% by Dec. 31, 2026 (9:26 p.m. ET, Nov. 5). The market has US$674,334 traded across all its dates. The same market gives 2.4% for a date by Nov. 30, so traders see any vote slipping into next year. A separate market on the next winner has opposition leader María Corina Machado at 67.5% and Rodríguez at 10.5%, The market has US$68,276 traded across all candidates.

These prices are bets, not polls. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely.

We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for US Readers

For holders of Venezuelan government bonds, Rubio’s message is that a restructuring comes with the transition and may outlast it. That points to a long road, not a quick rebound.

Companies weighing a return must plan around a timetable that depends on court and election-body reforms.

Two signals come next: the negotiators’ meeting next week and the mid-December court target. A newly named electoral council would confirm progress, while a slipped deadline would support the traders’ doubts. The Dec. 31, 2026 deadline, priced at 8.5%, is the next hard test.

What Is Not Known

No election date is set, and Rubio would not promise one before Trump leaves office. It is unclear whether the wider opposition accepts a plan negotiated with only one sector.

The reports we reviewed gave no reaction from Caracas or from opposition leaders outside the talks. We will update this report when Washington or Caracas adds detail.

More: Venezuela news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

When could Venezuela hold elections?

Rubio said "ideally" in 2027, but he gave no date and no guarantee. Reforms of the Supreme Court and the electoral council come first.

What must happen before a vote?

A renewed Supreme Court and electoral council, a debt restructuring and security-force reforms. Then Rodríguez would declare the presidency vacant, opening a six-month window to call elections.

Sources: US State Department, Consejo Nacional Electoral (Venezuela’s electoral council), Polymarket.
