World.title: Costa Rica Voted World’s Most Desirable Country by 250,000 Travelers
World.content:
Costa Rica has been voted the most desirable country in the world by readers of British travel magazine Wanderlust, taking gold in the worldwide category of the publication’s Reader Travel Awards. The result was announced at a ceremony in London yesterday and confirmed by the Costa Rican Tourism Institute (ICT).

The awards, now in their 25th edition, are decided by reader votes, and this year’s edition drew about 250,000 ballots. The win moves Costa Rica up from second place in the 2025 rankings, when it finished behind Japan, and returns it to the top spot it also claimed in 2022. In 2021, the country placed third.

ICT Executive President Marcos Vargas Borges received the award in London and described it as a strategic opportunity for the country’s tourism sector. He is leading a delegation of 45 Costa Rican tourism businesses at World Travel Market, one of the industry’s largest trade fairs, held in the British capital this week.

Other winners in this year’s awards included Spain, named the most desirable country in Europe, and Tokyo, chosen as the most desirable city. California took the top region award, Belize was named the leading emerging destination, and Tasmania and Corsica were recognized among the islands.

The recognition comes as Costa Rica’s visitor numbers continue to grow. ICT figures show 2,310,320 international visitors arrived from January through September 2026, an increase of 4.8% over the same period last year. The United States remains by far the largest source market, with 1,288,001 visitors, followed by Canada with 239,065. Together, the two countries account for 66% of all arrivals.

Europe is a key target for the London trip. The ICT reported earlier this year that air arrivals from Europe rose more than 8% from January to August, even as Lufthansa plans to drop its Costa Rica route in 2027 while its sister airline adds flights. The Wanderlust vote caps a week of international attention for the country. National Geographic named Costa Rica Central America’s ultimate nature escape in a new guide, and Forbes recently highlighted a Pacific coast resort as a way to beat the crowds during the shoulder season.

With the December-to-April high season weeks away, the ranking offers a snapshot of how travelers abroad see Costa Rica, and a reminder of how much its natural reputation continues to carry its tourism economy.

World.title: Peru’s Ignacio Buse Stuns Medvedev in Landmark Paris Masters Victory
World.content:
Peru’s Ignacio Buse delivered one of the biggest upsets of the Paris Masters on Wednesday, defeating world No. 5 Daniil Medvedev 6-4, 6-4 to reach the round of 16 at an ATP Masters 1000 tournament for the first time in his career. The 22-year-old Peruvian, ranked No. 33 in the world, needed just one hour and 40 minutes to eliminate the fourth-seeded Russian, a former world No. 1 and the 2020 Paris Masters champion.

The victory marked another milestone for Peruvian tennis. Buse became the first Peruvian man to defeat a top-10 opponent since Luis Horna beat Richard Gasquet at the Italian Open in 2008. He also became the first Peruvian player to reach the round of 16 at the Paris Masters.

Buse controlled the opening set with patient baseline exchanges, staying close to Medvedev before breaking serve in the final game to take it 6-4. The second set presented a more difficult challenge. Medvedev moved ahead 4-2 and appeared ready to force a deciding set, but Buse responded by winning four consecutive games to complete the upset.

Speaking after the match, Buse described the result as the biggest victory of his career. He said he had become increasingly comfortable playing on indoor hard courts and credited his patience during important points for helping him overcome one of the tour’s most experienced competitors.

The result continued a remarkable 2026 season for Buse, who began the year inside the ATP top 100 and climbed as high as No. 30 in August. He has already captured two ATP singles titles this year, winning in Hamburg and Winston-Salem. His Paris campaign began Monday with a 6-2, 6-4 victory over Belgium’s Zizou Bergs. The win over Medvedev then secured a place among the final 16 players at the last Masters 1000 tournament of the season.

Buse earned a third-round meeting with Portugal’s Nuno Borges, who advanced after defeating Russia’s Karen Khachanov. Borges entered the main draw as a lucky loser after initially falling in qualifying. Buse was not the only South American making headlines in Paris. Argentina’s Tomás Martín Etcheverry also produced a major upset Wednesday, defeating world No. 9 Alex de Minaur 7-6(2), 6-3.

It was Etcheverry’s first career victory over a top-10 opponent after losing his previous 20 meetings against players in that group. The Argentine had already defeated Andrey Rublev in his opening match, but his tournament ended Thursday when Australian qualifier Rinky Hijikata rallied for a 2-6, 6-3, 7-5 victory. Hijikata had eliminated seven-time Paris champion Novak Djokovic in the previous round.

The unexpected results have reshaped the final Masters 1000 draw ahead of the ATP Finals in Turin, scheduled for November 15-22. For Buse, the victory over Medvedev stands as another important step in a season that has established him among Latin America’s leading young tennis players. His performance in Paris also strengthens his position heading toward the 2027 Australian Open.

World.title: Costa Rica Unemployment Climbs to 6.5% With 20,000 More Out of Work
World.content:
Costa Rica’s unemployment rate rose to 6.5% in the July-to-September quarter, up from 5.7% a year earlier, according to the National Institute of Statistics and Census (INEC). The agency’s Continuous Employment Survey, released Thursday, counted 154,736 unemployed people, 20,276 more than the 134,460 recorded in the same period of 2025.

The increase was concentrated among men. Their unemployment rate climbed from 5.0% to 6.0%, adding roughly 15,000 jobless men for a total of about 88,000, according to INEC. Among women, the rate stood at 7.4%, compared with 6.9% a year earlier, a change the institute did not consider statistically significant. About 67,000 women were unemployed during the quarter.

Total employment held steady at about 2.21 million people, within a labor force of roughly 2.37 million. The employment rate slipped to 51.3% from 51.7%, while the net participation rate was unchanged at 54.9%. Participation remains sharply divided by gender, at 67.6% for men and 42.2% for women.

Underemployment, which counts workers who want more hours than they are getting, rose significantly to 3.3% of the employed population from 2.8%. The rise was steeper among women, whose underemployment rate reached 4.4% from 3.3%, while the rate for men was 2.6%. Informal employment, which covers jobs without social security registration or formal contracts, included about 811,000 people, or 36.7% of all workers. INEC reported no significant change in that figure from a year earlier.

The year-on-year rise comes despite some easing within 2026. INEC figures show unemployment at 7.1% in the January-to-March quarter and 7.0% from April to June before falling to 6.5% in the most recent period. The data arrive as several sectors report pressure on hiring. Exporters and manufacturers have warned that the strong colón is threatening jobs, and this week a call center operator scaled back a Costa Rica hiring pledge, citing competition from Asia. Costa Rica’s record dollar supply has kept the exchange rate low, reducing the value of earnings for businesses that sell abroad in dollars and pay their costs in colones.

The Central Bank of Costa Rica had already lowered its growth forecast for the year, citing the risks of El Niño to agriculture, food prices and electricity generation. The next quarterly survey will show whether the easing seen since the start of the year continues, or whether the gap with 2025 widens as the economy cools heading into 2027.

World.title: National Geographic Names Costa Rica Central America’s Ultimate Nature Escape
World.content:
National Geographic has published a new essential travel guide that shows Costa Rica as Central America’s ultimate nature escape, a country where rainforest meets reef and volcanoes rise above cloud forest. The guide, written by New York and Lima-based journalist Nicholas Gill and published Oct. 22, credits decades of environmental stewardship for protecting that natural wealth.

It holds Costa Rica up as a model for sustainable tourism and maps six regions for visitors, from Arenal to the Caribbean coast. It is the latest in a string of international nods from the publisher this year. National Geographic named Costa Rica a forest bathing paradise in August, and the country took two top honors at the National Geographic UK Travel Awards in October.

Gill describes Costa Rica roughly the size of West Virginia that packs misty cloud forest, surf beaches, active volcanoes and jungle into a short drive. He points to scarlet macaws, three-toed sloths hanging from cecropia trees and howler monkeys calling at dawn as the everyday backdrop.

The guide splits the year into two seasons. The dry months from December to April bring the best beach weather on the Pacific coast, along with higher prices and bigger crowds. The rainy months from May to November bring greener landscapes, fuller rivers and waterfalls, and thinner crowds, with September and October singled out as especially good on the Caribbean side.

Hans Pfister, co-founder of the Cayuga Collection hotel group, told the magazine that the stretch from mid-April to mid-December is what he calls “wildlife season.” He said the rainforest is at its most active then, with migrations and nesting cycles at their peak. Arenal and the northern highlands lead the regional tour.

The guide highlights trails across old lava fields in Arenal Volcano National Park, canopy ziplines, rappelling down waterfalls, rafting on the Balsa and Sarapiquí rivers, and the hot springs around La Fortuna. In the Tilarán Mountains, Monteverde’s cloud forest gets attention for its hanging bridges, moss-draped trees, glasswing butterflies and the resplendent quetzal.

The guide also recommends night walks for kinkajous, tarantulas and glowing fungi, and notes the area’s Quaker dairy-farming roots. Quetzals have been turning up beyond the classic hotspots too, including a first recorded sighting at a little-known Cartago refuge last month.

Guanacaste is shown as the home of Tico cowboy culture, with the surf of Tamarindo, the turtle nesting beach at Ostional, the resorts of the Papagayo Peninsula and the bubbling mud pots of Rincón de la Vieja National Park. Next door, the Nicoya Peninsula draws praise for Santa Teresa, Nosara, the year-round surf at Playa Guiones, Cabo Blanco Absolute Natural Reserve and its status as one of the world’s Blue Zones.

On the Central Pacific, Manuel Antonio National Park anchors what the guide calls the most cinematic mix of rainforest and beach. On the Caribbean coast, it points readers to Puerto Viejo de Talamanca, the reefs off Cahuita National Park, cacao farms and Afro-Caribbean cooking built on coconut milk and seafood.

Food gets its own section. Gilberto Briceño, chef and owner of Road Less Traveled Cuisine in Playa Potrero, told the magazine that the roadside sodas keep Costa Rica fed day to day, and he named Soda y Mirador Cinchona in Alajuela as home to the best tortilla aliñada he has tasted. Chifrijo, casado, Caribbean rondón and ceviche round out the list.

Three hotels are named. El Remanso is an eco-lodge above the canopy on the Osa Peninsula, Hotel Belmar is a family-run Monteverde retreat with its own microbrewery and regenerative farm and The Springs Resort & Spa sits on 67 hectares (165 acres) of hot springs facing Arenal Volcano.

The practical advice is standard but useful. The guide recommends a 4×4 for rural roads in the rainy season, learning some Spanish before arriving, and the 16-day Camino de Costa Rica trail for hikers who want to cross the country from the Caribbean to the Pacific. It also notes that Costa Rica abolished its army in 1948.

On safety, Gill calls Costa Rica one of the safest places in the Americas but warns of organized and petty crime in parts of San José and in port areas, and advises against flashing phones or jewelry or walking empty streets at night. The Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) recorded 873 homicides in 2025 and has projected fewer than 800 for 2026, with most killings tied to the local drug trade and score-settling between gangs.

The sustainability section asks travelers to book lodges certified under the Costa Rican Tourism Board’s Certification for Sustainable Tourism, hire official guides in fragile areas, stay on marked trails, use reef-safe sunscreen and never feed wildlife. It notes that nearly a third of the country’s land is protected.

The spotlight lands as the tourism industry heads into high season on uneven footing. Figures from the Costa Rican Tourism Board (ICT) show 2.31 million international arrivals through September, up 4.8% from a year earlier, but September arrivals fell 2.4%, the second monthly decline in a row, after air arrivals from the United States dropped 13.9% in August.

The promotion group Proimagen Costa Rica has pointed to the country’s high prices compared with its neighbors and the strength of the colón against the dollar as pressures on demand. Rivals to the north are also competing harder for nature travelers.

For a destination that sells itself on forests, wildlife and protected land, a high-profile guide from one of the world’s best-known nature brands is the kind of attention money struggles to buy. Whether it translates into arrivals will show up in the ICT’s numbers over the coming dry season.

World.title: Pacific Low Has a 60% Chance of Turning Tropical as Costa Rica Braces for Rain
World.content:
A broad low-pressure area off Central America’s Pacific coast now has a 60% chance of becoming a tropical depression within the next week. Whether it develops or not, it could bring heavy rain to parts of the region through the weekend. The odds climbed in less than a day. Yesterday morning, the U.S. National Hurricane Center gave the system a 30% chance of forming within 48 hours and 50% within a week. By its late Wednesday outlook, those numbers had risen to 40% and 60%.

The low is producing a wide, disorganized area of showers and thunderstorms. Forecasters expect it to develop gradually while drifting slowly north, and a depression could form by this weekend. A tropical depression is the first stage of a tropical cyclone, with an organized circulation and sustained winds below 63 km/h (39 mph). For Costa Rica, the bigger concern is water, not wind.

Costa Rica’s National Meteorological Institute (IMN) flagged the system’s cyclonic potential last evening. The low sits next to an already very active band of tropical moisture, the Intertropical Convergence Zone, which has kept afternoons and nights stormy across much of the country this week.

Under that setup, IMN forecast 20 to 50 millimeters (0.8 to 2 inches) of rain in six hours, with peaks of 60 to 80 mm (2.4 to 3.1 inches) in the Caribbean mountains and near the Pacific coast. Storms can bring gusts of up to 80 km/h (50 mph), strong enough to bring down branches and power lines.

As we have mentioned in multiple previous articles, the ground is why this rain matters more than usual. Soils are already 70% to 90% saturated in the South Pacific, on the Nicoya Peninsula and in the mountains of the Northern Zone, and they have had little time to dry since October’s nationwide rain alert. When the ground can’t absorb more water, rain runs straight into streams and drains. Creeks rise fast, culverts back up and slopes along roads can give way.

That is what happened in mid-October, when soil saturation reached 85% to 100% and flash floods trapped people in Heredia and Escazú. The National Emergency Commission (CNE) put the whole country on green alert on Tuesday, which keeps emergency committees active in all 84 cantons.

IMN expects cloudier conditions from Friday through Sunday, with fog on the Pacific slope early in the morning and cooler starts to the day. The hurricane center says heavy rain could reach parts of Central America through the weekend even if the low never becomes a depression.

If you plan to drive or hike, build your day around the morning. Storms this week have been strongest in the afternoon and at night. Don’t cross a swollen river or a flooded road, on foot or by car. You can’t tell how deep or fast the water is until you are in it. Keep away from riverbanks and steep slopes during and after heavy rain.

On the Pacific coast, expect rough seas on top of the rain. Small boats, fishing trips and water tours face the most risk, so check with your operator before you head out. Forecasts for developing systems can change quickly. The hurricane center updates its outlook every six hours, and the CNE can raise its alert level if conditions get worse.

World.title: Kilos of Marijuana Seized Off Costa Rica’s Border With Panama
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Coast Guard intercepted a speedboat carrying 2,648 packages of marijuana in the South Pacific this week in an operation coordinated with the US Drug Enforcement Administration, according to the Ministry of Public Security. Two Ecuadorian crew members were detained.

Public Security Minister Gerald Campos Valverde said the vessel was stopped about 52 nautical miles (96 kilometers, or 60 miles) southeast of Punta Burica, the peninsula that straddles the border with Panama. According to the minister, the operation began Tuesday and concluded Wednesday, Nov. 4.

The ministry said each package weighed roughly one kilogram (2.2 pounds), putting the load at more than 2.6 metric tons (about 5,800 pounds). Agents also seized 11 drums of fuel and other items that authorities consider relevant to the case.

The interception was carried out by the Coast Guard’s special operations group, known as GOPES, which stopped a 38-foot (11.6-meter) go-fast boat. The ministry said the DEA coordinated the operation, while the US Joint Interagency Task Force South and Panama’s National Aeronaval Service (SENAN) provided air and intelligence support.

Costa Rica’s Drug Control Police (PCD), the Special Support Unit (UEA) and the Directorate of Intelligence and Criminal Analysis (DIAC) also took part, according to the ministry.

The suspects were identified by their surnames as Trejos Domínguez, 25, who allegedly captained the vessel, and Flores Bawi, 49. Both were placed at the disposal of the Public Prosecutor’s Office, which will determine their legal situation. As of Thursday morning, authorities had not said whether prosecutors would request pretrial detention.

The boat was towed to the port of Golfito in Puntarenas province, where Drug Control Police agents inspected the cargo alongside prosecutors. The investigation continues into where the drugs came from and where they were headed, the ministry said. Authorities have not said whether the shipment is linked to other international cases or to any criminal group operating in Costa Rica.

The seizure adds to a run of maritime interceptions along Costa Rica’s southern Pacific coast, a stretch of water that has emerged as a prime drug route for shipments moving north from South America. Last month, a US surveillance plane helped authorities seize 1.5 tons of cocaine off Osa, a short distance up the same coastline.

Joint operations with US agencies have become a fixture of Costa Rica’s anti-drug strategy. Under a joint maritime patrol agreement in place since 1999, US aircraft and vessels regularly support Costa Rican interceptions at sea. The country authorized US Coast Guard vessels to take part in 2026 anti-drug operations, and in September a US military plane flew 45 tons of seized drugs out of Costa Rica. Seizures have climbed this year, with cocaine seizures up nearly 50% in 2026.

For a country that sits between South American producers and North American markets, the steady pace of seizures at sea reflects both the volume of drugs moving past its coastline and the growing reach of the international cooperation built to stop them before they land.

World.title: Cristiano Ronaldo Announces Portugal Retirement at 41
World.content:
Portuguese football legend Cristiano Ronaldo announced on Thursday he was retiring from international football at the age of 41. Ronaldo made his debut for Portugal in 2003 and went on to play a world record 234 times for his country, scoring 146 goals. But the forward’s powers have been waning in recent years and he fell out with national coach Jorge Jesus last month after refusing to play him in a Nations League match.

Ronaldo immediately left the team camp and was handed a 30-day suspension. He apologized and it was rumored he intended to return to the international fold, but on Thursday the five-time winner of the Ballon d’Or released a video on his Instagram account in which he said he had played his last match for Portugal.

“To the Portuguese people, the day has come for me to hand back the number seven shirt of our national team,” Ronaldo said, as images of his career were played. “I never felt it belonged to me alone, but for 23 years I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it, defending it and carrying it with me into stadiums all around the world.

“Today the time has come to pass it on to the future. It was not an easy decision, because some decisions are not made with the mind alone — they are also made with the heart. “A journey that began in August 2003 and changed my life forever has come to an end,” he added.

Will stay with me forever

The Portuguese Football Federation said it would organise a “fitting tribute” to Ronaldo’s “immense career”. Ronaldo will continue to play for his current club in Saudi Arabia, Al-Nassr, where he is under contract until June 2027. In the highlight of his international career, Ronaldo won the European Championship with Portugal in 2016 in France, although he had to leave the field during the final with an injury.

“I won Euro 2016 and, for me, that’s just as important as the World Cup. It will stay with me forever,” he recalled. At this year’s World Cup in the United States, Canada and Mexico, he scored three goals but Portugal were knocked out in the last 16 by eventual winners Spain.

In a notorious moment at a previous World Cup, a 21-year-old Ronaldo was caught by TV cameras winking at his bench after appearing to exhort the referee to send off his then Manchester United teammate Wayne Rooney as Portugal faced England in the 2006 quarter-finals in Germany.

Rooney was red-carded and Ronaldo scored the winning spot kick in the penalty shootout to send Portugal into the semi-finals where they lost to Zinedine Zidane’s France. His departure from the international stage follows that of his long-term rival, Lionel Messi, who played his final match for Argentina last month.

World.title: Call Center Cuts Costa Rica Job Pledge Over Asian Competition
World.content:
A US-owned customer service company operating under Costa Rica’s free trade zone program has cut its minimum employment commitment by more than half. It told the government it can no longer compete on cost with call centers in India and the Philippines. TTEC Customer Management Costa Rica, which began operating here in 2007 as Teletech Customer Care Management, received approval from the Ministry of Foreign Trade (Comex) to lower its required workforce from 111 employees to 45.The original commitment dates from executive agreement 067-2007.

In its request, the company said it faces growing competitive pressure in international markets, chiefly from firms in India and the Philippines. It said operating costs and salary structures there are far lower than in Costa Rica. The company described that gap as a significant structural disadvantage. It said the disadvantage had weakened its ability to keep international contracts and attract new clients.

TTEC carried out a partial reduction of its staff before seeking the change. It has not disclosed how many people it currently employs in the country. Companies in the free trade zone regime receive tax and customs incentives in exchange for minimum investment and employment commitments. Those commitments are written into executive agreements and can be modified at the company’s request.

TTEC is far from the only company to ask for that change. Executive agreements published in La Gaceta show that at least 38 free zone companies have lowered their employment targets since 2023. Their combined commitments fell from about 38,450 jobs to about 19,864. The largest adjustment came from Amazon, which halved its commitment from 16,450 positions to 8,225 in January. Align Technology lowered its minimum from 4,992 to 2,500 under an agreement published in May. Align said artificial intelligence and automation had raised output per worker.

Service firms make up most of the companies that have reduced their targets. They include IT consultancies, technical support providers, back-office centers, call centers and data processors. The reasons the companies gave vary. Several, like TTEC, pointed to lower labor costs in Asia. Others cited automation and artificial intelligence, or a shortage of specialized talent.

A smaller group blamed the strong colón, which raises costs for companies that earn in dollars but pay salaries and local bills in colones. One of them, Sistemas Globales, estimated that its operating costs had risen by 23.6%. TTEC did not cite the exchange rate in its request. The pullback is now showing up in the overall numbers. Direct employment in free zone companies fell from 197,101 to 195,410 jobs through August, a 0.9% drop, according to Central Bank data published in its monetary policy report.

Central Bank president Róger Madrigal attributed the decline mainly to fewer jobs in administrative support, professional and technical services, and information and communications. A lower commitment does not always translate into an equal number of layoffs. Some companies are revising targets set at peak hiring rather than cutting existing staff, as Align said in its request.

Even so, the trend points to mounting pressure on service jobs in a regime that directly employs nearly 200,000 people. Those jobs have been among the steadiest sources of formal private-sector employment.

World.title: Emilio and Elvis Zabaneh, Tersi Aguilar charged with human trafficking in Dangriga
World.content:
Emilio and Elvis Zabaneh, Tersi Aguilar charged with human trafficking in Dangriga

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Three members of the well-known Zabaneh family of southern Belize, including an 88-year-old businessman, his son and his son’s common-law wife, have been charged with human trafficking following disturbing allegations involving a Salvadoran woman recruited to work as a caregiver.

Emilio Quinonez Zabaneh, 88, his son Elvis Christian Zabaneh, 36, and Tersi Amini Aguilar, 34, appeared in the Dangriga Magistrate’s Court on Thursday, November 5, where they were each granted bail of $7,000.

The charges stem from a September 2023 investigation by the Belize Police Department’s Anti-Trafficking in Persons Unit.

According to police documents, the Salvadoran woman claims she was recruited by Emilio Zabaneh in El Salvador with the promise of earning US$500 monthly to care for him, along with accommodation and paid travel expenses.

However, after arriving in Belize on August 15, 2023, she allegedly experienced verbal abuse, sexual harassment, forced labour and threats of imprisonment.

The woman told investigators that Emilio demanded sexual acts, including sexual intercourse, which she refused. She alleged that he subsequently threatened to report her to immigration authorities and have her jailed.

She further claimed that Elvis withheld her passport despite repeated requests for its return and threatened to have her imprisoned if she attempted to leave the family’s Havana Street property.

According to the police summary of facts, the woman was fed only twice daily, made to sleep on a small sofa and permitted to shower only once a day.

She also alleged that Elvis and Aguilar required her to perform extensive household chores, including sweeping, mopping, ironing and cleaning bathrooms, despite her employment agreement being specifically for caregiving.

Although promised US$500 monthly, she reportedly received only BZ$150 during her stay, which she transferred to relatives in El Salvador.

On September 10, 2023, police conducted a rescue operation at the Zabaneh residence in Dangriga, removing the woman and placing her in the care of the Department of Human Services.

More than three years later, police formally arrested and charged the three accused.

Emilio faces one count of trafficking in persons for allegedly harbouring the woman through threats and coercion for the purpose of exploiting her through prostitution.

Elvis and Aguilar were jointly charged with a separate count of trafficking in persons for allegedly harbouring the woman through threats and coercion to compel her to perform forced labour.

The trio appeared before Senior Magistrate Mannon Dennison. Emilio was represented by attorney Andrew Bennett, while Elvis and Aguilar were represented by attorney David Morales.

No pleas were taken pending instructions from the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions on whether the cases will proceed summarily or on indictment before the High Court.

Each was granted bail of $7,000 with sureties and conditions restricting international travel and prohibiting contact with the complainant or her family.

The three are scheduled to return to court on November 18, 2026.

The allegations have not been proven in court.

World.title: AI could add US$48 million to Belize’s economy, study finds
World.content:
AI could add US$48 million to Belize’s economy, study finds

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Artificial intelligence could make Belize’s economy US$48 million larger within ten years, but the country has work to do to get its young people ready, according to a new study.

The Ayre Index, launched at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda, ranks Belize 35th out of 56 Commonwealth countries for youth AI readiness. Belize scored 42.8 out of 100, below the study’s readiness benchmark of 53. Only 15 Commonwealth countries reached that level.

The research, by the Ayre Think Tank founded by Antiguan Canadian entrepreneur Calvin Ayre, found strong internet access among young Belizeans. About 92.2% reported using the internet, 82.4% own a mobile phone and 4G coverage reaches 87% of the population. Belize scored 8 out of 10 for meaningful access.

But the picture changes when it comes to education and jobs. Belize scored just 2 out of 10 for education and training, with computing not recorded as part of the curriculum measure used. The study also found 22.5% of young people are not in employment, education or training.

Using International Monetary Fund scenarios, researchers estimate AI could lift Belize’s GDP by US$48 million after ten years. The conservative estimate is US$23 million, while the optimistic case reaches US$73 million.

Belize has about 112,000 young people aged 15 to 29.

World.title: Black Orchid Resort still hiring front desk and driver positions
World.content:
Black Orchid Resort still hiring front desk and driver positions

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Black Orchid Resort has filled its housekeeping position, but two other jobs are still open.

The riverside resort in Burrell Boom is looking for one Front Desk Agent and one Driver/Maintenance Personnel.

Applicants should send the following:

A cover letter.

A resume with two updated references.

A recent valid police record.

A valid Social Security card.

Applications should be emailed to [email protected].

The resort is reminding applicants to submit all required documents, as failure to follow instructions may result in their application being rejected.

World.title: Need new glasses? Courts Optical is coming to San Pedro November 12–13
World.content:
Need new glasses? Courts Optical is coming to San Pedro November 12–13

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): San Pedro residents looking to check their eyesight or purchase new prescription glasses can mark their calendars for November 12 and 13, when Courts Optical brings its Vision Clinic to Ambergris Caye.

The clinic will be held at Mahogany Bay Resort and will feature comprehensive eye examinations alongside a special promotion offering free lenses with qualifying frame purchases.

According to Courts Optical, the free lenses offer is available on select prescriptions and is subject to conditions.

The initiative gives residents an opportunity to address their vision care needs while exploring eyewear options closer to home.

Regular eye examinations can help identify changes in vision and detect potential eye health concerns, making routine checks an important part of preventive healthcare.

Whether experiencing blurry vision, difficulty reading or simply needing an updated prescription, residents can contact Courts Optical to inquire about available appointments.

The clinic takes place on Thursday, November 12, and Friday, November 13.

To book an appointment, call or WhatsApp 615-4146.

World.title: International News: Paraguayan President Santiago Peña resigns amid banking crisis
World.content:
International News: Paraguayan President Santiago Peña resigns amid banking crisis

By Zoila Palma: Paraguayan President Santiago Peña has announced his resignation amid a financial scandal surrounding Ueno Bank, which was shut down following a solvency crisis that left millions of customers unable to access their money.

Today, Peña announced his decision saying it was intended to protect the country’s stability, social peace and public institutions.

In a statement posted on social media, Peña said his priority was the security of Paraguayans who had entrusted their savings to the country’s financial system.

He also apologized to the public, acknowledging that history would ultimately judge the events surrounding his administration. Peña took office in August 2023 for a five-year term, CNN reports.

Shortly after his resignation announcement, Paraguay’s Chamber of Deputies unanimously voted to initiate impeachment proceedings against him during a special session.

The charges were brought by 35 opposition lawmakers and members of the ruling party, who accused the president of alleged serious and systematic dereliction of duty. The Senate will determine whether the impeachment proceedings advance or whether to accept his resignation.

The controversy erupted following the intervention of Ueno Bank, a private financial institution to which Peña has been linked and which reportedly received millions of dollars in public funds during his administration. Among the institutions that placed funds with the bank was the Social Security Institute (IPS), which manages pensions for most Paraguayan workers.

Paraguay’s Central Bank reported that Ueno Bank’s solvency ratio had fallen below 50 percent of the required minimum following adjustments to its financial statements during a regularization process.

The bank serves approximately 2.9 million customers in a country of 6.1 million people, and its closure resulted in thousands of customers having their savings frozen.

World.title: Belize advances development of National Employment Policy for 2027–2031
World.content:
Belize advances development of National Employment Policy for 2027–2031

By Zoila Palma: The Ministry of Immigration, Governance and Labour, through its Labour Department, is advancing the development of Belize’s National Employment Policy 2027–2031 through a three-day stakeholder consultation workshop held from November 3 to 5, 2026.

The workshop was organized in collaboration with the International Labour Organization (ILO), with funding from the European Union, and brought together national stakeholders to help shape the country’s employment priorities for the next five years.

The opening ceremony featured remarks from Chief Executive Officer Tanya Santos and CEO Valentino Shal of the Ministry of Rural Transformation, Community Development and Local Government.

Minister of Immigration, Governance and Labour Kareem Musa delivered the keynote address and officially opened the workshop. Abdelmalik Muhummed, Employment and Labour Market Policies Specialist with the ILO Decent Work Team and Office for the Caribbean, also introduced the objectives and consultation process.

Throughout the 3 days, participants examined eight key policy areas, including youth employment and the transition from school to work, women’s participation in the workforce, skills development, productivity, job quality, formalization and foreign labour. Discussions also addressed the inclusion of underrepresented groups, workforce development and labour market governance.

The final day focused on identifying policy priorities, institutional responsibilities, implementation gaps and the resources needed to put the proposed policy into action. The consultations provided an opportunity for stakeholders to share experiences, identify challenges and make recommendations toward developing a comprehensive employment framework that responds to Belize’s changing labour market.

The Ministry acknowledged the leadership of Labour Commissioner Rissela Dominguez Patt and the Labour Department, as well as the technical assistance provided by the ILO and financial support from the European Union.

Special recognition was also given to CEO Valentino Shal for his early vision and support in initiating the policy’s development.

World.title: Escape the winter cold with an Ambergris Caye vacation at Las Terrazas Resort and Residences

Escape the winter cold with an Ambergris Caye vacation at Las Terrazas Resort and Residences

Located on one of Belize’s most popular island destinations, Las Terrazas offers a tropical retreat for couples, families and travellers seeking a memorable winter getaway.

Ambergris Caye is known for its beautiful Caribbean waters, access to the Belize Barrier Reef, snorkeling, diving, fishing and laid-back island atmosphere. Visitors can spend their days exploring the sea, enjoying local cuisine or simply relaxing beneath swaying palm trees.

This winter, Las Terrazas is making the experience even more attractive with three special vacation offers.

Stay four nights, get the fifth night free. Travellers booking a five-night getaway can enjoy the fifth night complimentary. The offer is advertised as valid through December 15, 2026.

Stay four nights and receive US$100 resort credit. Guests booking four consecutive nights or more can receive a US$100 resort credit per room, per stay, adding extra value to their island vacation.

Complimentary couples massage. Couples booking three consecutive nights or more can enjoy a complimentary 60-minute couples massage, making the resort an appealing option for romantic escapes.

Beyond the special offers, Ambergris Caye provides an excellent base for exploring Belize’s marine attractions, including snorkeling excursions and visits to the surrounding reef.

For travellers planning a December holiday or an early winter escape, the resort’s promotions offer several ways to enjoy more of Belize while adding value to their stay.

World.title: Bahia Principe Explore Jamaica to reopen in Runaway Bay on December 1
World.content:
Bahia Principe Explore Jamaica

Bahia Principe Explore Jamaica, formerly Bahia Principe Grand Jamaica, will reopen in Runaway Bay on December 1 following a comprehensive renovation carried out over approximately one year, the hotel chain announced in a press release Thursday.

The reopening brings 647 rooms back into operation and approximately 1,000 jobs on Jamaica’s north coast ahead of the winter tourism season, the release stated.

According to Bahia Principe, as part of the Explore sub-brand, the renovated property is designed for families and groups who travel together and want to enjoy their vacation at their own pace.

It said the renovations covered rooms, common areas, dining, leisure and entertainment spaces, “with a stronger connection to Jamaican culture and local identity.”

The hotel chain said the reopening of Bahia Principe Explore Jamaica reinforces a new chapter for Bahia Principe, marked by the evolution of its brand architecture, clearer positioning and a more premium hotel offering, segmented and connected to culture and destination. In this context, the release stated, the Explore and Escape sub-brands help organise Bahia Principe’s offering and make it easier for each guest to identify which hotel best fits their needs, motivations and travel style.

Explore is aimed at families, groups and travelers who want to combine relaxation, leisure,

entertainment and a connection with local culture, while Escape is geared toward an adult audience

seeking a more relaxed, sophisticated stay focused on disconnecting.

“This differentiation strengthens the identity of each property and builds a more coherent experience from the moment of choice, in line with a more current, experiential way of traveling that is tied to the surroundings,” the release stated, adding that the initiative is part of the 50 per cent joint venture between Hyatt and Piñero, which manages the Bahia Principe resorts and owns the brand.

Bahia Principe maintains its brand identity and hotel essence, and Hyatt integrates its resorts into the inclusive collection, strengthening its international reach and connecting them with the company’s global platform, the release stated.

Julio Pérez, CEO of Bahia Principe Hotels & Resorts, highlights that the reopening as a significant step in strengthening the company’s presence in Jamaica.

To mark the reopening of Bahia Principe Explore Jamaica, the brand has launched a promotional

campaign for the hotel, with exclusive discounts of up to 50 per cent.

World.title: Haunted House?
World.content:
GREEN... I think what we have happening too much is that where a decision is made and it does not find favour with the Opposition, they resort to some form of protest.

WHAT should be a place for elected representatives to challenge one another through debate has been interrupted, on several occasions over the past year, by protests, walkouts and heated exchanges, with Tuesday’s confrontation over the Cuba censure motion being the latest flashpoint.

However, Leader of Government Business Floyd Green and Leader of Opposition Business Phillip Paulwell have expressed contrasting views over what is driving the repeated breakdowns in order.

In separate interviews on Wednesday with the Jamaica Observer following Tuesday’s sitting, Green blamed what he described as a lack of discipline and leadership among Opposition members, while Paulwell argued that the management of Parliament, particularly the Speaker’s handling of proceedings, was increasingly putting the Opposition at a disadvantage.

Their contrasting accounts have brought into focus the growing strain between the two sides of the House and raised questions about whether the country’s Parliament can return to more orderly proceedings.

Green said members of Parliament were responsible for maintaining proper conduct, even when disagreeing with decisions made by the Speaker or other parliamentary authorities.

“I think what we have happening too much is that, where a decision is made and it does not find favour with the Opposition, they resort to some form of protest, and that is more than unfortunate, that is unparliamentary, quite frankly, and should not be the approach,” he told the Observer after speaking at a post-Cabinet press briefing on Wednesday.

Green said he could not recall a previous period in Jamaica’s parliamentary history when an Opposition had responded to unfavourable decisions by attempting to halt proceedings.

He pointed to past Opposition responses, including walking out of the chamber or holding press conferences, as ways of expressing disagreement without stopping the business of Parliament.

He also rejected the suggestion that the problem was with the House itself, instead placing responsibility on the Opposition’s leadership to ensure its members followed parliamentary rules.

“It’s a challenge with the Opposition not appreciating that they too are bound by the principles of the House, and it’s unfortunate because every opposition wants to be Government, and when you set a precedent like this it just creates a very difficult situation,” he said.

Green said the way forward was for Opposition leader Mark Golding to exercise greater control over his members and encourage them to use other avenues when they felt aggrieved by a parliamentary decision.

He also suggested that Golding was sometimes contributing to the conduct he was criticising, making it difficult for him to correct the behaviour of his members and also blamed him for not allowing Paulwell to do his job as leader of opposition business effectively.

However, Paulwell rejected Green’s assessment, arguing that the repeated confrontations were rooted in how Parliament was being managed and the treatment of the Opposition.

He said the minority had been increasingly disadvantaged over the past year, particularly in its efforts to question decisions and hold the Government accountable.

“Well, I believe that the Parliament has declined into a state of disrepute, and it has to do with largely the management of the Parliament, all the affairs of the Parliament. I believe from our standpoint that we are seeing greater oppression of the minority in Parliament over the last year or so, when in fact there has always been a presumption that to enable greater accountability, and transparency, great leeway ought to be given to the minority in Parliament,” he said.

Paulwell said the interpretation of the standing orders, which govern how the House conducts its business could place Opposition members at a disadvantage depending on how the Speaker applies them.

He argued that the Speaker, who has the final authority to interpret the rules in the chamber, should remain above the political rivalry between Government and Opposition members.

“What I think has happened, and it might be due to the inexperience of the leader of government business, is that the Speaker is now embroiled in the cut and thrust of the democratic process that results from the two-party rivalry and competition,” he said.

“Now, the practice of the past, the leaders of Government business and Opposition business, they work things out, and it is true that he and I have a cordial relationship, and I believe that if he and I are allowed to manage the affairs of the Parliament, things wouldn’t go much further. But it cannot be that the Speaker, who is to be the final arbiter, the umpire, that person ought not to be engaged in the rivalry,” Paulwell added.

He said he had previously called for regular meetings involving himself, Green and Speaker Juliet Holness to settle disagreements away from the public proceedings of the House.

He also rejected Green’s suggestion that he was unable to maintain discipline among Opposition members, pointing to his own experience serving as both leader of Government business and leader of Opposition business.

“That is absolute nonsense, there are only a few persons on their side with the level of experience that I have, having served as leader of Government business for years, and also leader of Opposition business, and what has happened in the past is for the leader of opposition business and government business to work out the accommodation and the facilitation, and to make sure that there is greater harmony in the running of the Parliament,” he expressed.

Paulwell is therefore calling for a cooling-off period and renewed discussions involving the parliamentary business leaders, with the possibility of Prime Minister Andrew Holness and Golding also participating.

He said the matter could be addressed through renewed engagement between the country’s political leaders, including as part of the Vale Royal talks on constitutional reform.

World.title: Lower the temperature!
World.content:
HENRY-WILSON...I’m not sure if we are at a stage where, because of a person’s political persuasion, they can’t be civil towards other people

TWO former prominent Members of Parliament (MP) — Maxine Henry-Wilson of the People’s National Party (PNP) and Othneil Lawrence of the Jamaica Labour Party (JLP) — are appealing to politicians currently serving in the nation’s Parliament to “lower the temperature”, and bring civility back to the legislature.

The two have called for a reset in the Parliament, while highlighting the approaches taken by former prime ministers PJ Patterson and Bruce Golding who were able to maintain order during some of the most robust debates in the country’s recent history when they served in the Parliament.

Their appeal follows Tuesday night’s dust-up in the House of Representatives that saw two senior MPs having to be separated by their colleagues after they appeared to come close to exchanging blows. The two are Mikael Phillips, PNP MP for Manchester North Western, and JLP’s Desmond McKenzie, MP for Kingston Western, who’s also minister of local government and community development.

The incident followed the adjournment of the parliamentary sitting after a tense and disruptive debate on a motion centred on the Government’s decision to abstain from a recent United Nations vote on the punishing United States economic embargo on Cuba. The MP for St Andrew Western Anthony Hylton who moved the motion, even called for the Government to be censured.

Both Henry-Wilson and Lawrence credited the prime ministers under who they served for keeping things in line when they threatened to go off the rails. Henry-Wilson served two terms as MP for St Andrew South Eastern during the Patterson era, while Lawrence served one-term under Golding from 2007-2011.

“One of the things that Patterson did was to try and bring down the tempo and the animosity between the two sides because there was a period when the animosity was really high, Henry-Wilson recalled.

“One of the things he did was to have social events where they [PNP and JLP members] interacted with each other. And, also downstairs, in the dining room, we actually ran jokes and we knew who and who were friends and so on,” she shared. The former minister of education and information minister, who was also the first female general secretary of a major political party in Jamaica, said the level of hostility and polarisation was abated by the deliberate social interactions.

“I’m not clear how that goes now, I’m not sure if we are at a stage where, because of a person’s political persuasion, they can’t be civil towards other people,” she said, while pointing out that, “We have to work in the best interest of the nation”.

“It’s a question of respect also, and a question of understanding that politics is about bargaining and compromise and negotiation and nobody ever gets everything they want,“ Henry-Wilson added. “It seems like some of that has gone and issues have become intensely personal. Why would you in Parliament talk about anybody’s mother? They’re not a part of the debate, the discussion or the cut-and-thrust. We can’t stoop to that level,” she remarked.

“We must understand what the parliamentary debate is about; it’s not about personal attacks. As Norman Manley said, “elevate the thing, take it up off the ground,” she added.

Henry-Wilson said it appeared MPs are not taking the time to learn about parliamentary rules.

“Some of the things that I hear people talking about, they contravene the parliamentary standing orders but whether you like the standing orders or not the fact of the matter is that it is there and you have to observe it”.

She opined that the breakdown in the Parliament also has to do with the exercise of leadership of the House of Representatives. She recommended that the Leader of Government Business in the House, Floyd Green, sit with the Leader of Opposition Business Phillip Paulwell and “come up with some kind of ground rules about how you interact with each other. I think it is important”.

For his part, Lawrence said he is “very disappointed seeing what has been taking place — not only yesterday [Tuesday] but previously”.

Although two senior multiple-term MPs were at the heart of Tuesday’s altercation, Lawrence seemed to point the finger of blame for disruptions in recent parliaments squarely at the feet of younger, inexperienced politicians. “I don’t know if proper training needs to apply,” he said.

A former minister of state, Lawrence said when he was elected, training sessions were organised for the incoming class of parliamentarians. “It guided us as to how we should conduct ourselves,” he said. “I served on about eight different committees including the Ethics Committee and that has guided me well,” he added.

“I’m wondering if we [serving politicians] are not cognisant of the fact that from the moment you walk through those doors [of the Parliament] each day, we must remember that the country is looking at us.“

He recalled experiencing robust debates involving members of both sides “and at the end of the day persons who just had a heated debate were seen sitting together having lunch”.

He told of a particularly heated exchange between the late Roger Clarke of the PNP and Robert Montague who serves in the current JLP cabinet. “It was really heated but I can tell you that at the end of the day, five minutes after that, Roger was downstairs giving joke”.

Like Henry-Wilson, Lawrence believes the leadership of the Parliament needs to take charge.

“I don’t know if they need to be a bit more firm but at the end of the day, they must understand that while we want to rule, we still must respect each other regardless of which side we sit on”.

He went further to suggest that politicians may be influenced by the crassness that is played out daily on social media. And going back to the younger parliamentarians, Lawrence opined that youthful exuberance was taking over.

“Because if you go back to the persons who are behaving a certain way, the younger ones are showing disrespect to the seniors and it’s a concern that’s creeping into the Parliament.“

He worried that with increasing conflicts in schools, with some turning physical with deadly consequences, it is becoming increasingly difficult to tell young people how to conduct themselves properly “when we’re not setting any example”.

“After [Tuesday’s] behaviour, how do we speak to students about proper behaviour? It cannot continue, we have to set a better example”.

Having sat through some of the most contentious debates, including during the global recession of 2008-2009 and the Christopher ‘Dudus’ Coke extradition saga which ultimately ended Prime Minister Golding’s political career, Lawrence said he never saw the disrespect like what is being played out today.

“We debated robustly, we didn’t always see eye to eye but there was mutual respect. When I watched yesterday I cannot understand how they almost got physical. I’m saying, lower the temperature because the world is watching us”.

World.title: Shauna Chin: An actress with a diplomatic vision
World.content:
Jamaica’s honorary consul to Los Angeles Shauna Chin.

For Shauna Chin, becoming Jamaica’s honorary consul to Los Angeles was never a far-fetched ambition. It was a matter of time.

In March 2008 the actress sat down with Headline Entertainment’s Jerome Hamilton to discuss the future of her career. During that conversation, she voiced an aspiration she had previously shared only with her family — becoming a diplomat.

Nearly two decades later, that long-held vision has become reality, placing Chin in a position to represent Jamaica and its nationals in Los Angeles and Southern California, while opening doors for greater collaboration between the island and one of the world’s most influential centres of entertainment, business, and culture.

“Most people can’t see the vision of how an actress can also be a diplomat, but, to me, it’s so clear. I’m actually late on this goal, but I always knew it was coming,” she told the Jamaica Observer. “I guess my first reaction, then, is gratitude that this current Jamaican Administration also sees the vision clearly and supports that.”

For Chin, the appointment represents more than the fulfilment of a personal ambition. It is an opportunity to bring together the different parts of her professional life in service of Jamaica, while challenging conventional ideas about who can occupy a diplomatic space.

“I’m actually pretty excited to be the first and set the benchmark on what is possible,” she said.

It is a considerable undertaking, but one she does not regard as an abrupt departure from her previous work. Since 2010, Chin has served the Jamaican Diaspora in several capacities, including three years as an ambassador for the National Association of Jamaican and Supportive Organisations (NAJASO), five years volunteering with the Los Angeles Consulate, and six years as a representative of the Global Jamaica Diaspora Council (GJDC).

Her experience as a diaspora leader, including her tenure as vice-chair of the GJDC, has given her insight into the needs of Jamaicans overseas and the possibilities for stronger partnerships with their homeland.

“A nuh today me a work,” she said with a laugh.

Chin’s responsibilities include representing the interests of Jamaican nationals in Los Angeles and Southern California through passport and citizenship services, emergency assistance, and other official government services. She is also responsible for fostering trade relations between Los Angeles and Jamaica at the Government level.

Having previously pursued such connections as a cultural ambassador, she views the appointment as a natural progression.

“It’s been 16 years in the making. Today is just me continuing walking in my purpose,” she said.

That accumulated experience is now informing nine strategic priorities she has identified for her tenure. Developed from gaps and opportunities she observed during her years of service, the priorities have also been shaped through discussions with government officials, including the prime minister, the minister of foreign affairs and foreign trade, and other senior personnel.

Chin has already begun engaging several government ministries and agencies on initiatives spanning trade, agriculture, labour, policing, and film production.

Among the possibilities are collaboration between the Jamaica Constabulary Force and the Los Angeles Police Department, opportunities within California’s agricultural sector for Jamaica’s farm work programme, and stronger export links for Jamaican produce.

The film industry, however, offers a particularly natural meeting point between her official responsibilities and artistic experience.

Jamaica has long attracted international productions, but Chin wants the relationship with Hollywood to evolve beyond the island serving primarily as a location for overseas productions.

“One major goal with a partnership is to see our creatives, from crew to talent, as primary production players and not just background support,” she explained.

She is also measuring the success of her tenure by the tangible benefits it delivers to both countries.

“I’m starting from scratch with these priorities, so at the end of my third year each of the priorities should show initiation established with key partners, and tangible financial progress and intellectual gain to both Los Angeles and Jamaica’s benefit. My priorities focus on equal benefit to both countries,” she said.

For Chin, that means creating opportunities for Jamaican actors, writers, directors, and technical professionals to participate more meaningfully in international productions, while helping local films secure financing and distribution. She is equally interested in broadening the stories that reach international audiences

Jamaican cinema has no shortage of narratives shaped by crime and violence, she acknowledged, but she believes the country’s storytelling possibilities extend far beyond them.

“We have love stories, comedies, and stories about redemption that are also very colourful for mainstream audiences,” she said.

Her familiarity with both the creative industry and government processes, she believes, could give her an advantage in bridging the gap between the two.

“Los Angeles is renowned for Hollywood being a blueprint for the creative industries. This is why it’s exciting for Jamaica that the representative is an actress,” she said.

“For example, where Hollywood might pass on filming in Jamaica, I can speak clearly to the Ministry of Industry and Commerce and explain why carving out a tax incentive would be beneficial, and help them shape what that can look like. Same for musicians seeking to get Grammy nominations and wins, my office is positioned to facilitate more collaboration to get our musicians in the rooms with voters,” Chin continued.

It is an approach that reflects the breadth of a career that has moved through entertainment, military service, and health care. Still, representing a country while remaining an artist requires careful negotiation. Chin acknowledges that her new position has made her more restrained, particularly when it comes to the projects she accepts and the opinions she expresses publicly.

“It’s a hard daily balance that I evaluate on a case-by-case basis,” she said.“My ambitions are already overzealous, so I have to pace myself. I’ll get it done, but I have to pace myself,” she said.

Among the most significant opportunities on the horizon is the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles. With Jamaica’s celebrated track-and-field tradition likely to draw considerable attention, Chin wants the country’s engagement with the Games to extend beyond its athletes and sporting achievements.

She is already holding preliminary discussions with government representatives, sports business leaders, and community stakeholders, while preparing to engage Los Angeles partners on how Jamaica’s vision can align with the city’s plans.

Her broader ambition is to use the international spotlight to promote Jamaica as a destination for tourism, investment, and business partnerships, while creating opportunities for its creative industries.

World.title: No big bill
World.content:
Minister of Mining and Geology Floyd Green speaks at a post-Cabinet press briefing on Wednesday as Information Minister Dr Dana Morris Dixon looks on. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

AS the Government tightens its belt and orders a review of public spending, it has created a new Ministry of Mining and Geology. But Minister Floyd Green insists taxpayers will hardly feel the cost, arguing that the ministry is being built largely from resources and positions that were already in place.

Green, who also has responsibility for agriculture and fisheries, said the new ministry would not require the Government to recruit additional staff, establish new agencies or provide separate office accommodation.

He made the comments at Wednesday’s post-Cabinet press briefing, where he outlined the ministry’s plans and defended its creation against the backdrop of the Government’s drive to reduce expenditure and redirect resources towards national recovery.

Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness recently announced a series of spending restrictions, including a moratorium on non-essential overseas travel and a pause on official vehicle purchases until March 31, 2027.

The Government has also ordered a review of public-sector property leases, discouraged hotel retreats and reinstated restrictions on official Christmas parties.

The measures are part of a wider effort to control spending as Jamaica continues to recover from last year’s Hurricane Melissa.

The creation of another ministry therefore raised questions by many about the cost of expanding the Government’s administrative structure at a time when it is urging public bodies to spend less.

However, Green, said mining already had much of the technical structure needed to operate as a ministry because it had previously been a ministry before being reduced to a division.

“So mining used to be a ministry years ago, and then it moved and became a division. But it never changed its structure in relation to the various technical officers that you have. So we have a director of mining who happens to be here with us, we have a commissioner of mining who is here with us, we have two deputy commissioners of mining, [and] all of those positions were already there,” Green said.

He also noted that the Jamaica Bauxite Institute and Jamaica Bauxite Mining Limited are also existing agencies, while the new ministry will share human resources and accommodation with the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries.

“So no new entities have been established or are being established. Additionally, we are practising a shared service model. Again, this is something that the Ministry of Finance has been pushing forward. So we are not developing new human resources and new accommodations. All of that will be shared with the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries. So when you look at the cost for the new ministry, it is genuinely minimal,” he said.

He said the new structure was intended to speed up work in a sector that the Government believes can play a greater role in economic growth, particularly as Jamaica rebuilds following Hurricane Melissa.

He revealed that the ministry’s main task will be to expand the country’s mining industry beyond its traditional focus on bauxite and alumina, while improving the benefits Jamaica receives from its mineral resources.

Green said the bauxite and alumina sectors had been affected by two major hurricanes, setting back production and making a fresh approach necessary.

One of the areas being targeted is the system used to collect revenue from bauxite production. Green said the Government was reviewing the levy formula, which dates back to the 1980s, with work already involving the Jamaica Bauxite Institute, the mining division and the Ministry of Finance.

He said the proposed changes were expected to be brought to Parliament in the coming weeks.

But the Government also wants to make greater use of Jamaica’s limestone resources by encouraging companies to process the material locally instead of exporting it for further manufacturing overseas.

Green said Jamaica had chemical-grade limestone, which is used in products such as antacids and toothpaste, and that the ministry would develop incentives to attract investors to process it here.

Green said the intention was to encourage companies to invest in Jamaica and create more value from the resource before it is sold.

“How do we get companies to invest in Jamaica to do the value-adding here? In order to do that, we need to craft an incentive regime that will say to investors, this is what we have to offer, this is what we think can work, and we want you to come here,” he said.

The ministry is also expected to play a role in preparing the country for possible gold and copper production. Green said international companies were working with Jamaican firms to explore the potential, but stressed that it was too early to say whether commercially viable deposits existed.

World.title: EARN YOUR WAY BACK!
World.content:
West Indies’ Nicholas Pooran reacts after being run out during the ICC men’s Twenty20 World Cup 2024 group C cricket match against Afghanistan at Daren Sammy Cricket Ground in Gros Islet, St Lucia on Monday, June 17, 2024. (Photo: AFP)

FORMER West Indies and Jamaica bowlers Daren Powell and Nehemiah Perry say Cricket West Indies (CWI) must reach a suitable agreement with Trinidadian batter Nicholas Pooran should he decide to return to international cricket.

Pooran has seemingly softened his stance to play for the West Indies again after his decision to retire last year at age 29.

The power-hitting left-hander, who made over 160 appearances for the Windies between 2016 and 2024, didn’t give reasons when he announced his decision in June 2025 but opted to focus on global franchise cricket, including the Indian Premier League and the Caribbean Premier League.

However, on the opening day of his “Nicky P” Batting Academy in Trinidad last Saturday, Pooran, a former T20 captain said, “I’ve never shut that door completely. Time changes fast. I don’t know what the future holds.”

Powell, who picked up 156 wickets in 92 caps for the Windies, says Pooran needed time off to realise his worth to the Caribbean team.

“He probably heard the cry of the people on wanting to see more of him in West Indies colours and he had thought about it, probably fleshed out what the problem was and came to this consensus that he potentially wants to represent West Indies again,” Powell told the Jamaica Observer. “When you look at what has happened in the last few weeks, there is a pay cut which is going around for the players and if he is making his intention clear to come back as a West Indies player, it has nothing to do with salary. It has something to do more with the love of cricket and him wanting to represent the West Indies.

“I don’t think that Pooran has any stripes to earn. When you look around the region, we don’t have that X-factor like Pooran. He’s competing against nobody to get into our city’s team. We have good talent, yes, but good talent alone can’t bring success in sport. Pooran has proven himself in the region that he is not any ordinary cricketer, he is somebody who is way above the rest.”

Recently, CWI President Kishore Shallow told the Super Over podcast that he had conversations with Pooran before he announced his retirement and said, “You just have to accept the direction people want to take.”

With the ICC T20 World Cup two years away, Perry, who played 25 times for the Windies, says CWI needs to have a serious meeting with Pooran before potentially bringing him back into the fold.

“At the end of the day you don’t want a man to have West Indies cricket as a patty shop where you hop in and out and can do anything you want. You need to make a commitment and if the commitment is to represent your region at the highest order and perform, then we don’t have a problem with that,” Perry told the Observer.

“At the end of the day, if a man wants to apologise to the public, then he just apologises and says he made a mistake and he misses the game, he misses the camaraderie with his teammates, and he misses the competitiveness of the cricket and wants to see if he can win a World Cup for us, then fine, I don’t have a problem with that. We have to develop that sort of culture that you have to be committed to our cause — and when I say ‘our,’ I mean West Indies.”

Powell shared similar sentiments, that Pooran could help generate more revenue for CWI, which is facing financial challenges. However, he says a proper agreement must be reached to avoid future complications.

“I am not saying that they should accept him with open arms,” Powell said. “They have to have a good agreement. Not just take him and just say come play because you’re going to the World Cup and we’re going to need you. Don’t come and play because we need sponsorship and the sponsors need you. If that is the situation and that’s the agreement, he’s going to go back to square one, he’s going to pack up and leave when he wants to leave.

“He is a star player; West Indies need him, we need him, but it should not be a case you just walk in. There has to be some rules of engagement and some way in which no parties will be uncomfortable when he returns or is at a disadvantage to the other. It should be a mutual agreement with every other player, if anything should happen, it’s the same rules and regulations for the rest of the players.”

Perry says Pooran, the West Indies’ second-highest run-scorer in T20 internationals with 2,275 runs, must be fully committed if he decides to return to the team.

“He has to have that discussion with whoever — whether it’s the coach, the president, vice president or whoever the hierarchy of CWI designates to have that discussion with him and set some parameters and some conditions. And they need to say if you are not on the same page then we’ll do without you because cricket will always be here,” he said.

“We are not bigger than the game, we have to show that respect for the game itself because persons were before you and persons will be after you. So, it is imperative that we have that sit down and then we can shake hands and then we chart our way forward as a body.”

World.title: Flavours Of Japan
World.content:
Saki Salmon roll (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

Foodies, take note. Koi Sushi has arrived at the Super Valu Towne Centre on 144 Constant Spring Road. Marrying traditional Japanese finesse with bold Jamaican flair, the new outpost promises maximum flavour in every bite.

Eager for our own Japanese fix, Thursday Food visited the stylish new spot last week Thursday.

The offerings cater to every palate, bridging raw indulgence — consider Sashimi Sampler with tuna, yellowtail, and salmon — and cooked specialities like Teriyaki Chicken roll or the island-accented Scotchie Shrimp roll, boasting a spicy Scotch bonnet punch. For substantial mains, look no further than the miso-glazed salmon or the beef yaki noodles.

Behind the bar, the Japanese influence remains unmistakable with sake-infused mixology. Cocktails like the Lychee Sake Spritz and the Tokyo Mule offer a crisp, inventive alternative to conventional drink menus, delivering a refreshing balance of traditional finesse and modern flair.

What began in 2021 as a pandemic-era takeout concept on Hillcrest Avenue took full flight in 2022 as a complete dining destination. Through co-principals Lisa-Gaye and Kirk Chin and Chef Shuzo Hanasaki, the brand swiftly cemented its presence, captivating local palates whose appetite for premium sushi remained steadfast — even amidst limited opening hours and without a dedicated dining space.

“Our patrons didn’t mind eating [sushi] from boxes because of how great the sushi was. And the partnership that we shared with Chef Hanasaki was because of the love that he puts in his food as well,” Lisa-Gaye told Thursday Food. “So, we said, you know what? People love this so much, let’s turn this into a sushi restaurant.”

That success is evident in the brand’s steady evolution for the past four years, which culminated in a move to the more spacious Super Valu Towne Centre. The relocation answers a clear surge in consumer demand while bringing a refreshed ethnic dining experience to the neighbourhood.

“In the stretch between Constant Spring and Manor Park, we were really lacking options because Kingston 6 is usually where all the different ethnic restaurants are based,” Lisa-Gaye noted. “We just thought, ‘You know what? This is exactly where we need to be.’”

A departure from her signature Fromage brand, the venture is a passion project for Lisa-Gaye, driven by her deep love for Japanese cuisine.

“Usually, you’d have to travel for such great cuisine, especially Japanese, because it’s so hard to get the right ingredients here in Jamaica. We were up to the challenge, however, and decided to go all-in,” she said.

Indeed, Chef Hanasaki’s unwavering insistence on authentic, high-grade ingredients and meticulous attention to detail elevates every plate. Yet, the true secret to the brand’s success lies deeper: in the absolute trust Lisa-Gaye places in Hanasaki’s expertise, and the genuine passion he pours into every dish.

“He just formed this love for what we do. I was always pushing him to do it [open a restaurant] for himself and he said, ‘I won’t do it unless I do it with you’. And he believed in me, I believed in him. So here we are… a great partnership.”

Thursday Food raises a Lychee Sake Spritz toast to the continued success of this latest venture. Kanpai!

World.title: WATCH: US midterm results unlikely to shift Holness’ diplomatic approach – Chang
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica – Political commentator Kevin O’Brien Chang does not expect the results of the United States midterm elections, which saw the Democrats take control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, to influence the Jamaican government’s approach to diplomacy.

Chang, in an interview with Observer Online reporter Carlysia Ramdeen, suggested that Jamaica’s foreign policy direction is unlikely to be altered by the shifting political balance in Washington, noting the Holness administration’s approach to “get along” with the superpowers of the world.

“Mr Holness himself and Ms Kamina Johnson Smith, they’ve been very good diplomats in my view. They’ve made no enemies, they get along with the three great powers of the world,” Chang said. “They get along with America, they get along with China, and they get along with the EU [European Union].

“We’re a little small country. Why do we want to have any quarrel with any bigger country than us?”

The Holness administration has been widely criticised for its recent abstention at the United Nations on the resolution calling for an end to the United States embargo against Cuba, raising questions about the shift in policy as the island has long voted for the resolution.

World.title: Trump’s final two years: Is the UK ready?
World.content:
After a Democratic wave in the U.S. midterms, Westminster is wondering whether Trump’s domestic setbacks could make him more unpredictable on the world stage — and how Britain should handle the final two years of his presidency.

Patrick Baker speaks to Simon McDonald, the former top civil servant at the Foreign Office, who takes us inside Britain’s diplomatic response to the 2018 midterms and explains what lessons can be learned from Trump’s first term.

Then Ed Roman, who recently left his role as director of communications at the British Embassy in Washington, reveals how diplomats are already preparing for the next U.S. president — and how to court Trump’s potential successors without upsetting the man currently in the Oval Office.

And POLITICO’s senior foreign and defence correspondent Esther Webber explains why she thinks Andy Burnham will take a different approach to the Trump White House than his predecessor.

World.title: How to curry favor with the next US president — without annoying Trump
World.content:
1) Don’t be late to the party

“If you’re doing it now, you’re kind of too late,” Roman says of efforts to schmooze key Democrats who have made it into both the Senate and House this week. The British Embassy has, he says, already been doing its homework, tracking potential Democratic Party contenders throughout the year in anticipation of a wave.

But there’s stiff global competition to build those links first. “The French competitors, the German competitors, the Korean competitors — each embassy is trying to build a network that allows them a level of access,” he says.

In addition to the embassy in D.C., Britain uses its eight U.S. consulates — strategically placed across the country — to help it identify rising politicians outside Washington.
