As Roman puts it: “Real politics in America happens in America, out in the states, out in the districts. Knowing those Senate hopefuls ahead of time is always the name of the game.”

2) Don’t put all your eggs in one basket

Roman worked under former British Ambassador Karen Pierce, whose team invested considerable effort in cultivating relationships with Trump’s circle during the Biden administration.

Roman believes that work paid “dividends” for Britain in the years that followed, including in landing a U.K.-U.S. trade deal as Trump slapped tariffs on a host of allies.

World.title: US voters’ warning to European politicians
World.content:
The Democrats scored a resounding victory in this week’s U.S. midterm elections. But will their triumph actually change anything for Europe?

With the balance of power shifting in Congress, could the incoming lawmakers move the needle on issues Europe cares about, from tariffs to support for Ukraine? And what do MAGA’s bruising losses mean for Europe’s own nationalist and populist parties? Are they a warning for Europe’s far right? Or could the very issues that battered Republicans — affordability and the cost of living — end up propelling Europe’s far right into power?

Joining host Sarah Wheaton to discuss this is POLITICO Europe’s Executive Editor Carrie Budoff Brown, who also led our U.S. newsroom during Donald Trump’s first term. We’ll also speak with Gregor Schwung, a reporter at WELT currently on the ground in Washington, D.C., and POLITICO’s Foreign Affairs columnist Jamie Dettmer.

Questions? Comments? Let us know on WhatsApp here or at +32 491 05 06 29.

World.title: The curse of Liz Truss brings down the MAGA movement
World.content:
If you concentrate very, very hard, you may remember that Truss was the actual prime minister of the actual U.K. in 2022 for about 7 seconds. But despite that short time frame, two major events happened on Truss’ watch.

First, she crashed the U.K. financial markets. That’s the opinion of just about everyone, it seems, except for a certain Elizabeth Truss, whose new book “Bank Job” claims it was the fault of, well, anyone else.

She’s often blamed the “powerful economic establishment” for the abrupt end of her premiership; a run, you may recall, so short she was outlasted by a lettuce (that lettuce, incidentally, got a job as a senior economist at the World Bank).

This week, Truss told Sky News that the U.K.’s economic problems were not because of her mini budget but down to “a spike in the gilt market.” It just so happens, A Spike In The Gilt Market was the name of my teenage progressive rock band (our sole album — “Quantitative Easing” — is, unfortunately, not available on any streaming service).

A zero-star review of the Truss book in sister publication the Telegraph ends thus: “Of all the books I have ever reviewed that purported to offer a serious thesis, this is without question the most deranged. If you are seeking a Christmas present for someone you really don’t like, give them a copy.”

The second major event that occurred during Truss’ tenure was the death of Queen Elizabeth II (my lawyers — Sue M. Hall and Bill Able-Hours — want me to make it very clear that Truss had nothing to do with the queen’s death).

World.title: From Madrid to MAGA: How Spain’s Vox forged a right-wing network with global reach
World.content:
The Spanish party has forged strong links among far-right groups stretching from Buenos Aires to Washington — and is wielding growing influence in Brussels.

With Hungary’s Viktor Orbán gone, Spain’s nationalist Vox party is set to play an increasingly central role as a bridge linking Europe’s far right to political allies worldwide — from South America to MAGA in Washington.

Unlike Orbán’s Fidesz or Marine Le Pen’s National Rally in France, which have spent decades shaping national and European politics, Vox is a relative newcomer, having only entered Spain’s parliament in 2019.

But it is a force on the march. Pollsters expect Vox to double its parliamentary representation in Spain’s upcoming Nov. 29 election, potentially making it an indispensable partner in a coalition government led by conservative People’s Party chief Alberto Núñez Feijóo.





If the polls hold true, Vox would then arrive in government with an outsized global influence relative to its domestic footprint — all thanks to an international network it has quietly cultivated over the past few years.

Through its Madrid-based Disenso Foundation, the party has established ties with Latin American leaders such as Argentina’s Javier Milei and Chile’s José Antonio Kast, while forging relationships with influential figures in the MAGA movement in Washington.

Though distinct, the movements are bound by a common rejection of the political establishment. “This isn’t about occupying more space. This is a movement,” Jorge Martín Frías, a Vox member of the European Parliament and director of the Disenso Foundation, told POLITICO in Madrid. Vox’s allies, the lawmaker said, “face the same obstacles, the same labels, the same desire to annihilate them … And that’s how a sense of brotherhood develops.”

Vox leader Santiago Abascal and Jordan Bardella, president of France’s National Rally, in Ceuta on Oct. 12, 2026. | Thomas Coex/AFP via Getty Images

That same spirit of cooperation has helped Vox establish itself as a trusted partner to Europe’s right. Its leader, Santiago Abascal, now heads Patriots.eu, the pan-European political group that brings together Fidesz and the National Rally, as well as other far-right parties like Italy’s Lega, Belgium’s Vlaams Belang and Portugal’s Chega.

Frank Furedi, president of the Brussels-based Freedom & Sovereignty Initiative Europe, a conservative think tank formed by the core team behind MCC Brussels, said Vox had “been remarkably effective in carving out a niche for themselves as a movement that’s open to other political forces.”

Guillermo Fernández Vázquez, a political scientist at Madrid’s Carlos III University, said Vox’s strategy had allowed it to amass international influence well beyond what its electoral strength would suggest.





“Vox is an electorally modest party in the European context of the far right,” he said. “But it’s nonetheless become a communications node, a bridge, a hinge between the new Latin American right, the European far right and the Trumpist right.”

Across the Atlantic

Vox has been vocal about its interest in Ibero-America, which comprises Spain, Portugal and the Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking countries of the Americas.

The “continent of hope,” Martín Frías says, is “already ahead of Europe, including in economic terms,” pointing to Milei’s chainsaw approach to deregulation in Argentina and Kast’s efforts to attract foreign investment in Chile through tax incentives and regulatory changes.

Right-wing leaders on the continent “are showing that it is possible to challenge the politics of resignation that have prevailed here — the status quo of the People’s Party and the Socialists,” he added.

Abascal hugs Argentina’s President Javier Milei at a Vox rally in Madrid on May 19, 2024. | Óscar del Pozo/AFP via Getty Images

Through the Disenso Foundation, created in 2020, the party has built an institutional network of conferences, political contacts and training programs. One of its main initiatives, Foro Madrid, brings together right-wing parties, politicians and organizations from across Latin America.

Vox has funneled millions of euros into Disenso over the last six years, giving it substantial resources to nurture its relationships across the pond.

According to political scientist Fernández Vázquez, Vox identified and reached out to figures like Milei and Kast when their respective movements were still relatively small. Those early contacts have since developed into relationships with leaders who now hold power or occupy prominent positions in their countries.

The network has also given Abascal direct access to some of the region’s most prominent political figures, such as Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado. During an April visit to Madrid, she met with the Vox leader while notably declining an offer to meet Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.





Martín Frías attributed Vox’s success in building an international network to its refusal to simply export a Spanish political model and its ability not to get caught up in disagreements over national interests.

He pointed to Argentina’s support for the EU-Mercosur trade deal, which Vox opposes. “Each country, and each leader, applies its own rules to defend its national interests, which in some cases will be contrary to ours,” he said. “That’s only logical … That’s the game we’re all playing.”

For Vox, Latin America is part of a wider network that includes Washington. Indeed, Martín Frías has taken the party’s message directly to the American conservative establishment, attending the Conservative Political Action Conference in Washington in 2024 alongside Abascal and speaking at events organized by the right-wing think tank The Heritage Foundation, including the 2026 Miami Security Forum.

Furedi said Vox’s most prominent members have displayed a level of interest in Latin America rarely found among their European far-right counterparts. The party, he argued, was interested not just in building political alliances but in fostering “a more dynamic contemporary Hispanic culture.”

Balázs Orbán, Viktor Orbán’s former political director and a senior figure in Hungary’s MCC, told POLITICO that Vox had been able to forge a transatlantic “connection” through the party’s “sophisticated” approach and its members’ ability to speak both English and Spanish.

Back to Brussels

Vox’s approach to language and identity has undoubtedly given it an edge in Brussels.

The party has taken note of others’ mistakes, including those of Le Pen’s National Rally, whose failure to build strong ties with the wider far right has been partly attributed to its members’ refusal to engage in languages other than French.

“[The National Rally] may speak English, but they refuse to speak English … With Vox, there isn’t this desire to speak Spanish and make a big deal out of the fact that they’re very proud of their language. They’re much more relaxed about it,” Furedi said.





Fernández Vázquez said this had helped Vox position itself as a broker in Europe and led other far-right figures to view Abascal as a safe choice to lead Patriots, capable of balancing Le Pen and Orbán’s rival ambitions.

With Orbán’s fall, many are now competing for the influence he once wielded.

“Fidesz obviously wants to maintain its relevance and authority,” Furedi said. “The Italians — [Brothers of Italy] in particular — are also quite keen, with Meloni wanting to be seen as the equivalent of what Orbán was at a certain point.” But Vox stands out due to its consolidated role as both an “honest broker” and global interlocutor, he added.

Vox’s Martín Frías rejected the suggestion that his group was simply waiting to inherit Fidesz’s mantle. Instead, he said, the goal was to unite like-minded parties against institutions such as the European Commission, which he accused of undermining the European Union — a political project which he described as “a good invention.”

Abascal and other European far-right leaders at a meeting of Patriots for Europe in Madrid on Feb. 8, 2025. | Thomas Coex/AFP via Getty Images

The National Rally’s Jordan Bardella similarly said earlier this year his party would not seek to leave the EU, but instead transform it from within and “change everything without destroying anything.”

Like Martín Frías, Balázs Orbán rejected the notion of a far-right handover and referred to the beginnings of a broader alliance, including Hungary’s former prime minister and his party.

“Viktor Orbán always played a very important role in the patriotic movement. He is the founding father and one of its intellectual leading figures,” he said, adding that now that Fidesz is “no longer in government, we have more time to spend in Brussels and speed things up.”

Martín Frías expressed optimism for what Spain’s upcoming election would mean for Vox’s broader mission in Europe.





“Changes of government in European countries can lead to changes in the European Council,” he said, outlining a vision of an EU made up of sovereign nations that pursue their own interests while cooperating where their goals align. “There is an opportunity there to correct everything that is wrong, and to even regain citizens’ trust in the institutions.”

That shift, he argued, is already visible in the European Parliament, where the center-right European People’s Party increasingly “has no choice” but to work with the Patriots.

“They don’t do it out of principle,” Martín Frías said. “They do it because they’re afraid of the electorate.”

World.title: Don’t try to ‘please the dictator,’ Estonian leader urges Europe about Putin
World.content:
The Estonian premier — whose country of 1.3 million people borders Russia and has been subject to Moscow’s persistent attempts to stoke internal unrest — warned against the idea of direct talks, saying it would weaken Europe’s position with Putin.

“For once, Europe has a plan which is actually working” by suffocating Russia economically with sanctions, Michal said. Being a mediator means “you are willing to lower the standards, for example, for Russia,” including when it comes to imposing and enforcing punitive sanctions, he said.

“You cannot [have] two roles. One role is backing up Ukraine and pressuring Russia. A second one is trying to have a form of mediation,” the Estonian leader said.

“Putin should understand that Europe is strong, keeping together and we have one voice,” he added.

U.S. officials will sit down with Ukrainian and Russian representatives next week. The talks, which will be the first face-to-face negotiations since February, will be held in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff said Monday.

The Estonian leader said Europeans “appreciate” the Trump administration’s attempts to broker a peace deal, “but the pressure should be very much on Russia,” he said. “The problem [is] sitting in [the] Kremlin. Nowhere else.”

World.title: Andy Burnham’s cost-of-living COP
World.content:
Burnham will be there — now as British prime minister. And that little-noticed article, published five years ago in the Evening Standard newspaper, says plenty about his political instincts on climate change.

2021 was the high point of the U.K. consensus on net zero. But the then-future prime minister criticized the summit for giving a “pulpit” to billionaire Jeff Bezos (who had earlier that year “burnt more carbon in a trip to space than most people consume in a lifetime”) and took aim at protesters “with the time to glue themselves to roads … reprimanding ordinary people under work and time pressures for using their cars.”

Burnham backed climate action, he insisted. But with its technocratic focus on “percentages and far-off dates, with remarkably little reference to the struggles of ordinary families,” there was a danger COP would send the wrong message: “That the drive to net zero will mean cost and inconvenience for ordinary people.”

Several years and one big job change later, those views have not changed.

Interviews with more than a dozen advisers, government officials, pollsters and MPs around Burnham reveal a PM convinced of the dangers posed to Britain and the world by runaway global warming — yet whose first instinct, sometimes to the frustration of climate advocates, is to prioritize cost of living and energy security worries at home.

“I think Andy does get the big picture climate emergency, the urgency with which we need to act,” said Dale Vince, a clean energy entrepreneur and former New Age traveler who has advised Burnham on energy. But “millions of people in our country are asking: ‘How do I pay the bill?’”

World.title: EU targets large firms to unlock budget deal
World.content:
Lourtie overhauled an unpopular corporate tax known as CORE — which charges a lump sum on companies’ revenues exceeding €100 million — that the European Commission proposed last year.

According to his proposal, the EU would charge a 0.05% levy, as opposed to a lump sum. It would also only apply to firms with an annual turnover of more than €750 million.

These changes are expected to soften opposition among a group of countries led by Germany that challenged CORE on the grounds that it undermines competitiveness and takes a toll on medium-sized enterprises.

Going further

But two diplomats fear these concessions will not be enough to muster support for the new levy. “I don’t think this is going to solve the problem on CORE,” one told POLITICO. They, like others in this story, were granted anonymity to discuss the sensitive negotiations.

France is pushing to introduce new taxes to reduce contributions to the EU budget.

In a concession to Paris, Costa’s team indicated that they won’t cut down on the total revenue projections from the Commission’s tax proposal from last year, which was expected to generate €65 billion annually.

World.title: Zelenskyy urges Latin American leaders to help repair Ukraine's power grid
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Thursday urged Latin American leaders to send help "as soon as possible" to save his country's power grid from relentless Russian attacks.

 

Speaking at a summt in Madrid, Zelenskyy said every power plant in Ukraine has been damaged "in one way or another by attacks".

The Ukrainian leader asked for international cooperation to help rebuild and repair its energy system.

"We need equipment that works with our power grid and we need it fast. So please support directly to have connections with your companies, with your productions and get these supplies to Ukraine as quick as possible," Zelenskyy said at the 30th Ibero-American summit.

The summit brought together a 22-nation group of mainly Latin American Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking countries.

Those attending included Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, Guatemalan President Bernardo Arevalo, Honduran President Nasry Asfura, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and European Council President Antonio Costa.

"Since the start of the war, Ukraine has sought integration and the right kind of communication about this war with countries on the African continent and in Latin America," Zelenskyy wrote on X, adding that it is the first time Ukraine is represented at the summit.

"We need the diplomatic support of these countries. Every day, every month, and every year, relevant issues are raised at the UN General Assembly, and we are getting more and more votes from Latin America," he added.

Ukraine faces another difficult winter

Speaking at the summit, Zelenskyy called on leaders across the region to speak out against what he described as Russian "mass killings" that it carries out throughbombings and drones.

The Ukrainian president, who thanked Spain for its continued support, set out the urgent need for technical equipment, such as transformers, power cables, electronic equipment and diesel and gas generators to maintain the country's infrastructure.

Repeated Russian strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure in recent weeks have raised fears of another difficult winter ahead, and on Tuesday Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said supplies in the capital were "extremely difficult".

Zelenskyy's visit to Madrid comes amid US-led efforts to revive peace negotiations between Kyiv and Moscow, with trilateral talks set to resumse next week in the United Arab Emirates.

In addition to meeting with Sanchez, Zelenskyy also met with King Felipe VI to offer his condolences over the train collision in Toledo, as well as brief him on the consequences of Russia's daily attacks on Ukraine.

"We are now actively working with our partners to strengthen our air defense and better protect people. We count on Spain’s support in this regard," Zelenskyy wrote.

World.title: West Bank: Palestinians harvest olives under Israeli military restrictions
World.content:
Israeli soldiers stood guard near olive groves in the occupied West Bank village of al-Mughayyir on Thursday as Palestinian families gathered what they could during one of the few days they are permitted to harvest their crops. Footage showed troops firing tear gas near the olive pickers, with smoke drifting through the trees as a boy threw a canister aside.

 

Home to around 3,000 people, the village lies north-east of Ramallah and has some 4,300 hectares of land, yet residents say they can access barely 100 hectares. Reaching their groves requires prior Israeli military approval, with access restricted to a handful of days and subject to age limits and bans on equipment. Villagers say such brief visits are not enough to maintain their trees, which need year-round care.

Al-Mughayyir has faced mounting pressure from nearby Israeli settler outposts. Six residents have been killed in 2026, its eastern entrance has been closed by the army for more than two years, and around 12,000 olive trees were uprooted from its eastern plain in 2025.

Across the West Bank, the UN has recorded 377 settler attacks causing casualties or property damage since September, the highest figure since records began in 2006. The incidents have left one Palestinian dead, more than 200 injured and 3,850 trees damaged.

The olive harvest provides a vital source of income for an estimated 80,000 to 100,000 Palestinian families. Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are considered illegal under international law by most countries.

World.title: Spain: Zelensky urges Latin America to help repair Ukraine's power grid
World.content:
Speaking to Spanish, Portuguese and Latin American leaders, he appealed for transformers, power cables, generators and electronic equipment to restore infrastructure damaged by Russian attacks. Zelensky specifically identified Brazil, Mexico, Argentina and Colombia as potential suppliers of transformers, Chile for power cables and Spain for electrical equipment and generators. He stressed that Ukraine needed supplies compatible with its electricity grid and urged governments to establish direct contacts with manufacturers to accelerate deliveries.

 

At the summit, Zelensky was seen speaking with UN Secretary-General António Guterres and attending talks alongside Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, Honduran President Nasry Asfura and other international leaders.

The Ukrainian leader also met Spain's King Felipe VI at the Zarzuela Palace, where he was welcomed alongside Spanish Defence Minister Margarita Robles.

His appeal placed Ukraine's energy needs at the centre of discussions, highlighting the importance of cooperation beyond Europe as Russian strikes continue to damage essential infrastructure. Zelensky emphasised that restoring the power network required not only international support but also rapid access to specialised equipment.

World.title: Paraguayan president resigns amid bank collapse leaving 3M people without access to bank accounts
World.content:
Paraguayan President Santiago Peña has resigned on Thursday amid a banking crisis just before the Chamber of Deputies voted unanimously to impeach him.

 

Ueno Bank, the bank that was placed under intervention earlier this week, had close to three million customers, who have suddenly found themselves without access to their accounts.

Protests have roiled the South American nation after its central bank took control of Ueno Bank on Tuesday, citing a severe capital shortfall.

Peña, a close ally of US President Donald Trump, announced his decision in a video posted to X as lawmakers debated his impeachment, saying he was stepping down in the interest of "the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions."

"I want to apologise to the people if at any point I failed. It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me," the right-wing president said in the video.

The Paraguayan president, who until last year held a stake in a company related to Ueno Bank, expressed contrition but stopped short of accepting responsibility for the banking crisis that has plunged a South American nation long prized by foreign investors for its stability into financial and political turmoil.

People protest against the government and Ueno bank, which Paraguay's central bank has seized amid a solvency crisis in Asuncion, Paraguay, Wednesday, 4 November, 2026. AP Photo/Jorge Saenz

Some three million people lost access to bank accounts

Long lines of people trying to withdraw their money from Ueno branches snaked down Asuncion's streets on Tuesday and Wednesday, while angry protests swarmed the capital on both evenings.

Regulators investigating the bank found poorly documented lending and expenses wrongly accounted for as assets. But once the books were corrected, Ueno's capital fell half below the legal minimum, which led to the central bank seizing the lender.

Ueno’s app, cards and transfers went dark, and its branches locked their doors, leaving desperate depositors lined up outside with no way to cash out their savings. On Wednesday, a rush to open new accounts elsewhere crashed other banks’ mobile apps, fueling public panic.

"In the face of these accusations, I can't pretend to be oblivious," said ruling party deputy Alejandro Aquilera during the debate. "We have more than three million Paraguayans who have been harmed, who feel betrayed, swindled, deceived," she said.

A demonstrator holds a mock U.S. dollar bill depicting Paraguayan President Santiago Peña during a protest against the government and Ueno Bank in Asuncion on 4 November 2026. AP Photo/Jorge Saenz

Ueno claimed 60% Paraguay's adults as customers

Ueno Bank, which exploded from an obscure finance company to a household name in less than five years, claimed more than 60% of Paraguay’s adults as customers. They are now left scrambling to recoup their savings, government pensions, and, for 7,000 employees impacted by the bank's closure, unpaid wages.

Many Paraguayans are left asking how a bank linked to the president, who until last year had a stake in Ueno’s holding company, could grow so rapidly in size and importance despite repeated warnings about its dubious lending practices.

The answer lies in the uncomfortable proximity of Peña’s long-ruling Colorado Party to the country’s regulators and business elite, a weakness that has endured even as steady economic management and rapid growth made Paraguay a darling of international investors in recent years.

“Santiago Peña and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings,” said Luis Pineda, one of the protesters marching to Congress on Wednesday. “We are fed up with 70 years of plunder.”

Soon after winning its banking license in 2023, Ueno seemed to be everywhere in Paraguay. The digital lender, a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company, lured customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries, grew to more than 70 locations, sponsored Paraguay's national soccer team and plastered its name on the country's main stadium.

Ueno highly financed by Peña's government

Government money poured into Ueno’s coffers under Peña. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, president of Financiera Ueno, the predecessor to Ueno Bank, to run the central bank, the agency charged with supervising the digital lender.

As of last month, Ueno reported holding roughly $800 million (€712 million) in public deposits, about a quarter of its total, including money from the state pension and health fund and the operators of Paraguay’s giant hydroelectric dams.

Even as retirees’ savings and other public money piled up at Ueno, worries were escalating inside the central bank. In June, its inspectors found a pattern of risky lending to insiders, reported ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper.

Ueno had extended large sums to companies tied to its owners, beyond what the law allows and without enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad. On a single day in September 2025, nearly $39 million (€35 million) had gone to three such companies.

Peña repeatedly brushed off the warnings. As recently as last month, he defended Ueno and the central bank’s oversight, dismissing the concerns as a smear campaign that was spooking the public.

World.title: British comedian Russell Brand found guilty of rape and three sexual assaults by London jury
World.content:
British comedian Russell Brand has been found guilty of rape and three sexual assaults by a London jury on Thursday, the offences involving four women in total.

 

Eyes closed when the verdict was delivered, Brand showed no emotion as he was also cleared of two rapes and one count of attempted indecent assault.

The 51-year-old actor who turned into a conservative, religious online guru faces "significant custodial term," as said by Judge Joel Bennathan.

Brand's wife Laura watched from the public gallery as the jury at London's Southwark Crown Court delivered their four unanimous guilty verdicts. He was remanded in custody and will be sentenced on Monday. The maximum sentence in the UK for rape is life imprisonment.

Russell Brand and his mother, Barbara, arrive before the 83rd Academy Awards, in the Hollywood section of Los Angeles, 27 February 2011. AP Photo/Matt Sayles

Briefly married to US pop star Katy Perry, Brand reportedly also faces accusations of raping two other women, including a 16-year-old schoolgirl. These allegations were revealed during previous hearings of his four-week trial, thus not included in the trial.

'Courage' of victimes

After the verdicts, the Metropolitan Police paid tribute to the "extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward and reported what happened to them."

"Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women," the Met's Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy said in a statement.

"As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement. I hope this conviction sends a clear message that no one is above the law, no matter how famous or powerful they may be," Furphy added.

Brand's bail refused

Senior prosecutor David Roberts said outside the court Thursday that Brand's behaviour was "predatory" and that he "used his celebrity status to commit sexual crimes."

"He was a manipulator with an insatiable desire to get what he wanted regardless of whether consent was given or not," Roberts added.

Russell Brand attends Cosmopolitan Magazine's 'Fun Fearless Males of 2011' event in New York, 7 March 2011. AP Photo/Evan Agostini

His offences involved four women between 2005 and 2009 in different locations, a radio station, the set of a DVD recording and Brand's home. He had pleaded not guilty to all the charges saying that although he used to be promiscuous he had always had consensual sex.

The prosecution had earlier described him as a "ruthless, calculated and manipulative" sexual predator. Following the guilty verdicts, Brand's lawyer Ian Winter urged the judge to renew his bail over the weekend as "an act of humanity" and to "put his affairs in order and in particular to say goodbye to his three young children."

But Judge Bennathan refused to grant bail, saying Brand had "considerable resources" and whatever his good intentions might be, there was "fear he might in the end not feel able to come along and face his sentence."

From the dock, Brand signalled to his defence team that he was okay, adding: "I'm good, I'm good, I'm good" before being led out of the dock.

World.title: Greece: Students march in Athens demanding more education funding
World.content:
The rally began at 11am outside the University of Athens, then wound to Syntagma Square, where crowds gathered in front of parliament behind police lines. Protesters carried banners declaring "From Greece to France, we fight for free public education" and placards bearing the French slogan "Étudier ou survivre?" ("Study or survive?"), borrowed from France's school student protest movement. Outside parliament, some dumped sacks of rubble from deteriorating schools to highlight the conditions pupils face, from leaking roofs and crumbling plaster to broken radiators.

 

Police put turnout at about 4,000 across Athens and Thessaloniki combined, well below the 20,000 who marched in 50 Greek cities on 21 October; organisers disputed the figure.

The demands are concrete: more state funding, urgent inspections and repairs of school buildings, permanent posts to fill thousands of vacancies, smaller classes, and withdrawal of new national exams and of a proposal to remove Article 16 of the constitution, which protects public higher education. The secondary teachers' union, OLME, staged a four-hour walkout from 10am so staff could join.

Behind it lies the cost of living. Students describe rents of 800 euros a month and say many can no longer afford to study at all, with unions demanding a monthly housing allowance and rent caps.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | November 5th, 2026 – Evening
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: World Investment Forum in Doha examines what attracts investment and what holds it back
World.content:
The World Investment Forum brought governments, investors and business leaders together in Doha to discuss how countries can attract investment and create jobs. Organised by UN Trade and Development, the event examined why investment reaches some countries more than others and what governments can do to improve their chances.

 

Discussions covered practical needs, from ports and reliable infrastructure to skilled workers and clear rules. Speakers also addressed the difficulties businesses face when expanding, including rising costs and disrupted supply chains. For smaller countries, working with their neighbours could offer investors access to a larger market.

The forum also examined how public institutions could encourage investment in countries considered riskier. Options included guarantees to cover some potential losses and funding projects alongside other partners. Beyond attracting money, speakers highlighted the importance of creating jobs, supporting local businesses and measuring whether investments improve people’s lives.

World.title: Ex-lawmaker jailed in Macau's first national security trial
World.content:
Pro-democracy former lawmaker Au Kam San was found guilty of "subversion against the political power of the State." He was handed a prison sentence of 12-and-a-half years.

A court in Macau on Friday sentenced former lawmaker and pro-democracy campaigner Au Kam San to 12 years and six months in jail in the Chinese territory's first national security case.

The 69-year-old was convicted of several offences including "subversion against the political power of the State".

What were the charges against Au Kam San?

Au was accused of providing false information to anti-China organizations outside Macau to incite hatred against the city's government and Beijing.

The teacher-turned-lawmaker was detained in July 2025, in what was the first publicly known prosecution under Macau's national security law since it was implemented in 2009.

Au "personally provided, over a long period of time, assistance and collaboration to external hostile organisations in the collection, preparation, and public dissemination of various images and information that were manifestly filled with political claims of a subversive nature against the political authority of the State," a court statement said.

The court added that Au also sought to "incite hatred among Macau residents against the Central People's Government, with the intent to overthrow and undermine the fundamental system of the State enshrined in the Constitution of the People's Republic of China."

What have critics said about Au's trial?

Au's closed-door trial — which ended in September in three days — had raised concerns about fairness.

An open trial was ruled out by a judge to safeguard national security interests, the court had said earlier.

Critics say that Au's case illustrates China's emphasis on security and its intolerance of dissent, even though Macau's pro-democracy movement has never been as influential as its neighbor Hong Kong.

Last year, the European Uniondenounced Au's arrest, saying it added to the concerns about the "erosion of political pluralism" in Macau.

Au served in Macau's legislature dominated by pro-China loyalists for two decades and stepped down in 2021.

He co-organized Macau's vigils commemorating the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown in Beijing.

Macau is a former Portuguese colony which reverted to China in 1999. Like Hong Kong, it operates as a special administrative region of China.

World.title: Asian stocks slump after US tech rout amid AI jitters
World.content:
Concerns that Democrats in the US will push back against data center projects are weighing on an AI trade that is already on shaky footing amid growing doubts about profitability.

Japanese and South Korean shares tumbled on Friday, following a massive selloff in tech stocks on Wall Street the previous day.

Tokyo's benchmark Nikkei 225 index fell 5.5% in early trade, while Seoul's tech-heavy Kospi index slid as much as 8.8%, triggering a circuit breaker which suspended trading for 20 minutes. Taiwan's benchmark TAIEX index was also down more than 8%.

Asian tech giants including Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) have borne the brunt of the artificial intelligence-related selloff.

Samsung plunged nearly 10% while SK Hynix slid over 11%.

Chip-related shares in Japan also took a beating, with Tokyo Electron stock trading down around 9% and Kioxia shedding 13%.

European stock futures fell 1%, indicating that the selloff was likely to spread across to Europe.

Data centers face backlash from US communities To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What's behind the stock rout on Wall Street?

On Thursday, US markets were hammered by a sharp retreat in tech stocks, particularly those involved in the buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure like data centers.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 5.52% and shed as much as $2.5 trillion (roughly €2.23 trillion) in market value, while the broader S&P 500 index plunged 4.4%.

The rout occurred as investors grow increasingly anxious about the colossal AI spending plans and whether they will eventually produce commensurate profits.

The results of the US midterm elections, which saw Democrats seize control of both houses of US Congress, added to the concerns.

A number of Democratic governors-elect campaigned on slowing artificial intelligence development and promised to stop or pause the construction of data centers amid growing public opposition to such projects.

"It's pretty clear there's been a real shift ​in sentiment," Michael McCarthy, chief executive for Australia and New Zealand at online brokerage Moomoo, told the Reuters news agency.

"Market turning points are often accompanied by strong disagreement, and that shows up in the market ​by huge swings in either direction," he said. "That's what we appear to have had — and last night's emphatic sell-down suggests that is the direction that we're now headed in."

World.title: Trump raises prospect of 'big, beautiful' Russia-Ukraine deal
World.content:
US President Donald Trump said the Ukraine war was close to being settled and that ending it might involve "all of Europe." Trump has previously made several similar promises, with no resolution to the conflict in sight.

US President Donald Trump on Thursday said a "very big" deal is in the works with Russia to end the Ukraine war.

Trump made the comments after he had an unscheduled meeting with Russian ⁠President Vladimir Putin's special envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House.

What did Trump say?

Speaking to ​reporters later, the president said the Russia-Ukraine war was ​very close to being settled and that bringing it to an end might involve "all of Europe."

"I can't tell you what I discussed. But I'm just telling you, it's going to be an agreement, it's going to be a big agreement," Trump said in the Oval Office.

"It's going to be very big. It's going to involve more than Ukraine, and I could even say it might involve all of Europe. It's going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone's going to be thrilled."

Trump said he had not met with Ukrainian officials who were also at the White House on Thursday.

Trump weakened: Is Europe safer now? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Meanwhile, Trump's son-in-law and US envoy Jared Kushner said the United States, NATO, ⁠and European ⁠partners held ​"productive and substantive ​discussions" on resolving ​the war in Ukraine Thursday.

"Our objective is to address the security concerns of all sides through practical, mutually agreed arrangements that reduce the risk of future conflict," he wrote on X, ​ahead of ⁠discussions ​next ​week in ​Abu Dhabi involving Kyiv and ​Moscow.

Even before his return to the White House, Trump has made similar promises regarding an imminent end to the conflict, famously saying he would end the war in one day upon becoming president.

Ukraine, Russia praise Melania Trump for brokering Oleshky truce

Delegations from both Russia and Ukraine were at the White House on Thursday for an event honoring First Lady Melania Trump's work brokering a recent ceasefire in the war-ravaged city of Oleshky.

Speaking at her invitation, Russian envoy Dmitriev thanked the first lady for her "distinguished humanitarian role" in securing the six-day truce.

Dmitriev added that Putin personally gave instructions as part of the operation and sent his thanks to Melania Trump.

The head of the parliamentary faction of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's party, Davyd Arakhamia, and Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, also spoke at the event.

Arakhamia told the first lady she did an "amazing job" and encouraged her to keep helping the Ukrainian people.

"Definitely we would like to ask you to keep going and to find new missions and to de-escalate more as much as possible," Arakhamia said.

World.title: Austrian tycoon Rene Benko sentenced to 2 years in prison for fraud
World.content:
Austrian businessman Rene Benko, who suffered a major fall from grace after his real estate empire, Signa Holding, went bust, was handed two more years in prison.

Rene Benko, an Austrian businessman whose legacy as a property tycoon collapsed with the fall of his real estate empire Signa Holding three years ago, was sentenced to two more years in prison on Thursday.

The Innsbruck Regional Court found Beko guilty of defrauding €5 million from the private foundation of Austrian industrialist Hans Peter Haselsteiner. The payment from Haselsteiner arrived just weeks before Signa Holding declared insolvency.

It was the third criminal proceeding against Banko, coming after two earlier convictions. He was sentenced in the first case in October 2025 on charges of insolvency-related fraud. In September 2026, he received a 30-month term for harming creditors.

The new sentence against Benko, 49, comes just ‌three weeks ⁠after ⁠he was released to house arrest to serve out a previous conviction.

Rene Benko with his lawyers at the trial Image: Johann Groder/Expa/APA/dpa/picture alliance

Benko's lawyer said he would assess whether to appeal the conviction over the weekend.

Benko was acquitted on a second charge that he had hidden a luxury rifle worth €80,000 from creditors.

The fall of Signa Holding

Benko was once thought to have been a wunderkind for having established himself as a self-made entrepreneur after dropping out of college.

At its peak, Signa Holdings accumulated a portfolio worth more than $30 billion, with stakes in New York's Chrysler Building and Berlin's KaDeWe department store.

In 2023, Signa Holdings declared bankruptcy, dealing a blow to a myriad of European property investors and others.

The fall of Signa was considered the single biggest financial earthquake to have hit the European property market since the global financial crisis of 2008.

World.title: Gavin Newsom commutes sentences of all death row inmates in California
World.content:
Gavin Newsom, a Democrat and a rumored presidential candidate, moved to commute the death sentences of 548 inmates in California for one of his last acts as governor of the state.

California Governor Gavin Newsom said Thursday that he will change all death sentences in the state to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

"I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us," Newsom said in a letter to Californians.

There are 548 people on death row in California.

The outgoing governor added in the letter that he has long opposed the death penalty and issued a moratorium on executions in 2019.

The California state constitution requires the California Supreme Court's approval to grant clemency to anyone convicted of a felony more than once, which means the court would have to approve 382 of those commutations, or roughly 70%, according to numbers provided by Newsom's office.

Newsom's announcement also comes after the failed execution of Christa Pike renewed scrutiny of the death penalty.

Newly released 911 calls reveal chaotic response to save Christa Pike To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Newsom acknowledges 'difficulty' of decision

Newsom, who is rumored to be considering a run for president in 2028, said the decision was among the most difficult choices of his career because it will surface painful memories for crime victims' families.

"As Governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution," Newsom wrote.

He acknowledged that Californians had voted to keep the death penalty. In 2016, 53% of people rejected a ballot measure that would have abolished the death penalty in the state.

"But the constitution also gave every governor clemency authority, and that power exists for moments when law as applied cannot be squared with justice," Newsom said. "For me, this is that moment."

The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), who has said the implementation of the death penalty reflects racial bias, applauded the announcement.

"These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long," said Anthony Romero, the executive director of ACLU.

In 2025, 17 countries carried out a total of at least 2,707 executions, according to Amnesty International.

World.title: Americans voted against Trump's Iran war. Gulf countries hope that means an end to the conflict
World.content:
The US midterm results showed how unpopular Donald Trump's Iran war is. Now, Gulf countries, trapped for months in the middle of the war between the US and Iran, see reason for optimism.

After his party's resounding defeat in the US midterm elections this week, President Donald Trump conceded that the war with Iran had likely played a part.

"I think a part of it was Iran, but, at the same time, people understood the importance of what I've done with Iran," Trump told Fox News, conceding that US voters were unwilling to accept the impact of the war on gas prices.

Observers say the United States and Israel had been holding off on major attacks on Iran until after both had held elections.

At the end of October, the Wall Street Journal reported that the Trump administration was already warning Gulf state governments to brace for a short, intense military campaign after the midterms.

Could conflict escalate again?

While foreign policy is a US president's purview, analysts have pointed out that a Congress controlled by the Democratic party could ostensibly withhold funding for Trump's military expeditions. However newly-elected Democratic politicians won't take their seats until early next year.

The US has been moving military assets into the Middle East and limited attacks on Iran have been ongoing Image: Menelaos Hadjicostis/AP Photo/picture alliance

As two US professors of political science wrote for Foreign Affairs magazine this week, past American presidents, like Trump, who become "lame ducks" — that is, a president who loses control of Congress and can't run for another term — have often ramped up international interventions.

"As they think about their legacy, lame ducks often turn to foreign policy, where the power of the presidency allows them to act unfettered by pesky domestic politics," they explained. And one of the places where Trump is most likely to act is Iran, the professors argued.

On the other hand, Trump also told several media outlets that he was in "no rush" to start bombing Iran again.

Opinions on Iran's next moves are also divided.

The Iranians have said they're ready for any attack and rhetoric from senior leaders indicates they may be willing to strike a wider range of targets than previously. That could include regional energy and economic infrastructure and even undersea telecommunications cabling or data centers.

If Iran thinks there is an existential threat to its leadership, then "all bets are off," Ross Harrison, a senior fellow at the Washington-based Middle East Institute, or MEI, and an expert on Iran, said during a virtual briefing hosted by MEI this week. "I think they will target differently in the Gulf states [this time] … so it really depends on how all this unfolds."

But other experts believe Iran was deliberately holding out to pressure Trump before the midterms. Now the election is over, the Iranians may be more willing to negotiate a peace deal.

Unwilling participants

All this leaves the Gulf states, who have been the main targets of Iranian attacks since the conflict began, in a difficult position.

"We find ourselves drawn within a crisis that we worked diplomatically very hard to try to avert," Anwar Gargash, a foreign policy adviser to United Arab Emirates leadership, said at a security conference in Bahrain last weekend, the Manama Dialogue hosted by the International Institute for Strategic Studies, or IISS. "We are clearly seeking a political off-ramp."

Qatar has been trying to negotiate between the US and Iran but has also been conducting emergency drills at its airport. The Emiratis have been doing similar drills. And Saudi Arabia is looking at a war on two fronts: The oil-rich state is already under attack from the Houthi militia in neighboring Yemen. Even Egypt has reacted, reportedly strengthening air defenses around the Suez Canal.

Still, no matter what happens next, the US-Israel-Iran war has already made Gulf states evaluate defense partnerships with the US. Rather than making them safe, US bases have made them a target.

"There is widespread disappointment across the region with the US over the folly of the war, the erratic nature of Washington's military and diplomatic conduct, and its decision to prioritize Israel's defense over that of its Gulf partners," Hasan Alhasan, a senior fellow at the IISS, told news agency Bloomberg this week. "If the US liberation of Kuwait in 1991 was the moment that established America's role in the region, the 2026 war may be remembered as the moment that undid it."

Replacing America?

Gulf states are widening their outreach with, for example, the UAE getting closer to Israel and the Saudis entering the Mecca defense pact with Pakistan and Turkey.

"The Gulf states have already moved toward strategic autonomy and self-reliance," Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer at the School of Security Studies at King's College London, wrote for online outlet Middle East Eye this week. "A lame-duck Trump will speed that process."

That's even though a Democrat-led Congress might make the US a slightly more reliable partner again.

Krieg argues that Gulf states should come together to pressure the US not to attack Iran and then negotiate a non-aggression pact with Iran — without US involvement.

Whether that kind of unity is possible in the Gulf is dubious, Ryan Crocker, a former US ambassador to the region and distinguished fellow with MEI, replied to a question from DW during the MEI's online briefing.

Reevaluating the relationship? Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan (left) and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio at a recent G20 meeting in the US Image: Megan Varner/AFP

"I'm afraid that meaningful Gulf unity is not coming to a theater near us anytime soon," Crocker said. The Qataris remain untrusting because of how other Gulf states acted against them in 2017. And, he added, "there are well known differences between Saudi Arabia and the UAE we see in Sudan [and] in Yemen, and, of course, the profound differences … on relations with Israel. So I would not expect any meaningful moves toward [Gulf] security cooperation."

What's more likely in the long term is Gulf states eventually coming to some kind of understanding with Iran.

"The Gulf states understand that they probably can't buy their security only from Washington, and that they're going to have to buy it, to some degree, by some kind of a relationship with Tehran," the MEI's Harrison added. "It's inevitable. Geography reigns."

What that sort of non-aggression pact looks like remains to be seen, he added. That's why one of the big concerns for Gulf leaders now, is the conflict escalating again to a point where the path back to some sort of diplomacy is lost, Harrison concluded.

World.title: Pete Hegseth under fire as Republicans trade blame for midterm debacle
World.content:
Iran war hawk Pete Hegseth is facing the fallout from Republicans' midterms losses as high energy prices turned voters toward Democrats. US President Trump continues to support his embattled defense chief — for now.

Republicans in Washington continued to assess the damage on Thursday, after a resounding electoral defeat in the midterm elections two days prior saw Democrats take over Congress by large margins.

Republican Party insiders told US outlets CNN and The Washington Post that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is feeling the heat over criticism that the war in Iran, which he supports, cost his party the elections.

Trump on Wednesday acknowledged that the Iran war affected the midterms, saying that voters were frustrated how the 8-month-long conflict has cause gas and diesel prices to skyrocket.

"The Iran thing we had to do, and we continue to do it," Trump told reporters, but he ultimately defended the war effort and denied any plans to fire his defense secretary over it, saying Hegseth was "doing a very good job."

On Wednesday, Trump said it was 'likely true' the Iran war led to the Republicans' midterm rout Image: CNP/AdMedia/picture alliance

But US Vice President JD Vance has sought to distance himself from the war, questioning whether it was worth the cost.

"The ⁠reason ⁠we lost is the war," Vance said on X. "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so."

'Knives out' at the Pentagon

Hegseth has been a loud voice in Washington for the US attacking Iran, and has publicly chastised lawmakers and journalists for raising questions about the conflict's strategic objectives, cost and lack of congressional authorization.

The defense secretary has also been accused of not being forthright about the damage to US bases in the Middle East and the severity of troop casualties. He has also purged dozens of high ranking military officers, while denying promotions to others on dubious grounds.

Hegseth was in hot water even before the Iran war. In October 2025, a Signal group chat between himself and Vice President JD Vance discussing a military strike on Yemen in October 2025 accidentally included a journalist, and led to calls for Hegseth's dismissal.

According to CNN's reporting, multiple Republicans told the network on condition of anonymity that many in their party are now turning against the defense secretary.

Sources also told the Washington Post that the political situation at the Defense Department appears "very dynamic at the moment," with "knives out."

With Trump backing Hegseth for now, The Post reported that those close to the Trump administration have floated the notion that the president might dismiss General Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, or Admiral Brad Cooper, who has overseen the war, instead of the embattled Hegseth.

House plans Hegseth impeachment vote

Pressure is mounting in Capitol Hill, as Hegseth's critics from both sides of the aisle turn their focus on him.

CNN reported that House Republicans are expected to hold an impeachment vote to directly repudiate the defense secretary in a matter of days.

Republican Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky, who has been a critic of Trump, told CNN he plans to trigger the impeachment, which multiple GOP sources say is expect to pass.

In September, Massie had said he would force a vote in the House on impeaching Hegseth, which led to House Speaker Mike Johnson sending Congress into recess until after the midterms.

On Thursday, Massie posted on X that his impeachment resolution is a "much gentler" version of what's coming when the Democrats take over Congress in January.

"They'll have hearings & trials," he wrote.

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said that Hegseth "will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists."

"We will continue to drive President Trump's agenda at the Department of War — despite threats of sham witch hunts from Democrats — and Secretary Hegseth is 100% committed to leading the Department until the end of President Trump's term in office," Parnell added, using the administration's name for the Department of Defense.

Incoming Democrats plan probes

Fresh off their sweeping wins, Democrats will have the power to launch investigations on Hegseth and even slash funding for the Defense Department and the Iran war.

"I'm going after Pete Hegseth. Not only is he incompetent and corrupt, he's undermining our national security and the safety of our troops," said Representative Jason Crow, a Democratic member of the House Armed Services Committee.

Representative Adam Smith, the top Democrat on the committee, said a top priority would be "to conduct vigorous oversight of the Department of Defense and the Trump Administration," including on "the illegal war against Iran."

World.title: Does the Oleshky ceasefire signal progress to come in Ukraine?
World.content:
Hundreds of civilians were evacuated from the city of Oleshky after Russia and Ukraine agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire. Some observers have expressed optimism that more such humanitarian missions might follow.

Nearly 800 residents have been evacuated from the Russia-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine. This was announced by US first lady Melania Trump, who was credited with helping to mediate the ceasefire. The mission was coordinated by Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets and his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova.

Most evacuees chose to be sent to Ukrainian-controlled territory, although some opted for transfer to Russia. Currently, more than 1,000 people remain in Oleshky, according to Kherson's regional administration. They were supplied with food, water and medicine.

Melania Trump hailed the mission as a success, taking to social media to thank Kyiv and Moscow for their "leadership and cooperation." She said the Oleshky ceasefire could go on to inspire a "lasting peace between the two peoples."

Dmytro Lubinez similarly wrote on the Telegram messaging platform that it is "important to maintain this cooperation mechanism," adding that "we are currently exploring options with Yana Lantratova to continue similar humanitarian efforts."

Ukraine's Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets (center) poses for a photo with residents evacuated from the Russian-controlled city of Oleshky Image: Genya Savilov/AFP

The Kremlin, however, was quick to dampen any such expectations, making clear that no further plans for humanitarian missions exist at this stage.

Did Russia exploit the ceasefire to strengthen military hold?

One day after the ceasefire ended, Ukraine's general staff stated that Russia had "used the humanitarian pause to fortify its positions." It also said Russia had carried out troop rotations, expanded its anti-drone defenses, and brought in ammunition.

British broadcaster Sky News aired drone footage, produced with the support of the Ukrainian army, showing the Russian army transporting heavy equipment, weapons, personnel and food to Oleshky and neighboring villages.

"It was clear to the Ukrainian government and international mediators that Russia could exploit the pause in this way. But it was the right thing to do to allow people to leave the country," Volodymyr Vyatrovych of the Ukrainian European Solidarity opposition party wrote on Facebook.

Oleshky evacuees recount survival under occupation To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

He believes Russia would do the exact same thing if Kyiv were to withdraw its troops from the Donetsk region, as Russian President Vladimir Putin is demanding.

"Russia would use this to prepare for its next offensive, to further destroy Ukraine," Vyatrovych wrote. That said, humanitarian missions have their place, says Ihor Chalenko of the Ukrainian Center for Analysis and Strategies. "We shouldn't speak ill of the Oleshky mission, even though it's clear that the Russians have used the ceasefire in the occupied territories to their advantage," Chalenko told DW. That's why he says Kyiv should insist on banning such behavior in future ceasefires.

What did Washington and Moscow gain from the pause in fighting?

The Oleshky mission took place just shortly before US voters headed to the polls in the midterm elections. Dmytro Levus of the United Ukraine research center believes the timing was no coincidence. "The Russian side played right into the hands of US President Donald Trump, whose Republican Party was expected to face a crushing electoral defeat," Levus said.

Involving Melania in the mediation was a "subtle public relations move" for Trump, through which he hoped to score points ahead of the election, Levus explained. First Lady Melania Trump has long been an advocate for humanitarian causes.

First Lady Melania Trump played a leading role in the ceasfire deal Image: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Chalenko says the Oleshky ceasefire was in Washington's interest because it allowed Donald Trump to cast himself as a "peacemaker."

Moscow also hoped it could improve its image through the humanitarian mission, especially as it caused Oleshky's humanitarian catastrophe in the first place, Chalenko said. Rescuing civilians is intended to serve as proof that "not everything is bad in Russia."

What can the Ukrainian and Russian human rights commissioners accomplish?

Cooperation between the two human rights ombudspersons had reached "a new level," Chalenko said, adding that the Oleshky case was just one of several noteworthy examples that also included prisoner swaps and foreign representatives gaining access to Ukrainian political prisoners held in Russia.

He does not, however, believe that Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova makes her own decisions. "We are seeing a certain top-down realignment of Russian policy," Chalenko told DW. He also said it was important to further develop this communication channel. The lessons learned from the evacuation of Oleshky could be applied to other towns along the front, Chalenko believes.

Dmytro Levus says the Oleshky mission has proven that, if Moscow were so inclined, a ceasefire could be established along the entire front line. Yet Russia has so far shown no willingness in doing so, partly because Ukraine has not agreed to Putin's terms, Levus explains.

Will the ceasefire inject momentum into the upcoming talks?

Preparations are underway for a new round of negotiations between Ukraine, the US and Russia on November 10 and 11 in Abu Dhabi. Dmytro Levus believes the Oleshky ceasefire could provide substance to talks on humanitarian issues. He does not, however, think there will be much progress on a political level, even though he does see scope for a ceasefire at sea, for example.

Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpark Dmytro Lubinets speak to the press ahead of the evacuation Image: Office of the Ombudsman of Ukraine/AP Photo/picture alliance

Levus says that the US will be particularly keen to present further humanitarian successes. Ukraine may use the talks to negotiate a new prisoner exchange, though Levus says Russia will likely only budge under pressure.

Ihor Chalenko says one should not expect too much of the upcoming talks. He believes that Russia is looking for a pretext to withdraw from the negotiations, preferring instead to expand its cooperation with the US, without wanting to make any concessions to end the Ukraine war.

Samuel Greene of King's College London is similarly skeptical. "I assume that at some point, the Kremlin will come to realize that there is nothing left to gain on the battlefield and that they will have to reach an agreement."

"That moment hasn't yet come though," Greene told DW, adding that Russia was still trying to buy time by feigning a willingness to engage in dialogue with the US.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: El ‘gurú’ de las deportaciones masivas prepara su desembarco en España ante un posible gobierno de PP y Vox
World.content:
El austríaco Martin Sellner, referente de la ultraderecha europea, quiere abrir un centro de estudios para apoyar la expulsión de millones de personas de origen migrante, sobre todo africanos y latinoamericanos

Martin Sellner (Viena, 37 años) es uno de los intelectuales más influyentes en la política europea actual. Licenciado en Filosofía, condenado en su adolescencia por acciones neonazis, es el principal ideólogo detrás de la remigración, el concepto que enarbola la extrema derecha en media Europa para referirse a deportaciones masivas incluso de nacionales europeos. “La remigración, la desregulación y la prioridad nacional serán los ejes de Vox para el 29-N”, afirmó el 11 de octubre el partido de Santiago Abascal. Sellner explica en una entrevista con EL PAÍS que el centro de estudios que lidera, el Instituto para la Remigración, iniciará pronto sus actividades en España para promover la expulsión masiva de extranjeros.

La remigración de Sellner es un plan detallado para sacar de la Unión Europea “a muchos, muchos millones de migrantes”. No solo esto: su esquema para proteger “a los nativos, la cultura de referencia y la identidad nacional” de cada país europeo pasa por retirar la ciudadanía a millones de personas nacionalizadas y devolverlos al país de origen si no demuestran que se han asimilado.

El canciller alemán, Friedrich Merz, calificó la remigración el pasado septiembre como “sinónimo de limpieza étnica”.

“Estoy contento de que Merz reconociera la remigración como su archienemigo; dijo que la remigración es un ataque a la Alemania contemporánea, lo que significa que entiende que todo lo que él representa está en entredicho con la remigración”, afirma Sellner. Este niega que su idea sea una limpieza étnica pese a que, en su libro Remigración, una propuesta, plantea la expulsión de Alemania de siete millones de extranjeros en 15 años y varios millones de alemanes con raíces internacionales en tres décadas: “Hablar de limpieza étnica es algo muy grave y no es para tomárselo a la ligera. Lo que estamos exigiendo, aunque no les guste, aunque lo consideren cruel o extremista, no tiene nada que ver con matar a personas arbitrariamente ni expulsarlas de sus tierras por su origen étnico”.

Sellner actúa a partir del Instituto para la Remigración. Su sede se encuentra en Austria y en verano abrió su primera filial europea, en el Estado alemán de Sajonia-Anhalt. El centro de estudios llegó a este land poco antes de que AfD, el partido de la extrema derecha alemana, arrasara en los comicios generales de septiembre. AfD tiene altas probabilidades de gobernar en Sajonia-Anhalt y de ello se puede beneficiar, como comenta Sellner, el trabajo de su instituto.

Martin Sellner, fotografiado cerca del Palacio de Schönbrunn en Viena, Austria, el 27 de octubre. Fabian Weiss

Desde los partidos de izquierdas, Die Linke, SPD y los Verdes, se ha pedido la ilegalización del Instituto para la Remigración en Alemania. “Existen pruebas suficientes de que las propuestas inhumanas de remigración de Sellner atentan contra los pilares mismos de nuestra democracia”, afirmó en septiembre al medio Correctiv Marcel Emmerich, portavoz parlamentario de política de interior de Los Verdes.

La remigración formulada en etapas por Sellner es uno de los mantras de la extrema derecha alemana. La copresidenta de AfD Alice Weidel, en el pleno parlamentario en el que Merz la acusó de querer llevar a cabo una limpieza étnica, exigió la deportación inmediata de un millón de extranjeros solicitantes de asilo.

Mapa de la Reconquista

Que España es del interés de Sellner lo prueba también un detalle de su despacho: en una de las paredes cuelga un mapa de la Península Ibérica que ilustra las diferentes etapas de la Reconquista hasta el siglo XV.

Siguiendo el ejemplo de Sajonia-Anhalt, la próxima sede del Instituto para la Remigración que quiere inaugurar Sellner es en España, a rebufo de un hipotético futuro gobierno de PP y Vox: “Mi esperanza es que un próximo gobierno de derechas en España pueda ser más avanzado en materia de remigración”. De lo que está convencido es de que el país está dando señales de que cambiará a favor de sus tesis: “La situación es única en España porque ahora hay un Gobierno de izquierdas en pleno despertar paneuropeo en materia de remigración. Tenemos la crisis en Ceuta, que sigue muy presente. Cuando estuve en Málaga [a mediados de octubre], vi banderas de Ceuta por todas partes, en los balcones de los malagueños”.

Sellner está elaborando un documento sobre la crisis migratoria con propuestas específicas para España de la cantidad de personas que deben ser expulsadas. El grupo principal afectado sería el de los procedentes de todo el continente africano, aunque también la comunidad latinoamericana. El informe lo están elaborando colaboradores españoles de los que no quiere revelar su identidad.

La idea de Sellner es compartir este documento con partidos políticos. Confirma que mantiene contacto con Vox, pero tampoco quiere precisar cuáles son sus interlocutores. Sí cita la participación de la diputada responsable de política migratoria de la formación, Rocío de Meer, en la Cumbre de Remigración, una conferencia que organizó en Porto en mayo y a la que asistieron políticos de la ultraderecha europea.

De Meer reproduce en sus discursos muchas de las ideas que Sellner lleva años desarrollando, sobre todo las que hacen referencia al supuesto lastre económico de los extranjeros. El 21 de octubre, en la presentación de su candidatura a las elecciones por Almería, compartió la diputada de Vox un mensaje bajo el lema “remigración y prioridad nacional”: “La migración masiva y descontrolada es de una gravedad absoluta, es un mito que llevan tanto tiempo contando, que los migrantes vienen a contribuir a nuestro estado del bienestar”. “Todas estas personas que han venido a vivir del cuento, del esfuerzo de los españoles que madrugan, tendrán que marcharse a sus países”, añadió la diputada ultra.

De Meer copó titulares en 2025 al cuantificar en hasta ocho millones las personas que deben ser deportadas de España.

“Estoy en contacto con el ala prorremigración de casi todos los partidos políticos de derechas”, prosigue Sellner. “Intentamos unir a todos los afines, ayudarlos con datos, argumentos y sesiones informativas. Queremos hacerlo especialmente en España, teniendo en cuenta las elecciones que se avecinan”.

Sellner indica que sabe de la existencia de otro partido de extrema derecha en España, Aliança Catalana, pero cree que su independentismo hace de la relación con este “una cuestión complicada”.

Sellner visitó España en octubre para dar los primeros pasos de su desembarco. Celebra que pudo abrir sin problemas una cuenta bancaria. Según sus propias estimaciones, más de 130 sucursales bancarias en Alemania, Francia, Polonia, Lituania, Austria y Hungría le han vetado como cliente a él y a sus organizaciones.

La Sparkasse de Chemnitz, en el land de Sajonia, es una de estas entidades bancarias. “Como caja de ahorros, defendemos la diversidad y la democracia, defendemos los derechos humanos y la convivencia entre diferentes culturas. Nuestros empleados y clientes proceden de 80 países de todo el mundo”, dijo en junio una portavoz de la caja al diario Süddeutsche Zeitung para justificar el veto.

Sellner también tiene prohibida la entrada al Reino Unido y Canadá porque sus Gobiernos consideran que sus propuestas atentan contra los derechos humanos. El 29 de octubre, al aterrizar en Francia en avión procedente de Viena, la policía lo retuvo y le obligó a salir del país. Las autoridades habían cancelado una conferencia y una manifestación por la remigración convocada en París para el 31 de octubre.

En Alemania, además de deportar a millones, establece Sellner en su libro que una cifra correcta de nuevos migrantes sería de 20.000 personas al año, una cifra residual que llevaría al país, en términos de flujo de población, a cifras nunca vistas en su siglo y medio de historia.

“Cuando comes mucho durante mucho tiempo, sabes que luego tienes que comer menos, tal vez menos de lo que has comido nunca para que tu cuerpo vuelva a estar en forma”, dice Sellner, “esto sería una respuesta a las cifras masivas de migración de las últimas décadas, por eso tiene que reducirse a casi cero”. Su planteamiento es que España debe seguir este camino, y para ello confía en un cambio de gobierno.

World.title: Así se prepara la banca para los próximos años
World.content:
El avance de la inteligencia artificial en bancos como CaixaBank convive con iniciativas de inclusión como SVisual, el servicio de videointerpretación en lengua de signos.

Más educación financiera, planes acordes con la mayor longevidad de la población y digitalización inclusiva. En el horizonte, las entidades bancarias quieren pasar de un papel reactivo a otro más proactivo que acompañe, oriente y anticipe las necesidades de los clientes

La banca del futuro se imagina a menudo dominada por los algoritmos. Sin embargo, cuando se escucha a los expertos y a quienes la construyen, brota un cariz más humano: todos coinciden en que será híbrida. La tecnología es eficaz en lo cotidiano, está disponible a cualquier hora, concede una autonomía impensable hace unos años, cuando la relación con el banco tenía el rostro del trabajador y no una interfaz. Sin embargo, hay circunstancias —las decisiones más vitales— en las que se prioriza el trato personal. Son momentos en los que la conversación con alguien que orienta adquiere un valor irremplazable. Por eso, entidades como CaixaBank entienden el mañana como una suma compleja: más tecnología y más innovación sin desdeñar la posibilidad de acceder a especialistas y gestores cuando sean necesarios.

La inteligencia artificial (IA) permitirá que la relación sea más sencilla y personalizada, pronostican desde CaixaBank. Su cambio estructural consistirá en pasar de una banca principalmente reactiva, en la que el cliente busca una solución cuando surge una necesidad, a una banca con mayor capacidad para acompañar, orientar y anticiparse. Imaginan una relación en la que el banco tenga más capacidad de acompañar de forma proactiva.

Las funciones de esos modelos inteligentes ayudarán a traducir información compleja, a facilitar la comparación entre alternativas y a generar recomendaciones más adaptadas a cada perfil, como anuncian desde este banco. Como concreta Alejandro San Nicolás, docente del máster en Formación Permanente en IA para el Sector Financiero de la Universidad Internacional de Valencia (VIU), la banca conocerá mejor al usuario a través de sus hábitos, comportamientos, emociones y tendencias de consumo. Este docente añade que los entornos bancarios evolucionarán hacia una suerte de marketplace, donde el cliente podrá contratar productos, realizar compras o acceder a financiación directamente desde la plataforma digital bancaria pertinente: “El propio banco va a empezar a lanzarte ofertas basadas en tus necesidades y en lo que te gusta”, explica San Nicolás.

Las entidades financieras aspiran a esa hiperpersonalización que, como señalan desde CaixaBank, “da la oportunidad de reducir ruido y proporcionar al cliente sólo la información apropiada para su situación personal”. Por eso, insisten en que la formación en competencias digitales, la educación financiera y la prevención del fraude son también una parte crucial de ese nuevo acompañamiento.

Habla

Cómo construir una banca integradora, según CaixaBank La evolución de la interfaz Habrá una generalización del móvil como canal financiero. Las plataformas digitales seguirán en constante cambio. Evolucionará con los agentes de IA, que podrán interpretar necesidades, mantener conversaciones complejas y simplificar procesos completos. Su actuación reducirá la complejidad de gestiones que hoy requieren múltiples pasos. Una longevidad diversa Llegados a la jubilación, se generan necesidades que van más allá del dinero. Por eso, desde la entidad se trata de fomentar el ahorro desde edades tempranas, complementar ingresos en la jubilación, ayudar a optimizar el patrimonio financiero e inmobiliario o acompañar a las personas durante toda esa etapa posterior a la laboral. Un error común es considerar que todas las personas mayores son iguales, señalan desde CaixaBank. Algunos se sienten cómodos con los entornos digitales, otros prefieren la atención telefónica y algunos exigen presencialidad. El colectivo senior es especialmente diverso en cuanto a autonomía financiera y uso de canales. Atención a las necesidades específicas CaixaBank hace hincapié en la inclusión: el 94% de sus oficinas, el 99% de sus cajeros y su aplicación móvil CaixaBankNow son accesibles.
