Además, dispone de la Tarjeta Braille para personas con discapacidad visual, el servicio de videointerpretación en lengua de signos SVisual para clientes con discapacidad auditiva, TPV accesibles, comunicaciones en lectura fácil, una guía adaptada para ayudar en la toma de decisiones financieras y el programa Día a Día Apoyo Capacidad Jurídica. La transformación de las sucursales Las oficinas físicas evolucionarán, aunque seguirán desempeñando un papel importante. CaixaBank tiene más de 4.200, repartidas por España. Además, la entidad tiene presencia en cerca de 3.700 municipios: en 2.234 localidades con el modelo tradicional y en más de 1.420 poblaciones a través de 32 oficinas móviles. Estas permiten a clientes (y no clientes) realizar las operaciones bancarias más habituales en localidades sin oficina bancaria o con restricciones que limitan el acceso a los servicios financieros en poblaciones en las que residen más de 632.000 personas. El 70% de los usuarios tienen más de 65 años.

Mantener la confianza... ‘online’

Dar cierta credibilidad a la IA es fundamental para que su implantación sea efectiva. Pero trabajar en entornos tecnológicos plantea riesgos relacionados con la privacidad, la seguridad de los datos y la posible sensación de vigilancia excesiva, como enumera Juan Carlos López-Robles, profesor de ESIC University que imparte en ámbitos como la Informática Aplicada, las Tecnologías de la Educación y las Tecnologías Móviles e Internet de las Cosas (IoT).

Los ingredientes para que la IA tenga una buena integración, según López-Robles, son tres: que sus respuestas sean útiles, que se comprendan sin necesidad de tener un alto nivel de conocimientos específicos y que sean transparentes. “Los usuarios aceptamos mejor una recomendación cuando entendemos el porqué, el para qué y tenemos la sensación de control sobre la decisión final”. Y añade: “La confianza se construye con explicaciones claras y resultados consistentes “. Hay una necesidad de entender los criterios, de conocer las reglas del juego de algoritmos.

Los usuarios están dispuestos a compartir información cuando perciben un beneficio claro y confían en la entidad. Por eso, para CaixaBank, “la personalización solo tendrá recorrido si va acompañada de seguridad, privacidad, transparencia y capacidad de control por parte del cliente”. Un ejemplo de su compromiso es su nueva Dirección de IA y Datos, que coordina de forma transversal esta área y facilita el desarrollo de soluciones escalables, seguras y responsables. Gestiona todo el ciclo de vida de las iniciativas, desde la identificación de oportunidades hasta su diseño, implantación y supervisión. Además, integra el cumplimiento normativo y la gestión de riesgos desde las fases iniciales; se asegura de que los desarrollos sean responsables.

La IA se emplea con criterio, pero también permite al banco ser más seguro. La han incorporado a sus sistemas de defensa para reforzar las tareas de detección, análisis, actuación y para proteger los nuevos entornos. También vigila los agentes, una función que, más allá de responder a preguntas como un chat tradicional, razona, planifica y ejecuta acciones de forma autónoma para cumplir un propósito. Estos sistemas incorporan herramientas como la identificación y corrección automatizadas de vulnerabilidades, la evolución de su centro de operaciones de seguridad y el empleo de sistemas capaces de detectar indicios de actividad sospechosa, correlacionar señales, evaluar amenazas y activar medidas de protección de manera autónoma.

Sobre todo, inciden en que combinan la capacidad analítica de la IA con la supervisión y responsabilidad humanas. En esa mezcla está la virtud, secunda López-Robles: “Nadie quiere pedir cita para hacer una transferencia o revisar los movimientos de la cuenta, pero casi todo el mundo quiere hablar con una persona antes de firmar una hipoteca o una cartera de inversión”.

La atención presencial no puede desaparecer, reconocen los expertos, pero su transformación es inevitable. “Dará paso a una red mucho más reducida, orientada a un trato más personal, en un espacio con sofás y en los que le ofrecen un café”, describe San Nicolás. De ahí que sean fundamentales las citas previas; serán más puntuales, planificadas y especializadas.

Las entidades financieras se adaptan a los nuevos hábitos y refuerzan sus servicios digitales. CaixaBank aumentó en un 30% las altas digitales en el ejercicio 2025, en gran parte gracias a imagin, el banco digital del grupo dirigido especialmente a clientes jóvenes, que cuenta con alrededor de 4,3 millones de clientes. La penetración en el Grupo CaixaBank de clientes financieros de edad de entre 16 y 34 años alcanza el 42%. La tendencia online también se aprecia en los hábitos de pago. En junio, CaixaBank superó el récord histórico de pago con el móvil en España, con 139,7 millones de operaciones en un mes.

La generación de transición

¿Quiénes son los que se pueden sentir más abrumados por los cambios? San Nicolás, como experto en IA para el sector financiero, señala que los que están “en tierra de nadie”. Por ejemplo: “Los mayores de 50 años, una generación que ha visto llegar toda esta transformación cuando ya tenía gran parte de su vida financiera construida”.

La tecnología puede convertirse en una nueva forma de exclusión, advierte López-Robles, profesor de ESIC. “A medida que aumente el número de personas mayores, la clave no será ofrecer más tecnología, sino hacerla accesible, dinámica, sencilla y fluida”, sostiene. Es uno de los motivos que lleva a CaixaBank a ir más allá de la jubilación, que les mueve a planificar una etapa de la vida cada vez más larga y diversa y apostar por un acompañamiento integral. Para López-Robles, el objetivo que se deben proponer las entidades es construir una banca “no solo más digital, sino más inteligente, más sencilla y, sobre todo, más relevante para cada cliente”.

World.title: El euríbor me está comiendo. ¿Puedo vender mi vivienda y comprar otra acogiéndome a las ayudas del Gobierno?
World.content:
Los lectores envían sus preguntas al consultorio de vivienda de EL PAÍS en colaboración con Legálitas

Pregunta. Quiero preguntar por las ayudas para la compra de vivienda aprobadas por el Gobierno. Quiero vender la mía porque las subidas del euríbor me comen. ¿Podría acogerme a esta ayuda si compro una casa, después de vender mi vivienda habitual? S. Navarro

Respuesta. Los programas de ayuda para la adquisición de la primera vivienda se diseñan bajo el principio de “primer acceso a la propiedad”. Por ello, vender una vivienda para comprar otra no permite recuperar la condición de comprador de primera vivienda a efectos de estas ayudas.

En el caso de las ayudas específicas para la primera vivienda, la norma general es clara: no podría acogerse a ellas si ya es o ha sido propietario de una vivienda. Tanto el préstamo público al 0% para comprar la primera vivienda como la línea de avales que cubre hasta el 20% del valor de tasación del inmueble, permitiendo que la entidad financiera pueda llegar a conceder una financiación de hasta el 100% del precio de compra, están destinados a la compra de la primera vivienda.

Por lo que nos indica, ya es titular de una vivienda que actualmente constituye su residencia habitual. Por lo tanto, la adquisición de una nueva vivienda tras la venta de la actual no tendría la consideración de primera vivienda, requisito esencial para acceder a estas ayudas. Así que, en principio, no podría acogerse.

En cuanto a la edad, el límite general suele situarse en los 35 años, aunque algunas comunidades autónomas y determinados programas lo amplían hasta los 40 años. Entre ellos destacan:

Avales ICO (hasta el 20% de la entrada): exigen tener, con carácter general, 35 años o menos en el momento de la solicitud, si bien algunas comunidades autónomas permiten acceder hasta los 40 años.

Plan Estatal de Vivienda (ayudas directas a la compra): las subvenciones destinadas a la compra de vivienda en municipios de menos de 10.000 habitantes requieren que el solicitante sea menor de 35 años.

Respecto a la ayuda de 50.000 euros, se trata de la Línea TU CASA (Real Decreto-ley 29/2026). Es importante señalar que no es una subvención a fondo perdido, sino un préstamo que debe devolverse. Estos son los requisitos de la Línea TU CASA:

Que sea primera vivienda. Está destinada a quienes acceden por primera vez a una vivienda en propiedad. Que constituya vivienda habitual. No puede destinarse a segunda residencia ni a inversión. Que la compra se formalice mediante hipoteca. Esta línea complementa la financiación bancaria, pero no la sustituye. No existe límite de edad. La normativa establece expresamente que puede solicitarse con independencia de la edad del comprador. Superar el análisis de solvencia del ICO. El Instituto de Crédito Oficial evaluará cada solicitud conforme a los criterios y condiciones establecidos para esta línea de financiación.

Por tanto, si ya ha sido propietario de una vivienda, aunque la venda para adquirir otra, no cumpliría el requisito de acceso como comprador de primera vivienda, exigido por la mayoría de estas ayudas.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: Unfair rent clauses: why thousands of tenants may get money back
World.content:
Did you know that, as a renter, you may be entitled to money back? Read on to see if you qualify.

It all centres on unfair clauses regarding rent increases and recent legal rulings – to the benefit of renters.

Dutch courts, including the Supreme Court, have ruled that a clause in private-sector leases allowing an annual rent increase in line with the Consumer Price Index (consumentenprijsindex, CPI) plus a surcharge of up to 3% is, as a rule, not unfair.

A higher surcharge, though, may be deemed unfair: in December 2025, the Amsterdam Court of Appeal held a surcharge of up to 5% unfair.

“If you believe you paid too much based on an unfair rental clause, you can claim money back,” says Robert Berendsen, founder of Mr. Berendsen Advocaten in Amsterdam. “Many tenants don’t realise they have strong protections in this tight housing market.”

The high court rules

When the Supreme Court made that ruling in November 2024, it set a legal precedent: the CPI and the additional surcharge can be split, meaning that even if the CPI is legal, the surcharge can be seen as unfairly burdensome.

“Until then, that was deemed legally impossible,” says Berendsen of the fair-unfair division. “There was huge interest in the outcome of this case. Hundreds of thousands of tenants may be owed money. Which means potentially hundreds of millions of euros paid out. It has a huge economic impact.”

Most affected would be landlords, housing associations and investors, who would have to return the money.

DIY

Berendsen advises tenants to check their leases and see what surcharge on top of inflation the rent increase clause allows. If it’s more than 3%, enter your data into your AI program of choice and let modern technology do the rest.

“Enter the start date of your lease, the initial rent excluding service charges and every annual increase,” says Berendsen. “Then ask: ‘suppose the rent had only been increased with inflation each year, without the surcharge. What would the rent be today, and how much did I overpay?’”

Only the surcharge can be reclaimed; the inflation increases stand.

“If you believe you are owed money for the unfair surcharges only, write a letter to your landlord. If they don’t react or decline, says Berendsen, you (the tenant) can take the claim to the subdistrict court (kantonrechter). In all cases concerning a lease, even those brought by a landlord, the court must check whether the surcharge clause is unfair, even if the tenant does not raise the issue.”

The future

In July 2026, the Amsterdam District Court referred questions regarding “the splitting of the rent change clause and whether the clause is unfair or not” to the Court of Justice of the European Union in Luxembourg in the cases of 19 tenants seeking a refund.

While any decision is likely years away, Berendsen advises tenants not to worry. “The Supreme Court’s ruling is the starting point for tenants; I do not expect the EU court to make their position worse,” he says.

“The idea behind the rules is that tenants operate in a tight market, and it’s not reasonable to expect them to vacate their rental homes if they don’t agree with rent increases,” says Berendsen. “Tenants must be protected from unfair practices.”

If you want legal help from an actual person, contact Mr. Berendsen Advocaten.

World.title: KLM to cut 5,000 jobs amid high fuel prices and global unrest
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

National airline KLM is slashing around 5,000 jobs, almost 15% of its workforce, in a move the company says is necessary to survive.

CEO Marjan Rintel announced in a press release on Thursday that without serious action the airline, which was founded in 1919 and is one of the oldest in the aviation industry, could fold.

High fuel prices and global unrest are major factors in pressure the company is facing.

KLM was effectively taken over by Air France in 2004, though the Dutch brand kept its own name and management. Of the jobs being cut, 2,000 will be moved to the Air-France KLM group.

Labour unions have expressed concern about the move, with FNV and CNV saying workers are footing the bill for a major corporation.

KLM says compulsory layoffs likely won’t be needed, and that voluntary departure schemes and not replacing staff who leave will help make the needed cuts.

World.title: Human rights orgs cut ties with ICC under US sanctions pressure
World.content:
At least 20 human rights organizations have ended or considerably reduced cooperation with the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague over US-imposed sanctions against the court and its employees, and that may just be the tip of the iceberg.

So found investigative journalism platform Investico and German daily Süddeutsche Zeitung after surveying 100 non-profit organizations, including big names like Human Rights Watch and the Center for Constitutional Rights.

The Trump administration has declared war on what it calls a “rogue court”, sanctioning judges, prosecutors, human rights organisations and, in October, the court as a whole.

“They want more power, and they want it at the expense of our sovereignty as a nation,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio wrote on X at the time.

“And President Trump will never allow the ICC to prosecute Americans… We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources, and crippling their ability to operate against us. The United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC.”

ICC employees have faced visa restrictions, a loss of access to their American property and financial assets and seen their accounts with American financial service institutions cut as a result of the sanctions, with one judge saying she lost access to all her American credit cards earlier this year.

Human rights organizations

While human rights organizations don’t work directly for the court, they provide valuable information in criminal cases, including eyewitness testimony and local law knowhow.

“They are a very important part of our work,” former Chief Prosecutor Fatou Bensouda told Investico. “They do not conduct investigations on our behalf, but they do provide us with leads, which help us find ways to substantiate evidence.”

Bensouda worked at the ICC until 2021 and was herself sanctioned by the US in 2020, which froze her American assets.

Chilling effect

Some organizations not directly covered by the sanctions have also stopped cooperating with the ICC.

“We cannot accept the risk of being sanctioned ourselves and that all our other work is at risk,” a German NGO told the researchers.

Save the Children Netherlands also says it is struggling to find new ways of working with the court.

As the host country of the ICC, the Netherlands is obliged to protect the court’s work from “interference”. But a spokesperson for the foreign affairs ministry told Investico that the country bears “no special responsibility as a host country” to protect NGOs from the consequences of sanctions.

Midterm elections

While Democrats won control of the US House and Senate in this week’s midterm elections, that won’t change the current sanctions.

“That foreign policy is firmly in the hands of the White House,” legal historian Iva Vukušić from Utrecht University told Dutch News. “But the election results may distract the White House with domestic issues and investigations against them and whatnot. It also changes the mood of invincibility of the White House and that may hold them back a bit.”

World.title: Half of rental agents willing to exclude foreign tenants: study
World.content:
Almost half of rental agents contacted for a government-commissioned study were willing to discriminate against potential tenants with foreign roots, researchers have found.

The study, conducted by the Verwey-Jonker Institute, used actors posing as landlords to phone rental agents and ask them if they could avoid renting to “foreigners; Moroccans, Turks or Poles”.

They found that 97 out of 200 agreed outright with the request. Another 30% didn’t refuse, mostly saying it was up to the landlord, and only 20% said no.

“Expat” privileges

In 36 of the cases, agents distinguished “expats” as good foreign tenants, describing them as highly educated and well paid, with reliable employers. Some also said they tend to leave after a while, which they presented as a way around the 2024 ban on most temporary leases.

“Let me put your mind at rest, neither do we,” one agent told an actor who said they did not have a good feeling about foreigners. “The foreigners we usually talk about are the expats, who just come here to work for the big companies.”

Another said: “Officially we’re not allowed to discriminate, of course, but if you say you don’t want people from certain types of countries, I don’t need to put them forward to you.”

Moroccan-sounding names

In separate tests on 1,662 listings on the rental site Pararius between December and May, applicants with Moroccan-sounding names were invited to viewings less often than otherwise identical applicants with Dutch-sounding names.

For men, there were 14% of cases where only the Dutch-named applicant got an invitation, and 16% for women. Last year’s monitor found no significant discrimination against any group for the first time. The researchers found none this year against Polish-sounding names or same-sex couples.

Findings of the investigations were sent to MPs on Wednesday.

A majority of MPs are seeking to have soon-to-be-redundant civil servants at the education, culture and science ministry (OCW) retrained as teachers.

The VVD will bring the proposal, which also has the backing of political parties D66, CDA, JA21 and 50Plus, the to the cabinet Thursday.

VVD MP Arend Kisteman believes the plan will “kill two birds with one stone”.

“The announced cuts are a great opportunity to have these enthusiastic people voluntarily retrained for a job in education at the expense of the government,” Kisteman told broadcaster NOS.

The cabinet plans to eliminate 25,000 civil servants over the next nine years, a cut of some 16% by 2035. The OCW will not be spared.

Supporters say retraining already enthusiastic education workers as teachers will help alleviate chronic teacher shortages nationwide, especially in the country’s big cities.

But similar past initiatives have gotten low marks over schools’ reluctance to hire people with little to no classroom experience and civil servants’ reluctance to take salary cuts.

World.title: Disgruntled estate agents plan rival to property site Funda
World.content:
A group of disgruntled real estate brokers is starting a rival online real estate marketplace to the dominant Funda, saying it is “building a platform in which the broker is no longer a cash cow but is at the helm.”

The new platform, called Homek, is expected to launch in March 2027. For now, it’s appealing to brokers to join the platform, with RTL Z reporting that it won’t launch until at least 1,000 agents have bought in or the foundation has raised €1 million.

The increasing price of placing a property on Funda is one of the irritants that led the brokers to start the rival site.

“Homek is the fair, transparent alternative to Funda, without expensive packages or paid priority,” says Homek’s website, which currently doesn’t list any properties for sale or rent.

Only certified brokers affiliated with industry associations can use Homek, unlike Funda, where unaffiliated real estate agents who meet the site’s conditions can place properties.

Brokers on Homek will also share in the profits.

“The high placement costs and priority paid at Funda require an alternative: a housing platform where real estate agents themselves are in charge,” says Homek’s website. It promises “fair rates, equal opportunities and control for the affiliated brokers and offices.”

Supply problems

Funda was established in 2001 by the brokers’ association NVM.

“As brokers, we came up with Funda ourselves,” says Toine Naber, former chairman of the NVM branch in West-Brabant and a past member of Funda’s advisory board. “With Homek, we get the chance to do it again, but this time without giving away control of our own future.”

Sven Heinen, who is slated to be chairman of the Homek Foundation, told RTL Z he recognises that to become successful, Homek must have the goods to offer home buyers or renters.

“In the past, there have been plenty of competitors of Funda who wanted to take a piece of this market, but they all stalled because the supply was too limited,” Heinen says. “Only when many real estate agents join us and share their housing supply…can we become a serious competitor of Funda.”

Heinen says that within 48 hours, they’ve already raised €200,000.

Funda says it’s not worried about the competition for now. “In a healthy market, there is competition, and sometimes new players join,” spokesperson Claire Verhagen told RTL Z. “We look forward to that with confidence.”

World.title: Coalition parties ready to vote against each other on tax plans
World.content:
The ruling coalition parties have signalled they could vote against one another on amendments to the 2027 tax plan before parliament votes on it next week, after a debate that went ran late into Wednesday night.

Prime minister Rob Jetten’s centrist social-liberal D66 and the centrist Christian Democrat CDA said they could back opposition amendments even if their coalition partner, the right-wing liberal VVD, voted against them, broadcaster NOS reported.

“It is not an unthinkable situation,” D66 finance spokesman Henk-Jan Oosterhuis said after repeated questions from MPs. “The coalition is not a merger party.” CDA MP Inge van Dijk said split voting was “certainly not the intention” but did not rule it out.

Senate hurdle

The tax plan sets income tax rates and other levies for next year, and must be passed in time for the tax office to bring in the changes. If it fails, the cabinet will almost certainly fall, NRC reported.

Earlier this week the cabinet offered about €350 million in concessions to opposition parties on the left and right, which have formed rival blocs and demanded that the coalition choose between them.

The coalition holds 66 of the 150 seats in parliament. It now looks likely to win next week’s vote with the help of the ChristenUnie, 50PLUS and the group led by former PVV MP Gidi Markuszower. But that is not enough in the senate, where it needs the support of either Pro and Volt or the BBB.

Left-wing parties attacked the coalition for relying on Markuszower, after MPs, including the coalition parties, voted earlier this year against deals with politicians who call for violence against refugees. Markuszower had said Palestinian refugees should be stopped “with maximum violence”, the Volkskrant reported. Pro, Denk and the PvdD said extra police funding credited to him amounted to buying his support.

Oosterhuis said there was “no agreement” with Markuszower, but added: “If Mr Markuszower wants to support the tax plan, I am not going to ask him to vote against it.”

Wealth tax offer

The Pro and Volt alliance used the debate to table an amendment that would shift €1.5 billion of tax from workers to the wealthiest. Income tax would be lowered, paid for by a higher tax rate on the largest fortunes, higher tax on business owners’ income from their companies and an end to tax breaks on passing on family businesses.

The VVD’s Wendy van Eijk said it was “unthinkable” that any coalition party would back the proposal “in this form”, and that her party would not support higher taxes on wealth.

Parliament votes on each amendment before voting on the plan as a whole. That means the VVD could vote against a wealth tax rise but still back the final plan, if D66 and the CDA help the amendment through.

MPs vote on the tax plan on November 12, and the senate in the week before Christmas.

World.title: Sunny end to week, but near-freezing nights ahead
World.content:
Thursday and Friday will be sunny and dry across the Netherlands, but temperatures won’t rise past 10° and could drop close to freezing overnight, according to the KNMI forecast issued at 6am on Thursday.

The national weather institute KNMI said Thursday afternoon would bring plenty of sunshine, with a high of around 10°. Wind from the east will make it feel colder.

Thursday night will stay dry. Temperatures will fall to near freezing in the east, and stay at about 6° on the Wadden islands. Fog is possible in the far southwest.

Friday will be sunny and dry again. Highs will range from 8° in the far north to 12° in the southeast. Clouds will build in the southwest late in the afternoon.

Saturday may start with fog, mainly in the south and southwest, and some frost is possible inland, the KNMI said.

Chinese fast fashion platform Shein has announced a €500 million (2.2 billion zloty) investment to expand its logistics centre in Poland, a move it says will create around 2,000 new jobs by the end of this year. The announcement comes amid growing controversy over the impact of Chinese e-commerce platforms on European businesses and follows a recent decision by the European Union to introduce a special fee on low-value parcels sent from outside the EU and European Free Trade Area. SHEIN investește 500 mil. euro în Polonia. Extinde hub-ul logistic europeanhttps://t.co/WNbib4dFta pic.twitter.com/KiI1AB4wFM — Cristi Dorombach (@piticu21) November 4, 2026 The investment will expand Shein’s existing logistics facility in Magnice, near the city of Wrocław in southwestern Poland, which has been operating since 2022. The expansion will bring total employment at the site to around 10,000 by creating 2,000 jobs in logistics, supply chain management, technology and warehouse operations, according to local news service Wroclaw.pl. The facility will also host 6,500 autonomous robots for sorting items. Shein says that the move will help it cut delivery times in Europe, allowing some orders to arrive within 48 hours. “This investment in Poland clearly demonstrates our commitment and belief in the potential of the European market,” said Leonard Lin, the firm’s global head of public affairs. “Poland has become one of the pillars of our operations in Europe,” he added. “This latest investment is a testament to our confidence in the country’s potential, the competencies of its workforce, and its business environment.” The expansion comes as Shein faces a tougher trading environment in Europe. Its sales in the region fell by 13.9% year-on-year to $3.77 billion in the second quarter, while net profit dropped by 67%. The decline comes as the EU steps up efforts to curb the influx of low-cost imports from Chinese platforms such as Shein, Temu and AliExpress, which European retailers say pose unfair competition. In July, the bloc introduced a €3 fee on parcels worth less than €150. From 1 November, a further €2 handling fee was added to all imported parcels, regardless of their value, to cover customs processing costs. China overtook Germany to become Poland’s biggest source of imports for the first time in July, ending a period of around 35 years in which Germany had consistently held top spot https://t.co/U6rQwfEJ7I — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 16, 2026 Shein has also faced accusations of labour-law violations at its facilities in China, including concerns that it may use cotton produced through forced labour. The company disputes many of the allegations, saying that it prohibits forced and child labour and regularly inspects working conditions at its suppliers. China is an increasingly important trading partner in Poland. In July, it overtook Germany to become Poland’s largest source of imports for the first time, driven by rising purchases of cars, computer hardware and consumer goods. Poland has detained and charged six people – five Poles and one Russian – suspected of running an operation to illegally supply Russia with military components. Investigators say that over 2 million zloty (€450,000) worth of equipment was smuggled into the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. The arrests, which took place on 21 October and 2 November, were announced on Thursday morning by Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) and National Prosecutor’s Office. 🚨 ROSYJSKI WYWIAD. PRZEMYT CZĘŚCI DO PRODUKCJI UZBROJENIA. 6 ZATRZYMANYCH.@ABW_GOV_PL rozbiła grupę podejrzaną o działalność na rzecz rosyjskich służb specjalnych. 🔴6⃣ osób zatrzymanych, 🔴2⃣1⃣przeszukanych lokalizacji, 🔴 4⃣osoby z zarzutami szpiegostwa – wszystkie trafiły… pic.twitter.com/L90n3rf5rY — ABW (@ABW_GOV_PL) November 5, 2026 Prosecutors report that all six suspects have been charged with participating in an organised criminal group that sought to export weapon components from Poland to Russia in violation of a ban on such trade. Four of the suspects have also been charged under Poland’s espionage law, accused of acting on behalf of Russian intelligence in return for financial benefits. Those four individuals have been placed in pretrial detention. The other two were released with preventative measures put in place. The ABW says that the criminal group “illegally supplied Russia with significant quantities of military components, including those used in the production of ammunition and weapons systems”. “This type of activity may lead to the strengthening of the Russian arms industry and the military capabilities of the Russian Federation, and thus pose a serious threat to Poland’s security and interests,” wrote the agency. Prosecutors say that the group operated at least between June 2023 and December 2025 in Poland, Lithuania and Russia. Members were responsible for procuring goods and transporting them to Kaliningrad, which borders Poland and Lithuania. “Vehicles equipped with hidden compartments were used to transport the goods,” wrote the prosecutor’s office. “The suspects repeatedly crossed the Polish-Russian border, and some of the transports were intercepted by Polish border guards.” Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister in charge of the security services, revealed that the six suspects include five Polish citizens, aged 25 to 52, and one Russian woman, aged 37. Onet, a leading news website, reports, based on unnamed sources, that the Russian citizen acted as a liaison between the group and the foreign intelligence agency behind the operation. Funkcjonariusze @ABW_GOV_PL zatrzymali 6 osób podejrzanych o udział w zorganizowanej grupie przestępczej działającej przeciwko Rzeczypospolitej Polskiej. Wśród zatrzymanych jest pięciu Polaków w wieku od 25 do 52 lat i 37-letnia Rosjanka. 🛑 Sąd – pod zarzutem szpiegostwa -… — Tomasz Siemoniak (@TomaszSiemoniak) November 5, 2026 Poland has seen a huge rise in espionage cases in recent years. The ABW launched 48 investigations related to espionage last year, more than twice as many as in 2024. In those two years taken together, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined. Last month, a Polish man was jailed for five and a half years for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of an airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland. In July, a Russian married couple with refugee status in Poland were convicted of working as spies on behalf of Moscow. In October, a member of Poland’s military reserve, who holds both Polish and Ukrainian citizenship, was detained on suspicion of espionage. World.title: Polish far-right leader Braun to face second trial
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun will again stand trial, after prosecutors filed an indictment against him for a series of anti-Ukrainian, anti-Jewish, anti-LGBT and anti-EU acts committed during his presidential election campaign last year. Braun is already separately on trial for a number of other alleged crimes, including an attack on a Jewish religious ceremony in parliament. He is also facing further charges for a range of other alleged offences. Grzegorz Braun stanie przed sądem. Prokuratura Okręgowa w Warszawie skierowała dziś akt oskarżenia za zuchwałą kradzież flag Ukrainy w Białej Podlaskiej i Unii Europejskiej w Katowicach, zniszczenie wystawy LGBT w Sejmie oraz zniesławienie organizatorów akcji Żonkile i Muzeum… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) November 4, 2026 On Wednesday, the district prosecutor’s office in Warsaw announced that it had indicted Braun for four alleged crimes. It was able to do so after the European Parliament, where Braun sits as an MEP, stripped him of immunity earlier this year. One of the charges, for criminal defamation, stems from Braun’s claim, during a televised presidential debate in April last year, that the yellow paper daffodils distributed each year in Warsaw to mark the anniversary of the 1943 Jewish Ghetto Uprising against German Nazi rule are “symbols of shame”. Prosecutors say that Braun’s words were “extremely xenophobic, manipulative and aggressive”, and that they defamed the organisers of the daffodil campaign, in particular the POLIN Museum of the History of Polish Jews in Warsaw. During the same debate, Braun also warned about the “Judaisation” of Poland, saying that “Jews have far too much say in Polish affairs”. That prompted protests by some of his opponents, one of whom filed a notification to prosecutors. Two other charges relate to thefts of flags. In one incident, Braun and his supporters removed a Ukrainian flag hanging outside city hall in the town of Biała Podlaska during a campaign event. In another, he removed a European Union flag from the industry ministry in the city of Katowice and set it on fire. Braun regularly rails against what he calls the “Ukrainisation” of Poland, warning of the supposed dangers of having so many Ukrainian refugees and migrants in the country. He is also a vocal critic of the EU. On those and other issues, Braun’s rhetoric often echoes Russian propaganda. The final charge, of destruction of property, relates to an incident in June 2025, when Braun vandalised an exhibition about the LGBT+ community in the Polish parliament. He regularly condemns what he calls the “perversions” of LGBT+ people, and has called for homosexuality to be criminalised. The European Parliament has again stripped Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun of immunity to face charges of denying Nazi crimes. The decision marks the sixth time it has lifted Braun’s immunity, and the second time for charges of Holocaust denial https://t.co/O9FN1YbchE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 16, 2026 The charges Braun faces carry prison sentences of up to five years in the case of destruction of property, and up to one year in the case of criminal defamation and theft. Additionally, the deputy leader of Braun’s Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party, Roman Fritz, was indicted for assisting in the theft of the EU flag, while four other men (who have not waived their right to anonymity under Polish law) were indicted for their alleged roles in stealing both the EU and Ukrainian flags. All four incidents for which Braun has been indicted took place when he was campaigning for the May 2025 presidential elections, in which he finished a surprise fourth, with 6.3% of the vote. Since then, KKP has continued to perform strongly in polls, with its support currently standing at around 9%. If it obtained that kind of result at next year’s parliamentary elections, it would be likely to play a major role in deciding what kind of government could be formed. Our essential guide to Poland's parliamentary elections, which will take place one year from now. How does voting work? What do polls suggest the outcome will be? Which issues may animate the campaign? And what role will President Nawrocki play? https://t.co/fmdoFpBaxz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2026 Much of Braun’s political brand has been built around provocative statements and actions. The politician is already on trial for his attack on a Jewish Hanukkah ceremony taking place in parliament, at which he put out the candles with a fire extinguisher. In their statement on Wednesday, the Warsaw prosecutor’s office noted that the latest hearings in that trial had been cancelled after Braun presented a medical certificate justifying his absence. However, the prosecutors pointed out that, last Friday, the day that the hearings had been due to begin, Braun attended a protest by opposition supporters outside the Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw, which that evening had been taken over by government-backed judges. Braun was pictured “jostling with police riot police, addressing the crowd and giving interviews”, showing “no signs of health problems that would prevent him from attending the hearing”, wrote the prosecutors. They have therefore asked the court to investigate the doctor who issued the medical certificate. Polish political leaders have reacted to the results of Tuesday’s US midterm elections, in which the Democrats won control of both houses of Congress from President Donald Trump’s Republicans. The outcome was welcomed by Poland’s ruling coalition, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk declaring that “democracy won”. The response was more muted from the right-wing opposition and the office of conservative President Karol Nawrocki, who is a Trump ally. 🚨 🇺🇸 Tusk gives Trump some great advice. But will the US president listen? Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk urged the US president to seek compromises after the Republicans' defeat and not to rely on vetoes as his main way of governing. Trump had earlier threatened to become… pic.twitter.com/s3E6G5zIQT — NEXTA (@nexta_tv) November 4, 2026 Tusk addressed the election results on Wednesday afternoon local time at a press conference alongside his Czech counterpart, Andrej Babiš. “Today, democracy won in America,” said a smiling Tusk. “I love democracy; it is a beautiful thing.” “As President Donald Trump himself said just after the election, the Democrats did a good job, and I really could not agree more with him this time,” added Tusk. “I hope that the result will stabilise the situation also in our region.” Although the United States remains Poland’s most important security partner, Tusk’s government – a broad, pro-EU coalition that ranges from left to centre right – has at times had uneasy relations with the Trump administration. It has been critical of Trump’s conciliatory approach towards Russia, his often tough stance on Ukraine, as well as his pursuit of US control over Greenland. Meanwhile, the head of the parliamentary caucus of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, Zbigniew Konwiński, told broadcaster Polsat News that “personally, I was happy with the Democrats’ victory”. “We know how Donald Trump behaves, how volatile he is in his political declarations, how he can sometimes put Ukraine in a more difficult position than Russia, so I would rather look for the positives in what happened,” said Konwiński. “If we look at recent years, the more Democrats, the stronger the Democrats, the better for Poland,” he added. .@Konwinski_PO: Cieszę się z wygranej Demokratów w USA, bo to lepszy scenariusz dla Polski. @marcinfijolek pic.twitter.com/gJ3TnlMn0l — Graffiti_PN (@Graffiti_PN) November 4, 2026 The speaker of Poland’s parliament, Włodzimierz Czarzasty, who is also the leader of one of KO’s junior coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), has clashed with the US ambassador to Poland twice this year over Czarzasty’s criticism of Trump. Today, Czarzasty shared and commented on a social media post by Trump, published in the wake of the Democrats’ victory, in which the US president showed an image of his signature red cap with the word “VETO” on it. “Where have I heard this before?” wrote Czarzasty, referring to the fact that Nawrocki has vetoed a record number of bills passed by parliament, where Tusk’s coalition has a majority. Czarzasty then went on to list a series of characteristics that he suggested both Trump and Nawrocki share, including “arrogance”, “lack of respect for women”, a “suspicious past”, “transactional exploitation of their position”, and “admiration for politicians with fascist tendencies”. Skąd ja to znam? Arogancja. Buta. Nieuzasadniona pewność siebie. Brak szacunku dla kobiet ( a to popchnę jakąś dwojga nazwisk, a to zakpię prymitywnie). Dziwna przeszłość. Instrumentalne traktowanie dziennikarzy. Pieniądze za spotkania. Transakcyjne wykorzystywanie funkcji.… pic.twitter.com/ryT2BMOZb2 — Włodzimierz Czarzasty 📚📖 (@wlodekczarzasty) November 4, 2026 Nawrocki has closely aligned himself with Trump. During last year’s Polish presidential election campaign, Trump invited Nawrocki for a private meeting at the White House. His then-homeland security secretary, Kristi Noem, visited Poland to endorse Nawrocki. Nawrocki himself has not thus far commented on Tuesday’s midterm election results. However, Marcin Przydacz, the head of the president’s International Policy Bureau, did address the issue in a social media post. “As predicted, in the US midterm elections voters decided on change,” wrote Przydacz. “Poland will continue its good cooperation with the US, because it is our ally, and collaboration is in our mutual interest.” Przydacz also added that the results were “a reminder for Tusk” that “no government lasts forever”. In Poland, too, “the moment will come when voters will decide on change – and it might be quite soon”, added Przydacz, in a nod to next year’s Polish parliamentary elections. Zgodnie z przewidywaniami w wyborach połówkowych w USA wyborcy zdecydowali o zmianie. Wcześniej wygrywali Republikanie, dziś Demokraci. Polska będzie kontynuować dobrą współpracę z USA, bo jest to nasz sojusznik, a kooperacja jest w naszym wspólnym interesie. O tym, kto sprawuje… — Marcin Przydacz (@marcin_przydacz) November 4, 2026 Tusk’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, meanwhile, used the US election results to revive his long-running feud with Elon Musk, who is no longer part of the Trump administration but donated enormous amounts of money to support the Republicans ahead of the midterms. Last year, Musk and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio criticised Sikorski after he suggested that Musk had threatened Ukraine. In a post on his social media platform, X, Musk told Sikorski to “be quiet, small man”. On Wednesday, Tusk shared a screenshot of a tweet he had published last year, after Musk left the Trump administration, in which Sikorski wrote: “See, big man, politics is harder than you thought.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. The International Commission of Jurists (ICJ) has criticised the takeover of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) by a group of government-backed judges. It says that the move “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary”. However, the ICJ, a Swiss-based NGO led by judges, lawyers and academics from around the world, also chastised Poland’s opposition-aligned president, Karol Nawrocki, for his role in the crisis surrounding the TK, in particular his refusal to swear in judges elected by parliament. 🚨#Poland’s constitutional crisis must be resolved through the rule of law. The ICJ urges all authorities to respect judicial independence, follow lawful procedures, and comply with European court rulings. 🔗More information: https://t.co/NWmca9mpUx — ICJ (@ICJ_org) November 3, 2026 On Friday, eight judges who were elected to the TK this year by the government’s parliamentary majority effectively took over the tribunal. They announced that the chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański, had been suspended for failing to properly fulfil their duties. Meanwhile, large numbers of riot police were deployed outside the court, holding back protesters, including opposition politicians, and preventing Święczkowski and Sochański from entering the grounds. Święczkowski denounced the takeover of the court as an illegal “coup d’état”. He has been backed by the tribunal’s remaining six judges, who, like him, were appointed under the rule of the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which brought the TK under its political influence. Nawrocki has likewise denounced the actions of the government-backed judges. In the early hours of Saturday, he dramatically forced his way into the court, where he clashed physically and verbally with the judges who had taken over the TK. During a visit to the Constitutional Tribunal last night, President Nawrocki clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of the court. The president is today seeking talks with political leaders to discuss the crisis https://t.co/7HmBnuIaDG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026 In a statement on Tuesday, the ICJ expressed regret that the latest developments have “deepened the crisis over the tribunal”. It called on Polish “state institutions to seek solutions…that comply fully with the rule of law, including the principle of the independence of the judiciary”. The ICJ’s secretary-general, Santiago Canton, noted that Nawrocki has refused to swear in five of the eight TK judges elected by parliament this year. That “violates international standards and is contrary to the interim measures indicated by the European Court of Human Rights”, said Canton. In May, the ECHR issued an interim order for all judges elected by parliament to be allowed to serve on the court. However, that has been ignored by Nawrocki and Święczkowski, who argued that the ECHR does not have the authority to make such a decision. The ICJ also noted that the roots of the crisis at the TK date back a decade, to the time when the PiS government took actions – including unlawfully appointing judges to the tribunal – that rendered the court illegitimate. “At the same time,” continued Canton, “the suspension of the president and vice-president of the tribunal without a fair and appropriate procedure established by law, carried out with the involvement of the police, contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary.” In its statement, the ICJ added that “criminal and disciplinary proceedings must respect all the guarantees of a fair trial and must never be used as a means to change [a court’s] composition”. Later on Tuesday, after the ICJ had issued its statement, the eight government-backed judges held their first general assembly, at which they moved forward with disciplinary proceedings against Święczkowski and Sochański. The justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, has also submitted six requests to the TK to lift Święczkowski’s immunity from prosecution so that he can face charges for a range of alleged crimes relating to both his time as chief justice and his previous role as a senior prosecutor under the PiS government. Skierowałem do Trybunału Konstytucyjnego kolejny, szósty już wniosek o uchylenie immunitetu Bogdanowi Święczkowskiemu, dołączając go do pięciu wniosków przekazanych w piątek. Dzisiejsza sprawa dotyczy zakupu systemu szpiegowskiego Hermes w czasie, gdy pełnił funkcję Prokuratora… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) November 3, 2026 The takeover of the TK has also stirred controversy among Polish legal experts. The issue has even caused an unprecedented split at the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights (HFPC), a well-respected NGO. On Saturday, the HFPC’s management board issued a statement, signed by its president, Maciej Nowicki, saying that it “sees no clear legal basis” for the actions taken on Friday by the government-backed judges to suspend Święczkowski and take control of the tribunal. It warned that the situation “set a dangerous precedent” and “does not contribute to fixing the tribunal”. However, HFPC also made it clear that the crisis at the court dates back a decade and reiterated its view that Nawrocki “has no right to block or invalidate the election [of judges] by parliament”. That statement prompted six of the eight members of HFPC’s council – a separate body from the management board – to resign. Those to depart included a former chief justice of the TK, Andrzej Rzepliński, and a former deputy human rights commissioner, Hanna Machińska. Machińska announced their resignation in a social media post. She said that the reason for her decision had been the management board’s statement, “with which I disagree”. Speaking later to broadcaster TVN, Machińska said that “we believe that the legal basis [for the TK takeover] was clearly defined”. Poland’s government, including Prime Minister Donald Tusk, has also argued that the takeover of the tribunal was necessary to ensure that legally appointed judges can take up their seats and that the court’s legitimacy can be restored. However, on Tuesday evening, Tusk shifted to a more conciliatory tone, offering to hold a one-on-one meeting with Nawrocki to discuss the crisis around the Constitutional Tribunal and “try to find solutions that will protect Poland from any political upheaval”. World.title: Disputed Polish constitutional court holds first meeting after takeover by government-backed judges
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The group of eight government-backed judges who last week took control of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) have held a meeting at which they made a number of key decisions, including moving forward with disciplinary proceedings against the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski. However, the situation is mired in controversy and uncertainty. Święczkowski and the opposition-aligned president, Karol Nawrocki, do not recognise the judges who are now claiming control of the court, describing their actions as a “coup d’état”. Meanwhile, there are doubts as to whether today’s general assembly even had a valid quorum, given that the chief justice and six other judges appointed under the former government did not attend. PILNE: Zgromadzenie Ogólne Sędziów TK przyjęło, że kworum to osiem osóbhttps://t.co/SYEf9Ead3L — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) November 3, 2026 The meeting was called by Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who on Friday declared that Święczkowski and the deputy chief justice, Bartłomiej Sochański, had been suspended for failing to fulfil their duties. Korwin-Piotrowska said that she herself, as the longest-serving judge on the court, was taking control. Large numbers of riot police were deployed outside the court, holding back protesters, including opposition politicians, and preventing Święczkowski and Sochański from entering the court. However, Nawrocki himself did enter the premises, where he clashed physically and verbally with Korwin-Piotrowska. For a general assembly of the TK to be valid, two thirds of the court’s judges need to be present. Normally, given that the tribunal has 15 positions, that would mean at least 10 judges being present. However, only eight judges attended today’s meeting. They were all appointed to the TK by the government’s parliamentary majority this year. But Nawrocki has refused to swear in five of them, meaning that their legal status has become disputed. The TK’s seven other judges, including Święczkowski and Sochański, were all appointed to the court under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under its political control, including by unlawfully appointing three judges. None of them attended Tuesday’s general assembly. Nevertheless, the eight judges present at the meeting, which was broadcast live for the first time in the TK’s history, decided that a quorum had been reached. They did so on the basis that three of the TK’s judges were not authorised to attend: Święczkowski and Sochański, because they are suspended, and Jarosław Wyrembak, because he inherited his position from one of PiS’s unlawfully appointed judges. That meant only 12 judges were authorised to attend, and two thirds of that number is eight, meaning that a quorum had been reached. Zgromadzenie Ogólne TK: JEST KWORUM! 👏 Według przedstawionej interpretacji liczy się je od 12 uprawnionych osób. 2/3 × 12 = 8. Prawo i matematyka.👏 pic.twitter.com/77v2ep9HbT — Pani Prezes 👠 (@PaniNaSzpilkach) November 3, 2026 Once that issue was agreed, the eight judges present proceeded to decide upon a number of key issues. First, they adopted a draft budget for the TK for 2027, something that Święczkowski had been unable to achieve, which was used as an argument for his ousting. Second, they drew lots to decide which of the TK’s judges would sit on disciplinary panels for Święczkowski and Sochański in relation to their suspension from the court. However, some legal experts have expressed doubt as to whether a legal quorum was established at today’s meeting. Ryszard Piotrowski, a prominent constitutional scholar, called the meeting “illegal”, reports news website Onet. Przemysław Rosati, the president of the Supreme Bar Council, also expressed his doubts. Obniżenie progu kworum na skutek zawieszenia prezesa i wiceprezesa otwiera puszkę Pandory. To jest mechanizm, który pozwala dowolnie obniżać kworum na Zgromadzeniu Ogólnym TK – wystarczy, że prezes zawiesi 10 sędziów i będzie mógł na Zgromadzeniu podejmować decyzję w trzy osoby.… — Marcin Matczak (@wsamraz) November 3, 2026 Święczkowski himself rejected the legitimacy of what he called a “social gathering”, saying that Korwin-Piotrowska is a “usurper” who has no right to call a general assembly at all, reported Polsat News. Shortly before the meeting at the TK, Nawrocki also met with the prime minister, Donald Tusk, for the first time since the crisis at the court broke out last Friday. They had convened at the presidential palace for a meeting of the National Security Council that Nawrocki had called before the TK crisis. During public remarks broadcast before the confidential meeting got underway, Nawrocki accused the government of “illegally taking over the Constitutional Tribunal”. He added that Tusk “bears full responsibility for…all these illegal actions”. Grubo! Karol Nawrocki do Tuska: „Pełną odpowiedzialność za wszystkie nielegalne działa w Trybunale Konstytucyjnym ponosi jeden człowiek, który jest obecny – premier Donald Tusk” pic.twitter.com/WMPnWTZIKt — chrzanik (@chrzanikx) November 3, 2026 Tusk and his government have argued that the source of the crisis is, in fact, Nawrocki’s refusal to swear in judges appointed by parliament, as he is required to do, and then Święczkowski’s resultant refusal to accept those judges onto the court. They also note that the TK has not been legitimate for a decade, since PiS unlawfully appointed judges and brought the court under its political influence. Speaking to broadcaster TVN on Tuesday before the general assembly, justice minister Waldemar Żurek said that the actions being undertaken by Korwin-Piotrowska are the only way “to rebuild the independence of the tribunal”. World.title: Poland has EU’s second-highest electricity prices accounting for cost of living
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland had the second-highest household electricity prices in the European Union in the first half of 2026 after adjusting for differences in the cost of living, new Eurostat data show. Prices in Poland were also among the fastest-rising in the bloc. Poland’s relatively high electricity costs reflect the country’s continued reliance on coal, which results in EU charges for carbon emissions, and its taxes and levies, which make up the largest share of household electricity bills anywhere in the EU. In nominal terms, Polish households paid €29.99 per 100 kilowatt-hours (kWh) for electricity in the first half of 2026. This was the seventh-highest price among the EU’s 27 member states and above the bloc-wide average of €28.32. Ireland (€38.71 per 100 kWh) had the highest prices, followed by Germany (€36.18) and Belgium (€35.75). The lowest costs were recorded in Hungary (€11.39), Malta (€12.68) and Bulgaria (€13.41). However, when adjusted for purchasing power standards (PPS), which account for differences in the cost of living, Poland ranked second in the EU, at 41.12 PPS per 100 kWh. Only Romania had higher prices, at 46.89 PPS. The lowest prices when measured in PPS were recorded in Malta (13.75), Hungary (14.7) and Luxembourg (15.47). Poland’s electricity prices, in PPS terms, rose by 10.7% compared with the second half of 2025, which was the second-biggest increase in the EU after Finland. They were also up 17.6% compared to the first half of 2025, the fourth-largest rise in the bloc. One reason why electricity prices in Poland remain high is the country’s continued reliance on coal, which last year generated just over half of power, by far the highest proportion in the EU. Almost all coal used in Polish power plants is mined domestically and is among the most expensive in the world to extract. Additionally, burning it also produces high carbon emissions, which power generators must pay for under the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS). These costs contribute to the high taxes and levies included in household electricity bills, which accounted for 39% of the final price in Poland in the first half of 2026. This was the highest share in the EU, ahead of Germany (23.6%) and well above the bloc-wide average of 18.6%. “In Poland, only one-third of our electricity generation is carbon-free. We have to pay for the rest – often dearly,” noted Polish energy journalist Jakub Wiech, commenting on the data. Without taxes and levies, the nominal price of electricity in Poland would have been just under €16 per 100 kWh, below the EU average of €20.27. However, Bartłomiej Orzeł of the Project Tempo think tank notes that electricity prices in Poland would, in fact, be even higher were it not for the huge state subsidies paid to support the unprofitable coal mining sector, which amount to billions of zloty a year but also shield end consumers from the full cost of extracting coal. He told news website Interia that mines actually sell coal to power stations at a price below the cost of extraction. Poland will from next month be the last remaining EU country still mining hard coal, after the Czech Republic – the only other producer – announced the closure of its last mine https://t.co/0sfMDQb19N — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 30, 2026 According to Wiech, the high tax burden also reflects the costs of transforming Poland’s energy sector while continuing to support coal-fired power stations and the state budget. He says Poland needs “on the one hand, to fund the accelerated but delayed transformation and modernisation of the electricity sector; on the other hand, to maintain the fleet of coal-fired power stations; and thirdly, to contribute to the state budget”, which is struggling with persistently high deficits. Wiech expects, however, that politicians will come under pressure to reduce electricity bills ahead of next year’s parliamentary election. He says they may be tempted to “interfere with electricity bills” and that “it is therefore quite likely that certain charges (e.g. the distribution charge) will be reduced in 2027”. Komisja Europejska wrzuciła dane o cenach prądu za I półrocze 2026 roku i – boy, oh, boy – niesamowita jest to lektura. Na początek mocne uderzenie: w ujęciu standardu siły nabywczej polskie gospodarstwa domowe mają drugie najwyższe ceny prądu w całej Unii Europejskiej.… pic.twitter.com/yKvt5251i7 — Jakub Wiech (@jakubwiech) November 1, 2026 Energy prices and the wider energy transition have already become increasingly politicised this year, with the right-wing opposition criticising EU climate policies. The national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, recently called for Poland to unilaterally withdraw from ETS, claiming that it treats “Poles as a cash machine for the absurd leftist climate policy of the EU”. Opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki has twice attempted to call national referendums on rejecting EU climate policy, but in both cases his proposals were rejected by the more pro-EU government’s majority in parliament. Poland's right-wing opposition wants to withdraw from the EU Emissions Trading System, saying it makes Poles "a cash machine for absurd leftist climate policies"@PStrzalkowski explains what costs ETS really brings, and what prospects there are for reform https://t.co/UxpMWpG1pE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 4, 2026 However, when PiS was in power from 2015 to 2023, it recognised the need to move Poland away from coal and towards a mix of renewables and nuclear. Solar energy installations boomed under the PiS government, and the overall share of renewables in the energy mix rose from around 9% in 2015 to a record 29% in 2024. The current government has continued with PiS’s plans to shift towards nuclear and renwables. This year, Poland’s first offshore wind farm in the Baltic Sea began generating electricity, with a number of other offshore projects set to follow. Poland’s national energy and climate plan, approved in June, envisages coal accounting for 0-5% of the energy mix by 2040. Around 15-16% will come from nuclear, 7-8% from gas, with most of the rest from renewables: onshore wind (22-27%), offshore wind (18-21%) and solar (14-18%). World.title: Polish journalist held at Ukraine border and handed three-year entry ban
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A prominent Polish journalist and commentator, Łukasz Warzecha, has been prevented from entering Ukraine and handed a three-year ban on crossing into the country. Warzecha, who is primarily associated with right-wing weekly Do Rzeczy, says he was told that the decision had been made for “security reasons”. Polish journalist Łukasz Warzecha was travelling to Kyiv on a study visit jointly organised by Poland’s @MieroszewskiPL Centre and the Ukrainian Institute @UA_Institute an institution affiliated with Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry. According to head of @MieroszewskiPL Dr Łukasz… https://t.co/Tawp2hEJ5u — Sławomir Dębski (@SlawomirDebski) November 2, 2026 Warzecha had been due to join a study visit to Ukraine for Polish journalists organised by the Mieroszewski Centre, a Polish state institution, and the Ukraine Institute, a Ukrainian public body affiliated with the foreign ministry. The head of the Mieroszewski Centre, Łukasz Adamski, revealed that the list of journalists attending the tour had been agreed between the two organisers and forwarded to the relevant Ukrainian state authorities, who previously raised no objection. However, on Monday afternoon, Warzecha announced on social media that he had been held at the Ukrainian border and told to wait in a room. The journalist remained there for over seven hours before being informed that he was banned from entering Ukraine for three years. Proszę państwa, oto miś. Miś jest bardzo grzeczny dziś. pic.twitter.com/aVEUnkGhM7 — Łukasz Warzecha (@lkwarzecha) November 3, 2026 Adamski revealed that his organisation had sought to intervene with the foreign ministries of both countries, but to no avail. Warzecha said on social media that he had been told the decision, which was issued by the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), was made due to “security reasons”. Adamski commented that, while he “recognises Ukraine’s sovereign right to decide whom to grant entry…restricting journalists’ work on state security grounds…creates fertile ground for unfriendly commentary”. At the time of writing, there had been no comment from the SBU regarding its decision to issue an entry ban against Warzecha. In his journalistic work, Warzecha has at times been critical of Ukraine, for example over its honouring of historical nationalist figures, and has called for a reduction in social benefits given to Ukrainian refugees in Poland. However, those views are within the Polish mainstream. Warzecha has also voiced support for Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression. In February 2023, on the first anniversary of Russia’s full-scale invasion, he expressed satisfaction that Ukraine defended itself so effectively. However, Do Rzeczy, with which Warzecha has been associated for around a decade, has taken a tougher position on Ukraine. In 2024, its front cover warned of the “Ukrainisation of Poland”, a phrase often used by the far right to warn against the growing presence and influence of Ukrainians. OKŁADKA "Do Rzeczy" nr 35: Ukrainizacja Polski. Raport "Do Rzeczy" o groźnym procesie pic.twitter.com/SUYy1GhIat — DoRzeczy (@DoRzeczy_pl) August 25, 2024 Speaking to Do Rzeczy after the ban against him was issued, Warzecha said he had “wanted to confront my own views with open-minded politicians and opinion leaders in Ukraine. Unfortunately I was not given the opportunity to do so”. Ukraine’s decision was criticised by Andrzej Śliwka, an MP from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s main opposition party. He asked if Warzecha had been banned “because he dared to criticise Ukrainian corruption, the confrontational policy toward Poland, and the distortion of history”. “One can agree with editor Warzecha or not, but such a decision demands explanations and a firm response from Polish authorities,” wrote Śliwka. At the time of writing, Poland’s government had not commented on the case. Polski dziennikarz, red. Łukasz Warzecha, otrzymuje od ukraińskich służb trzyletni zakaz wjazdu na Ukrainę. Dlaczego? Czy dlatego, że odważył się krytykować ukraińską korupcję, konfrontacyjną politykę wobec Polski i zakłamywanie historii? Można zgadzać się z red. Warzechą albo… https://t.co/JvuhLL9O8F — Andrzej Śliwka 🇵🇱 (@SliwkaAndrzej) November 2, 2026 Adamski said that the visit to Ukraine had been arranged specifically with the aim of “representing diverse editorial perspectives”. The Mieroszewski Centre last month arranged a similar visit for Ukrainian journalists to Poland. The aim was “to enable Polish journalists to gain direct knowledge of the situation in Ukraine, engage in conversations with representatives of various communities, and achieve a better understanding of the challenges facing Ukrainian society”, wrote Adamski. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has been one of Kyiv’s closest allies, providing extensive military, humanitarian and diplomatic support. However, there have also been regular tensions between the two countries, in particular over their difficult shared histories. This year has seen the two sides clash over the unresolved issue of large-scale massacres during World War Two.
