NEW DELHI: NCP leader Praful Patel on Thursday visited Nationalist Congress Party (SP) chief Sharad Pawar at Mumbaiâs Breach Candy Hospital and enquired about his health. Patel said the veteran politician was stable and expected to return home in a day or two after completing his medical check-ups.The visit by Patel has triggered political speculation as he is among the NCP leaders reportedly "unhappy" with party boss Sunetra Pawarâs leadership. The meeting comes amid signs of internal discord within the party, adding a political dimension to Patelâs hospital visit.Sharad Pawar was admitted to Breach Candy Hospital on Wednesday night with a respiratory and chest infection, after being discharged from Puneâs Ruby Hall Clinic. Dr Pratit Samdani, a doctor at the hospital, said on Thursday that Pawar was stable and undergoing treatment."Sharad Pawar was admitted yesterday at Breach Candy Hospital for a respiratory and chest infection. He is stable and under treatment. He was admitted last night; he had a cough and an infection, something like bronchitis trouble. His treatment is ongoing, and he is currently stable," Dr Samdani told reporters.After meeting Pawar, Patel said the hospital admission was part of his routine medical check-ups and that his health was good. He also dismissed speculation that their meeting involved political discussions, saying he continued to meet Pawar and his daughter, Supriya Sule, because of their family ties.In a post on X, Patel said, "I visited the Breach Candy Hospital in Mumbai to pay a courtesy call on the esteemed Shri Sharad Pawar Saheb and inquired about his health."Providing an update on Pawar's condition, Patel said, "Sharad Pawar due to fatigue two days ago, was taken to Ruby Hall Clinic in Pune for a checkup. After that, he came to Mumbai, and here his health is fine. Naturally, a checkup happens once or twice a year, for a complete checkup, so in that context only he is admitted here at Breach Candy. His health is good. I am also happy that I came here, but everything is fine, and sahab was also in good spirits. He was asking about what is happening in politics in the country and state, as that is his interest. We had a good conversation, and I am happy that in a day or two all his checkups will be completed, so he will return home soon so he can rest."Patel also commented on Prime Minister Narendra Modi's conversation with Pawar, describing their relationship as long-standing and cordial. He said Modi's call to enquire about Pawar's health was natural given their association over the years.âSharad Pawar and Narendra Modi have had a very long-standing relationship. I have also known Modi ji for many years and personally know about the relationship between him and Pawar sahab... I have witnessed their very good, cordial and respectful relationship over the years, even when we were in the UPA government in Delhi, and Modi ji was the Chief Minister of Gujarat... Modi ji is such a senior leader of the country today. So, if he received information about Sharad Pawar ji's health, it was natural for him to enquire about his well-being and speak to him...âEarlier, Pawar was admitted to Ruby Hall Clinic on November 2 after complaining of a cough and pleuritic chest pain. According to a statement issued by Dr Purvez K Grant, Chief Cardiologist, Chairman and Managing Trustee of the hospital, Pawar was stable and doing well at the time of his discharge."Mr Sharad Pawar has been discharged from Ruby Hall Clinic today. He is stable and doing well. He will be travelling directly from the hospital to his residence in Mumbai. We wish him good health and a speedy recovery," the statement said.His daughter, Baramati MP and NCP (SP) working president Supriya Sule, had earlier said that Pawar was undergoing medical tests and that his health parameters were stable. Ruby Hall Clinic subsequently said he would remain under observation as a precautionary measure. Doctors cleared him for discharge after his condition remained stable and his discomfort subsided.The developments come amid growing concerns within the BJP over organisational differences in its ally -- NCP. Union home minister Amit Shah met several senior NCP functionaries late Sunday who are believed to be unhappy with party president Sunetra Pawar and her son Parth, and urged them to resolve their differences in the partyâs interest.Those who met Shah included NCP national working president Praful Patel, Maharashtra unit chief Sunil Tatkare, ministers Chhagan Bhujbal and Hasan Mushrif, and leaders Dhananjay Munde and Dilip Patil. Deputy chief minister Sunetra Pawar and her son Parth were absent from the meeting.Following the meeting, Sunetra Pawar convened a core committee meeting in Mumbai.

World.title: 'No impact on India-US ties': Tharoor says Trump retains power on tariffs, Iran war
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Congress MP

on Friday said the results of the US midterm elections would have little impact on India-US relations, asserting that President Donald Trump retains considerable powers to pursue his foreign policy agenda despite the ruling party's electoral setback.

Speaking in Thiruvananthapuram, Tharoor said the US election results would not change Washington's approach towards key issues such as tariffs, sanctions on countries buying Russian oil, the Iran war or the Ukraine conflict.

"Whether it comes to tariffs, whether it comes to sanctions for buying Russian oil, whether it comes to the Iran war itself, whether it comes to any initiative he takes on the Ukraine war. All of this, he's completely unaffected by the election result," Tharoor said.



Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

He explained that while Congress has significant powers over budgetary matters and can restrict or approve government spending, the President enjoys considerable discretion in foreign policy and international affairs.

Tharoor said that even when it comes to military action, the President can proceed without seeking approval for an initial period of up to 60 days. However, Congress can exercise its financial powers to restrict expenditure, particularly in the case of an expensive military campaign.





"Those in India who are expecting this to have some impact on our relationship with the US, I think, are completely mistaken," he said.

Commenting on the election outcome, Tharoor described it as an extraordinary setback for the ruling party, pointing out that midterm elections traditionally serve as a course correction for the party in power.

He also highlighted the gains made by candidates from minority communities and people of Indian origin, including the election of a mayor of Indian origin in Los Angeles.

Tharoor said the results reflected the vibrancy of American democracy but maintained that the outcome would not significantly alter Trump's ability to take decisions on international affairs.

IYC sources said organisational office-bearers from assembly to the central level were directed to attend the rally with

World.title: Party after gun buy ends in a death
World.content:
A late-night liquor party among friends to celebrate the purchase of an illegal firearm ended in the death of a 25-year-old man during celebratory firing in Bhubaneswar early Thursday.

Eight friends of the deceased, Tapu Nayak, were arrested. All the accused were employed at a private construction company. Despite indications that the firing may have been accidental, police booked all accused for murder. While drinking together, one of the accused allegedly fired. The bullet struck Nayak. He was rushed to a hospital. As Nayak's condition deteriorated, he was shifted to a private hospital, where doctors declared him dead. Preliminary investigation suggested no apparent motive to target Nayak. His wife has sought an impartial probe.

World.title: Elephant calf with genetic bone disorder to be flown from Keralam to Gujarat’s Vantara for specialised treatment
World.content:
An 18-month-old elephant calf suffering from a genetic bone disorder and unable to stand or walk will be flown to Jamnagar in Gujarat on Friday (November 6, 2026) for specialised treatment at Vantara, the Kerala Forest Department said.

The calf, weighing around 125 to 130 kg, was shifted from its treatment facility at Kodanad elephant centre in Kochi to an animal ambulance with the help of 10 to 12 people and a crane.

The calf was subsequently loaded onto a specially arranged animal ambulance and taken to the Nedumbassery airport in Kochi, from where a chartered flight, accompanied by veterinary experts, was scheduled to depart for Jamnagar by noon, officials said.

Chief Wildlife Warden P. Pugazhendi told reporters that the calf had been brought to Kodanad soon after its birth and was being provided treatment there.

“Unfortunately, it fell once, following which we realised that it had certain genetic disorders. It was found to have osteopenia, a bone-related disorder,” he said.

Mr. Pugazhendi said Keralam did not have the facilities required to provide the calf with specialised treatment and the department had held discussions with experts, including veterinary specialists at Vantara.

“We are sending our calf to another State with great hope for specialised treatment. We are hopeful that it will recover and we will certainly bring it back to Keralam once it regains its health,” he said.

He said the initial treatment period was expected to last four to six months, depending on the calf’s progress.

Treatment plan

A treatment plan involving hormonal therapy and hydrotherapy had been prepared by the specialists at Vantara, he said, adding that the outcome could not be predicted with certainty as the calf was suffering from a genetic disorder.

A team comprising a veterinary officer from Keralam, Forest department officials and the mahout who had cared for the calf since its early days would accompany it and assist in its treatment.

The department had also constituted a monitoring committee to review the progress of the treatment and submit reports at least once a week, Mr. Pugazhendi said.

While the mahout would remain with the calf throughout, the assistant forest veterinary officer and other officials would also visit and monitor its condition, he added.

Mr. Pugazhendi said Vantara had agreed to bear the entire cost of the treatment.

World.title: Architecture students learn practical challenges of urban planning at DULT Monsoon Design Studio 2026
World.content:
“Thoughtful urban planning is vital for sustainable development of cities,” Commissioner, Urban Development, Shakeel Ahmed said in Belagavi on November 4.

“We need to realise the importance of thoughtful urban planning, sustainable development and collaborative efforts in shaping the city’s future,” he told the gathering after inaugurating the three-day DULT Monsoon Design Studio 2026 at Karnatak Law Society’s Gogte Institute of Technology in Belagavi.

Mr. Ahmed shared valuable insights into urban development initiatives and emerging urban challenges in Belagavi. He cited examples from every day problems faced by residents and the solutions attempted by officers of various urban development agencies. He provided participants with a broader understanding of the opportunities and responsibilities involved in creating better urban environments.

The three-day event was organised by the Directorate of Urban Land Transport (DULT) in association with KNMTA (Karnataka Non-Motorised Transport Agency) and in collaboration with The Department of Architecture, KLS GIT.

Shamanth Kuchangi, head, TETC, DULT, said the collaboration between DULT and the Department of Architecture, KLS GIT, aims to provide students with an opportunity to engage with real-world urban issues and understand the practical dimensions of urban design and development.

Jyoti Patil, HoD, Architecture, highlighted the significance of the workshop in bridging academic learning with professional practice and encouraged students to actively participate, explore innovative ideas, and contribute meaningful design perspectives towards urban development. “It will bring together students, urban design professionals, and experts to explore urban challenges, exchange ideas, and develop design-oriented approaches towards improving the urban environment of Belagavi,” Dr. Patil said.

Speakers included senior urban designer Sandeep Venkataramu, DULT coordinators, and faculty members of the Department of Architecture, KLS GIT, and Priyadarshini Honnur.

Among those present were faculty coordinators Roopali Kavilkar, Priyanka Rajput and Nikhil Bastwadkar, and faculty members.

World.title: Trump blames Democrats’ midterm win for U.S. stock market selloff
World.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump attributed Thursday’s (November 5, 2026) stock market selloff to the electoral victory of the rival Democratic Party in the midterm elections on Tuesday (November 3, 2026).

“The Stock Market crashed today because the Dumocrats had a big Tuesday — So sad to see, you only have yourselves to blame!” Mr. Trump posted on his Truth Social platform after U.S. markets closed for the day.

Analysts attributed Thursday’s selloff to fears that Democrats would threaten the AI data centre investment boom, with the tech-focused Nasdaq suffering its worst session, percentage-wise, since April 2025.

Data centres have faced broad opposition from U.S. voters regardless of political affiliation, and many midterm winners have pledged to put the brakes on such projects.

World.title: China's Macau jails ex-lawmaker in first national security trial
World.content:
A Court in the Chinese territory Macau sentenced on Friday (November 6, 2026), ex-lawmaker and democracy campaigner Au Kam San to 12 years and six months in prison for subversion and other offences.

Au, 69, is the first person convicted under national security laws widened in 2023 in Macau, the former Portuguese colony and casino hub which reverted to China in 1999.

He co-organised annual vigils for victims of the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown in Beijing, something previously tolerated only in Macau and neighbouring Hong Kong.

Au, detained in July 2025 and whose closed-door trial concluded in September in three days, was found guilty of "subversion against the political power of the State" among other offences, a Court statement said.

Au "personally provided, over a long period of time, assistance and collaboration to external hostile organisations in the collection, preparation, and public dissemination of various images and information that were manifestly filled with political claims of a subversive nature against the political authority of the State," it said.

He also sought to "incite hatred among Macau residents against the Central People's Government, with the intent to overthrow and undermine the fundamental system of the State enshrined in the Constitution of the People's Republic of China," it added.

The European Union last year condemned his arrest, saying it only heightened concerns about the "erosion of political pluralism" in Macau.

The organisation Justice Abroad said in July that Au's family, including his wife and three daughters, have not been permitted to see or speak with him since shortly after his detention.

The family received only one telephone call from him, lasting less than one minute, on the day after his arrest, Justice Abroad said.

"My father dedicated more than 30 years of his life serving the people of Macau. Nearly a year has passed, and we are still unable to communicate with him," his daughter was quoted as saying in the statement.

"All we ask for is a fair trial, due process, and for his more than three decades of dedication to the people of Macau not to be erased or forgotten... (We) must be allowed to visit him or, at the very least, communicate with him," she said.

Au was a teacher but after the 1989 crackdown in China, he came to believe that Macau urgently needed to become an open, democratic society, and entered politics.

"I admit that in the fight for democracy we have accomplished nothing, but I believe in sowing seeds and giving them a chance to grow," he told AFP in 2024.

"Even though we are in a bitter winter, if there are changes to the external environment, these seeds in Macau may yet have a chance to sprout and forge a new path towards democracy," he said.

World.title: Bengal Biennale 2026: Artists, theme, dates and venues
World.content:
Jibanananda Das, often regarded as the Charles Baudelaire of Bengali Surrealist poetry, captures in his poem Banalata Sen the journey of a traveller wandering through centuries and civilisations, across seas and the dark corridors of history, carrying the solitude of a world grown impossibly vast. Then, in a moment that seems to suspend time, he encounters Banalata Sen of Natore — her face offering stillness after the day’s long drift. The poem’s enduring tenderness lies in this fleeting reprieve: the possibility of finding, amid the tumult of history, a place to rest, a presence that makes the wandering worthwhile.

It is this poem that lends its name to the second edition of the Bengal Biennale, which runs from November 25, 2026, to January 2, 2027, in Shantiniketan, with its Kolkata edition opening on November 28. Organised by the Gameplan Foundation, founded by Jeet Banerjee and Malavika Banerjee, the event will unfold across multiple venues in Kolkata and Santiniketan, bringing together established cultural institutions, historic sites, artist-led spaces and alternative locations.

Venues across Kolkata and Shantiniketan Shantiniketan: Nandan Art Museum & Gallery (Kala Bhavan), Tokaroun, Santiniketan Society of Visual Art & Design (SSVAD), Arthshila, Sculpture Park, Somnath Hore Studio and Krittika Arts Space Kolkata: The Alipore Museum, The Indian Museum, TRI Art & Culture, Lalit Kala Akademi (AJC Bose Road), Victoria Memorial Hall, The Red Bari, The Dockyard Co, Siddhi & Muni Art Studios (Stephen Court), New Empire and the Kolkata Centre for Creativity (KCC)

Under the curatorial framework Banalata, the Biennale turns towards the tangled ecologies of memory, displacement, resistance and belonging. Like the wild forest creepers that inspire its theme, its artworks seek out unexpected connections, winding through buried histories and overlooked spaces, binding people, places and stories that might otherwise remain apart.

The line-up brings together modern masters such as Rabindranath Tagore, Nandalal Bose, Benode Behari Mukherjee, Bikash Bhattacharjee and Chittaprosad with contemporary practitioners including Atul Dodiya, Arpita Singh, Jitish Kallat, Paresh Maity, Jogen Chowdhury, Shilpa Gupta, Amar Kanwar and Amol K Patil. They share the Biennale’s canvas with international artists, collectives and emerging practitioners, alongside collaborative projects and group exhibitions exploring diverse artistic practices.

Speaking about the Biennale, Jeet and Malavika say, “The more polarised our world seems, the more urgent is the need to acknowledge the lessons of resilience that Nature offers us, if we wish to learn from it. The unseen entanglements that unite us, the neurons that make us feel for each other, and the hope that green shoots hold out to us — Bengal Biennale’s Banalata was born, and grew from these thoughts.”

Art beyond gallery walls

At the curtain-raiser on October 28 at Kolkata’s Alipore Museum, a panel discussion moderated by Sumona Chakravarty deputy director, DAG museums brought together Paula Sengupta, head, Department of Graphics-Printmaking and dean, Faculty of Visual Arts, Rabindra Bharati University; Devina Swarup, director, Paharpur Group; and Bhabatosh Sutar, co-curator of the Biennale and part of the artist collective Chander Haat. Their conversation explored the possibilities of taking art beyond conventional gallery spaces, the responsibility of preserving Bengal’s artistic histories, and the role of a biennale in opening up new encounters between artists and audiences.

For Paula, who participated in the previous and the first edition called Anka-Banka: Through Cross-Currents in 2024-2025 , that encounter was particularly significant. Her work, previously exhibited in fragments, was brought together as a complete body of work on a politically sensitive subject: the loss of home and forced migration. She wanted it to reach audiences beyond the familiar confines of galleries and museums.

“I also decided that I did not want to exhibit it in a gallery, but in a public space,” she said, explaining that the subject and the number of people it concerned made it important to reach as wide an audience as possible. The biennale, she felt, offered the right platform.

The exhibit coincided with a film festival, which helped draw large numbers of visitors at times, as many as 1,500 a day.

Paula also underlined how a biennale can free artists from some of the expectations attached to commercial exhibition spaces. “When you move into a non-commercial, not-for-profit space that is not necessarily connected to the market, it can liberate an artist,” she said.

The second edition seeks to extend these possibilities through Banalata, a framework that brings ecology and poetry into conversation with the subterranean histories of Bengal. Co-curator Ritika Biswas describes the project as an exploration of the often unseen networks through which people find kinship, refuge and ways to resist. The biennale turns towards grief, war and persistent loss, but also towards the possibilities of joy, solidarity and alternative forms of exchange.

“I envision the second Bengal Biennale as a slightly strange, slightly dissonant, slightly dark ecology which embraces the full spectrum of being alive in and to a burning world,” Ritika has said. She adds, “Banalata foregrounds emotion, rest, and poetics, as modes through which we might critically examine the systems and selves within which we are entangled. It endeavours to create new knottings of kinship and solidarity across Bengal and beyond. This Biennale attempts to hold poetics and politics as inherently and generatively entwined forces.”

More than 40 projects in this edition are new works conceived for the Biennale; others are site-responsive iterations of existing works or loans from collections. The programme brings together established Indian and international contemporary artists with practitioners who may never have had a solo exhibition or worked with a gallery. Rather than arrange artists within a hierarchy, the curatorial vision asks how their practices might inform and alter one another.

For Bhabatosh Sutar, the project also offers a way to draw attention to Bengal’s distinctive artistic trajectory — its histories, political concerns and generations of practitioners — while bringing those conversations into contact with the wider art world. The biennale’s ambition is not simply to showcase art but to create relationships between artists, institutions and audiences, and to make visible the cultural histories that have shaped the region.

Art, access and Bengal’s cultural legacy

That responsibility extends to the institutions supporting the event. Devina said the decision to support the biennale was deliberate. She argued that a city’s well-being cannot be measured by its physical infrastructure alone. “But what about the mind and the soul?” she asked. Devina also emphasised the importance of public art in making artistic encounters accessible beyond exclusive spaces, giving people across social and economic backgrounds the opportunity to respond to what they see.

Sumona sees DAG’s engagement with the biennale as part of a wider responsibility towards the artistic histories from which its collection has grown. She recalled DAG’s Ghare Baire exhibit which presented around 700 works from its collection across Kolkata and Chandernagore. The collection itself had been built through relationships with people in Bengal, including families who needed help preserving artists’ works.

Perhaps this is where Banalata finds a deep resonance. A vine does not grow in a straight line; it reaches, coils, crosses and catches hold. Across Bengal’s old walls, public spaces and buried histories, the biennale follows a similar impulse — asking what can be recovered when art leaves its familiar enclosures, what stories emerge when people are invited to participate, and what forms of kinship might take root when memory is allowed to travel.

In a world marked by displacement, fracture and forgetting, the promise is not that art can undo history. It is that, for a moment, it can bring us closer to the lives history has scattered — and offer, amid the long wandering, the possibility of finding one another.

World.title: Bihar’s new regulations for government school teachers, non-teaching staff and students | Explained
World.content:
The story so far: The Bihar government on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) imposed new regulations for school teachers, non-teaching staffs and students instructing them not to make or upload reels on social media without permission from concerned authorities. A week back on October 30, 2026, the Department had also enforced a formal dress code for them. The condition of government schools in Bihar, of late, had hit national headlines and subsequently, has caused major embarrassment for the State government.

Bihar has approximately over 76,000 government schools out of which about 47,000 are primary schools, 25,000 are upper primary and around 5,000 are higher secondary schools. There are about 6.6 lakh government school teachers employed in all these schools. Recently, the BJP-led NDA government painted all (551) government-model schools with saffron colour and said they would be equipped with all modern facilities for the students studying there.

World.title: Why this Lanka in a Keralam panchayat is betting on people-powered solution to tidal flooding
World.content:
Lanka, a small idyllic island tucked away in Ezhikkara panchayat in North Paravur, is set to get what is probably the first community-led high-tide flood mitigation project aimed at addressing a problem that has been collectively taking a toll on the property and livelihoods of the coastal population in Ernakulam district of Keralam.

The community co-designed project, named Resilient Lanka, will be jointly implemented by Equinoct, a Kochi-based, community-sourced environmental and climate-modelling technology solutions provider, and Happiness Project, a newly formed foundation, under the overall supervision of the Ezhikkara panchayat. The project is an extension of the collaboration between Equinoct and the Ezhikkara panchayat over the last five years to document, monitor and assess the impact of tidal flooding with the active participation of local communities. Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan will inaugurate the project on November 15.

“The project may prove critical for the small local community in Lanka, which has been badly affected by tidal flooding. The panchayat is committed to ensuring transparent implementation of the project. If found successful, the project will be extended to more tidal flooding-prone areas of the panchayat,” said Seena Sajeev, president of the Ezhikkara panchayat.

The project seeks to translate the evidence and understanding built through years of community engagement into locally appropriate mitigation measures. Its defining approach is to place the people experiencing tidal flooding at the centre of planning and implementation. Residents’ lived experiences, local knowledge and priorities will inform the identification, design and implementation of measures suited to the specific conditions of the settlement.

“The preparation of a Detailed Project Report (DPR) will mark the first phase of the project, and it will be ready by the end of the year. We have requested the State Planning Board to recognise this pilot as a demonstration model for locally led climate adaptation, showcasing community-driven approaches to strengthening climate resilience across coastal Kerala.,” said C.G. Madhusoodhanan, chief executive officer of Equinoct.

The initiative will focus on three aspects: preventing flooding, facilitating the smooth receding of water in the event of flooding, and ensuring that houses and properties are not affected. Short-term solutions are already being worked out ahead of the tidal flooding predicted for three days from November 9. Lessons from the implementation of these measures will be incorporated into the drafting of the DPR for a long-term solution.

L.G. Gireesh, a 48-year-old fisherman who was born and brought up in Lanka, hopes the project will finally bring relief from tidal flooding, which has been taking a toll on the properties and livelihoods of residents.

“Earlier, there was a pattern to tidal flooding and it was largely seasonal. But now it has become almost a daily phenomenon, and on some days it happens more than once. The time taken for the water to recede has also increased,” he rued.

World.title: Air quality of Delhi worsens, many parts reel under ‘severe’ level air pollution
World.content:
The overall air quality of Delhi worsened and continued to be in the “very poor” category on Friday (November 6, 2026) morning, while many parts of the city reeled under “severe” level of air pollution, according to official data.

Many parts of the national capital, including IIT Delhi, ITO, Dwarka, Rohini, Punjabi Bagh, Alipur, Bawana, and Jahangirpuri, witnessed “severe” level air pollution.

Other cities and towns in north India, including Noida, Gurugram, and Faridabad also witnessed overall “very poor” air quality, on Friday (November 6, 2026) morning.

The 24-hour average Air Quality Index (AQI) of Delhi was 391 (very poor) at 9 a.m. on Friday, as per Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) data.

“Severe” level air pollution affects healthy people and seriously impacts those with existing diseases, as per the CPCB.

The overall air quality of Delhi is likely to be in the “severe” category for three days, as per the Central government’s ‘Air Quality Early Warning System for Delhi’.

The 24-hour average overall Air Quality Index (AQI) of Delhi stood at 369 (very poor) on Thursday at 4 p.m. on Thursday, slightly down from 377 (very poor) a day earlier, as per the Central Pollution Control Board’s daily bulletin, which is treated as the day’s AQI. A higher AQI means worsening of air quality.

A higher AQI means worsening of air quality.

Every winter, air pollution spikes in Delhi-NCR and many parts of the larger Indo-Gangetic Plains, mainly due to meteorological factors such as lower wind speeds and a drop in temperature. Also, pollution from stubble burning during October and November and bursting of firecrackers during the festive season add to existing pollution from vehicles and dust, worsening the air quality.

World.title: Country’s external debt nearly doubles in a decade
World.content:
• World Bank’s global debt report shows figure climbed from $68.7bn in 2015 to $135.1bn in 2025

• China remains Pakistan’s largest single creditor

• Developing economies’ external debt rises to record high of $9.4tr

ISLAMABAD: Pakistan’s total external debt almost doubled to $135.1 billion over the decade ending in 2025, according to the World Bank’s Inter­national Debt Report 2026.

The report noted that Pakistan’s external debt increased from $68.673bn in 2015 to $135.107bn in 2025. This included public and publicly guaranteed debt of $107.076bn, private non-guaranteed debt of $17.58bn and short-term debt of $10.45bn.

Of the public and publicly guaranteed debt, $56.83bn was owed to multilateral creditors, $42.43bn to bilateral creditors and $7.8bn to private creditors.

China was Pakistan’s largest individual creditor, with $22.4bn outstanding, followed by the World Bank with $19.2bn and the Asian Development Bank (ADB) with $16.83bn.

The report put the average maturity of loans from official creditors at 16 years, with a four-year grace period and an average interest rate of 3.6 per cent. On the other hand, private credit carried an average interest rate of 8.6pc, with a three-year repayment period and a one-year grace period.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (Menap) region recorded improvements in debt-service and interest ratios. However, its external debt-to-gross national income (GNI) ratio rose from 26.7pc to 29.4pc in 2025, the largest single-year increase of any region, indicating continued debt accumulation.

In 2025, China extended the maturities on $2bn in loans to Pakistan, while the International Monetary Fund (IMF) provided $2.3bn in new disbursements under the Extended Fund Facility and Resilience and Sustainability Facility arrangements to support the country’s long-term economic stability.

Global debt at record high

Overall, the borrowing by low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) surged in 2025, marking the sharpest increase in external debt in four years and a forceful return of private creditors to developing country markets.

External debt climbed 5.5pc to a record $9.4 trillion as bond issues rebounded, the US dollar weakened and investors again showed greater willingness to lend. But the reopening of capital markets came at a steep price, especially for the poorest countries, which faced some of their highest borrowing costs in decades.

Debt service payments also rose for a fifth consecutive year. Even so, stronger economic growth helped stabilise some debt ratios and net long-term debt transfers turned positive after years of outflows.

The increase in external debt was even faster for countries eligible for International Development Association (IDA) financing, rising 8.1pc to $1.3tr, and for low-income countries, climbing 8.9pc to $262.4bn, the biggest increase since 2020.

A weakening dollar amplified the rise in debt. The dramatic depreciation of the US dollar during the year accounted for 28.2pc of the increase in LMICs’ external public and publicly guaranteed debt.

For several of the largest borrowers from concessional windows, currency valuation gains in 2025 not only offset principal payments made during the year but also, in some cases, partially reversed the stock reductions achieved through repayments in 2024, leaving reported balances higher at end-2025 despite continued debt servicing.

Private lending, which is more susceptible to fluctuations in financial market conditions, pricing conditions, and perceived creditworthiness of borrowers, saw a strong rebound in 2025.

LMIC debt stock owed to private creditors increased 5.2pc in 2025 to $5tr, a significant acceleration from the 0.6pc increase recorded in 2024. This increase was due to a combined increase in debt owed to bondholders and debt owed to commercial banks and other private creditors, which increased by 5.7pc (to $2.4tr) and 4.7pc (to $2.7tr), respectively.

LMIC economies, measured by gross national income, grew by 5.1pc. This strong economic growth encouraged lenders to return to these countries, and many LMIC governments were willing to borrow despite relatively high interest rates. The countries that can least afford it are paying the most to borrow.

Increased borrowing from private creditors hardened lending terms disproportionately for IDA-eligible countries, which faced an average interest rate of 8.2pc on new commitments during the year, the highest since the late 1980s. The difference in interest rates that this group of borrowers pays when borrowing from official creditors and rates on debt from private creditors widened significantly over the past decade, from 3.4 percentage points in 2016 to 5.5 percentage points in 2025.

International Bank for Reconstruction and Development borrowers, by contrast, saw improvements in the terms on new commitments, with an improved 5.5pc average interest rate, down from 5.8pc the previous year.

The report noted that the debt service burdens remain a pressure point for LMICs. Total debt service payments (interest plus principal) rose for the fifth year in a row, increasing 1.9pc to $1.4tr in 2025.

Payments to private creditors drove the increase, with payments to bondholders rising 13.7pc to $363.1bn.

Between 2022 and 2025, LMICs paid about $436.1bn more in debt service than they received in new financing. However, the trend reversed in 2025: long-term debt flows shifted from a net outflow of $118.4bn in 2024 to a net inflow of $45.4bn.

World.title: Petrol price slashed by Rs9.41 per litre, high-speed diesel by Rs5.56
World.content:
The government on Thursday dropped the price of petrol by Rs9.41 per litre and that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs5.56, in the fourth consecutive reduction in fuel prices.

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs352.59 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs382.25 on Nov 6 (Friday), according to a notification by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra).

The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel.

Under an arrangement announced on Monday for 30 days, oil refineries will contribute to the petroleum levy by bearing a cumulative impact of Rs15 billion, according to the government. This allows a Rs14.71 reduction in the petrol price at the consumer end.

Addressing a press conference on Tuesday, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik said efforts were being made to introduce a similar system for liquefied petroleum gas (LPG).

Meanwhile, the Jamaat-i-Islami and the government are set to follow up on their recent discussions on possible relief in petroleum prices and hold another round of talks on Thursday, the party said.

Rise in fuel prices

The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on Feb 28.

The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March.

Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm, and fuel allocations for official vehicles have been cut by 50pc for three months.

On Sept 13, PM Shehbaz also announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices.

Previously, on July 17, the petroleum minister announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US.

Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel.

The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give Ogra the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends.

Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes.

Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators.

Petrol and HSD are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

World.title: Eight killed, 30 injured in bus-truck collision on Hazara Motorway
World.content:
ABBOTABAD: At least eight people were killed and 30 others injured when a passenger bus collided with a dumper truck near the Havelian Interchange on the Hazara Motorway early Friday morning, rescue officials said.

The bus was travelling from Gilgit to Rawalpindi when the accident occurred. Initial reports suggested that a tyre burst caused the driver to lose control of the vehicle before it collided with the truck.

Following the incident, Rescue 1122 Abbottabad dispatched seven ambulances and a rescue vehicle to the scene to carry out relief operations.

The rescue operation, led by District Emergency Officer Hafeezur Rehman, was completed successfully. Rescue personnel provided first aid to the injured before shifting them to nearby hospitals for treatment.

The bodies of the eight deceased, who reportedly belonged to Gilgit, were transported to different hospitals. One body was taken to Type-D Hospital in Havelian, while four were shifted to Ayub Medical Complex and three to the District Headquarters Hospital (DHQ) Abbottabad.

All 30 injured passengers, including five children and six women, were shifted to Ayub Medical Complex for medical treatment. The condition of four injured passengers was reported to be critical.

A day earlier, a collision between a passenger bus and truck claimed the lives of 11 people and left 33 others injured near Pakpattan.

Last week, at least five people were killed and 27 others injured when a passenger bus plunged into a drain in Punjab’s Hafizabad district.

World.title: Asia stocks tumble after AI rout rocks US markets
World.content:
A rout in Asia’s tech-heavy markets deepened on Friday as fear of increased regulatory scrutiny and a slowdown in AI build-out precipitated the steepest decline in US stocks since the tariff-triggered “Liberation Day” selloff in April 2025.

Japan’s Nikkei slumped 7 per cent immediately after the opening bell while benchmark share price indices in South Korea and Taiwan dropped more than 8pc. Stocks across the region then appeared to stabilise as dip buyers emerged.

European stock futures also cut initial loss and were last down 0.6pc. Nasdaq futures were up 1.4pc though sentiment remained fragile.

Wall Street’s volatility “fear gauge” soared, the Nasdaq sank 5.5pc and $3 trillion was wiped off S&P 500 firms, with investors worried Democrats, who dominated midterm elections this week, will apply brakes to the AI boom.

The political jitters are hitting an AI trade already on shaky footing due to worry about return on companies’ enormous investment in artificial intelligence-related infrastructure.

“There is also clearly an element of panic in the selling, and positioning is making the adjustment much more violent,” said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo.

“When investors begin unwinding these positions simultaneously, the selling can become self-reinforcing, particularly if leverage and forced liquidations are involved.” The meltdown spooked retail investors and hedge funds alike, while policymakers and regulators scrambled to stem the selling.

AI chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix fell nearly 10pc and 12pc respectively in South Korea. Kioxia plunged 14pc in Japan while TSMC fell as much 8.5pc in Taiwan.

AI investor SoftBank Group slid 11pc, while the cost of insuring against the Japanese firm defaulting on debt jumped to its highest in four years.

“The selloff shows that AI stock prices had been built on rosy illusions about the future, and now that illusion is gone,” said Dong Baozhen, chairman of asset manager Lingtong Shengtai.

“The US stock market has been the standard-bearer and backbone of the global AI bull run. Now that backbone has snapped. Can AI bull markets elsewhere hold up on their own?”

Sentiment shifts, cracks emerge

Investor fear also centred on whether a stalling AI infrastructure expansion could hurt smaller firms whose capacity to raise funds has already been limited by higher interest rates and tighter financial conditions.

Neocloud firm CoreWeave, which has become a barometer of investor anxiety over heavy AI spending and borrowing, slumped 10pc, while its five-year credit default swap spreads widened to a record level.

“It’s pretty clear there’s been a real shift in sentiment,” said Michael McCarthy, chief executive for Australia and New Zealand at brokerage Moomoo.

The selling indicates investors are starting to factor in increased local opposition to data centres, with analysts saying markets have yet to fully consider the cost such building has imposed on communities.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index slumped 12.2pc overnight and the Nasdaq, which reversed an initial swing higher after the midterms before dropping, has now shed 12pc from its record close a month ago.

Still, some analysts said the selloff was overdone and the bottom was not far off.

“Today we are bound to see further liquidation of margin accounts, which suggests we are likely in the final stage of capitulation,” said Allen Huang, a vice president of Mega Financial Holding’s equities trading department.

“Even TSMC hit its daily limit down circuit breaker at one point, which typically marks the tail end of a downturn. When TSMC gets sold off, that means all stocks have been thoroughly dumped,” Huang said.

Finding refuge in bonds and Yen

Bonds gained in Asia, with US Treasuries as well as government bonds in Japan and China rising, while the US dollar slipped against haven currencies such as the yen and Swiss franc.

“Treasuries can probably rally a lot further,” said Nick Ferres, chief investment officer at Vantage Point Asset Management.

The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note was at 4.838pc, hovering near the lowest level since September 9. The 10-year JGB yield dropped as much as 9 bps to 1.795pc, the lowest since June 30.

World.title: Pakistan builds record reserves amid Gulf war
World.content:
KARACHI: Despite the Gulf war’s impact on weaker economies and uncertainty over high oil prices, Pakistan’s foreign exchange reserves climbed to a record high of more than $26.8 billion, the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) reported on Thursday.

The war started on Feb 28, jolting many economies, including Pakistan, but the SBP has since improved its reserves and added over $5bn.

The SBP’s reserves were $16.568bn in February, rising to $21.568bn on Oct 30.

The central bank reported that the foreign exchange holdings of the SBP and commercial banks increased during the week. During the week, SBP reserves rose by $39m.

The financial sector considers the State Bank’s current reserves sufficient to keep the exchange rate stable and to encourage exporters to repatriate export proceeds without delay. A stable exchange rate also provides confidence to importers.

However, currency experts believe the rupee is overvalued, allowing importers to get cheaper dollars, which is why the trade deficit is widening each month.

The trade deficit during July-Oct FY27 reached $14.6bn. The imports were $26bn and exports $11.4bn.

It is also believed that the exchange rate is being kept stable at the expense of remittances, which have been increasing each year.

The government or the State Bank has not devised a policy to use remittances better; instead, they are used to fill the trade gap.

SBP data showed that commercial bank reserves also increased by $70m during the week, reflecting that outflows from Pakistan were less than inflows into the banks.

The State Bank reported that the total reserves of the country reached a record high of $26.864bn, compared to $26.754bn last week, an increase of $110m.

Published in Dawn, November 6th, 2026

World.title: CJ shows displeasure over cops making TikTok videos
World.content:
LAHORE: Lahore High Court Chief Justice Aalia Neelum on Thursday expressed her displeasure over police officers making TikTok videos about missing girls and uploading them on social media.

“How police officers engaged in such activities [making video clips] would trace the missing girls,” the chief justice questioned, hearing a petition filed by a woman, Salma Bibi, seeking recovery of her allegedly missing daughter.

The chief justice also expressed dissatisfaction with the committee formed to recover the missing girls and summoned Inspector General of Police (IGP) Abdul Karim in person on Nov 11.

Earlier, police officials, including Punjab DIG (Crimes) Ali Janbaz and DIG (Legal) Awais Malik, appeared before the court.

A law officer submitted a report on cases involving the abduction and recovery of girls.

He said the police recovered 2,810 girls, while 452 remained missing, adding that four of the outstanding cases dated back to 2021.

“Where would police look for the cases registered in 2021? We are now in 2026. We cannot wait until 2032 to examine cases registered in 2024,” Chief Justice Neelum observed.

The police officers told the court that a social media application had helped trace a considerable number of missing girls.

An officer of the investigation wing stated that most of the outstanding cases were reported from Rawalpindi, Sialkot and Nankana Sahib. The chief justice was informed that action would be taken against the police officials involved in making and uploading TikTok videos.

She adjourned further proceedings till Nov 11.

Published in Dawn, November 6th, 2026

World.title: Shafay says standing by his younger brother
World.content:
LAHORE: Punjab Commerce and Investment Minister Shafay Hussain of the PML-Q has said that he is standing by his younger brother Salik Hussain, Federal Minister for Overseas Pakistanis, come what may.

In response to the ongoing controversy involving Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz and Salik Hussain, Mr Shafay said: “I have and will never distance myself from my younger brother. My brother is an independent person with his own independent views,” he told Dawn on Thursday. Maryam Nawaz has served a Rs5 billion defamation notice on Salik over his corruption allegations against her government, demanding that he retract his remarks. Salik, however, has maintained that he will respond to the notice.

Defending his brother, Mr Shafay said he (Salik) might be privy to information (about corruption), which he was not aware of.

“Salik Hussain never named Maryam Nawaz and never intended to say anything about her nor the Punjab government, but I believe he was referring to the systematic corruption that we all agree exists,” he said and added all politicians should be “more tolerant and should sit together to clear things.”

He hoped that both sides should try to defuse and clear misunderstandings.

On Wednesday, Information and Culture Minister Azma Bokhari said: “Shafay Hussain’s recent interviews have been supportive of Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, so we have no plan to denotify him from the Punjab cabinet. Shafay Hussain has rejected Salik’s allegations,” Ms Bokhari said responding to Dawn’s queries.

The latest exchange comes against the backdrop of a political split within the Chaudhry family following the ouster of Imran Khan’s government through a no-confidence vote in 2022. While Chaudhry Parvez Elahi and his son former federal minister Moonis Elahi aligned themselves with the PTI, Chaudhry Shujaat Hussain’s sons, Salik and Shafay, chose to side with the Sharifs.

Published in Dawn, November 6th, 2026

World.title: First Marble City being set up in Karachi
World.content:
KARACHI: Sindh Minister for Information, Transport and Mass Transit Sharjeel Inam Memon has said that Pakistan’s first Marble City is being established in Karachi to create new investment opportunities, promote industrial activities and generate employment.

He said the project would enable the processing of marble and granite reserves found in different parts of Sindh and other areas of the country through modern industrial techniques to produce high-quality products for export to international markets.

Addressing the pre-launch ceremony of the Karachi Marble City Industrial Park at a local hotel, he said investors would be provided with opportunities to establish industries equipped with modern facilities.

The project would promote the local processing of natural resources and the production of finished goods instead of exporting them as raw materials, which would also benefit the national economy, he added.

Sindh minister says project will promote local processing of stone and granite for exports

The formal inauguration of the project would be performed by Pakistan Peoples Party Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari and Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah.

Mr Memon said the average price of land in Marble City was being set at approximately Rs25 million per acre. Investors would not be required to pay the entire amount in a single instalment, as those unable to make a one-time payment would also be offered the facility to pay in installments.

According to a press release, Mr Memon said that despite the country’s vast reserves of marble and granite, these resources had not been utilised to their full potential.

He said agriculture also held fundamental importance in Pakistan’s economy, with a large segment of the population depending on the sector for employment. Pakistan needed to increase its agricultural exports and align agricultural production with modern industrial requirements.

He said the Sindh government would welcome other provinces, including Punjab, adopting successful projects initiated by Sindh. Similarly, if the provincial government found any policy or project of Punjab to be more effective, it would be happy to adopt it.

“We are all part of the same country and should encourage each other’s positive initiatives,” he added.

He claimed that several industrialists who had established businesses in other cities of the country were now also interested in shifting their operations to Karachi and making fresh investments in the city.

Special Assistant to the Chief Minister on Investment and Public-Private Partnership Qasim Naveed Qamar said the Marble City project covered an area of more than 300 acres along the Northern Bypass, with an estimated cost of $250 million. The project was being developed under a public-private partnership framework.

He said the Sindh government was working on a proposal to provide electricity at Rs20 per unit for its projects, particularly in Dhabeji and Khairpur.

He said efforts were also underway to provide industrialists in Marble City with facilities at the lowest possible cost, make machinery available on rent and provide access to the world’s most advanced equipment.

Arrangements were also being made to offer electricity at rates lower than those charged by K-Electric, he added.

Mr Qasim said the process of registration of investors and industrialists was being initiated, with registration scheduled to begin next month. Further facilities would also be extended to investors following registration.
