World.title: Hong Kong’s Joshua Wong: From teenage protest leader to a decade behind bars
World.content:
DEMOCRACY ACTIVISTS. File photo shows pro-democracy activists Joshua Wong and Agnes Chow arrive at the Eastern Court by police van after being arrested on suspicion for organizing illegal protests, in Hong Kong, China August 30, 2019.

He will be approaching 40 when he leaves jail, a long way off from his days as a one-year-old toddler in 1997, when Britain handed his city back to China with a promise of extensive autonomy and freedom of speech and assembly

HONG KONG – Hong Kong democracy activist Joshua Wong, once a leader of the 2014 Umbrella Movement that posed one of the boldest populist challenges to the leaders of China’s Communist Party in decades, was sentenced on Thursday, November 5, to 10 more years in jail.

Wong, who has been behind bars since 2020, pleaded guilty to a charge of collusion with foreign entities under the Asian financial hub’s national security law, ushered in that year.

He will be approaching 40 when he leaves jail, a long way off from his days as a one-year-old toddler in 1997, when Britain handed his city back to China with a promise of extensive autonomy and freedom of speech and assembly.

“One national security officer said he and I were ‘enemies’ and lamented that he had lost many friends because of me,” Wong said on Thursday, recalling the day he was charged.

“I replied: ‘You are not my enemy. We are all Hong Kongers; there is no antagonism between us,'” he added in his mitigation comments.

Activist journey started at 14

Wong’s activist journey started at just 14, as he emerged on Hong Kong’s democratic stage by co-founding a group called Scholarism that held mass protests and ultimately forced the government to shelve plans for a pro-China national education scheme in schools.

By age 17, as a thin youth with bowl-cut hair and dark-rimmed glasses, Wong was the international face of the pro-democracy “Umbrella Movement,” referring to how protesters warded off riot police volleys of tear gas and pepper spray.

Wong’s activism and vocal dissent landed him in jail numerous times, not least after the Umbrella Movement drew hundreds of thousands of protesters at its peak to paralyze streets in the city’s heart for 79 days.

Prosecutors in the latest case accused Wong of working along with others to solicit foreign sanctions or hostile actions against Hong Kong and China between July and November 2020.

Though he pleaded guilty to the charge, Wong said he mistakenly thought his actions were within the law, adding that he had never advocated Hong Kong independence nor the collapse of China.

The timeframe of the events is key, since Beijing in late June of that year had imposed the National Security Law on the city following months of sometimes-violent pro-democracy protests in 2019.

The law effectively outlawed or put at risk many of the political activities that Wong and his peers once took for granted.

‘Black hand’

Wong became a familiar face on the international scene and a thorn in the side of authorities in Beijing and Hong Kong, featuring on the front cover of Time magazine in 2014 and in a Netflix documentary in 2017 that chronicled his political life.

Along with other Hong Kong critics of mainland China, including media tycoon Jimmy Lai, he was repeatedly nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize.

He made it a mission to drum up support for Hong Kong’s democracy movement at home and overseas, meeting politicians from the United States and Europe, drawing the wrath of Beijing, which called him a “black hand” of foreign forces.

Outsiders who met him during this time recall his striking air of quiet determination, and apparently unshakable convictions.

When Wong left jail in June 2019 at the height of the protests, he was not a leading figure in organizing the rallies, but he once again became one of the movement’s most globally recognized faces.

Scholarism had morphed into Demosisto, a political party that once backed a referendum on Hong Kong’s sovereignty and installed the youngest candidate ever on the city’s Legislative Council before he was disqualified.

Demosisto was disbanded within hours after the National Security Law was passed.

In 2017, just before another sentencing, Wong told more than 100 supporters who thronged the court lobby, some weeping, that he had no regrets.

“I hope Hong Kong people won’t give up,” he said. “Victory is ours. When we are released next year I hope we can see a Hong Kong that is full of hope. I want to see Hong Kong people not giving up. This is my last wish before I go to jail.”

Nearly 10 years on, Wong’s extended term in prison is the latest blow for a movement whose followers find themselves in detention, exile or, in the case of some, cowed into silence.

Standing in the dock on Thursday, Wong was silent as the judge sentenced him to 10 years in jail that will keep him in prison after his current term ends in January. The sentence will be served concurrently, effectively shortening it by two months.

Wong mentioned a desire to eventually look after his ageing parents above all.

This, along with the fact that books on Chinese history and Hong Kong’s mini-constitution were among the hundreds he was reading in jail, prompted the judge to hail Wong’s efforts at rehabilitation as “commendable.” – Rappler.com

World.title: US warns of ‘ongoing cyber threat’ to industrial refrigeration systems
World.content:
REFRIGERATORS. View of empty refrigerators at the frozen food aisle inside an Intermarche supermarket in Paris the day after a cyberattack targeted refrigeration systems at French supermarket chains, causing food losses and fires at several stores, France, October 13, 2026.

FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman says the government is 'seeing these systems targeted across critical infrastructure sectors globally'

WASHINGTON, USA – The United States is warning of an “ongoing cyber threat” to industrial refrigeration systems, saying in a statement issued on Thursday, November 5, that every organization that depends on cold storage should assume it could fall into the hackers’ crosshairs.

The statement, which follows a spate of hacks against commercial freezers in the United States and Europe, said that unidentified “malicious cyber actors” were targeting vulnerabilities in internet-accessible electronic temperature and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities.

Although short on detail about the hackers involved, the statement suggested that the threat to commercial cold storage was ongoing.

“If successfully exploited, the actors could change the temperature and possibly cause physical impacts such as fire hazards, loss of inventory and changes to the service life of the system,” said the statement, which was jointly issued by the FBI, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and the departments of health, transport and agriculture.

“Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target,” said Chris Butera, CISA’s acting executive assistant director for cybersecurity.

FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman said that the government was “seeing these systems targeted across critical infrastructure sectors globally.”

The government urged operators of industrial refrigeration control systems to pull their devices off the public internet, isolate them from their corporate networks and promptly apply software updates.

At least three waves of hacks have hit commercial fridges and freezers in the past few months. Pentagon investigators are treating a series of mysterious malfunctions that hit grocery store refrigeration units on US military bases in August as a cyberattack, Reuters first reported last week. A sweeping hack of French freezers last month dealt tens of millions of euros’ worth of damage, while a second wave of hacking affected more than 100 stores across Europe on Monday.

The hacks have raised concerns over the ability of hackers to remotely tamper with refrigerators and other critical devices. – Rappler.com

World.title: Unemployment edges up to 5.4% in September 2026
World.content:
Pasay residents looking for work queue for interviews during a job fair at the Pasay City Astrodome on April 13, 2026.

Part of the increase in unemployment is due to job creation lagging behind a growing pool of workers

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines’ unemployment rate slightly rose to 5.4% in September 2026 as the number of Filipinos joining the labor force continued to outpace employment growth.

Around 2.86 million Filipinos were unemployed in September, up from 2.77 million in August, according to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) on Friday, November 6.

The latest figure is also much higher than the 3.8% unemployment rate recorded in September 2025, when around 1.96 million Filipinos were unemployed. This meant an additional 909,000 Filipinos were without jobs compared with a year before.

Part of the increase in unemployment is due to job creation lagging behind a growing pool of workers.

National Statistician Dennis Mapa said the country’s labor force grew by around 1.63 million year-on-year to 53.19 million in September. However, employment increased by only 721,000 to 50.32 million over the same time.

Most of the increase in labor force participation came from younger Filipinos aged 15 to 24, with around 988,000 more people in this age group joining the labor force compared with September 2025. Among them, not everyone found employment, with only 606,000 securing a job.

Despite the higher unemployment rate, several industries posted substantial employment gains.

Accommodation and food service activities recorded the largest year-on-year increase, adding around 834,000 workers. Mapa said much of the increase came from restaurants, mobile food services, and canteens, as part of more economic activity ahead of the Christmas season.

Transportation and storage added another 254,000 workers, while other service activities gained 174,000.

Construction, however, continued to weaken, losing around 271,000 workers year-on-year and another 416,000 compared with August alone.

Mapa attributed the decline partly to slowing government construction projects and higher construction material costs. Employment losses were particularly pronounced in the construction of buildings, electrical installation, and construction of utility projects.

The PSA also reported a substantial drop in employment of clerical support workers, which fell by 582,000 year-on-year, the largest decline among the major occupational groups.

Asked by Rappler about the decline, Mapa said around 289,000 of the reduction came from contact center information clerks, an occupational category that includes some business process outsourcing (BPO) employees.General office clerks accounted for another 149,000 of the decline.

Underemployment, meanwhile, improved to 11% in September from 11.9% in August and 11.1% in September 2025. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Puso at Diwa] Wanted: Integrity dividend
World.content:
The Philippines does not need another political savior. It needs an integrity dividend.

The flood control scandal, the investigations involving powerful political figures, the impending arrest of Senator Bato de la Rosa, and the impeachment proceedings against Vice President Sara Duterte may appear to be separate political developments. But they raise one fundamental question: Can the Philippines finally move beyond political personalities and confront the deeper problems of corruption, weak institutions and poor governance?

This is not just a political question. It is an economic one.

At a time when the economy needs more investment, stronger consumer spending and renewed business confidence, the country is caught in a cycle of political controversy and institutional uncertainty. The consequences are being felt not only in government but also in businesses, households and the broader economy.

Consider what is happening. The economy grew by only 2.3% in the second quarter of 2026. More troubling, investment declined by 9.2%. Household consumption continued to grow, but at a slower pace of 2.8%, extending a four-quarter slowdown.

These numbers have several explanations, including surging inflation, higher borrowing costs and persistent external shocks. But governance and political uncertainty are also part of the problem. And we should not underestimate their economic cost.

Corruption is more than stolen money

The flood control anomalies have exposed how public funds intended to protect communities from flooding and disasters may have been wasted or diverted through questionable projects and contracts.

The damage goes far beyond the money allegedly lost.

Every peso wasted on an overpriced, substandard or nonexistent project is a peso that could have built a better road, protected a community, improved a school or supported a hospital. When flood control projects fail, families lose homes and livelihoods, businesses suffer disruptions, and farmers lose crops. The economy pays repeatedly for infrastructure that should have protected it in the first place.

This is why accountability matters. Investigations, audits and the filing of cases against those implicated are necessary. No public official or contractor should be above the law.

But catching the people responsible is only half the job. We must also change the system that allowed these things to happen.

How can questionable projects pass through government approval? Why are procurement and project monitoring safeguards inadequate? Why can public funds be allocated without sufficiently transparent and independent scrutiny?

Unless these questions are answered, the country risks repeating the same scandal under different names and political personalities.

The danger of turning accountability into another political fight

The impeachment proceedings against the Vice President present another test of our democratic institutions.

The issue should not be whether one belongs to the administration or the opposition, or whether one enjoys greater political support. The issue is whether constitutional processes are followed fairly, transparently and consistently.

The same standards must apply to everyone implicated in corruption allegations, regardless of political position or affiliation. The presumption of innocence and the right to due process must be respected. Impeachment must be decided on constitutional and evidentiary grounds, not political alliance or convenience.

There is a danger that these proceedings will become another contest between political factions, with each side more concerned about winning power than strengthening institutions.

If people come to believe that investigations and impeachment are simply weapons used against political opponents, public trust will suffer further. Even legitimate efforts to establish accountability can lose credibility when they are perceived as selective or partisan.

The country needs justice, not political revenge. It needs accountability, not another round of political score-settling.

The economy pays for uncertainty

Why should ordinary Filipinos care about these political and institutional developments?

Because confidence matters to economic activity.

Businesses invest when they believe the rules are predictable, contracts will be honored, government policies will be consistent and public institutions can be trusted. When uncertainty rises, businesses hesitate. They postpone expansion, delay purchases of equipment, defer hiring and sometimes move their investments elsewhere.

Households behave similarly. When people worry about their jobs, incomes, prices and the country’s economic direction, they become more cautious. They postpone buying a house, a car or appliances. They reduce discretionary spending and save more for emergencies.

When businesses invest less and households spend less, economic activity weakens. Companies earn less, employment opportunities become limited, and government collects less revenue. This can reinforce the very economic difficulties that created the uncertainty in the first place.

This is the connection between governance and the everyday lives of Filipinos. Corruption and political instability are not abstract problems confined to Congress, Malacañang or government agencies. They affect jobs, incomes, prices, public services and opportunities.

The cost of corruption is not only the money stolen. It is also the investment that never happens, the job that is never created and the economic opportunity that is lost.

We must change the system, not just the personalities

Perhaps the most difficult truth is that Philippine politics remains heavily driven by personalities, political dynasties, patronage and narrow vested interests.

Political alliances change, personalities rise and fall, and elections rearrange the balance of power. But the underlying incentives often remain the same.

We cannot expect meaningful transformation simply by replacing one group of politicians with another of their kind. Unless we reform the way political power is exercised and public money is allocated, the same problems will return.

We need more transparent political financing, stronger procurement safeguards, independent auditing, meaningful legislative oversight and greater public access to information about government spending.

The budget process itself deserves serious reform. Public funds must be allocated according to clear national priorities and measurable economic and social benefits, not political accommodation. The 2027 national budget provides an immediate opportunity to demonstrate that government has learned from the flood control scandal.

Political dynasties and the concentration of political power should also be squarely addressed, as contemplated by the Constitution. Ultimately, public office must be treated as a responsibility to serve, not an opportunity to accumulate power and resources.

Wanted: Integrity dividend

There is an argument that aggressively pursuing corruption cases and confronting political controversies could further unsettle the economy. There may indeed be short-term costs when questionable projects are suspended, government spending is reviewed and powerful political interests are challenged.

But avoiding accountability in the name of economic stability would be a much greater mistake.

The solution is not to abandon investigations or compromise justice. It is to ensure that accountability is pursued fairly, efficiently and without political interference, while legitimate public investments and essential services continue.

The Philippines needs what may be called an integrity dividend: the benefits that come when people trust government, public funds are used properly, businesses feel secure investing, and households believe that the future is worth preparing for.

This dividend cannot be produced simply by arresting a few prominent personalities or removing one political figure from office. It requires institutions that work regardless of who occupies public office.

The real measure of success is not only about how many politicians are investigated, arrested or impeached. It is also about how public money is better spent, government services improve, businesses invest with greater confidence, and ordinary Filipinos enjoy more opportunities.

The country does not need another political savior. It needs a political and economic system that does not depend on saviors in the first place.

Good governance is not an obstacle to economic growth. It is one of its most important foundations. And when governance fails, it is ultimately the ordinary Filipinos who pay the price. – Rappler.com

Diwa C. Guinigundo is the former deputy governor for monetary policy and other aspects of central banking. He was a former alternate executive director at the IMF in Washington, DC in 2001-2003. He is the author and editor of several books on political economy, regional crisis and cooperation, debt and economic growth and public policy agenda.

He serves as independent director of several corporate and financial institutions with focus on corporate governance, risk oversight and audit.

He also serves as principal advisor for New York-based GlobalSourcePartners. He remains in the advisory board of ASEAN Macroeconomic Research Office and Singapore Management University’s Sim Kee Boon Institute for Financial Economics.

He is the senior pastor of the Fullness of Christ International Ministries in Mandaluyong.

World.title: [Market Rider] Essential market insights on the recent GCash IPO
World.content:
Last month’s P60.9-billion GCash initial public offering (IPO) or more precisely of Mynt Inc., the parent company of GCash, was the largest in the history of the Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE). It was also the biggest for Southeast Asia for 2026.

When the idea came out for the first time, many thought it was not possible. The market has been poor that it slowly but surely became the region’s bottom dweller in recent years. During this time, the PSE was said to “operate under a P30-billion domestic liquidity ceiling.” Public equity offerings exceeding this threshold routinely drained capital from other index stocks. It was suffering from a market structural anomaly where massive IPOs exhausted domestic liquidity, resulting in immediate post-listing price collapses. (READ: [Market Rider] Buy when there’s blood in the streets, even if it’s your own blood)

But the incredible happened. The IPO shattered local capital-raising records. The market withstood the stress test and presented an optimistic financial ecosystem for both present and future big ticket market debuts.

Let’s look at how it happened.

Essentially, the operational mechanics of the GCash debut offer definitive structural lessons in pricing discipline, liquidity management, and retail participation, fundamentally redrawing the blueprint for big-ticket public equity offerings. It also provided a glimpse into the local market’s actual capacity to absorb multi-billion-peso digital assets, frameworks that will directly dictate the strategy especially for future technology listings in the country.

Initially, the GCash IPO demonstrated that massive scale demands conservative pricing discipline; for in the past, large-cap listings on the PSE suffered from post-debut sell-offs due to overwhelming market supply.

In 2021, Monde Nissin maximized its valuation on day one by pricing at the absolute top of its range, leaving no “money on the table.” The resulting lack of a secondary market cushion triggered a multi-year valuation reset. Similarly, during its 2020 debut, Converge ICT resisted trimming its initial offer price despite pandemic-induced market volatility. When institutional selling intensified on Day 1, its local stabilization agent was forced to exhaust 85% of its defense fund within a fortnight just to establish a static floor.

True enough, even with the conservative anchoring, the trading price of GCash experienced a post-debut slump, hitting an intraday low of P5.95 or nearly 10% below offer on October 26. It required heavy post-IPO intervention from its stabilization agent (UBS) to steady the stock back to P6.61.

In this regard, GCash bypassed this market constraint through two distinct structural pillars. This is through the employment of a massive global cornerstone book and decentralized retail onboarding. GCash secured over 20 top-tier global cornerstone institutional investors, including BlackRock, Fidelity, HSBC, and Capital Group, who absorbed nearly 70% of the offered shares. This is now the new structural “floor” for new-economy tech stocks.

Conversely, by embedding the IPO natively into the GStocks PH platform, GCash unlocked an entirely new tier of retail investors. Over 140,000 everyday platform users collectively contributed P1.1 billion.

Unlike traditional day-traders who flip shares for short-term arbitrage, these platform-native users behaved as long-term, sticky collectors, effectively neutralizing immediate open-market selling pressure.

Out of this experience, global banking intervention and conservative initial pricing to withstand the local market’s finite depth are critical to meet the demands of a massive public equity offering.

Regulatory and tailwinds

Believe it or not, PSE’s decision to lower the minimum public float requirement to 12% for exceptionally large corporations like those valued over P200 billion or over, also helped contribute to the success of GCash’s IPO and listing. This reduction in the minimum requirement for public float has truly created a safer buffer against market exhaustion.

By also allowing modern tech infrastructure and fintech assets to trade on forward-looking growth multipliers, the PSE and the Securities Exchange Commission (SEC) have as well contributed to the successful IPO of GCash.

This newly proven playbook for market absorption could serve heavily as market strategies for upcoming mega-public offerings. However, it appears also has that the market cannot do it in rapid, localized succession without causing investor fatigue.

Recognizing this local capacity constraint, the regulators, issuers and underwriters may have to work more to remedy the problem by introducing a delicate balance of disciplined localized pricing, decentralized retail distribution, and forging a strategic bridge to global institutional capital. – Rappler.com

World.title: Hurry Up With Our Investment Projects, China tells Myanmar Regime
World.content:
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has renewed Beijing’s call for the Myanmar regime to “steadily advance” key projects under the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC), which is designed to give Beijing direct access to Indian Ocean.

Wang made the remarks during a meeting on Tuesday with Myanmar Investment and Foreign Economic Relations Minister Aung Kyaw Hoe, who is in Beijing for the 11th Lancang–Mekong Cooperation Foreign Ministers’ Meeting.

A clearly exasperated Wang stressed the need for the two sides to “coordinate” development and security, as many parts of Myanmar are plagued by civil war, making it hard for the China-backed projects to proceed.

In turn, Wang promised Chinese support for the rebranded regime’s efforts to achieve international recognition. “China will always be a strategic partner that Myanmar can rely on,” he said.

The remarks come as the U.S. shows signs of re-engaging with Naypyitaw in search of business.

Wang also called for stronger efforts to combat scams and online gambling. He urged Myanmar to prevent the “resurgence of chaos” in Myawaddy, referring to online scam operations that flourished along the Thai-Myanmar border.

He urged Naypyitaw to do more to ensure the safety of Chinese nationals, organizations and projects operating in the country.

Aung Kyaw Hoe, for his part, promised that his regime does want to accelerate the CMEC projects and step up cooperation with China and regional countries in combating online scam operations. He duly thanked his hosts for supporting Myanmar in international forums, according to a statement from the Chinese Embassy.

When Myanmar’s putschist leader Min Aung Hlaing last visited Beijing in June after declaring himself president, Chinese President Xi Jinping also urged him to speed up the CMEC projects, a key component of Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI).

He too urged the regime to provide stronger security guarantees for Chinese personnel and investments in Myanmar, many of which are in areas now controlled by the resistance or ethnic armed organizations over which Beijing holds no sway.

The planned corridor includes several flagship projects, notably the Kyaukphyu deep-sea port in Rakhine State and a railway linking Kyaukphyu through Mandalay and Muse with China’s Yunnan Province.

The Kyaukphyu Special Economic Zone and deep-sea port project is particularly important for Beijing because it would provide China with direct access to the Indian Ocean while supporting economic development in Yunnan and other southwestern Chinese provinces.

But other than pay lip-service to the plans and hold out its hand for more investment, the Myanmar regime has done little to advance these projects, instead losing itself in dreams of reviving the long-mothballed Myitsone Dam Project in quite a different part of the country.

In its frustration, China has now reopened border crossings with areas controlled by ethnic armed organizations in northern Shan State to allow lucrative trade to resume, whether the regime likes it or not.

A China analyst told The Irrawaddy that Beijing “knows very well that Min Aung Hlaing’s stubbornness is holding everything up. The fighting is still going on, the peace talks haven’t delivered any results, there’s been no progress in northern Shan State, and the border crossings are still not operating normally.”

For the CMEC projects to move forward, Min Aung Hlaing “has to engage in talks with the ethnic armed groups first,” she added. “In that sense, I think China was quite deliberately sending that message.”

World.title: Kyat Slump Disrupts Thai Border Trade as Import Costs Rise
World.content:
The rapid depreciation of Myanmar’s currency has disrupted border trade with Thailand, prompting some traders and money changers along the border to suspend transactions as they struggle to cope with volatile exchange rates and mounting import costs.

The currency weakened to around 680 baht per 100,000 kyats this week, down from more than 700 baht in recent weeks. The currency also fell against the U.S. dollar, with the market exchange rate rising from just above 4,700 kyats per dollar at the end of October to more than 4,900 on Wednesday. The rate was just around 4,400 kyats in early October.

The latest slump is fueling concerns over another wave of inflation in a country heavily reliant on imports from Thailand. Myanmar imports a wide range of goods from its neighbor, including electrical appliances, household products, cosmetics, construction materials and foodstuffs, making fluctuations in the baht exchange rate significant for consumers.

Market insiders attributed the kyat’s latest decline to the regime’s plan to borrow 2.1 trillion kyats from the Central Bank of Myanmar to finance a budget shortfall for fiscal year 2026-27, which ends on March 31. The regime has already sold treasury bonds worth trillions of kyats, leading to speculation that it will simply print banknotes to cover the deficit.

They also pointed to Myanmar’s continued inclusion on the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) blacklist, delays in export licensing and policy inconsistencies between ministries as factors undermining confidence in the market.

The swift depreciation of the kyat has left traders struggling to price goods and manage working capital.

“A gradual rise doesn’t create much difficulty. The problem is when rates surge rapidly,” a trader in Myawaddy told The Irrawaddy.

“If exchange rates rise further, we will need more capital to restock. Some traders have temporarily stopped trading and making payments, and are waiting to see where the market moves.”

The uncertainty has spread beyond traders. Some major money changers in Myawaddy and across the border in Thailand suspended transactions on Wednesday, opting to wait for the next day’s opening rates before resuming business, according to border exchange operators.

The volatility is not confined to the Thai border. Traders in Muse, on Shan State’s border with China, are facing similar difficulties as the kyat continues to weaken against the yuan, market sources said.

Traders warn that prolonged instability in foreign exchange markets could further squeeze trade. Importers say their profits are shrinking, but are reluctant to increase prices for fear that demand may decline further.

A trader in Myawaddy said transport costs remain a major contributor to rising prices, with expenses along trade routes increasing because of checkpoints and demands for unofficial payments.

“Price increases are caused more by transport costs than exchange rates,” he said. “Costs at checkpoints rise sharply whenever authorities announce crackdowns or tighter controls.”

Exporters also say the weaker kyat is raising shipping costs because freight charges, container fees and port services are paid in U.S. dollars. At the same time, they complain that mandatory foreign-exchange conversion rules prevent them from fully benefiting from higher market exchange rates.

Under existing regulations, exporters must convert 35 percent of their export earnings at the Central Bank’s official rate, creating a significant gap between official and market rates. The Central Bank’s official reference rate remains 2,100 kyats per dollar, while its market trading rate is about 3,660 kyats per dollar. The market rate was around 4,900 kyats on Thursday. Before the coup, the kyat traded at roughly 1,300-1,400 per U.S. dollar.

An exporter from Mon State explained that the depreciation of the kyat has sharply increased the capital required to buy export commodities such as corn and onions.

“Previously, we could buy a container of goods for 10 million kyats from local producers. Now it can require more than 15 million kyats,” he said.

Traders say prices of Thai imports, particularly electrical goods, household products, cosmetics, construction materials and food items, are already climbing as a result of the stronger baht and rising transportation costs.

World.title: Thai Foreign Minister to Visit Myanmar Ahead of ASEAN Summit
World.content:
BANGKOK—Thailand’s foreign minister said he will visit Myanmar on November 12, days before a regional summit where Bangkok will be pressing to normalize ties with the war-torn country.

Sihasak Phuangketkeow’s trip also comes during raised tensions along the countries’ shared border, where Bangkok said clashes between Myanmar’s military and ethnic rebels caused property damage and injured a Thai civilian in Thailand on Thursday.

His visit, announced late Tuesday, is scheduled shortly before a November 16-18 summit of leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in Manila.

Myanmar’s leaders have not been invited to high-level ASEAN meetings since former general Min Aung Hlaing led a 2021 military coup that ousted democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering a civil war.

Sihasak told reporters in Beijing his government wants to “hear Myanmar’s latest position” ahead of the summit.

“De-escalation by all parties will help create a conducive atmosphere for essential dialogue and the peace process,” he said.

“If there is progress on these fronts, it will be a positive factor for ASEAN to consider at the leaders summit, as we decide how to move forward on the situation in Myanmar, including Myanmar’s participation in ASEAN meetings,” he added.

Sihasak, who last visited Myanmar in April, said he would meet his counterpart, Tin Maung Swe, on November 12, and a meeting with Min Aung Hlaing was “in the works”.

In July, Bangkok hosted a meeting between Tin Maung Swe and foreign ministers of several ASEAN member states, the first such gathering since the 2021 coup.

The following month Min Aung Hlaing met with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul in Bangkok, with the two nations’ military chiefs holding talks two weeks after.

Min Aung Hlaing took over as civilian president in April following elections widely dismissed by monitors as a charade.

Since then he has been given a red-carpet welcome across the region, in India, China and several ASEAN nations.

Myanmar is expected to send a senior civil servant to the Manila summit.

Thailand has stepped up security on its western frontier following last week’s cross-border fire.

On Wednesday, Myanmar’s military blamed “terrorist insurgents”—the term it commonly uses to refer to ethnic-minority armed groups and pro-democracy forces—for wounding a Thai national, according to a statement in state media.

World.title: Myanmar’s NUG Warns US Against Prioritizing Its Interests Over Peace
World.content:
In response to the new U.S. Mission Strategy for war-torn Myanmar, the parallel civilian National Unity Government (NUG) and observers urged Washington to help solve the country’s political crisis first instead of prioritizing its own security and economic interests.

Speaking with The Irrawaddy, NUG Deputy Foreign Affairs Minister David Gum Awng said that if the U.S. had a genuine desire to see sustainable peace and economic development in the country, the root cause of the political crisis must be solved first.

“An approach that sidelines the core principles such as democracy, human rights and establishment of a federal union in favor of prioritizing its [own] security and economic interests is not sufficient and lacks the comprehensive scope needed to solve the Myanmar crisis,” he added.

The U.S. State Department recently published its latest strategy for Myanmar, prioritizing the fight against online scam networks that target Americans, increasing U.S. investment, and access to rare earth minerals. Additional objectives include expanding U.S. regional influence and brokering a peace agreement by 2030.

Recently, U.S. officials held talks with junta leaders in Naypyitaw and Tokyo, increasing Washington’s engagement with the internationally isolated coup regime that ousted the democratically elected civilian government led by pro-democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021.

Washington said in its latest statement that facilitating dialogue and supporting multi-stakeholder engagement would help lay the groundwork for lasting peace and national reconciliation.

However, Gum Awng argued that peace cannot be achieved simply by forcing stakeholders to sit together at a negotiating table, noting that the primary challenge is whether the regime is genuinely willing to give up its dictatorship and accept real change.

“Without the definitive end of the military dictatorship, the emergence of an inclusive political process involving all stakeholders (including ethnic groups), and the establishment of robust monitoring mechanisms to guarantee agreements, any hastily brokered peace driven by a specific timeline will only temporarily de-escalate the conflict without solving the underlying root problem.”

Regarding the U.S. goal of building regional influence, the NUG minister said Myanmar cannot be viewed solely as a proxy battleground for U.S.-China influence, adding that the sovereignty and the right to self-determination of the nation’s people remain paramount.

“If the U.S. wishes to build long-term, sustainable influence, engaging with the military council alone is insufficient. The U.S. must respect the democratic will of the Myanmar people, increase its engagement with federal democratic forces, and prove through practical actions that it is a reliable partner,” Gum Awng said.

“U.S. influence cannot be measured solely by its ability to counter China. It depends entirely on earning the trust of the Myanmar people and participating constructively in the building of a future federal democratic nation.”

Regarding U.S. efforts to gain access to rare earth minerals through its peace efforts, the NUG’s deputy foreign minister warned that the country’s resources cannot be treated merely as a component of a peace process or a political compromise, since they are directly tied to the long-term interests of the people, the rights of ethnic groups, and the resource management rights of the future federal union.

Regarding Washington’s move to boost engagement with the regime, Debbie Stothard, founder and coordinator of the Alternative ASEAN Network on Burma, said a strategy based on appeasing the root cause of Myanmar’s notorious transnational crime hubs is doomed to fail. U.S. citizens, along with the people of Myanmar and the region, continue to suffer due to this irresponsible approach, she said.

“It is like engaging serial killers in order to persuade them to kill fewer people instead of acting to stop their crimes,” she said.

“It is both illogical and immoral to bribe [coup president] Min Aung Hlaing’s junta with trade and aid to secure rare earths while looking away from the security, economic and humanitarian crises he is intensifying every day.”

She also warned that the U.S. was in danger of falling into Min Aung Hlaing’s trap, in which he is able to pit Moscow, Beijing and Washington against each other to secure more weapons, more cash and more legitimacy without concrete solutions.

Regarding U.S. peace efforts, Myanmar political analyst Htin Kyaw Aye said, “I don’t think it [a U.S.-brokered peace plan] will work. Myanmar’s political situation and its underlying problem cannot be resolved easily or quickly. Its peace plan is likely either a strategic miscalculation or merely a gesture to show the U.S. is interested in it.”

World.title: Is Myanmar’s Regime Preparing Another ‘Summit Surprise’?
World.content:
As regional leaders finalize their itineraries for this month’s Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila, a grim and familiar pattern is playing out in Myanmar. For four years, the military junta has delivered a “summit surprise”: a sharp escalation in violence, usually deadly airstrikes on civilians, timed to coincide with high-level diplomatic gatherings.

Human rights organizations and UN bodies have documented this cycle extensively. Ahead of the May 2023 ASEAN Summit in Indonesia, the military bombed the village of Pazigyi, killing more than 160 people. Human Rights Watch cited the attack as evidence of the junta’s disregard for ASEAN’s peace plan for Myanmar, known as the Five-Point Consensus. Later that year, as leaders were still managing the diplomatic fallout, the military struck a displaced persons camp in Kachin State, killing 28 civilians, including children. Amnesty International described the attack as a likely war crime. The brazenness grew ahead of the October 2024 summits in Laos, when the military launched some of its heaviest aerial campaigns since the 2021 coup. In September 2024 alone, monitors recorded 153 airstrikes, which destroyed schools and hospitals among other civilian targets. A report by the OHCHR, the UN’s human rights body, confirmed that airstrike fatalities nearly doubled that year.

Shortly before his visit to Malaysia in October this year, Min Aung Hlaing’s regime intensified its bombardment of Rakhine State, where an airstrike on a crowded local market killed at least 50 people, including children. The attack was so bloody that UN human rights chief Volker Türk said, “This latest attack raises serious concerns about respect for international humanitarian law with respect to the conduct of hostilities.”

The gap between diplomatic theater and reality on the ground has rarely been wider. Last week, Philippine Foreign Secretary and ASEAN Special Envoy Maria Theresa Lazaro made a two-day visit to Myanmar, overseeing humanitarian aid in Shan State and discussing the restoration of Myanmar’s ASEAN status with regime officials. She left without meeting detained State Counselor Aung San Suu Kyi. Manila has repeatedly pressed for access to the 81-year-old Nobel peace laureate, but Lazaro reportedly did not even request a meeting this time, fearing the junta would cancel her trip.

The regime was quick to exploit the optics, projecting an image of cooperation through state media. It also continues to use Aung San Suu Kyi as a bargaining chip. Recent limited contact, including a brief consular phone call with her son and a package from Britain’s King Charles, appear aimed at softening its pariah status abroad while denying ASEAN any meaningful access. Soon after the envoy’s departure, the junta’s fighter jets were back over civilian areas.

This approach is now alienating even Naypyitaw’s most accommodating neighbors. In August, Thailand rolled out the red carpet for Min Aung Hlaing, the newly self-appointed president, in the hope of pragmatic dialogue. Many in Myanmar consider him a war criminal. Thailand is now facing the fallout of the regime’s violence. Its reckless operations along the frontier recently prompted the Thai military to summon Myanmar’s defense attaché to lodge a formal protest. The embarrassment has spilled into domestic politics, where the opposition has accused the Anutin government of being dangerously soft on Naypyitaw. Critics argue that accommodation not only undermines democratic values but also emboldens a junta willing to threaten Thai security and humiliate neighbors who extend a hand.

For the Philippines, this year’s ASEAN chair, the crisis has proven exhausting. Manila has tried to balance quiet diplomacy with firmer rhetoric, but the junta’s relentless violence has stalled any real progress. When the summit ends, Manila will likely be relieved to hand the “Myanmar headache” to incoming chair Singapore.

Singapore will inherit a deeply fractured regional approach to a crisis that continues to embarrass Southeast Asia. Though historically a champion of pragmatic diplomacy, it has grown more assertive as its chairmanship nears, and many hope it will take a firm stand against the regime. At an informal ASEAN foreign ministers’ meeting in Bangkok in July 2026, brokered by Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow, Singapore’s Vivian Balakrishnan pressed Myanmar’s representatives directly to release political prisoners, naming Aung San Suu Kyi, and to allow safe, unimpeded delivery of humanitarian aid. Singapore has also shown a growing willingness to scrutinize financial flows and aviation fuel reaching the junta. Yet the fundamental equation remains unchanged: the regime has proven immune to standard diplomatic persuasion and incremental sanctions.

When the gavel falls in Manila this month, there will no doubt be renewed expressions of “deep concern” and calls for an end to hostilities. But as the smoke clears over Rakhine State and diplomatic protests are filed in Bangkok, the truer story emerges. For the people of Myanmar, ASEAN’s diplomatic milestones are no longer opportunities for a breakthrough. They are dark omens of the violence that follows.

World.title: Thailand’s New Deals with Myanmar and Washington’s Changing Priorities
World.content:
As we approach the end of October, it is worth revisiting Myanmar regime leader Min Aung Hlaing’s official visit to Thailand in August, particularly in light of what has happened since. Within two months, Myanmar has concluded new technological cooperation arrangements with Thailand and Russia, while the United States has held two rounds of direct talks with the regime. These developments may look unrelated, but they point towards something considerably more interesting: the regime is expanding its international relationships, acquiring access to new technologies and developing opportunities for intelligence cooperation.

On August 6-7, Min Aung Hlaing visited Thailand, where the two governments exchanged four cooperation instruments. The most interesting, no doubt, was a Memorandum of Understanding between Thailand’s Geo-Informatics and Space Technology Development Agency (GISTDA) and the Myanmar Space Agency. The agreement concerns Earth-observation technology and satellite information, officially intended for natural-resource management, environmental monitoring and disaster response.

As I discussed in my previous article, Buying Gas or Buying Surveillance? Gas-Rich Myanmar’s Deal With Russia, Moscow is already providing Myanmar with access to satellite and communications technology. Thailand’s new agreement adds another dimension to Myanmar’s expanding international technological cooperation.

But Thailand’s agreement is particularly interesting because satellite technology is only one component of the cooperation it is offering Myanmar.

The joint statement issued during the August visit contains an important commitment: Thailand officially pledged to support Myanmar’s membership in the Egmont Group, an international network of financial intelligence units (FIUs) that facilitates financial intelligence sharing across jurisdictions.

Thailand has been an Egmont Group member since 2001. Its Anti-Money Laundering Office already participates in the international network, and Bangkok has now committed to strengthening cooperation with Myanmar’s anti-money-laundering authorities, including information sharing and capacity-building.

Through Egmont cooperation, financial intelligence units can exchange information concerning suspicious transactions, financial relationships and the movement of funds across jurisdictions. The information can also help establish connections between individuals, companies and organizations operating internationally.

And what transactions are considered suspicious? Pretty much all of them—unless the Myanmar regime has personally approved them.

For the regime, acquiring such capabilities would represent a significant institutional development, particularly when considered alongside its expanding access to satellite technology.

The official justification is combating transnational organized crime. Both governments agreed to intensify efforts against online scams, narcotics and criminal networks operating along their shared border, including disrupting illicit financial flows.

The United States is pursuing similar objectives.

In September and October, American officials held two rounds of discussions with representatives of Myanmar’s military-backed government.

Following the regime’s release of American businessman Adam Castillo in September 2026, Washington is believed to be seeking cooperation from Myanmar’s military authorities to shut down cybercrime operations targeting Americans. Same old story—we’ve heard it all before.

But the Trump administration has its own priorities. There is little reason to interpret these discussions through the political priorities of previous administrations. The United States has a different president, and his administration is pursuing different interests.

What deserves attention is the relationship between these developments. Russia is expanding cooperation on satellite technologies. Washington is engaging the regime on transnational crime. Thailand is explicitly identifying the disruption of criminal financial networks as a priority, promising to strengthen Myanmar’s financial intelligence capabilities.

On October 23, Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow went further, welcoming the renewed American engagement with Myanmar. He explained that Thailand did not want Myanmar isolated or turned into an arena for geopolitical rivalry. Bangkok therefore welcomes U.S. involvement alongside its own bilateral cooperation.

The regime is developing relationships with governments whose interests are not identical but whose cooperation could nevertheless strengthen its technological and intelligence capabilities.

And that brings us to the possible consequences of combating transnational crime.

Cybercrime networks along the Thai-Myanmar border are obvious targets for financial investigations. But what begins as an international effort against scam centers could provide the infrastructure for a much wider witch-hunt.

The same mechanisms that trace financial transactions involving criminal networks can expose financial relationships involving independent media or NGOs. Banking information, company records, beneficial ownership structures and cross-border transactions can reveal how organizations are financed and who maintains commercial relationships with them.

The regime could therefore strengthen its ability to investigate financial flows involving ethnic armed organizations, political opposition groups and businesses across Myanmar, including those entirely unrelated to cybercrime.

Combined with improved satellite information, these capabilities could provide the regime with considerably greater visibility over both the physical infrastructure and financial relationships of organizations operating against it.

Officially, the objective is disrupting organized crime. But the regime has fought ethnic armed organizations for decades. It would be rather optimistic to assume that expanded financial surveillance capabilities will never be directed against political or military opponents.

There is another dimension to Thailand’s growing role in Myanmar, particularly concerning the United States.

U.S. legislative policy towards Thailand has changed considerably over the past three decades.

Remember the three Burma acts?

In 1995, the proposed Free Burma Act was rather uncompromising. Section 6 would have required the U.S. president to withhold assistance to Thailand until Bangkok fully cooperated in supporting Myanmar refugees and exiles. Section 7 demanded reports on Thailand’s treatment of refugees, students and exiles. Although the bill was never enacted, the message was clear: Thailand’s treatment of Myanmar nationals could come at a financial cost.

By 2003, Washington had apparently discovered the virtues of diplomacy. The Burmese Freedom and Democracy Act described Thailand as a close U.S. ally and called for Washington to work closely with Bangkok on human rights, political freedom and coordinated sanctions against Myanmar. The threat of withholding U.S. assistance had disappeared, replaced by considerably friendlier language about cooperation.

The BURMA Act of 2022 was even more accommodating. It supported humanitarian assistance and refugee protection involving Thailand and neighboring countries, without imposing comparable financial penalties on Bangkok over its treatment of Myanmar refugees. By this point, Washington was more interested in financing cooperation with Thailand than threatening to cut off assistance.

So, in 1995, U.S. legislators contemplated withholding assistance from Thailand over Myanmar refugees. By 2003, Thailand was being treated as a partner in implementing U.S. policy towards Myanmar. By 2022, cooperation with Thailand had become part of the broader framework for cross-border humanitarian assistance.

Now, in October 2026, Washington is conducting direct negotiations with the regime, and Thailand has publicly welcomed those discussions.

For organizations operating against the regime, these developments should be taken seriously.

The regime is establishing international relationships that can provide technological assistance, institutional development, financial intelligence cooperation and new channels of diplomatic engagement. These relationships do not depend on the regime resolving its conflicts with ethnic armed organizations or reaching an agreement with the National Unity Government (NUG).

If the NUG is underestimating the regime’s ability to develop such relationships, or underplaying the strategic importance of the capabilities being offered, that would be a serious mistake.

Military strength is not measured exclusively by the number of soldiers, weapons or territorial positions an organization controls. Access to information, institutional capacity and sustainable financing can be equally consequential.

The financial situation of Myanmar’s democracy movement is becoming increasingly difficult. For FY2024 and FY2025, Washington allocated $121 million annually to democracy, governance, human rights and humanitarian assistance programs concerning Myanmar. However, the Trump administration’s foreign aid cuts in 2025 affected several programs supporting pro-democracy organisations, including those operating in exile.

A November 2025 study by the Stimson Center interviewed 30 Myanmar civil society leaders, all of whom reported insufficient or short-term funding. Some organizations have already suspended activities, reduced staff or closed offices. International funding is also increasingly directed towards humanitarian assistance rather than political advocacy and institution-building.

A September 2026 study published in Civil Wars highlights the NUG’s financial difficulties, particularly its limited access to stable revenue sources due to its lack of control over substantial territory and economic resources.

Meanwhile, the regime is building international partnerships that could help it monitor its opponents and trace their finances. The NUG could find itself with fewer resources while the military acquires better tools to track and undermine it.

Ana Brown is a nuclear lawyer, academic and intelligence analyst specializing in defense economics, and an ALM candidate at Harvard University.

World.title: Top UN Court to Rule November 19 on Myanmar Rohingya Genocide Case
World.content:
THE HAGUE, Netherlands—The top UN court will on November 19 deliver a landmark ruling on whether Myanmar’s crackdown against its mostly Muslim Rohingya minority constituted a genocide, officials said on Tuesday.

Judges at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) have for seven years been weighing accusations by Gambia that Myanmar’s brutal repression of the Rohingya breached the 1948 UN Genocide Convention.

While the ICJ has no means of enforcing its decisions, a ruling that Myanmar committed genocide would heap more international pressure on its military junta and be seen as justice for hundreds of thousands of Rohingya.

Legal experts are closely watching the verdict from the ICJ, which rules in disputes between countries, for clues as to how the court might rule in the seminal genocide case brought by South Africa against Israel over its campaign in Gaza.

Myanmar has always denied carrying out a genocide against the Rohingya, arguing its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents after a series of attacks left a dozen security personnel dead.

The crackdown by the Myanmar military and Buddhist militias forced hundreds of thousands of Rohingya to flee to neighboring Bangladesh, bringing with them harrowing accounts of gang rape and mass executions.

More than 1 million Rohingya still live across the border in Bangladesh, in the world’s largest refugee settlement.

‘Collective conscience’

During hearings on the case in January, Gambian Justice Minister Dawda Jallow told the court the Rohingya had suffered “the most horrific violence and destruction one could imagine.”

“It is not about esoteric issues of international law. It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow.

“The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction,” added the minister.

Gambia brought the case to the ICJ under the terms of the UN Genocide Convention, which allows any state to sound the alarm if it suspects genocide is being committed.

The alleged violations of the convention “are a stain on our collective conscience and it would be irresponsible to pretend that it is not our business,” Jallow said.

Myanmar retorted at the hearing that the allegations were “unsubstantiated.”

“Emotional language and blurry factual pictures are not a substitute for a rigorous presentation of facts,” said Ko Ko Hlaing, a minister in the President’s Office.

In a previous hearing in 2019, then-de facto civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi herself addressed the court, housed in the iconic Peace Palace in The Hague.

The Nobel peace laureate said the case risked reigniting the crisis that led to the Rohingyas’ expulsion and there was no “genocidal intent” behind the crackdown.

Aung San Suu Kyi, 81, will not be attending the verdict, however. She has been detained in Myanmar’s capital Naypyitaw since being unseated in a 2021 military coup.

The ICJ has already made one ruling in this case, ordering Myanmar in 2020 to “take all measures within its power to prevent the commission of all acts” described by the Genocide Convention.

These acts included “killing members of the group” and “deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part.”

ICJ judges also threw out a challenge to its jurisdiction by Myanmar, ruling that it did have the power to decide on the genocide question.

The ICJ is not the only court looking into possible crimes against the Rohingya.

In 2024, the chief prosecutor of the International Criminal Court, also based in The Hague, asked judges for an arrest warrant for Myanmar’s junta chief Min Aung Hlaing over alleged crimes against humanity.

A case is also underway in Argentina, under the principle of universal jurisdiction, the idea that some crimes are so heinous they can be heard in any court.

World.title: China’s Myanmar Policy at Crossroads After 5 Years of Failure
World.content:
China’s Myanmar policy rests on a central assumption: that the military remains the country’s decisive political and military force. That assumption may have been valid in previous eras, but Myanmar’s post-coup reality demonstrates Beijing has overestimated the military while underestimating the revolutionary movement that has emerged since 2021.

The revolutionary forces factor

Throughout Myanmar’s civil war since 1948, and again after the 1988 pro-democracy uprising, successive revolutionary movements have failed to establish dominance, leaving most of the country in control of the military. Beijing has shaped its Myanmar policy accordingly, viewing the military as the guarantor of stability in an otherwise fractured nation.

Yet Myanmar after the 2021 coup bears little resemblance to either of those earlier periods.

The political and military balance has shifted dramatically. The Kachin Independence Army (KIA), Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA), Arakan Army (AA), Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA), and Chin and Karenni resistance forces have emerged as formidable military actors capable of seizing and controlling large swaths of territory.

Even the Karen National Union (KNU), weakened by decades of internal splits and defections since the 1990s, has regained momentum, recapturing numerous military bases and inflicting significant losses on regime forces.

Meanwhile, armed resistance has spread into the Bamar-majority heartland, posing an unprecedented challenge to central rule.

The National Unity Government (NUG) and its People’s Defense Forces (PDFs) have emerged as a major parallel authority, reinforced by cooperation with ethnic armed organizations.

China’s Special Envoy for Asian Affairs Deng Xijun has reportedly warned the United Wa State Army (UWSA) that the NUG will never be a genuine rival to Myanmar’s military. That judgement has historical precedent. Revolutionary movements that emerged after 1948 ultimately failed because of military and political mistakes coupled with weapons and funding shortages. Likewise, the National Coalition Government of the Union of Burma (NCGUB) and the All Burma Students’ Democratic Front (ABSDF), which emerged after the 1988 uprising, never threatened military dominance.

Beijing has calculated that the NUG and PDFs will follow suit and collapse.

But today’s realities point in the opposite direction. Plagued by systemic corruption, declining battlefield effectiveness and shrinking troop numbers, the military has lost support among the Bamar majority amid growing public revulsion over its war crimes against civilians.

Resistance movement: Past and present

The post-1988 NCGUB enjoyed political leadership but little organizational structure on the ground. By contrast, NUG networks extend deep into local communities.

Meanwhile, the ABSDF lacked the strength to operate effectively in Myanmar’s heartland and depended on ethnic armed organizations for refuge. Today’s PDFs and Spring Revolution forces operate independently across Sagaing, Mandalay, Magwe, Bago and Tanintharyi regions, also pushing into Ayeyarwady Region and conducting urban guerrilla warfare in Yangon.

Their military expansion has been matched by broad support among rural Bamar communities. Ethnic armed organizations, meanwhile, increasingly credit PDFs and other Spring Revolution groups with contributing to their own battlefield successes. That combat strength is supported by a centralized command chain and disciplined organization. Battlefield setbacks and defections in 2025 barely dented the movement’s momentum and never matched the mass desertions seen within the Myanmar military in recent years.

While resistance forces still face constraints in weaponry and logistics, by historical standards they remain well equipped.

Also, while the NCGUB and ABSDF were bound by ideology, the link between the NUG and PDF is institutional and operational.

While the NCGUB and ABSDF subsided into political opposition groups within five years, the NUG and PDF remain a formidable military force — arguably the strongest and most expansive resistance movement in modern Myanmar history.

As such, China’s assessment that the NUG and its armed wing are not a serious rival to the military no longer reflects realities on the ground. In today’s Myanmar, it is impossible to understand the conflict without including the NUG and PDF in the equation.

Democracy and China’s concerns

If Beijing has underestimated the military significance of revolutionary forces, it also remains wary of their political agenda — particularly their commitment to democracy.

Yet democracy is hardly an alien concept in China. During its own revolutionary era, the Chinese Communist Party described its struggle as a “people’s democratic revolution” and promoted Mao Zedong’s concept of a “New Democracy.”

The fight against military dictatorship naturally carries democratic aspirations. But that does not mean importing a Western political model wholesale, nor would such a model be easily transplanted.

Myanmar’s revolutionary forces recognize the critical importance of relations with neighboring China. After all, long-term economic engagement with Beijing was also a cornerstone of National League for Democracy (NLD) government’s foreign policy.

New alliances

Chinese pressure has sidelined two major ethnic political and military alliances, namely the Federal Political Negotiation and Consultative Committee led by the UWSA and the tripartite Brotherhood Alliance. Yet new revolutionary coalitions have emerged.

One is the Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union (SCEF), which brings together the NUG and major armed organizations including Kachin, Chin, Karen and Karenni forces. Another is the Spring Revolution Alliance (SRA), which unites anti-regime forces that emerged after the coup. Both alliances pursue political and military objectives, and coordination between them appears to be steadily improving.

The Arakan Army — which controls most of Rakhine State and remains the biggest thorn in the regime’s side — is forging deepening ties with both groupings.

The trajectory of once-isolated resistance organizations is thus becoming increasingly interconnected, gradually evolving into a broader political and military bloc. These organizations are indispensable not only to achieving peace and nationwide stability, but also to safeguard long-term China-Myanmar relations and Chinese interests in the country.

Weaknesses of revolutionary forces

The resistance continues to suffer gaps in institutionalization, chain of command, logistics and weapons supply, and unification. Yet these are offset by substantial public support, a reputation largely unstained by atrocities, and high internal morale.

Most revolutionary groups also refrain from the systemic corruption that characterizes regime rule. Those who do profit from drug trafficking or online scam operations remain exceptions rather than the norm.

Close public scrutiny and critical supporters generally ensures that revolutionary misrule is generally harder to conceal and easier to correct. Myanmar’s military, by contrast, exhibits many of the opposite traits and has also repeatedly failed to unite the country’s ethnic communities or deliver lasting stability.

China’s Myanmar policy vs Myanmar’s reality

Taken together, these developments expose two fundamental errors in China’s reading of post-coup Myanmar.

While Beijing justifiably views the military as a key actor in Myanmar’s future, it overestimates its ability to achieve stability in the face of an increasingly entrenched and unified armed resistance. A military-centric policy no longer reflects a landscape transformed since the 2021 coup.

The second error lies in the timing of Beijing’s intervention. China moved to shore up the regime as Min Aung Hlaing faced mounting pressure from battlefield defeats, economic crisis and growing dissent within the military.

Had Beijing waited for his removal before backing the regime, more pragmatic figures may have taken the military helm.

Instead, China’s hasty support strengthened hardliners around Min Aung Hlaing while sidelining moderates and internal critics. In effect, Beijing’s scramble to preserve the military prolonged the rule of a failing strongman. Desperate to salvage his diminished authority and prestige, Min Aung Hlaing has vowed to reclaim all territory lost to revolutionary forces. As such, the civil war looks set to escalate rather than ease.

China’s policy has yielded gains for the regime, most notably by pressing ASEAN countries to reengage with Naypyitaw. But it has come at the cost of entrenching Naypyitaw’s hardliners, the root cause of instability.

The generals’ flawed policies and spiraling military spending have opened the door to economic collapse and poverty, while systematic corruption has fueled narcotics trafficking and online scam networks.

Despite China’s support, they have failed to achieve the military, political, and economic stability that Beijing craves.

Time for a policy shift?

Recent developments suggest Beijing may already be reassessing its Myanmar strategy. While China remains Myanmar’s largest foreign investor, new investment in fiscal 2025-26 fell to just US$ 158.2 million. Large-scale Chinese investment and lending failed to materialize even after the junta rebranded as a pseudo-civilian government in April.

Meanwhile, China’s Special Envoy Deng Xijun has broken off from frequent visits to Myanmar, where he has not been seen since March. Likewise, Chinese Ambassador Ma Jia, who regularly met Min Aung Hlaing and senior regime officials after taking up her post in August 2024, last met the junta chief in Naypyitaw on April 6, 2026.

The Chinese Communist Party regularly evaluates its policy outcomes. As pragmatists, Chinese leaders place considerable emphasis on results.

In Myanmar’s case, Beijing’s objective remains unchanged: stability. Yet stability remains elusive even as China’s core interests — including Belt and Road development and multibillion-dollar border trade — continue to face severe disruption. Under such circumstances, Beijing cannot afford to proceed with the status quo. While China’s core aim in Myanmar is unlikely to change, its strategic assumptions and methods must adapt.

Thet Htar Maung is a political analyst.

World.title: South Korea Makes its Central Asia Play
World.content:
Before the fall of 2026, South Korea-Central Asia relations were akin to a plot without main characters: bilateral relations primarily conducted at the ministerial level without institutionalized regional engagement. Now, the story features presidents and critical minerals overcoming complex customs procedures and inadequate transport infrastructure in a new regional integration play: The first South Korea-Central Asia summit.

The inaugural summit on Sept.16 brought together the presidents of South Korea and all five Central Asian countries under the theme “Walking Together Toward the Future: Partnership for Trust and Prosperity.” The summit and associated presidential visits resulted in the Seoul Declaration, which outlined areas for cooperation, and in multiple agreements and memorandums.

In Korean and Central Asian joint history, people and culture precede business. In the second half of the 19th century, many Koreans began moving to Russia, and later to the Soviet Union, following Japanese colonization. The Koryo-Saram, the ethnic Koreans of Central Asia, arrived in the region through Stalin’s mass deportations in 1937.

According to the Korean Ministry of Foreign Affairs, approximately 310,000 Korean descendants live in Russia and Central Asia today, with the greatest number of them, 178,000 living in Uzbekistan, followed by Kazakhstan at 110,000. A South Korea-inspired canal promenade, Seoul Mun, meaning “Seoul Gate” was even built in Tashkent in recent years.

Business interest has been active since the five countries’ independence ranging from South Korea’s Daewoo car assembly plant in Uzbekistan in the 1990s, to its New Northern Policy (2017) and the K-Silk Road initiative (2024).

The significance of September’s summit rests on the fact that it was the first at a presidential level and in that it signals a move from bilateral relations to more institutionalised regional engagement moving forward.

“Through this summit, relations between South Korea and Central Asia will be consolidated into a leader-level multilateral cooperation framework, and the New Northern Policy we have pursued is expected to gain momentum,” Korean President Lee Jae Myung commented on television according to Reuters.

Like most roads in international relations, this one, too, leads to security. Over 82% of South Korea’s mineral imports, needed for products from semiconductors to batteries and electric vehicles, come from China. Central Asia is rich in critical minerals and offers an opportunity for South Korea to diversify its trade partners and supply chains.

“There is an economic partnership because currently Kazakhstan is the first source of these raw materials, since Korea is short of raw materials,” Abagan Akerke, the head of the Far East Department at Farabi University in Kazakhstan told the state-associated broadcaster K24.

In addition to having an abundance of uranium reserves, Kazakhstan in particular is located at a strategically important point, being part of the Middle Corridor (Trans-Caspian International Transport Route) connecting Europe to Asia.

Further highlighting critical minerals, Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev proposed the establishment of a regional investment alliance for rare earth minerals during his visit to Seoul.

“This initiative is aimed at creating large industrial clusters in the region that will cover all stages of production – from geological exploration and extraction, to deep processing of raw materials and the production of high-value-added products,” he said in his address at the summit.

Central Asia is looking for critical mineral supply chains that go beyond just mere extraction, and into refining, smelting and higher-value processing.

How will minerals actually get to South Korea? A South Korean government-sponsored study found customs procedures and inadequate transport infrastructure to be a challenge. China’s Belt and Road is active, while Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev proposed an “end-to-end transport and logistics chain” tied to the Middle Corridor and Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov invited Korean firms to the China–the Kyrgyz Republic–Uzbekistan railway.

Other agreements and topics of discussion centered around talent, technology, investment and climate-related projects.

South Korea’s first C5+K meeting comes at an increasingly crowded space, following the United States’ and Europe’s multilateral interaction with the region.

The next summit is set to be held in Kazakhstan in 2028 and by then it is expected that deals potentially worth billions will have commenced.

The article was originally published in Montfort Eurasia’s LinkedIn.

London-based Montfort Eurasia is the management consultancy specializing in corporate communications and investor relations. It was established in Uzbekistan in 2023 to support clients in Central Asia and the Caucasus.
