World.title: Baker Hughes sees opportunities beyond ACG, Shah Deniz in Azerbaijan (Interview)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 6. Having supported Azerbaijan's energy sector for decades, Baker Hughes sees significant opportunities ahead, both in Azerbaijan and across the wider Caspian region, Baker Hughes Vice President of Europe and CIS Elena Akoltseva said in an exclusive interview with Trend.

“The region remains strategically important due to its resource base, established infrastructure, and growing role in supporting global energy security.

As one of the world’s oldest oil-producing regions, we see many opportunities to help operators in Azerbaijan and the Caspian region maximize value from their existing assets. As fields age, more technology-driven solutions are needed to improve efficiency, reliability, and recovery while reducing emissions and operating costs. Baker Hughes has a wide range of advanced well construction, production optimization and digital technologies to address the challenges our customers’ face in mature oil and gas fields,” she said.

The regional VP noted that the company also sees growing interest in electrification, methane reduction, asset performance management, and digital technologies that help operators achieve both operational and sustainability objectives.

”A good example is our ongoing collaboration with SOCAR, announced during COP29, to help reduce flaring and abate downstream emissions at the Heydar Aliyev Baku Oil Refinery. Projects like this demonstrate how technology can deliver both operational and sustainability outcomes,” she said.

Akoltseva pointed out that in the competitive landscape, localization remains a key priority in Azerbaijan.

“Baker Hughes employs more than 300 people in the country, approximately 95% of whom are Azerbaijani nationals. We believe our long-standing local presence, investment in talent, and partnerships position us well to further expand local capabilities in services, manufacturing, and field operations.

Looking across the Caspian region, we see continued investment in energy infrastructure and industrial development. Our focus is on supporting customers with technologies that enhance energy security, improve competitiveness, and reduce emissions through technology, local expertise and long-term partnerships,” she added.

Extending ACG’s productive life

Akoltseva noted that as large producing assets mature, technology becomes increasingly important in maintaining production performance and maximizing ultimate recovery.

“Long-producing fields such as ACG are becoming more complex and require advanced technological approaches. Azerbaijan’s offshore giants, including ACG, demand new technologies as operators focus on maximizing recovery and extending field life.

In the subsea domain, modern monitoring and intervention technologies can provide operators with improved visibility into well and reservoir performance, helping identify opportunities to manage pressure, optimize flow, and increase production efficiency. Recent vessel-based intervention campaigns in the ACG area demonstrate the industry’s focus on extracting greater value from existing infrastructure,” she said.



The regional VP noted that Baker Hughes also sees significant opportunities in integrated reservoir management, predictive analytics, condition monitoring, and data-driven well intervention planning.

“The combination of physical technologies and digital intelligence can help operators extend field life, improve recovery factors, and enhance overall asset economics,” she added.

Akoltseva pointed out that Azerbaijan remains one of Baker Hughes’ strategic markets in the Caspian region, and its portfolio today spans subsea and well construction technologies, production and intervention services, industrial and energy technology equipment, digital applications, and lifecycle services supporting both offshore and onshore operations.

“Baker Hughes has maintained a long-standing presence in the country and continues to support operators and national energy stakeholders across the value chain,” she said.

Expanding business beyond ACG and Shah Deniz

Akoltseva noted that Shah Deniz remains one of the most important gas developments in the region and continues to play a critical role in supplying natural gas to Azerbaijan, Türkiye, and European markets.

“The field is a highly sophisticated offshore development with extensive subsea infrastructure and ongoing drilling and production activities.

Baker Hughes continues to work closely with operators across Azerbaijan’s energy sector to identify opportunities where our technologies can create value. Our focus areas include mature asset solutions, production enhancement, digitalization, and other technologies that improve efficiency and reliability,” she explained.



The regional VP believes there is significant potential to apply these solutions not only to established producing assets such as ACG and Shah Deniz, but also to other offshore and onshore developments as operators seek to maximize recovery, improve operational performance, and support the long-term sustainability of Azerbaijan’s energy sector.

“Baker Hughes remains committed to collaborating with SOCAR, bp, and other industry stakeholders to bring innovative technologies and local capability development to the market,” she added.

Medium- and long-term business potential in wider Caspian region

Akoltseva noted that looking beyond Azerbaijan – Baker Hughes operates in Central Asia in Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.

“We see the Caspian region as an important growth market, underpinned by a strong resource base, continued investment in energy infrastructure, and the strategic role the region plays in supporting energy security and economic development.

In the medium to long term, we see significant opportunities across conventional oil and gas and natural gas development as operators focus on maximizing recovery from existing assets while improving efficiency, reliability, and emissions performance. As global energy demand continues to grow, these resources will remain essential to providing secure, affordable energy,” she said.

The regional VP pointed out that for Baker Hughes, the opportunity is not defined by any one segment.

“It lies at the intersection of energy growth, operational performance, and emissions reduction. Our focus is on helping customers across the Caspian unlock greater value from their assets, strengthen competitiveness, and meet evolving energy and sustainability objectives through technology, innovation, and long-term partnership, she said.

Akolsteva believes that the next wave of demand across Continental Europe and the Caspian will be driven by growing energy needs, infrastructure modernization, and the need to improve efficiency while reducing emissions.

“As energy systems become more complex, operators are increasingly looking for solutions that enhance performance, strengthen energy security, and improve the economics of existing and new projects.

Over the next five to ten years, technologies such as electrification, advanced turbomachinery, digitalization, AI-enabled asset management, and next-generation well construction solutions have the potential to be transformative. These technologies can help operators increase reliability, reduce downtime, optimize energy consumption, lower emissions, and extend asset life, all of which have a direct impact on project economics,” she added.

Akoltseva noted that Baker Hughes sees particular potential in electric compression and digital technologies that enable smarter, data-driven operations.

“The ability to produce more energy from existing infrastructure while reducing operational emissions will become an increasingly important competitive advantage.

Ultimately, the projects that succeed will be those that deliver on the energy trilemma: security, affordability, and lower emissions. We believe integrated technology solutions will play a critical role in helping operators achieve those objectives while unlocking greater value from their investments,” she explained.

Gains from incorporating AI

Akoltseva noted that Baker Hughes has been incorporating artificial intelligence (AI) in the software we use for both product development and service delivery for more than 20 years.

“We use it for a wide range of applications, including estimating downhole quantities that are difficult to measure directly, improving communications downhole, monitoring equipment and predicting failures, and transferring engineering and laboratory models to the field.

We also package AI methods in software for our customers to use. For example, our Kantori™ autonomous well construction solution uses AI workflows to help our customers improve their efficiency developing and executing drilling programs, while our Leucipa™ automated field production solution does the same to help our customers improve production, minimize deferrals, and manage interventions and well integrity. We also offer our Cordant™ industrial enterprise solution that uses AI to extend the life and improve utilization of assets,” she explained.

The regional VP noted that within the past year, agentic AI packages have been incorporated into these products.

“These packages enable natural language interaction with the data and the underlying program functionality. They also allow operators to run specific workflows with fewer mouse clicks and steps overall, as well as to automate follow-up on operational decisions with economic analysis once the actions have been completed, with minimal instruction and dedicated scripts.

Several large IOCs have shown substantial economic gains with these products, and AI continues to provide meaningful improvements in our underlying service delivery performance,” she explained.

Akoltseva noted that as Baker Hughes’ customers seek to maximize the value of existing assets while reducing emissions, the company’s priority is helping them achieve both objectives at the same time.

“We are investing in technologies that improve efficiency, reliability, and asset performance, from advanced turbomachinery and digital solutions to electrification and emissions reduction technologies.

The focus is on delivering practical, measurable outcomes: extending asset life, increasing production efficiency, reducing emissions, and lowering operating costs. In markets such as the Caspian, where existing infrastructure remains critical to energy security and economic growth, we see significant opportunities to unlock additional value from mature assets while supporting decarbonization goals. Technology-enabled productivity and emissions reduction will continue to guide our investment and innovation priorities,” she said.

Priority markets for increasing Baker Hughes’ presence

Akoltseva pointed out that Baker Hughes is increasing its focus in markets where energy demand is growing, existing infrastructure requires modernization, and operators are seeking to improve efficiency while reducing emissions.

“This includes key energy-producing regions such as the Middle East, the Caspian, and parts of Asia, where long-term investment in both conventional energy development and lower-carbon technologies continues to accelerate.

In the Western Hemisphere, we’re targeting opportunities in Venezuela. We recently entered into a strategic alliance agreement with PDVSA, Lindsayca and Fulcrum LNG, Inc. to revitalize and expand the country’s natural gas infrastructure. We also recently signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with New Stratus Energy Inc. to support the development of future oil and gas prospects in the country,” she said.

The regional VP noted that primary drivers for these decisions stem from the need for reliable, affordable, and lower-carbon energy.

“Our customers are looking for technologies that can enhance production, improve asset performance, reduce emissions, and support energy security. Baker Hughes is well positioned to meet these needs through our portfolio of turbomachinery, digital solutions, well construction technologies, and electrification offerings,” Akoltseva concluded.

World.title: The geography of cooperation: What drives transport ties between Turkmenistan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 6. Two important developments in regional transport infrastructure took place in Turkmenistan on November 4: President Serdar Berdimuhamedov opened a 44-kilometer section of the Turkmenbashi-Garabogaz-Kazakhstan border highway and approved the start of construction of the new Ashgabat-Dashoguz road, which will stretch for approximately 550 kilometers. The first project improves road links with western regions of Kazakhstan, while the second will strengthen transport connections between the capital and the northern part of Turkmenistan, which borders Uzbekistan. Both highways are intended to expand regional transport opportunities and strengthen the country’s position along the international North-South Transport Corridor.

In particular, the western route is important for expanding transport flows between Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan’s Mangystau Region, whose economy largely relies on the oil and gas sector. The region also has well-developed mechanical engineering, metallurgy and chemical industries. The ports of Aktau and Kuryk, located there, provide access to Caspian Sea shipping routes, creating additional opportunities for transporting industrial goods.

On the Uzbek direction, the new road will complement existing infrastructure for cross-border cooperation. In November 2025, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan opened the Shavat-Dashoguz trade zone, equipped with customs, veterinary and phytosanitary facilities, warehouses and a trade pavilion. The application of the single-window principle is intended to simplify trade operations between the border regions of the two countries, while improved road connections could further support the development of the facility.

The development of these routes is part of the transport agenda that Turkmenistan actively promoted throughout 2026 during its chairmanship of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). Ashgabat advocated the expansion of regional corridors and stronger logistical cooperation among CIS member states. In September, the 111th meeting of the CIS Economic Council was held in the Turkmen capital, where participants discussed the countries’ transport potential, the development of the North-South and East–West routes, and the use of opportunities offered by the Caspian region. At Turkmenistan’s initiative, 2029 was also declared the Year of CIS Transport Connectivity.

“The Caspian region is a key element of transport connectivity. Clearly, the eastern and western Caspian North-South transport corridors are of vital importance,” President Berdimuhamedov said, addressing a meeting of the CIS Council of Heads of State in October.

This policy is also reflected in the development of the country’s maritime infrastructure. In May, the vessel Gadamly, with a carrying capacity of 6,100 tons, arrived at the Baku International Sea Trade Port. It is the first dry cargo vessel built at the shipbuilding and ship repair yard in Turkmenbashi. The vessel is designed, among other things, to carry containers and will operate in the Caspian Sea, primarily on the Azerbaijan route. The development of its own fleet expands Turkmenistan’s maritime transport capabilities and complements efforts to strengthen overland transport links.

The regional dimension of this policy is becoming particularly evident against the backdrop of Central Asia’s growing geopolitical and economic importance. Speaking at the fourth Interparliamentary Forum of Central Asian States in Dushanbe, the Chairwoman of the Mejlis of Turkmenistan, Dunyagozel Gulmanova noted that the region is gradually becoming an important geopolitical center, opening up new opportunities for multilateral cooperation and strengthening stability. Her assessment reflects a broader trend: Central Asia’s location between major economic centers, its resource potential, and its growing role in international trade routes are increasing external partners’ interest in developing relations with countries in the region.

For Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, deeper cooperation with Turkmenistan is driven by their respective economic and strategic interests. As Trend previously reported in its analytical article, “Astana talks: business opportunities and transport corridors shape Kazakhstan-Turkmenistan agenda”, Kazakhstan is interested in expanding the presence of its companies in the Turkmen market, including through energy and infrastructure projects. The development of transport routes through Turkmenistan toward Iran also occupies an important place on the bilateral agenda.

In its article “Where Turkmenistan fits in Uzbekistan's next export phase”, Trend, highlighted Tashkent’s interest in industrial cooperation, supplies of construction materials and the participation of Uzbek enterprises in projects in the Turkmen market. The signing in October of the Treaty on the Establishment of the Supreme Council of Strategic Partnership between Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan marked an important step in giving this cooperation an institutional framework.

For Kazakhstan, the Turkmen route offers an additional opportunity to develop transit shipments through Iran to the markets of the Persian Gulf and South Asia. Uzbekistan, a landlocked country, is interested in using Turkmenistan’s territory to access the Caspian Sea, the South Caucasus and, further on, European markets. Turkmenistan, for its part, stands to gain opportunities to increase transit flows and expand transport services. Each of the three countries therefore has its own reasons to strengthen connectivity with its neighbors, while the convergence of these interests provides a basis for deeper regional cooperation.

As Central Asia gains increasing importance in international trade and transport logistics, the development of links among its states is becoming an independent driver of regional growth. According to the World Bank, investment in the Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor and improved coordination among countries could more than triple freight volumes along the route by 2040. Against this backdrop, the development of Turkmenistan’s road and maritime infrastructure, alongside deeper ties with Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, reflects the three countries’ intention to make greater use of the region’s geographical and economic advantages. Their ability to coordinate infrastructure projects, border procedures, and transit conditions will largely determine whether Central Asia’s growing importance can translate into sustainable trade and logistics links.

World.title: EDB says regional cooperation is increasingly important for Central Asia's energy security (Exclusive)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 6. Regional cooperation is not an alternative to national energy security but one of its instruments, according to a report by the Eurasian Development Bank (EDB), "Energy Without Borders: Architecture of Energy Connectivity in Central Asia," provided to Trend.

"Central Asia already has something that many regions have to spend decades creating: physical connectivity between power systems, experience in cross-border electricity flows, seasonal complementarity of resources, and institutional memory of parallel operation. However, under new conditions, this advantage is not enough. Growing demand, aging assets, reserve shortages, the accelerated commissioning of renewable energy sources (RES), water and energy constraints, and the development of external corridors are changing the very nature of the regional energy agenda," the report says.

According to the EDB's analysts, the main question is no longer whether Central Asia's power systems are interconnected, but how reliable, manageable, financially sustainable, and acceptable to all participants this connectivity can be.

"In this regard, regional cooperation is not an alternative to national energy security but one of its instruments. The countries of the region retain responsibility for tariff policy, security of supply, and the development of their own energy assets," the report says.

At the same time, the report notes that some challenges already extend beyond national systems: a shortage in one area affects neighboring systems, limited transmission capacity reduces the usefulness of new generation capacity, insufficient reserves increase emergency risks, and uncoordinated water and energy operating regimes diminish the value of hydropower resources.

"Therefore, strengthening national security in the electricity sector increasingly depends on the quality of regional coordination," the EDB report says.

The report shows that the economic value of integration arises not only from selling electricity across borders. A more significant benefit comes from the region's ability to use its resources as a unified reliability portfolio: the grid as a means of delivering capacity, hydropower as a source of flexibility, digital infrastructure as the foundation for confidence in data, market rules as a mechanism for allocating responsibility, and investment projects as a means of removing specific system constraints.

"This approach changes the investment rationale: a project's value is determined not only by its physical parameters, but also by the extent to which it increases available transmission capacity, reduces emergency risks, curbs renewable energy curtailment, improves settlement discipline, and expands opportunities for future trading," the EDB report says.

World.title: Trump links stock market decline to US midterm election results
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 6. US President Donald Trump has linked the decline in major stock markets to the results of the midterm elections, which could result in Democrats gaining control of Congress.

The American leader shared his views on the matter in a post on his Truth Social account.

"The stock market has experienced one of the worst days in its history due to the election results. It’s very sad to see! It took a lot of effort to get us to levels never seen before, and now this has happened," Trump wrote.

To recall, the US midterm elections were held on November 3. Voters elected 35 of the 100 members of the Senate and all 435 members of the House of Representatives. Gubernatorial elections were also held in 36 states.

On Wednesday and Thursday, shares of several leading US companies, as well as companies in a number of other countries, recorded significant declines.

World.title: 3.9-magnitude earthquake strikes Aegean Sea off Türkiye
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 6. An earthquake with a magnitude of 3.9 has struck the Aegean Sea.

The country’s Disaster and Emergency Management Authority (AFAD), operating under the Ministry of Interior, reported the incident.

The earthquake was reportedly felt in several major cities, including Istanbul.

The epicenter was located 55 kilometers from the Ayvacik district of Canakkale province, at a depth of 9.29 kilometers.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan’s foreign-invested firms lift 2025 trade 28.3% to $4.1B
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 6. Kyrgyzstan’s foreign trade turnover attributable to enterprises with foreign capital participation reached $4.1 billion in 2025, up 28.3% compared with the previous year.

The figure was calculated by Trend based on statistics published by the National Statistical Committee of the Kyrgyz Republic.

These enterprises accounted for 24.3% of the country’s total foreign trade turnover, the committee said, which is almost one-quarter of the total.

Their trade balance remained negative. The deficit reached $2.1 billion in 2025, compared with $1.4 billion in 2024. According to calculations based on the committee’s data, the deficit widened by about $0.7 billion.

Exports by these enterprises rose 6.4% year-on-year to $953.1 million, while imports increased 37% to about $3.1 billion. Imports were thus about 3.3 times larger than exports, according to the same calculations.

The growth patterns differed by group of partners. Exports to CIS countries rose 45.1%, while exports to countries outside the CIS fell 42.3%, and the CIS accounted for 75.9% of total exports. Imports from CIS countries rose 37.9% and imports from non-CIS countries rose 35.7%, with the CIS accounting for 60.5% of total imports.

Compared with 2021, the committee said, exports by these enterprises grew 1.5-fold, or by $320.5 million, while imports grew 1.9-fold, or by $1.5 billion.

World.title: Ex-CFMEU boss admits to illegal tirade against AFL umpiring boss
World.content:
Former construction union boss John Setka is unapologetic for breaking workplace laws, with his barrister saying he did not "deliberately" wage a public campaign against an ex-building regulator and AFL umpiring chief.

Mr Setka, the former powerful Victorian secretary of the CFMEU, faces a fine of up to $18,730, but could be hit with a much heftier legal bill because the union has refused to indemnify his court costs.

The Federal Court on Friday heard Mr Setka admitted breaching the Fair Work Act by trying to coerce the AFL into sacking its head of umpiring Stephen McBurney in mid-2024.

Mr McBurney was the Australian Building and Construction Commissioner and participated in more than 50 court cases against the union between 2018 and 2023.

Mr Setka's barrister Margo Harris said her client should not receive a severe penalty.

She said he was now retired, in the middle of a divorce, and spent most of his time looking after his elderly mother.

"He doesn't express any remorse but he has made an admission that what he did was wrong," Mr Harris said.

Mr Setka was not in court for Friday's hearing.

Former union boss admits to breaching law

The development comes three days before the start of hearings in Victoria's Royal Commission into the state government's "Big Build" construction projects, which have been dogged by claims of widespread corruption and crime.

Mr Setka, who left the CFMEU weeks after his verbal attacks on Mr McBurney, is also facing separate criminal charges over alleged harassment of the union's administrators.

In the Fair Work case, Mr Setka was still union boss when he made social media posts and gave media interviews over a two-week period, threatening that the CFMEU would disrupt or delay AFL building projects if it did not get rid of Mr McBurney, the court heard.

"This is going to cost the AFL a lot of f**king money. I hope it's worth it," Mr Setka said.

"Projects without our full co-operation are going to be a f**king misery for them. They will regret the day they ever employed him."

John Setka left the CFMEU weeks after his verbal attacks on Stephen McBurney. (ABC News)

The Fair Work Ombudsman (FWO) prosecuted Mr Setka and the CFMEU, alleging the demands to sack Mr McBurney were made because of his lawful work as ABCC commissioner.

On Friday, barristers for Mr Setka and the CFMEU admitted to the breaches.

Ms Harris said there was no evidence Mr Setka "actively sought" media attention, even though he made statements to newspapers, and appeared in radio and television interviews where he said the AFL should sack Mr McBurney.

Ms Harris also said Mr Setka did not "deliberately" engage in a media campaign against Mr McBurney, prompting Federal Court judge John Snaden to clarify what she meant.

"When I say deliberate, there's a range of deliberateness. It's not a question of being pregnant or not pregnant," she replied.

"It comes in the stream of the interview. There's a question asked of him, he answers it."

However, FWO barrister Marc Felman said Mr Setka was not forced to give interviews.

"There can be no question that this is a media campaign," he said.

During one press conference, Mr Setka said of Mr McBurney: "He's a zealot. He hates unions. He hates workers in general."

He also put up a social media post depicting Mr McBurney in a mock poster containing the words: "(Not) Wanted Dead or Alive".

Penalty to be set for Setka and CFMEU despite claims of new regime

Mr Felman said Mr Setka's breaches of the Fair Work Act were "very, very serious".

He said Mr Setka wasn't the first person to call for the sacking of an AFL umpire, but it became illegal because the demands were connected to Mr McBurney's lawful work in an old job.

Mr McBurney, who has umpired four grand finals, was backed by the AFL at the time and remains the league's head of officiating.

Stephen McBurney adjudicated 401 AFL games and is still employed as the league's head of officiating. (AFLUA Hall of Fame)

The CFMEU, which has since been taken over by administrators, could be fined up to $93,900.

Barrister Andrew White, for the CFMEU, called for the penalty to be moderated because the union's new regime no longer saw breaking the law as "the cost of doing business".

He said the cultural shift had occurred following hundreds of Setka-era officials being removed or leaving their jobs.

"A new culture of lawful but robust unionism is taking hold," he said.

Justice Snaden will set the penalty for Mr Setka and the CFMEU at a later date.

World.title: Paraguay's president tangled up in Ueno banking crisis
World.content:
It only took two days for Paraguayan president to resign after a banking crisis blocked nearly half of the small South American country's population from accessing their money.

The central bank's takeover of Ueno Bank plunged the country into a political crisis, sparking protests and a move to unanimously launch impeachment proceedings against President Santiago Peña in Congress.

The US-allied leader beat them to the punch by resigning on X minutes beforehand.

How did Paraguay get here?

It all came crashing down on Monday when regulators investigating Ueno Bank uncovered alleged excessive lending to companies linked to its controlling shareholder, Grupo Vázquez, and expenses wrongly counted as assets.

By Tuesday, the central bank seized control of the digital lender due to a severe capital shortfall, and authorities issued arrest warrants for eight of Ueno's top executives.

Executives of Ueno Bank arrive in custody at the anti-corruption prosecutor's office in Asuncion, Paraguay. ( AP Photo/Jorge Saenz)

The bank's president Miguel Vazquez turned himself into police and central bank president Carlos Carvallo stepped down at Mr Pena's request.

Mr Carvallo, who was president of Ueno's predecessor, was appointed the top job at the central bank — the agency charged with supervising Ueno — by Mr Peña.

As recently as last month, Mr Peña defended Ueno which reported holding roughly $800 million in public deposits, including money from the state pension and health fund and the operators of Paraguay's giant hydro-electric dams.

Mr Peña, a former International Monetary Fund economist, also owned shares in the group that controlled the digital lender until last year.

Peña scrambles to contain the situation

On Wednesday Mr Peña enacted a law to return most deposits within five days.

Thirty-five lawmakers meanwhile filed a motion to impeach him.

By Thursday, Mr Pena's own Colorado Party turned against him, with party leader Horacio Cartes announcing that he backed impeachment.

The Chamber of Deputies opened a session to debate the motion, but no sooner had it started than Mr Peña posted a video on X announcing his resignation.

Paraguayan President Santiago Peña signs his resignation letter at the government residence in Asunción, Paraguay. (AP Photo/Laura Fioravanti)

"I want to apologise to the people if at any point I failed. It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me," he said.

Minutes later, the 78 deputies present unanimously approved the impeachment motion against Mr Peña.

Both houses have since declined to accept his offer to resign, pressing forward with a trial that could result in the president's removal from office.

Opposition senators said allowing him to resign would preserve his eligibility to become a senator for life and grant him with legal protections preventing his prosecution.

If the presidency remains vacant, Vice President Pedro Alliana will complete the term until 2028.

Peña faces criminal investigation

Paraguay's Attorney General Emiliano Rolón Fernández has ordered three criminal investigations into the Ueno Bank crisis, including allegations involving Mr Peña and other current and former government officials.

The investigations will examine authorities' oversight of the bank, their handling of its failure and the placement of public funds in the lender.

Mr Peña said he would cooperate with investigators.

"Whatever the outcome of this process, I will act with responsibility and respect for the Constitution," he said on X.

What is Ueno?

Ueno Bank, exploded from an obscure local fintech company into a mid-sized Paraguayan bank in less than five years, claiming more than 60 per cent of Paraguay's adults as customers.

Ueno Bank says it has over 3 million customers in a country of 6.4 million people and manages millions of dollars in pensions and other state funds.

Soon after winning its banking licence in 2023, Ueno seemed to be everywhere.

The headquarters of Ueno Bank in Asuncion, Paraguay. (AP: Jorge Saenz)

The digital lender, a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company, lured customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries as it grew to more than 70 locations, sponsored Paraguay's national soccer team and plastered its name on the country's main stadium.

The bank's rapid expansion made it one of Paraguay's most visible financial success stories.

Its collapse has triggered days of protesting in the country.

"Santiago Peña and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings," said Luis Pineda, one of the protesters marching to Congress.

Police used tear gas and water cannons to disperse the crowds who shouted "give us our money back".

World.title: Teen faces court over alleged armed group attack on boy in Ellenbrook
World.content:
A 14-year-old boy has been refused bail after he was charged over a group attack in which a 13-year-old boy was allegedly bashed and threatened with a knife in Perth's north-east.

The incident was filmed and shared on social media.

The Perth Children's Court heard the boy met with the group of between six and eight offenders at an address in Ellenbrook on Sunday before an altercation began.

The 13-year-old was allegedly punched and kicked, before meeting with the group again at another Ellenbrook location, where he was threatened with a knife and assaulted in a prolonged attack that lasted between five and 10 minutes.

The court heard the 14-year-old boy who has been charged kicked the boy in the face, causing him to fall on his back.

The video shows a number of people punching and kicking a boy as he tries to protect himself. (Supplied)

The boy was then allegedly dragged along the ground, punched and kicked and forced to say "derogatory things", before his t-shirt and jumper were stolen.

He was able to walk home and later went to Midland Hospital with a concussion, multiple lumps on his head, black eyes and bruising to his upper and lower body.

The 14-year-old boy was charged with aggravated armed robbery and causing bodily harm.

Magistrate Joanne Andretich said while the alleged offender did not have a criminal record, the offending was extremely serious and the state had a "very strong case".

He was refused bail and will return to court in late November.

Video posted to social media

A graphic video shared on social media shows a group following a teenager asking "where's the vape?" before the alleged victim is pushed to the ground.

A number of people then punch and kick the crying teenager as he attempts to cover his face.

The boy was allegedly assaulted by several teenagers in Ellenbrook. (Supplied)

At one point someone can be seen holding a knife.

"There's been a bit of a disagreement that escalated way out of control, and as you can see on the video, the mob mentality came in," Detective Inspector Gary Butler told 6PR on Thursday.

"He's quite lucky that the injuries aren't more severe, but it's the whole mental anguish of being a victim of crime in this gang attack."

Vigilantism warning

Inspector Butler said the boy's family would "clearly" have been concerned about the repercussions of making a complaint.

"I think what we need to remember is that we're just not sure what's going on in this young fella's life or his family or his school or the social environment," he said.

"So we've provided significant support to him and the family."

Police say the victim received minor injuries in the attack and have identified other "persons of interest". (Supplied)

A police spokesperson said their investigation was ongoing, with a number of other "persons of interest" identified.

They called for calm, while acknowledging the "considerable concern" the incident had caused within the community.

"Members of the community are strongly urged not to take matters into their own hands, threaten retaliation or publish the names, photographs or personal information of the people believed to be involved," they said in a statement.

'Hard to watch': Minister

Education Minister Sabine Winton said her thoughts were with the 13-year-old and his family.

"It was pretty hard to watch, just absolutely outrageous and has no place," she said.

"It's hard to contemplate that anyone would do such a thing, but also the impact on the victim and his family.

"I've instructed, and I've received advice from the [education] department, that they're doing everything they can to support that young person, the family and of course his schoolmates."

Police Minister Reece Whitby said he was "disgusted and angry" to see the attack, particularly the person holding a knife.

"One slip, one wrong move, could have had tragic consequences that might have ended a life," he said on Wednesday.

"We're not going to tolerate this behaviour."

Laws which would have criminalised the sharing of video of the incident on social media are currently before parliament after a committee last year recommended changes to avoid unintended consequences.

World.title: Outrage from tiny town results in electoral commission backflip
World.content:
Kaniva will have a polling booth on election day after the Victorian Electoral Commission (VEC) reversed a decision that would have left residents facing an 80-kilometre round-trip to vote.

The initial decision decision drew criticism from residents of the town of 900, including Mayor Helen Hobbs and Lowan MP Emma Kealy, who would have had to drive to Nhill to cast their ballots.

Victorian Electoral Commissioner Sven Bluemmel said he was pleased to be able to provide a booth at the town's Senior Citizens Centre.

"We had always wanted to have a voting centre in Kaniva," he said.

" We had tried very hard to get that done, for whatever reason that hadn't worked out until today. "

Kaniva ranked 12th for votes cast among Lowan’s voting centres at the 2022 election.

The Uniting Church hall was ruled out but has been used for polling in the past. (Supplied: Helen Hobbs)

Change of plans

Kaniva normally hosts a voting booth in the town's Uniting Church Hall, which also operates as an op shop.

Remote polling cancelled for Nullagine Western Australia's Electoral Commission has backflipped on its decision to not have a polling station at the remote town of Nullagine for the election on March 8.

The volunteers who run the shop said it would be too hard to dismantle and reassemble.

The ABC understands the commission was told at least three times the venue was not available and that alternative venues were offered, including other church halls, the Senior Citizens Centre and the shire hall.

The VEC deemed them to be inappropriate, but Mr Bluemmel said that had changed.

"Once we actually had that discussion with the council today, we were able to land on that senior citizens' club, which we'll be able to operationalise with no problems," he said.

Cr Hobbs said she was initially told the centre was not necessary and that the decision not to host a voting centre was part of wider operational plans, which left her "absolutely shocked, gobsmacked, flabbergasted".

"We're just rapt that this decision has been reversed.. it could not be a better outcome," she said.

" We're talking about 600 voters out of that 1,100 catchment population, so couldn't be happier. "

Resident Fleur Maddern said the VEC's original decision was confusing and "rude".

Fleur Maddern can hardly believe the ddecision was reversed. (Supplied: Fleur Maddern)

She urged residents to complain to the VEC and credited locals who picked up the phone and sent emails.

"I'm really, really happy that people in this town did what I asked … and put their complaints in the appropriate place," Ms Maddern said.

" No point being complacent, no point complaining amongst ourselves, we actually have to make some noise. "

She said the result showed what a community can do when it speaks up.

"It's almost unbelievable that we've made a government department reverse the decision that is actually in our favour," Ms Maddern said.

World.title: 'Not a waste of money': Authority to be dissolved after decade of issues
World.content:
The troubled regional waste authority responsible for the collapse of Western Australia's first food organics and garden organics (FOGO) system is being dissolved.

The Bunbury Harvey Regional Council (BHRC) was in charge of operating two waste facilities, including the FOGO processing facility which began in 2013.

Banksia Road Organics Processing Facility near Dardanup, 180 kilometres south of Perth, closed indefinitely in late 2024 due to high levels of contamination in breach of composting standards.

Ratepayers were left with a $2 million bill to remove tonnes of FOGO waste at BHRC's organic processing facility in Dardanup. (ABC South West: Ella Lonergan)

The closure resulted in the South West's green-bin waste being sent straight to landfill.

City of Bunbury and Shire of Harvey have now made an in-principle agreement to disband the joint waste management authority.

Some of the South West councils have decided to continue to send their FOGO to landfill, while others have taken up a state government subsidy to have the waste trucked to the Perth processing facility.

Mayor denies failure

In a joint statement, both councils said they had agreed BHRC's governance model was no longer financially, operationally or environmentally sustainable.

Bunbury Mayor Jaysen Miguel said the dissolution did not amount to a failure.

"I wouldn't call this a failure. There has been a lot of work over this place for a long time," he said.

The future for the staff and management of the waste authority is yet to be decided.

BHRC's Banksia Rd organics processing facility stopped accepting FOGO in late 2024 due to high rates of contamination. (ABC South West: Bridget McArthur)

Both councils will now create a draft transition plan which is expected to be finalised early next year.

The cost of compliance

Financial reports show South West ratepayers have poured $14.7 million into BHRC's operations since 2022, when regulatory scrutiny began mounting over its operations.

In 2022, the Department of Water and Environmental Regulation (DWER) shut down on-site landfilling at BHRC's other waste facility, the Stanley Road Waste Management Facility near Australind.

The tip at Stanley Road was turned into a transfer station after issues with overflowing landfill and leaking contaminants. (ABC South West: Georgia Loney)

The regulator raised concerns about the "unacceptable" risk to human and environmental health from full and unlined landfill cells leaching contaminants into the surrounding area.

Both councils paid a combined $7.7 million in 2022/23 towards operating costs and remediation at Stanley Road tip to stop further contamination.

The Stanley Road tip has since operated as a household waste transfer and drop-off station.

The waste authority again got into trouble in 2023 for storing 15,000 used mattresses, creating an "extreme fire risk".

In November 2025, both councils agreed to contribute $2 million to remove a 20,000-tonne stockpile of contaminated FOGO waste at the Banksia Road site.

'Not a waste of money'

BHRC chairperson Wendy Dickinson defended the millions of dollars spent on remediation.

"The funding that has been put in by the member councils has been used to meet compliance issues, which we have been in the process of addressing and continuing to do," she said.

" So that has not been a waste of money. "

Ms Dickinson said the dissolution was simply recognition of changing legislation, compliance requirements and infrastructure needs since the authority was established in 1990.

Former Bunbury councillor and deputy mayor Brendan Kelly said the waste authority had been a "black hole" for ratepayer money.

The regulator intervened in 2023 when BHRC stockpiled thousands of old mattresses and created an "extreme fire risk". (Supplied: Bunbury Harvey Regional Council)

"Both of those councils have been bleeding money over the last decade on trying to manage their waste, and they're not getting anywhere," he said.

"Harvey and Bunbury need to get themselves together and do not leave the room until they have a well-thought-out plan," he said.

"There's no point in just saying, 'too hard'. That's not the solution."

The former councillor said the problems at BHRC were symptomatic of a much wider failure to plan for the South West's waste-management needs.

"The BHRC and Stanley Road are not the disease, it's the symptom," he said.

"Successive state governments have kicked the can down the road when it comes to waste management in the South West."

Brendan Kelly says the two councils need to work harder for a waste solution. (ABC South WEst WA: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet)

He said the region's councils needed to work alongside the state government to develop a centralised, long-term waste-management strategy.

The WA local government minister has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Baseballer loses sight in one eye in 'horrific freak accident'
World.content:
Adelaide's baseball community is rallying around a "tough cookie" player who lost sight in one eye after a "horrific freak accident" during a weekend game.

Veteran member of the Adelaide Angels Baseball Club, Tyler Forney, was struck in the eye by a foul ball off his own bat, during a double-header against Woodville on Saturday.

Close friend and long-time teammate Chris Congdon said Mr Forney was in the batter's box during the second game when the incident happened.

"His ball ricocheted off his bat and basically collected his right eye," Mr Congdon said.

"[It] resulted in him getting taken off to hospital by ambulance in a bad way and having significant eye surgery that evening.

"However, he's permanently lost vision in his right eye as a result of that.

"Anyone I've spoken to around the club that was there was just really mortified by the accident … it's a really horrific freak accident."

Mr Congdon said Mr Forney was an integral member of the club since joining back in 2016, after moving from Arizona in the United States.

He said Mr Forney had a gifted athletic ability which he had honed while playing college baseball.

"He's a really really tough cookie, Ty — I'm sure he played through a broken hand for parts of last season," Mr Congdon said.

"He was a walking highlight reel, he would make plays at shortstop that just no one else could make.

"He just stuck with us and [he's] a massive reason why the last five years we've had huge success."

'So grateful' for support

A GoFundMe page has since raised more than $16,200 by Friday afternoon to cover Mr Forney's medical fees.

"He [Mr Forney] did not realise how much of an impact that he has had on people — not only in our club, but the wider baseball community," Mr Congdon said.

" He's a very humble person, but this has really, really taken him taken by surprise and he's just so grateful. "

Mr Congdon said Mr Forney was being supported by his partner, two children and three stepchildren as he recovers.

He said while Mr Forney's playing career may have come to an end, the club is already talking about ways to transition him to a coaching role.

"He's the sort of person that is quite private and reserved, but when he speaks and he does, everybody listens, so I think he wouldn't have thought about coaching," he said.

"He had so much left to do as a player and still so valuable as a player."

World.title: Seasonal produce to make the most of this November
World.content:
"I'm definitely excited for more chopped salads with lots of different colours," Phoebe Thorburn says.

Thorburn, a writer and cook in Naarm/Melbourne, says spring produce "is easier to eat closer to its natural form", which also helps with the cooking "mental load".

Josh Ball, co-founder of home delivery grocer Farmers Pick, says shopping seasonally tends to leave you with the freshest, tastiest and cheapest produce.

Josh Ball says asparagus has had a plentiful season that will begin to wrap up in the next few weeks. (ABC News: Anna Chisholm)

"Cost of living is a massive consideration and following the seasons is the best way to get the best price," he says.

There's new produce, such as mangoes and cherries, to be excited about and year-round staples too.

While brassicas grow all year, "the more sunshine they get, the faster they grow" and November can see prices drop, Ball says.

What can you look for?

Vegetables:

Broccoli

Cauliflower

Cabbage

Asparagus

Broad beans

Corn

Zucchini

Avocado

Garden peas

Snow peas

Fresh garlic

Fruit:

Mangoes

Strawberries

Cherries

Other stone fruit, such as nectarines, peaches and apricots, are expected later this month

Brassicas (those old favourites)

Spring weather often brings on a good supply of brassicas, particularly broccoli, cauliflower and cabbage, Ball says.

"If there's some sunny days in a row, they come on really fast," he says, and you can suddenly have a flush of affordable and versatile cauliflowers.

And if you're shopping at smaller or independent grocers, prices can change quickly, he says.

Enjoy asparagus and broad beans (while you can)

Hamish Franklin, the buyer at Georgie's Harvest in South Melbourne Market, says white and green asparagus will be available for the next few weeks.

Four spring asparagus recipes From one-pot pasta to a crunchy green salad, these easy recipes will put spring asparagus on your weeknight menu.

"When you're buying regular asparagus, you want to find the bigger size [spears], which have got a deeper, richer flavour," he says.

But, Thorburn gets "really excited about the baby asparagus".

"I've been wanting to make, like, a warm, tangy, vinaigrette potato salad with asparagus," they say.

Ball says: "If you like asparagus, you've probably got a few more weeks to really enjoy it and then it'll probably start disappearing."

Broad beans have a "relatively short season" and will be "winding up as well", he says.

Alan Li, from Fruits on Coventry in South Melbourne Market, expects broad beans to be available until the end of the month.

Broad beans are also known as fava beans, particularly once dried. (ABC News: Anna Chisholm)

Corn and zucchini

While corn is reasonably priced currently, Li says the price will drop as the volume increases.

The zucchini supply will increase in Australia's south in the next few weeks too, he says.

Zucchini and corn are also among Thorburn's warmer weather favourites, and they recommend charring corn cobs on a griddle pan and using the kernels in salads and salsas or sautéing thinly sliced zucchini "coins" in olive oil and butter as a side.

"Sometimes adding peas in, sometimes asparagus, [and] seasoning it."

Phoebe Thorburn says they have "gone a bit hard" on turning zucchini into fritters and slice in the past. (ABC News: Anna Chisholm)

Mangoes

Making mango lassis and dicing mango for salads is great, but like a lot of us, Thorburn is most excited for just eating mangoes out in the sun.

Josh Ball says mango is "definitely a superstar fruit coming into summer". (ABC News: Anna Chisholm)

The first mangoes came from the Northern Territory in early spring. However, Ball says supplies are now beginning to come from Queensland.

"People can expect to see mangoes coming into that sort of affordable, bingeable territory over the next couple of weeks, which is pretty exciting," Ball says.

Li says the Kensington prides are "Australia's best-eating mangoes" and he recommends the firmer flesh of the R2E2 variety for salads.

Berries, cherries and other stone fruit

Li says a lot of interesting fruit is coming into season this month.

This includes Victorian strawberries, which are becoming less expensive, he says, as well as other berry varieties, such as raspberries, blackberries and mulberries.

Josh Ball says a lot of cherries are rejected for aesthetic reasons. (ABC News: Anna Chisholm)

Ball is already stocking cherries, which can be "volatile" to grow.

"If there's any poorly timed rain, or hail in particular, the whole crop can be destroyed pretty easily," he says.

You might not have seen other stone fruit on the shelves yet, but Ball says it's on the way, pointing to the Goulburn Valley and northern Victorian growing regions.

So expect nectarines, peaches and apricots later in November.

"And then obviously through summer they're everywhere and they can get pretty cheap if it's a good season," Ball says.

World.title: Man sues former AFL players Dion Prestia and Steven May
World.content:
A man is suing former AFL players Dion Prestia and Steven May over an alleged brawl on Victoria's Mornington Peninsula.

The two players were previously charged over an alleged streetside altercation with another group in the coastal town of Sorrento on Boxing Day in 2024, but the charges were dropped in May 2026.

Mr Prestia, a former Richmond premiership player, had been charged with recklessly causing serious injury and affray, while Mr May, an ex-Demons player who retired this year, was charged with affray.

The incident left two men in hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

Previously, both Mr Prestia and Mr May strenuously denied their involvement in the alleged incident.

A personal injury claim is now underway in the Supreme Court over the alleged assault.

It is understood medical costs are among the damages being sought by a single plaintiff, who claims he was assaulted.

His name has been restricted by the court.

Court documents containing the exact details of the claim are yet to be released.

At a directions hearing in the Supreme Court on Friday, lawyers confirmed two more defendants were being added to the civil case alongside Mr May and Mr Prestia.

Their criminal matters remain before the court which means civil action is unlikely to commence before their cases are finalised.

Mr Prestia played 254 games for Richmond and Gold Coast and is a three-time premiership player.

It was recently announced he would join Hawthorn's coaching line-up for the 2027 season as an AFL development coach.

Mr May played 251 AFL games for Melbourne and Gold Coast and was a member of the Demons' 2021 premiership-winning squad.

He retired suddenly on the eve of the 2026 season.

Mr Prestia's employer and Mr May have been contacted for comment.

World.title: The demise of David Jones leaves an empty feeling
World.content:
NationalDavid Jones collapse Editorial The demise of David Jones leaves an empty feeling The Herald's View Editorial November 6, 2026 — 4:47pm

November 6, 2026 — 4:47pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The black-and-white houndstooth print on a David Jones bag has been a badge of honour for generations of Australians. For many, growing up in the suburbs meant a train trip to the city for school uniforms or, come December, the window display and Santa, and lunch in the food hall. Dressed in their best clothes, children wandered the floors of this bastion of middle-class refinement with mothers who inspected and touched the racks of leading Australian fashion labels and had their own dreams. The iconic retailer was renowned for its lavish window displays and houndstooth shopping bags. Jessica Hromas Prue Acton, Sportscraft and Carla Zampatti were joined by the best global labels and, together with seasonal shows replete with big names on the runway and celebrity guests, made David Jones Australia’s fashion central. It was more than a shopping emporium too. The David Jones Art Gallery supported Australian artists; before television arrived in the 1950s, a staff amateur theatre group, the Dajonian Repertory Society, staged six plays a year; on her first visit to Sydney in 1954, Queen Elizabeth II attended a banquet dinner on the seventh floor of the Elizabeth Street store.



But after 188 years, David Jones’ future hangs in the balance, with the board calling in administrators and the lender sending in the receivers. The department store chain is still trading, but no one is sure for how long. David Jones employs about 6000 staff and has 38 physical stores, with 17 of those in Westfield shopping centres. Unions are concerned about layoffs before Christmas. Suppliers are under no delusions. Various businesses have been left in the lurch and the owners and agents of luxury brands have began removing stock from outlets where they have “concession pad” agreements with the store. The collapse is part of a worldwide phenomenon – department stores have been smashed by an alarming combination: the global financial crisis, the COVID-19 pandemic, the ongoing cost-of-living crisis; and, most painfully, the rapid rise of online shopping. They have also been hit by what’s termed the bifurcation of retail, where top-end shoppers have migrated to super-luxe stores and the bottom end of the market hunts for more bargain-basement offerings, with department stores taking the hit in the middle. David Jones’ problems were compounded by dubious business decisions that began during the 1980s takeover fad with the Jones family selling out, and continued on and off for years until the company was unable to pay rent to Westfield last September.



Twelve years ago, a South African company reportedly paid $2.1 billion to buy David Jones. Three years ago, Anchorage Capital Partners bought the department store chain for less than $100 million but still could not make a go of it. Related Article David Jones collapse Six things to know about David Jones on the brink It is a long way from 1838, when Welsh draper David Jones opened one of the world’s first department stores in Sydney. It remained largely a Sydney phenomenon for the first century or so, opening in Newcastle in 1957 and then expanding into the regions and metropolitan suburbs around the nation. David Jones arrived in Victoria in the 1960s, and in 1982 it acquired the three stores of Buckley & Nunn located in Bourke Street, Northland and Chadstone. In 1987, David Jones purchased the former GJ Coles store and building at 299 Bourke Street, Melbourne, converting it into a David Jones store. David Jones had always been Sydney’s most upmarket store, specialising in quality goods and elite customer services.



But in Melbourne, David Jones was slightly lower down the pecking order. Georges Store in Collins Street had long catered to the cream of Melbourne society and liked to think of itself as the equal to Harrods of London. In 1981, David Jones bought Georges and slowly squeezed it into oblivion, eventually closing it in 1995 in the hope of keeping much of the cream for itself. It did not happen. In the end, David Jones was slowly squeezed by rising costs, changing shopping habits and online technology, a vestige of a way of shopping out of step with the times. The sun is setting on an Australian retail icon. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: From Swans to the AFL’s ugly ducklings: Sydney’s shame is no one-off
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion From Swans to the AFL’s ugly ducklings: Sydney’s shame is no one-off Jake Niall Chief football writer, The Age November 6, 2026 — 4:25pm

November 6, 2026 — 4:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

That the Sydney Swans have vowed to change, to repair the damage wrought by the Pullman hotel scandal and Tom Papley’s alleged drug offence, confirms that they know something is genuinely amiss in their playing group. One way to view their far-reaching “examination” is that it represents a kind of cultural audit in which they are seeking to answer to this question – What are the underlying factors that have seen senior players make such poor and reckless choices? Tom Papley became a pin-up player for the Swans after the Pullman hotel scandal, but that has now changed. Steven Siewert Papley’s roadside drug test failure – the outcome of which is yet to be verified by a secondary sample – can be a positive for the Swans, so to speak, if it forces them to confront the root causes of the Pullman fiasco. Until Papley’s arrest, it was possible for the club to consider the Pullman as an anomaly – players took liberties, made terrible and unprofessional choices and embarrassed themselves and the club (and possibly crossed legal and ethical lines), but that this was out of collective character.



When the Swans responded so magnificently to the Pullman scandal on the field, by slaying the Brisbane Lions in that extraordinary qualifying final and then running Fremantle to the wire in the prelim, despite a scandal-depleted side, it was natural to think that their stirring response, not the Pullman, demonstrated their true cultural colours. The hierarchy’s handling of the Pullman was powerful, too, in that, as chairman Andrew Pridham rightly asserted, they had been willing to torpedo their finals campaign by suspending the five for the remainder of the season. Loading Commendably, they did not follow the expedient old-school footy club script for scandals, in which players would have missed only one or two games (or none) when the grail was within their grasp. It’s worth noting that Papley himself was outstanding in the upset of the Lions, booting five goals. The same senior player who summoned his best in September has subsequently embarrassed everyone with a poor choice (allegedly).



Herein lies the critical distinction that the Swans must surely understand now if they didn’t previously: That committed performance on the field isn’t necessarily conducive to the best behaviours or culture in the outside world. Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘Unacceptable and must change’: Swans hierarchy apologise, detail review into their AFL program Footy is replete with the mythology that great teams and players carry some moral purpose, that successful teams – and the Swans are relatively successful, albeit without a recent flag – win games and finals because they have a “good culture”, led by senior players who set foundational standards and lead them not into temptation. Geelong people sometimes spruiked a culture of “character over talent”, which this column considers to be bunkum. The cultural strength of the Cats, as with Collingwood, has been their competitive ethos. They have senior players who refuse to accept defeat. This does not mean they all refuse a drink card or quick buck. The truth is that, just as Shane Warne’s wizardry was immune to whatever missteps he made in his life, football performance is not reflective of cleanskin behaviours outside the field.



It is possible for a team to party hard and still perform. Indeed, there’s a possibility that the Swans’ (relative) success can lead players to entitlement, which, in turn, can spawn a feeling of invincibility, leading you to a hotel room with topless dancers, and whatever mood-altering substances were present (certainly alcohol), at 5am. Wisely, the Sydney board and CEO Matthew Pavlich have engaged an external company, Intersection, to assist them in their examination of club culture, and it is not confined to just the men’s players. They are speaking to the AFLW cohort and commercial partners - some of whom need reassurance. Sydney CEO Matthew Pavlich was forced to face the media again this week as his club found itself embroiled in a new scandal. Sitthixay Ditthavong Another scandal could well cost the Swans millions, just as the Pullman has cost Isaac Heeney a pretty penny in sponsorship. Many of the celebrated club reviews - Geelong (2006), Richmond (2016), Collingwood (2018) - have been focused on the playing group’s failures to achieve their potential, under-performances that were overcome by changes.



This examination (the club is avoiding the R word, review) differs in that the Swans are canvassing other stakeholders. It is not simply about extracting the best output from players on the field. Related Article CBD Latest Sydney Swans scandal means marquee name a late scratching Underlying the club’s self-examination is the fact that the Swans are a distinctive club, with different needs to the majority of AFL clubs. Consider the following unique traits of the Swans: 1. They play in a market where the AFL is not followed so intensely, where it is entertainment more than a binding faith. Players in Randwick and Coogee are left alone and can (and do) have a drink without repercussions.



2. They have a more educated, affluent fan base, in inner Sydney and consequently have more female engagement and a more progressive social flavour (see Pride games). 3. Their AFLW team attracts more interest - crowds are exceptional - and is more central to the club than at many rivals. 4. They have made a virtue, and profited from their purported contrast with the NRL clubs, who are viewed as more old-world and scandal-prone. Emotions were high after Sydney’s stirring qualifying final win over eventual premiers Brisbane in September. AFL Photos via Getty Images To own a fan base that values women – and is less apt to accept the “boys will be boys” excuses – creates a higher demand for more respectful behaviours in that realm; at Sydney, there was immediate condemnation from a hefty section of members when the Pullman incident erupted.



The Sydney hierarchy thus will have to consider whether their men’s playing group is capable of meeting the club’s broader values, in which good citizenship - respectful treatment of women, avoidance of drugs and excessive alcohol consumption and associated anti-social behaviours - is elevated. Related Article AFL 2026 Surprise twist in legal move by dancers against Swans players caught in hotel saga Given that three of the Pullman five and Papley are/were among their most valuable and elite players (counting Nick Blakey), it’s reasonable to question whether there’s a gaping leadership deficit, outside of skipper Callum Mills, who rose to the moment post-Pullman and whose season-long absence due to injury will be a major challenge. Sydney doesn’t need to repair what happens in those two and half crowded hours each week during the AFL season. As with the West Coast Eagles of 2007-08, whose issues (drugs mainly) were far more serious, as Dean Cox would know, and were willing to sacrifice a ladder position in the short-term and some of whom suffered long-term fallout, the change the Swans desire won’t be measured in wins and losses. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: People ‘need to be held accountable’ for police station debacle: minister
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland Police People ‘need to be held accountable’ for police station debacle: minister William Davis November 6, 2026 — 4:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The state’s police minister says he hopes people will be held accountable for “possibly the worst deal for taxpayers in the history of Queensland”. In 2023 the Queensland Police Service committed to about $116 million in lease costs over 15 years – or more than $500,000 a month – for 433 Logan Road in Stones Corner, which it later found was unfit for purpose as a station and never occupied. A Crime and Corruption Commission investigation released on Thursday found a superintendent without significant commercial property experience led negotiations for the exorbitant lease, when the building would have been significantly cheaper to buy outright. The lease for the Stones Corner building was signed without funding allocated for the deal. Nine News It also said QPS had not secured funding for the building before the contract was signed.



The investigation did not make findings of corruption, but identified significant governance and control weaknesses that led to the high-profile bungled agreement. Police Minister Dan Purdie spoke to reporters on Friday morning about the report, framing it as the responsibility of the former Labor government and now-opposition leader Steven Miles. Police Minister Dan Purdie. Catherine Strohfeldt “We now know that is the worst deal in Queensland Police history, possibly the worst deal for taxpayers in the history of Queensland,” he said. Purdie added: “Queenslanders are left with this bill. Labor … need to own it now, and I still think people need to be held accountable.”



The minister confirmed the government was exploring possible options to get out of the lease legally. Related Article Queensland Police Police paying more to rent empty building than cost to buy it: watchdog Acting police commissioner Brett Pointing spoke to reporters on Thursday afternoon, apologising for the failure and saying the QPS would accept all recommendations from the CCC. “I think there are two groups of people that I’d like to apologise to,” he said. “One is the Queensland community. This is a large waste of taxpayers’ money.



“[The other is] the men and women of the QPS. That’s a significant amount of money that I’d rather be spending on keeping the community safe.” He did not reveal how a superintendent ended up negotiating the deal, and declined to say if heads would roll over the scandal. NationalVictoriaAustralian Open Australian Open to begin a day earlier in 2027 – just don’t expect tournament tennis Brielle Kohlbeck November 6, 2026 — 4:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The gates to Melbourne Park will open a day earlier in 2027 – but there will be no Open tournament tennis played. Tennis Australia is badging Saturday, January 10 Kids Tennis Day. Children and families will be encouraged to visit the precinct to watch training and practice matches and pick up a racquet – and, Tennis Australia hopes, buy food, drink and merch. Lleyton Hewitt at the launch of Kids Tennis Day. Zoey Duchene Tennis Australia chief executive Andrew Abdo made the announcement at Melbourne Park, joined by tennis legend Lleyton Hewitt and, mysteriously, a koala and a kangaroo to go with the “Australian-inspired” theme for the 2027 tournament. “It’s an engine that can be used to reinvest back into the sport,” Abdo said. “Having a focus on a dedicated day for kids is symbolically important, but it’s also an opportunity where we might discover the next superhero, and that’s exciting for us.”



Lleyton Hewitt (left), Andrew Abdo and a wildlife carer brought a koala and a kangaroo to Kia Arena. Zoey Duchene The schedule change follows this year’s shift of the Australian Open, which ran from January 12 to February 1 instead of finishing on the Australia Day weekend in late January, as it has in the past. Abdo took over as Tennis Australia chief executive in August after leaving the NRL. This is one of his first major announcements since he got into hot water for getting a player’s name wrong at his first Australian Open launch. Tennis Australia could not give an exact cost for the extra day, but Abdo said it wouldn’t be possible without sponsorship. “There definitely is an investment into it, and it’s an investment we’re happy to make,” Abdo said.



The Australian Open is among the biggest economic drivers in Australian sport. This year’s tournament was estimated to have pumped more than $600 million into the Melbourne economy, according to NAB analysis, a rise of 7 to 10 per cent from 2025. Related Article Australian Open A translucent, climate-controlled dome over Melbourne Park? Tiley’s radical plan to reshape the Australian Open Revenue from the Open has steadily increased since 2010, apart from a three-year slump after COVID. But taxpayers have also helped foot the bill. More than a billion dollars has been spent on upgrading Melbourne Park since 2011, and an agreement between Tennis Australia and the Victorian government keeps the tournament in Melbourne until at least 2046. Growth is also not limited to revenue. Melbourne Park’s annual report shows media reach is vast and still expanding. More than 13 million viewers tuned in to Nine’s coverage in 2025, up from about 12.8 million the year before, while content on the Open’s channels generated 45 million engagements across 7000 posts. (Nine is the owner of this masthead.) Hewitt also supported the push to get more children involved in the sport, saying it was the best way to produce more top-level players like himself and Alex de Minaur.



“We’ve got to work through the pathway, obviously,” Hewitt said. “We’ve got to try and become a real high-performance group ... and try and transition the best kids through.” Hewitt reflected on his 2005 final and the “wave of excitement” from the Australian public, and said he remembered experiencing Kids Tennis Day himself and playing games in Rod Laver Arena. “The more that we can get out there and host Kids Day, put on a good spectacle that people want to be involved with and come out to, I think it helps the sport in Australia,” Hewitt said. Abdo said the 2027 Open was already shaping up to be a strong one. “We are ahead on ticket sales, which is terrific,” he said. “We’ve got more interstate, more international visitors than we’ve had before, which is terrific. All signs are leading to another well-attended event.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Failed legal battle to retain independence costs cash-strapped ATC $4.1m
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Failed legal battle to retain independence costs cash-strapped ATC $4.1m Craig Kerry November 6, 2026 — 4:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The merits of the Australian Turf Club board’s failed battle to retain its independence can now be weighed against a $4.1 million cost after the release of the cash-strapped organisation’s annual report. The ATC, which operates Sydney’s four metropolitan thoroughbred racetracks and owns all of them except Royal Randwick, lost $4.8 million in the 2025-26 financial year, up from $2.6 million in 2024-25. The Australian Turf Club operates the Randwick, Rosehill, Canterbury and Warwick Farm race tracks, and owns all except Randwick. Getty Images However, the deficit for last year would have been about $700,000 if not for the board’s legal costs from its fight to prevent regulator Racing NSW appointing an administrator over concerns about the club’s financial position, which included a $30 million bank loan, and corporate governance. That battle started when Racing NSW issued a show cause notice in September last year, following the sacking of ATC chief executive Matt Galanos and resignation of directors Ben Bayot and Natalie Hewson, and ended in June when the regulator won a NSW Supreme Court appeal to appoint Morgan Kelly as administrator.



The ruling included an order for the ATC to pay the legal costs of Racing NSW, which this week reported an operating surplus of $13.63 million in 2025-26, up from $12.96 million the previous year. Kelly’s review of the ATC started as a consultant in April, under an agreement with Racing NSW to resume its additional funding of the club, and he took over as administrator on July 8, effectively replacing the board. Chairman Tim Hale, vice-chair Caroline Searcy and newest board addition Bernie Brookes became part of advisory subcommittee with Racing NSW directors Simon Tuxen and Michael Crismale. ATC chairman Tim Hale. Steven Siewert Kelly noted in the annual report that the club’s revenue of $379 million was up on 2024-25’s $373.4

million and losses were down without the one-off legal costs, but there was work to do. “While the club’s underlying assets and operations remain strong, the continued loss-making performance highlights the need to strengthen financial and commercial discipline across the organisation,” Kelly wrote.



“Our review to date has identified opportunities to enhance commercial performance, improve operational efficiency and strengthen governance. In a number of areas, costs have increased over time and opportunities to maximise revenue have not been fully realised.” Related Article Horse racing Racing NSW appoints administrator, advisory panel at cash-strapped ATC Sources who spoke on the condition of anonymity have told this masthead the operational efficiencies have not included forced job cuts, but the club has reduced its staff slightly through natural attrition, although roles attached to horse welfare or safety have been untouched. An ongoing court case regarding alleged thefts of cash from raceday safes has not impacted the club, which is insured for those losses. A positive for the club in this year’s report was the absence of an auditor’s notice of concern, present in the previous year’s report, over the ATC’s financial viability.



Members will have the chance to address the club’s situation at the annual general meeting at Royal Randwick on November 26. The ATC board initially succeeded in blocking Racing NSW’s move to appoint Kelly in December before winning again in March when NSW Supreme Court Justice Francois Kunc ruled that the regulator’s move was not authorised under the Thoroughbred Racing Act. However, Racing NSW’s appeal was upheld when the panel found the club’s finances and corporate governance were within the definition of horse racing under the Act.
