World.title: Army members who allegedly gang raped Sydney teen granted bail to live on barracks
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWCrime Army members who allegedly gang raped Sydney teen granted bail to live on barracks Amber Schultz and Jack Gramenz Updated November 6, 2026 — 4:09pm ,first published November 6, 2026 — 8:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Two serving army members who allegedly held down, choked and gang raped a teenager in her Sydney inner-west home have been granted bail to live at the Holsworthy military barracks. Combat engineer Kayden Phillips, 20, and marine specialist Harrison Massie Knight, 22, appeared in Liverpool Local Court on Friday and face life in prison over the alleged assault. The accused are based at Holsworthy barracks in Sydney’s south-west. AAPIMAGE The pair met the 18-year-old woman on Saturday and were captured on CCTV entering her Camperdown apartment. The prosecution argued there was a “degree of planning” in the alleged attack, with the men taking off their shirts when the alleged victim went to her room. One allegedly restrained her, and she was choked to the point of unconsciousness, then raped, the court heard. The woman then managed to “flee” the apartment, the court heard, reported to police and underwent a Sexual Assault Forensic Exam, with DNA testing underway.



When Knight and Phillips were captured leaving the apartment some time later, one of the men was missing his shirt and his belt. The court heard that when confronted by a witness’s partner, the two men initially denied being in the apartment, before denying anything sexual happened. The pair, who are in the same army troop, were arrested at the Holsworthy military barracks in south-west Sydney on Thursday morning. Police seized phones and clothing from their two rooms. DNA testing is underway. ‘[The woman] fled the scene worried about her safety.’ Judge Andrew Miller The men were both charged with aggravated sexual assault in company depriving liberty, aggravated sexual touching of another person and choking a person with intent to commit an indictable offence. The incident is still under investigation, and police may bring more charges.



In applying for bail on Friday, defence lawyer Tandy Machisa conceded the prosecution’s case was strong, but questioned whether the woman’s conduct before fleeing the scene “raised questions” about her account. Judge Andrew Miller dismissed this line of argument. “She fled the scene worried about her safety,” he said, highlighting the Criminal Procedure Act gave directions about drawing conclusions around delays in reporting sexual assault. Machisa argued both of the accused had strong family support, strong ties to their community, no criminal history, and strong employment. A file photo of a training exercise at Holsworthy army base, Sydney. Kate Geraghty She said Knight, who the court heard was the “more serious” offender of the pair, recently achieved the rank of Lance Corporal.



“To achieve this rank shows a level of compliance, respect and authority,” she said. The prosecution argued the alleged facts of the case were strong, and the pair presented an unacceptable risk to the community. They face a non-parole period of 15 years. Miller found that confining the pair to the barracks would mitigate bail risks. The pair cannot leave the barracks unless under the supervision of their commanding officer, and only for military, medical, court or legal appointments. The pair are not to contact the complainant, witnesses or be in contact with one another. The prosecution is contesting their bail. The pair will remain in custody until the bail review is heard in a higher court in the coming days.



They were supported in court by their parents, with Knight’s family travelling from Melbourne overnight. Their matter will next be heard on January 14. A Defence spokesperson said that, as the matter is under an NSW Police investigation and before the courts, it would be inappropriate to comment. “There is no place for sexual violence or misconduct in Defence,” the spokesperson said. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. World.title: Babies made a comeback – but that was before the latest rate rises
World.content:
PoliticsFederalBabies Babies made a comeback – but that was before the latest rate rises Matt Wade and Shane Wright Updated November 6, 2026 — 3:52pm ,first published 3:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

High inflation and the Reserve Bank’s steep interest rate hikes could halt a small baby bounce with new figures showing a turnaround in Australia’s fertility rate that is being driven by women in regional parts of the country. Figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics, released on Friday, showed there were 299,903 births registered in 2025, a 2.6 per cent lift on the previous year and the biggest one-year increase since the post-Covid baby boom. Loading The increase arrested a long-term fall in the fertility rate which lifted marginally to 1.497 after dropping to a record low in 2024. A fertility rate of 2.1 is needed to naturally replace a nation’s population. It is the third consecutive year that it has been below 1.5. The fertility rate fell in every capital city bar Hobart, with the biggest declines in Perth, Brisbane and Adelaide which all recorded sharp increases in home prices through 2025. The lowest capital city fertility rate is in Canberra at just 1.29.





In the City of Melbourne the fertility rate was just 0.5, the lowest of any local government area in the nation. Other Melbourne LGAs with very low fertility rates were Yarra (0.79), Port Phillip (0.81) and Stonnington (0.81). But cheaper regional areas have much higher fertility rates with some areas actually going through a modest baby boom. In regional NSW the number of births jumped by 8 per cent in 2025 and the fertility rate was a relatively healthy 1.87. The fertility rate in regional Victoria was 1.91. Across regional Victoria, councils such as Swan Hill, Southern Grampians, Moyne and Moira have fertility rates above 2.1 which held steady or improved through 2025. In NSW, centres such as Cowra, Dubbo, Griffith and Yass also held fertility rates above replacement level.



KPMG urban economist Terry Rawnsley attributed Australia’s modest “baby bounce” in 2025 to improvements in the economic circumstances of families in that period. “There was a bit of an improvement in cost of living pressures at the back end of 2023 and in 2024…and interest rates were kind of softening a bit at that time, so people had the confidence to press go on the family and we’ve seen that baby bounce come through in 2025,” he said. “It shows a clear pattern between households’ disposable income and their propensity to have children.” But that could come to an end.



Inflation has climbed to 4.3 per cent, in part due to high oil prices, prompting the Reserve Bank to lift official rates five times this year. On a $600,000 mortgage, the rate rises will add about $500 to monthly repayments while higher petrol prices are costing households around $100 a month more. Rawnsley said rising cost of living pressures this year would likely put downward pressure on birth numbers. “Crystal balling for the next year’s numbers, we’ll probably see another dip as people feel squeezed by cost of living,” he said. Related Article Australian economy What is a recession and are we in one? A bluffer’s guide Rawnsley said the national fertility rate has now hovered around the 1.5 mark for the past three years.



“The fertility rate seems to have found a bit of a floor in the past few years but there’s no clear factor that might drive it back-up again towards the levels around 1.7 we had pre-COVID,” he said. “There’s no big policy lever or change pointing to a turning around.” The fertility slump is not unique to Australia – many nations in Europe and parts of Asia have had far steeper declines, triggering warnings of a “demographic winter” in some. Opposition leader Angus Taylor, a father of four, said a lift in hope could help boost the chances of more children. “For young Australians to want to have a family, they’ve got to have hope. They’ve got to believe that the economy gives them opportunities,” he said. The ABS figures showed fertility among young women continues to fall, hitting record lows among teenagers and those aged between 20 and 24. The lift in 2025 fertility rates was driven by women aged between 25 and 39. There were 4148 births of twins and 46 triplets or more, in line with previous years.

World.title: ‘Heartbreaking’: Holocaust survivor shot in Bondi terror attack dies in hospital
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWBondi shooting ‘Heartbreaking’: Holocaust survivor shot in Bondi terror attack dies in hospital Daniel Lo Surdo and Jack Gramenz Updated November 6, 2026 — 3:48pm ,first published 2:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Eva Geller, 90, survived the Holocaust. A 90-year-old Holocaust survivor who settled in Sydney’s eastern suburbs after fleeing from Europe has died in Prince of Wales Hospital following complications stemming from injuries suffered in the December 14 terrorist attack. Eva Geller, a great-grandmother who fled Romania with her mother and grandmother as a child, died on Thursday night, almost 11 months after she was hit by gunfire in the attack that targeted Jewish Australians celebrating Hanukkah at Bondi Beach. Geller was told by doctors she would never walk again after suffering multiple gunshot wounds in the attack, in which 15 victims died. She had been in and out of hospital since December, but remained active in the Jewish community, attending services as late as September, moving with a walking stick.



Geller raised a family with her husband, David, an Auschwitz survivor, in Sydney’s eastern suburbs. She attended Nefesh Synagogue in Bondi, where Rabbi Aron Moss became accustomed to her “very warm” character. “She was a child in the Holocaust years, she escaped but she lost a lot of family. She lost her husband at quite an early age but, despite all that, she maintained a real positivity and happiness and a zest for life that was there right up until the end,” Moss said. “This is just another big, massive loss.” Rabbi Aron Moss AAPIMAGE A large crowd is expected at her funeral on Monday, a source said. Premier Chris Minns described her death as “heartbreaking”. “My thoughts are with Eva’s family and the Jewish community as they face another painful loss,” he said. “Almost a year on, we’re still living with the pain and aftershock of that evil act.”



Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Geller’s death highlighted the continued devastation Australians confront in the months since the Bondi attack. “Eva should have been able to celebrate Chanukah in peace and safety and instead, her life was changed forever by an act of terror and antisemitism,” he said. “We are wrapping our arms around Eva’s family, friends and the Jewish community at this very sad time.” NSW Police are working with the coroner to establish the cause of Geller’s death, and if it may lead to further charges against Naveed Akram, the surviving alleged gunman behind the attack. His father, Sajid, died in the attack following a shoot-out with police. Get alerts on breaking news as it happens.

World.title: From Swans to the AFL’s ugly ducklings: Sydney’s shame is no one-off
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion From Swans to the AFL’s ugly ducklings: Sydney’s shame is no one-off Jake Niall Chief football writer, The Age November 6, 2026 — 4:25pm

November 6, 2026 — 4:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

That the Sydney Swans have vowed to change, to repair the damage wrought by the Pullman hotel scandal and Tom Papley’s alleged drug offence, confirms that they know something is genuinely amiss in their playing group. One way to view their far-reaching “examination” is that it represents a kind of cultural audit in which they are seeking to answer to this question – What are the underlying factors that have seen senior players make such poor and reckless choices? Tom Papley became a pin-up player for the Swans after the Pullman hotel scandal, but that has now changed. Steven Siewert Papley’s roadside drug test failure – the outcome of which is yet to be verified by a secondary sample – can be a positive for the Swans, so to speak, if it forces them to confront the root causes of the Pullman fiasco. Until Papley’s arrest, it was possible for the club to consider the Pullman as an anomaly – players took liberties, made terrible and unprofessional choices and embarrassed themselves and the club (and possibly crossed legal and ethical lines), but that this was out of collective character.



When the Swans responded so magnificently to the Pullman scandal on the field, by slaying the Brisbane Lions in that extraordinary qualifying final and then running Fremantle to the wire in the prelim, despite a scandal-depleted side, it was natural to think that their stirring response, not the Pullman, demonstrated their true cultural colours. The hierarchy’s handling of the Pullman was powerful, too, in that, as chairman Andrew Pridham rightly asserted, they had been willing to torpedo their finals campaign by suspending the five for the remainder of the season. Loading Commendably, they did not follow the expedient old-school footy club script for scandals, in which players would have missed only one or two games (or none) when the grail was within their grasp. It’s worth noting that Papley himself was outstanding in the upset of the Lions, booting five goals. The same senior player who summoned his best in September has subsequently embarrassed everyone with a poor choice (allegedly).



Herein lies the critical distinction that the Swans must surely understand now if they didn’t previously: That committed performance on the field isn’t necessarily conducive to the best behaviours or culture in the outside world. Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘Unacceptable and must change’: Swans hierarchy apologise, detail review into their AFL program Footy is replete with the mythology that great teams and players carry some moral purpose, that successful teams – and the Swans are relatively successful, albeit without a recent flag – win games and finals because they have a “good culture”, led by senior players who set foundational standards and lead them not into temptation. Geelong people sometimes spruiked a culture of “character over talent”, which this column considers to be bunkum. The cultural strength of the Cats, as with Collingwood, has been their competitive ethos. They have senior players who refuse to accept defeat. This does not mean they all refuse a drink card or quick buck. The truth is that, just as Shane Warne’s wizardry was immune to whatever missteps he made in his life, football performance is not reflective of cleanskin behaviours outside the field.



It is possible for a team to party hard and still perform. Indeed, there’s a possibility that the Swans’ (relative) success can lead players to entitlement, which, in turn, can spawn a feeling of invincibility, leading you to a hotel room with topless dancers, and whatever mood-altering substances were present (certainly alcohol), at 5am. Wisely, the Sydney board and CEO Matthew Pavlich have engaged an external company, Intersection, to assist them in their examination of club culture, and it is not confined to just the men’s players. They are speaking to the AFLW cohort and commercial partners - some of whom need reassurance. Sydney CEO Matthew Pavlich was forced to face the media again this week as his club found itself embroiled in a new scandal. Sitthixay Ditthavong Another scandal could well cost the Swans millions, just as the Pullman has cost Isaac Heeney a pretty penny in sponsorship. Many of the celebrated club reviews - Geelong (2006), Richmond (2016), Collingwood (2018) - have been focused on the playing group’s failures to achieve their potential, under-performances that were overcome by changes.



This examination (the club is avoiding the R word, review) differs in that the Swans are canvassing other stakeholders. It is not simply about extracting the best output from players on the field. Related Article CBD Latest Sydney Swans scandal means marquee name a late scratching Underlying the club’s self-examination is the fact that the Swans are a distinctive club, with different needs to the majority of AFL clubs. Consider the following unique traits of the Swans: 1. They play in a market where the AFL is not followed so intensely, where it is entertainment more than a binding faith. Players in Randwick and Coogee are left alone and can (and do) have a drink without repercussions.



2. They have a more educated, affluent fan base, in inner Sydney and consequently have more female engagement and a more progressive social flavour (see Pride games). 3. Their AFLW team attracts more interest - crowds are exceptional - and is more central to the club than at many rivals. 4. They have made a virtue, and profited from their purported contrast with the NRL clubs, who are viewed as more old-world and scandal-prone. Emotions were high after Sydney’s stirring qualifying final win over eventual premiers Brisbane in September. AFL Photos via Getty Images To own a fan base that values women – and is less apt to accept the “boys will be boys” excuses – creates a higher demand for more respectful behaviours in that realm; at Sydney, there was immediate condemnation from a hefty section of members when the Pullman incident erupted.



The Sydney hierarchy thus will have to consider whether their men’s playing group is capable of meeting the club’s broader values, in which good citizenship - respectful treatment of women, avoidance of drugs and excessive alcohol consumption and associated anti-social behaviours - is elevated. Related Article AFL 2026 Surprise twist in legal move by dancers against Swans players caught in hotel saga Given that three of the Pullman five and Papley are/were among their most valuable and elite players (counting Nick Blakey), it’s reasonable to question whether there’s a gaping leadership deficit, outside of skipper Callum Mills, who rose to the moment post-Pullman and whose season-long absence due to injury will be a major challenge. Sydney doesn’t need to repair what happens in those two and half crowded hours each week during the AFL season. As with the West Coast Eagles of 2007-08, whose issues (drugs mainly) were far more serious, as Dean Cox would know, and were willing to sacrifice a ladder position in the short-term and some of whom suffered long-term fallout, the change the Swans desire won’t be measured in wins and losses. World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland Police People ‘need to be held accountable’ for police station debacle: minister William Davis November 6, 2026 — 4:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The state’s police minister says he hopes people will be held accountable for “possibly the worst deal for taxpayers in the history of Queensland”. In 2023 the Queensland Police Service committed to about $116 million in lease costs over 15 years – or more than $500,000 a month – for 433 Logan Road in Stones Corner, which it later found was unfit for purpose as a station and never occupied. A Crime and Corruption Commission investigation released on Thursday found a superintendent without significant commercial property experience led negotiations for the exorbitant lease, when the building would have been significantly cheaper to buy outright. The lease for the Stones Corner building was signed without funding allocated for the deal. Nine News It also said QPS had not secured funding for the building before the contract was signed.



The investigation did not make findings of corruption, but identified significant governance and control weaknesses that led to the high-profile bungled agreement. Police Minister Dan Purdie spoke to reporters on Friday morning about the report, framing it as the responsibility of the former Labor government and now-opposition leader Steven Miles. Police Minister Dan Purdie. Catherine Strohfeldt “We now know that is the worst deal in Queensland Police history, possibly the worst deal for taxpayers in the history of Queensland,” he said. Purdie added: “Queenslanders are left with this bill. Labor … need to own it now, and I still think people need to be held accountable.”



The minister confirmed the government was exploring possible options to get out of the lease legally. Related Article Queensland Police Police paying more to rent empty building than cost to buy it: watchdog Acting police commissioner Brett Pointing spoke to reporters on Thursday afternoon, apologising for the failure and saying the QPS would accept all recommendations from the CCC. “I think there are two groups of people that I’d like to apologise to,” he said. “One is the Queensland community. This is a large waste of taxpayers’ money.



“[The other is] the men and women of the QPS. That’s a significant amount of money that I’d rather be spending on keeping the community safe.” He did not reveal how a superintendent ended up negotiating the deal, and declined to say if heads would roll over the scandal. World.title: Australian Open to begin a day earlier in 2027 – just don’t expect tournament tennis
World.content:
NationalVictoriaAustralian Open Australian Open to begin a day earlier in 2027 – just don’t expect tournament tennis Brielle Kohlbeck November 6, 2026 — 4:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The gates to Melbourne Park will open a day earlier in 2027 – but there will be no Open tournament tennis played. Tennis Australia is badging Saturday, January 10 Kids Tennis Day. Children and families will be encouraged to visit the precinct to watch training and practice matches and pick up a racquet – and, Tennis Australia hopes, buy food, drink and merch. Lleyton Hewitt at the launch of Kids Tennis Day. Zoey Duchene Tennis Australia chief executive Andrew Abdo made the announcement at Melbourne Park, joined by tennis legend Lleyton Hewitt and, mysteriously, a koala and a kangaroo to go with the “Australian-inspired” theme for the 2027 tournament. “It’s an engine that can be used to reinvest back into the sport,” Abdo said. “Having a focus on a dedicated day for kids is symbolically important, but it’s also an opportunity where we might discover the next superhero, and that’s exciting for us.”



Lleyton Hewitt (left), Andrew Abdo and a wildlife carer brought a koala and a kangaroo to Kia Arena. Zoey Duchene The schedule change follows this year’s shift of the Australian Open, which ran from January 12 to February 1 instead of finishing on the Australia Day weekend in late January, as it has in the past. Abdo took over as Tennis Australia chief executive in August after leaving the NRL. This is one of his first major announcements since he got into hot water for getting a player’s name wrong at his first Australian Open launch. Tennis Australia could not give an exact cost for the extra day, but Abdo said it wouldn’t be possible without sponsorship. “There definitely is an investment into it, and it’s an investment we’re happy to make,” Abdo said.



The Australian Open is among the biggest economic drivers in Australian sport. This year’s tournament was estimated to have pumped more than $600 million into the Melbourne economy, according to NAB analysis, a rise of 7 to 10 per cent from 2025. Related Article Australian Open A translucent, climate-controlled dome over Melbourne Park? Tiley’s radical plan to reshape the Australian Open Revenue from the Open has steadily increased since 2010, apart from a three-year slump after COVID. But taxpayers have also helped foot the bill. More than a billion dollars has been spent on upgrading Melbourne Park since 2011, and an agreement between Tennis Australia and the Victorian government keeps the tournament in Melbourne until at least 2046. Growth is also not limited to revenue. Melbourne Park’s annual report shows media reach is vast and still expanding. More than 13 million viewers tuned in to Nine’s coverage in 2025, up from about 12.8 million the year before, while content on the Open’s channels generated 45 million engagements across 7000 posts. (Nine is the owner of this masthead.) Hewitt also supported the push to get more children involved in the sport, saying it was the best way to produce more top-level players like himself and Alex de Minaur.



“We’ve got to work through the pathway, obviously,” Hewitt said. “We’ve got to try and become a real high-performance group ... and try and transition the best kids through.” Hewitt reflected on his 2005 final and the “wave of excitement” from the Australian public, and said he remembered experiencing Kids Tennis Day himself and playing games in Rod Laver Arena. “The more that we can get out there and host Kids Day, put on a good spectacle that people want to be involved with and come out to, I think it helps the sport in Australia,” Hewitt said. Abdo said the 2027 Open was already shaping up to be a strong one. “We are ahead on ticket sales, which is terrific,” he said. “We’ve got more interstate, more international visitors than we’ve had before, which is terrific. All signs are leading to another well-attended event.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Failed legal battle to retain independence costs cash-strapped ATC $4.1m
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Failed legal battle to retain independence costs cash-strapped ATC $4.1m Craig Kerry November 6, 2026 — 4:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The merits of the Australian Turf Club board’s failed battle to retain its independence can now be weighed against a $4.1 million cost after the release of the cash-strapped organisation’s annual report. The ATC, which operates Sydney’s four metropolitan thoroughbred racetracks and owns all of them except Royal Randwick, lost $4.8 million in the 2025-26 financial year, up from $2.6 million in 2024-25. The Australian Turf Club operates the Randwick, Rosehill, Canterbury and Warwick Farm race tracks, and owns all except Randwick. Getty Images However, the deficit for last year would have been about $700,000 if not for the board’s legal costs from its fight to prevent regulator Racing NSW appointing an administrator over concerns about the club’s financial position, which included a $30 million bank loan, and corporate governance. That battle started when Racing NSW issued a show cause notice in September last year, following the sacking of ATC chief executive Matt Galanos and resignation of directors Ben Bayot and Natalie Hewson, and ended in June when the regulator won a NSW Supreme Court appeal to appoint Morgan Kelly as administrator.



The ruling included an order for the ATC to pay the legal costs of Racing NSW, which this week reported an operating surplus of $13.63 million in 2025-26, up from $12.96 million the previous year. Kelly’s review of the ATC started as a consultant in April, under an agreement with Racing NSW to resume its additional funding of the club, and he took over as administrator on July 8, effectively replacing the board. Chairman Tim Hale, vice-chair Caroline Searcy and newest board addition Bernie Brookes became part of advisory subcommittee with Racing NSW directors Simon Tuxen and Michael Crismale. ATC chairman Tim Hale. Steven Siewert Kelly noted in the annual report that the club’s revenue of $379 million was up on 2024-25’s $373.4

million and losses were down without the one-off legal costs, but there was work to do. “While the club’s underlying assets and operations remain strong, the continued loss-making performance highlights the need to strengthen financial and commercial discipline across the organisation,” Kelly wrote.



“Our review to date has identified opportunities to enhance commercial performance, improve operational efficiency and strengthen governance. In a number of areas, costs have increased over time and opportunities to maximise revenue have not been fully realised.” Related Article Horse racing Racing NSW appoints administrator, advisory panel at cash-strapped ATC Sources who spoke on the condition of anonymity have told this masthead the operational efficiencies have not included forced job cuts, but the club has reduced its staff slightly through natural attrition, although roles attached to horse welfare or safety have been untouched. An ongoing court case regarding alleged thefts of cash from raceday safes has not impacted the club, which is insured for those losses. A positive for the club in this year’s report was the absence of an auditor’s notice of concern, present in the previous year’s report, over the ATC’s financial viability.



Members will have the chance to address the club’s situation at the annual general meeting at Royal Randwick on November 26. The ATC board initially succeeded in blocking Racing NSW’s move to appoint Kelly in December before winning again in March when NSW Supreme Court Justice Francois Kunc ruled that the regulator’s move was not authorised under the Thoroughbred Racing Act. However, Racing NSW’s appeal was upheld when the panel found the club’s finances and corporate governance were within the definition of horse racing under the Act.

World.title: Army members who allegedly gang raped Sydney teen granted bail to live on barracks
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWCrime Army members who allegedly gang raped Sydney teen granted bail to live on barracks Amber Schultz and Jack Gramenz Updated November 6, 2026 — 4:09pm ,first published November 6, 2026 — 8:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Two serving army members who allegedly held down, choked and gang raped a teenager in her Sydney inner-west home have been granted bail to live at the Holsworthy military barracks. Combat engineer Kayden Phillips, 20, and marine specialist Harrison Massie Knight, 22, appeared in Liverpool Local Court on Friday and face life in prison over the alleged assault. The accused are based at Holsworthy barracks in Sydney’s south-west. AAPIMAGE The pair met the 18-year-old woman on Saturday and were captured on CCTV entering her Camperdown apartment. The prosecution argued there was a “degree of planning” in the alleged attack, with the men taking off their shirts when the alleged victim went to her room. One allegedly restrained her, and she was choked to the point of unconsciousness, then raped, the court heard. The woman then managed to “flee” the apartment, the court heard, reported to police and underwent a Sexual Assault Forensic Exam, with DNA testing underway.



When Knight and Phillips were captured leaving the apartment some time later, one of the men was missing his shirt and his belt. The court heard that when confronted by a witness’s partner, the two men initially denied being in the apartment, before denying anything sexual happened. The pair, who are in the same army troop, were arrested at the Holsworthy military barracks in south-west Sydney on Thursday morning. Police seized phones and clothing from their two rooms. DNA testing is underway. ‘[The woman] fled the scene worried about her safety.’ Judge Andrew Miller The men were both charged with aggravated sexual assault in company depriving liberty, aggravated sexual touching of another person and choking a person with intent to commit an indictable offence. The incident is still under investigation, and police may bring more charges.



In applying for bail on Friday, defence lawyer Tandy Machisa conceded the prosecution’s case was strong, but questioned whether the woman’s conduct before fleeing the scene “raised questions” about her account. Judge Andrew Miller dismissed this line of argument. “She fled the scene worried about her safety,” he said, highlighting the Criminal Procedure Act gave directions about drawing conclusions around delays in reporting sexual assault. Machisa argued both of the accused had strong family support, strong ties to their community, no criminal history, and strong employment. A file photo of a training exercise at Holsworthy army base, Sydney. Kate Geraghty She said Knight, who the court heard was the “more serious” offender of the pair, recently achieved the rank of Lance Corporal.



“To achieve this rank shows a level of compliance, respect and authority,” she said. The prosecution argued the alleged facts of the case were strong, and the pair presented an unacceptable risk to the community. They face a non-parole period of 15 years. Miller found that confining the pair to the barracks would mitigate bail risks. The pair cannot leave the barracks unless under the supervision of their commanding officer, and only for military, medical, court or legal appointments. The pair are not to contact the complainant, witnesses or be in contact with one another. The prosecution is contesting their bail. The pair will remain in custody until the bail review is heard in a higher court in the coming days.



They were supported in court by their parents, with Knight’s family travelling from Melbourne overnight. Their matter will next be heard on January 14. A Defence spokesperson said that, as the matter is under an NSW Police investigation and before the courts, it would be inappropriate to comment. “There is no place for sexual violence or misconduct in Defence,” the spokesperson said. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. World.title: Babies made a comeback – but that was before the latest rate rises
World.content:
PoliticsFederalBabies Babies made a comeback – but that was before the latest rate rises Matt Wade and Shane Wright Updated November 6, 2026 — 3:52pm ,first published 3:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

High inflation and the Reserve Bank’s steep interest rate hikes could halt a small baby bounce with new figures showing a turnaround in Australia’s fertility rate that is being driven by women in regional parts of the country. Figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics, released on Friday, showed there were 299,903 births registered in 2025, a 2.6 per cent lift on the previous year and the biggest one-year increase since the post-Covid baby boom. Loading The increase arrested a long-term fall in the fertility rate which lifted marginally to 1.497 after dropping to a record low in 2024. A fertility rate of 2.1 is needed to naturally replace a nation’s population. It is the third consecutive year that it has been below 1.5. The fertility rate fell in every capital city bar Hobart, with the biggest declines in Perth, Brisbane and Adelaide which all recorded sharp increases in home prices through 2025. The lowest capital city fertility rate is in Canberra at just 1.29.





In the City of Melbourne the fertility rate was just 0.5, the lowest of any local government area in the nation. Other Melbourne LGAs with very low fertility rates were Yarra (0.79), Port Phillip (0.81) and Stonnington (0.81). But cheaper regional areas have much higher fertility rates with some areas actually going through a modest baby boom. In regional NSW the number of births jumped by 8 per cent in 2025 and the fertility rate was a relatively healthy 1.87. The fertility rate in regional Victoria was 1.91. Across regional Victoria, councils such as Swan Hill, Southern Grampians, Moyne and Moira have fertility rates above 2.1 which held steady or improved through 2025. In NSW, centres such as Cowra, Dubbo, Griffith and Yass also held fertility rates above replacement level.



KPMG urban economist Terry Rawnsley attributed Australia’s modest “baby bounce” in 2025 to improvements in the economic circumstances of families in that period. “There was a bit of an improvement in cost of living pressures at the back end of 2023 and in 2024…and interest rates were kind of softening a bit at that time, so people had the confidence to press go on the family and we’ve seen that baby bounce come through in 2025,” he said. “It shows a clear pattern between households’ disposable income and their propensity to have children.” But that could come to an end.



Inflation has climbed to 4.3 per cent, in part due to high oil prices, prompting the Reserve Bank to lift official rates five times this year. On a $600,000 mortgage, the rate rises will add about $500 to monthly repayments while higher petrol prices are costing households around $100 a month more. Rawnsley said rising cost of living pressures this year would likely put downward pressure on birth numbers. “Crystal balling for the next year’s numbers, we’ll probably see another dip as people feel squeezed by cost of living,” he said. Related Article Australian economy What is a recession and are we in one? A bluffer’s guide Rawnsley said the national fertility rate has now hovered around the 1.5 mark for the past three years.



“The fertility rate seems to have found a bit of a floor in the past few years but there’s no clear factor that might drive it back-up again towards the levels around 1.7 we had pre-COVID,” he said. “There’s no big policy lever or change pointing to a turning around.” The fertility slump is not unique to Australia – many nations in Europe and parts of Asia have had far steeper declines, triggering warnings of a “demographic winter” in some. Opposition leader Angus Taylor, a father of four, said a lift in hope could help boost the chances of more children. “For young Australians to want to have a family, they’ve got to have hope. They’ve got to believe that the economy gives them opportunities,” he said. The ABS figures showed fertility among young women continues to fall, hitting record lows among teenagers and those aged between 20 and 24. The lift in 2025 fertility rates was driven by women aged between 25 and 39. There were 4148 births of twins and 46 triplets or more, in line with previous years.

World.title: ‘Heartbreaking’: Holocaust survivor shot in Bondi terror attack dies in hospital
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWBondi shooting ‘Heartbreaking’: Holocaust survivor shot in Bondi terror attack dies in hospital Daniel Lo Surdo and Jack Gramenz Updated November 6, 2026 — 3:48pm ,first published 2:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Eva Geller, 90, survived the Holocaust. A 90-year-old Holocaust survivor who settled in Sydney’s eastern suburbs after fleeing from Europe has died in Prince of Wales Hospital following complications stemming from injuries suffered in the December 14 terrorist attack. Eva Geller, a great-grandmother who fled Romania with her mother and grandmother as a child, died on Thursday night, almost 11 months after she was hit by gunfire in the attack that targeted Jewish Australians celebrating Hanukkah at Bondi Beach. Geller was told by doctors she would never walk again after suffering multiple gunshot wounds in the attack, in which 15 victims died. She had been in and out of hospital since December, but remained active in the Jewish community, attending services as late as September, moving with a walking stick.



Geller raised a family with her husband, David, an Auschwitz survivor, in Sydney’s eastern suburbs. She attended Nefesh Synagogue in Bondi, where Rabbi Aron Moss became accustomed to her “very warm” character. “She was a child in the Holocaust years, she escaped but she lost a lot of family. She lost her husband at quite an early age but, despite all that, she maintained a real positivity and happiness and a zest for life that was there right up until the end,” Moss said. “This is just another big, massive loss.” Rabbi Aron Moss AAPIMAGE A large crowd is expected at her funeral on Monday, a source said. Premier Chris Minns described her death as “heartbreaking”. “My thoughts are with Eva’s family and the Jewish community as they face another painful loss,” he said. “Almost a year on, we’re still living with the pain and aftershock of that evil act.”



Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Geller’s death highlighted the continued devastation Australians confront in the months since the Bondi attack. “Eva should have been able to celebrate Chanukah in peace and safety and instead, her life was changed forever by an act of terror and antisemitism,” he said. “We are wrapping our arms around Eva’s family, friends and the Jewish community at this very sad time.” NSW Police are working with the coroner to establish the cause of Geller’s death, and if it may lead to further charges against Naveed Akram, the surviving alleged gunman behind the attack. His father, Sajid, died in the attack following a shoot-out with police. Get alerts on breaking news as it happens.

World.title: ‘Taken its toll’: First-term Liberal MP in shock departure
World.content:
Updated PoliticsNSWNSW State Parliament ‘Taken its toll’: First-term Liberal MP in shock departure Jessica McSweeney Updated November 6, 2026 — 3:44pm ,first published 2:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

First-term Liberal MP Jordan Lane has shocked colleagues by announcing he will quit state politics at the March election, saying his time representing Ryde had taken a toll as he joins the exodus from the NSW opposition ranks. Lane’s extraordinary departure after just one term will likely decimate Liberal chances of holding on to the seat, which the 32-year-old won on a margin of just 54 votes. Jordan Lane will quit state politics after just one term as member for Ryde. Janie Barrett He is the seventh Liberal MP to announce they will quit politics at the state election, leaving Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane to fight for the premiership with about a third of her lower house colleagues jumping ship. “Hey Ryde, it’s not you, it’s me,” Lane said in a social media video.



Lane, who is one of the youngest parliamentarians in Macquarie Street, said he had spent most of his adult life representing Ryde, including as mayor before he became the state MP. “That kind of time takes a toll and I’ve made a really difficult decision to step away from politics for a while,” he said. Senior Liberal sources not authorised to speak publicly said the party had already been panicked about their chance in Ryde, where a split of the conservative vote thanks to One Nation could hand Labor the seat. The party’s chief advantage in the seat, Lane’s incumbency, has now been taken away. Sloane said in a statement: “On behalf of the NSW Liberal Party, I thank Jordan for his service to the NSW Parliament, the Liberal Party and, most importantly, the people of Ryde.



“I have no doubt that we have not seen the last of Jordan in public life and wish him and his family all the best for the future.” Editor's pick Exclusive

NSW Votes Labor warns MPs party could lose a dozen seats at March election In his announcement video Lane said he believed Ryde Councillor and operator of the popular Humans of Eastwood meme page, Justin Li, should be the next Liberal member for Ryde. Li has not been officially selected as the Liberal candidate. Lane said this was not how he expected his time in politics to end, but “sometimes you just know in your heart when something is the right decision”. Liberal sources have expressed dismay that MPs were leaving it so late to announce their departure.



Earlier this week Mark Coure, who holds one of Sydney’s most marginal seats in Oatley, also announced he would retire from state politics at the March election. Coure is one of the Liberal Party’s key moderates and a senior member of shadow cabinet, who since 2011 has successfully withstood campaigns from Labor to take his marginal electorate. His decision came after being endorsed as the Liberal candidate in Oatley, leaving party headquarters to hunt for a new candidate. Senior frontbenchers Alister Henskens and James Griffin, and long-serving MPs Ray Williams, Tanya Davies and Mark Taylor have all announced they will depart at the election. World.title: Lightning strikes cause fires in Auckland during severe storm, rain passes over Far North
World.content:
Lightning strikes caused three fires in Auckland Friday afternoon, as violent thunderstorms moved across the region.

A red alert went out for Kaipara, Auckland City, Waitākere, Franklin, Rodney and Albany about 3pm and lifted just after 4pm but a thunderstorm watch remains in place.

MetService said 1170 lightning strikes were detected today before 5.30pm, including 280 over Auckland.

Fire and Emergency shift manager Colin Underdown said fire crews responded to about 30 jobs, including lightning-related blazes in Westhaven, Westmere and Albany.

Voting booths at the PAK'nSAVE Māngere supermarket carpark and at Old Flat Bush School Hall in Takanini closed early because of the weather.

There were also a small number of properties affected by surface flooding.

Lines company Vector reported a handful of power outages, mainly in the north and west of the region.

Delays and cancelations on the east-west and Onehunga-west rail lines from a storm-related power outage between Sunnyvale and Mangawhau was likely to cause further travel disruption.

The barrier arms at Rossgrove Terrace level crossing were down after a power cut caused a signaling fault.

An Auckland Airport spokesperson says a lightning alert was in place for around 20 minutes this afternoon, which meant a small number of aircraft were unable to refuel, in line with standard safety procedures.

There were no resulting impacts to flight schedules, they say.

Metservice has now cancelled the severe weather warning for the Auckland region though a thunderstorm watch remains in place until 11am Saturday.

Heavy rain in Northland

A band of heavy rain passing over the top of the Far North has so far caused no significant flooding, Kaitāia's fire chief says.

In fact, Craig Rogers said every farmer in the district and every homeowner relying on rainwater tanks would be delighted with the downpour after an unusually dry spring so far.

"We've had a good bit of warm rain, with thunder mixed in. It's not enough but the farmers will be happy."

Rogers said the rain peaked around 1pm and had now eased to showers.

The rain was light enough now that he was able to go back to his golf after taking shelter at the proverbial 19th hole.

"We just sat it out," he said.

Around 2pm the MetService rain radar showed the band of heavy rain making its way south over Northland with particularly intense falls over Doubtless Bay, inland from the Bay of Islands and over the Kaipara Harbour.

A severe thunderstorm watch is in place for all of Northland and Auckland until 9pm Friday, and again from midnight until 11am on Saturday.

Saturday's severe thunderstorm watch also applies to Aotea-Great Barrier Island, Coromandel Peninsula, Waikato, Waitomo, Taumarunui, Bay of Plenty, Rotorua, Taupō and Taranaki.

Northland Regional Council rainfall data shows the heaviest rain so far, 30mm per hour, was recorded near Pawarenga in North Hokianga in the hour to 1pm.

Further south, Hakaru, near Kaiwaka, and the often dry Pouto Peninsula, both in the Kaipara District, were also experiencing heavy rain.

Regional council records show the last significant rain in the Kaitāia area was in mid-September.

World.title: 'I want this for other people': Survivor calls for expanded breast cancer drug funding after study shows reduction in deaths
World.content:
Audio player for " Calls for expanded breast cancer drug funding " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/health/2388966%2Fi-want-this-for-other-people-survivor-calls-for-expanded-breast-cancer-drug-funding-after-study-shows-reduction-in-deaths

Calls for expanded breast cancer drug funding Nine To Noon Download MP3 12m

A breast cancer drug funded for some New Zealanders with advanced breast cancer could help those with an early-stage of the disease live longer, a study has found.

The large international study, funded by Novartis, the manufacturer of the drug Ribociclib also known as Kisqali, indicated the treatment in combination with hormone therapy reduced the risk of death by 19 percent compared with hormone therapy alone.

It also suggested the risk of the disease returning reduced by 26 percent.

The Breast Cancer Aotearoa Coalition said about 900 more patients with earlier-stage disease could benefit from the treatment if funding was expanded.

Psychiatrist Jo Pendergast, who was diagnosed with Hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer in 2021, told Nine to Noon, more access to the treatment in New Zealand could help a lot of people - even if it was too late for her.

Pendergast said Hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer made up about 70 percent of breast cancers and when hers was discovered it had already spread to a lymph node.

While she had now completed treatment, she said she was at higher risk of it coming back.

"It's difficult because everyone says 'oh it's amazing you made it to five years you must be so relived', but with hormone positive breast cancer the risk keeps going."

Pendergast said she was on hormone blockers now and would probably stay on them for up to 10 years to try and stop the cancer coming back.

She said in New Zealand hormone blockers were the only thing she could have, but if she lived in Australia and was diagnosed now she would be on a CDK inhibitor which would reduce her risk of the cancer coming back by about another 30 percent.

"It would reduce that recurrence anxiety hugely to know I was doing everything I could."

Pendergast said she was in a group of doctors with breast cancer and there were some considering moving to Australia with their families just so they could get the treatment.

"It would make a huge difference to have access for early breast cancer, while it's too late for me now, being five years down the track, I really want this for other people."

Breast Cancer Aotearoa Coalition chairperson Libby Burgess, told Nine to Noon, New Zealand needed these medicines to be rolled out more widely to treat people with early breast cancer to give them the best chance of curing the disease and not having it return as advanced cancer.

She said in New Zealand it was only funded for those with the advanced stage of the disease while that was not the case in other countries including the United Kingdom and Australia.

"It's great that they're available if you have an advanced disease but we need to offer them in earlier disease."

She said the budget needed to be found to pay for it.

World.title: 'A life sentence with no possibility of parole': Kyle Whorrall's mum on grief of losing son
World.content:
The mother of an American PhD student who was killed by a group of teenagers with a machete says while they will one day be able to move on with their lives, her family has a life sentence.

A jury at the High Court in Auckland last night found the teenagers guilty of aggravated robbery and the manslaughter of Kyle Whorrall.

Carole Whorrall said she was relieved at the verdicts.

Kyle Whorrall Supplied

"Kyle was a brilliant young American with a bright future, who came to New Zealand to chase his passion as an entomologist studying local beetles.

"Already holding two degrees and working hard on his PhD, he was a beloved son, brother, nephew, cousin, colleague, and friend. He came here to make a real difference in the world, not to become a statistic, and our focus is entirely on honoring his amazing life."

Whorrall said while the justice system moved its focus to sentencing, her family faced a tough future.

Carole Whorrall plants a pohutukawa tree in memory of Kyle in 2025. RNZ/Marika Khabazi

"The people who did this will eventually move on from their legal troubles, but for us, the grief of losing Kyle is a life sentence with no possibility of parole."

She paid tribute to her son's friends and flatmates who sat beside her through out the High Court trial.

World.title: NZ stocks hold up well in face of big Wall Street sell-off
World.content:
The sharp fall in tech stocks on Wall Street has so far not flowed through in a big way to the New Zealand market.

The Nasdaq fell more than 5.5 percent in trading on Friday on fears that the Democratic wins in the midterm elections might lead to greater regulation of data centres and AI technology.

The NZX is not heavily exposed to tech stocks and, in afternoon trading, was down just over 0.7 percent at 13,988.

On Thursday, the NZX hit a record high of 14,090.

New Zealand's market can follow the lead of Wall Street when it comes to sentiment, although there is more of a correlation with the Dow Jones index and its more traditional range of companies.

The Dow Jones also fell more than 3 percent in trading on Wall Street.

The Australian market has also fared relatively well after the sell-off on Wall Street and the ASX was down just under 1 percent.

Japan's Nikkei index, however, was down about 5 percent, while the volatile South Korean Kospi was also down more than 4 percent.

Both markets have large exposure to tech stocks and computer chips.

The Nasdaq fall put it into correction territory, which means it has fallen 10 percent since its highs last month.

Many of the world's big tech names fell heavily, including chip maker Nvidia, which was down 9.3 percent.

World.title: How exposed is your KiwiSaver to market wobbles?
World.content:
The effects of falling US technology stocks on your KiwiSaver balance will depend largely on the type of fund you are in.

Stocks dropped sharply on Thursday, US time. Media reports blamed the victory of anti-AI candidates in the US midterms, on top of existing fears about how sustainable technology companies' share prices are.

A small number of technology companies' share market returns have risen recently, such as Nvidia, which has increased in price by more than 500 percent over five years, and Apple, which is up 127 percent over five years.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq index dropped 6.3 percent on Thursday, cutting more than US$2 trillion in market value.

The S&P500 also had its worst day since the introduction of US President Donald Trump's tariffs last year.

In New Zealand, KiwiSaver investors in growth and high-growth funds generally tend to have the most exposure to share markets. How much exposure they have to technology stocks within that depends on the approach of managers.

Audio player for " What will cost me more, cooling my house down or heating it up? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/personal-finance/2388401%2Fhow-exposed-is-your-kiwisaver-to-market-wobbles

What will cost me more, cooling my house down or heating it up? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 11m

Passive funds tend to track indices. As technology stocks have become larger parts of those indices, they will have been added to KiwiSaver funds in larger allocations. Active managers decide what they believe is appropriate. Milford, for example, has limited its exposure to technology stocks through its active growth fund because of its concerns about the risk.

An analysis of the top 10 holdings of high growth KiwiSaver funds, as reported by Sorted's Smart Investor tool, shows variation in how much of investors' money was in tech companies.

Milford's aggressive fund had 26 percent in companies including Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Broadcom and Micron. Generate's focused growth fund had 22.5 percent. Quay Street's High Growth had 21.6 percent and Kernel's 20.16 percent.

While Milford has been cautious with its active growth fund, its aggressive fund was 5.4 percent invested in Microsoft, 4.56 percent in Nvidia and 4 percent Amazon.

Pathfinder's High Growth had17.5 percent tech exposure and Simplicity's high growth 19.4 percent.

The best performing of those funds over the past year has been Koura' Strategic High Growth fund, which founder Rupert Carlyon credited to being invested offshore.

Kernel founder Dean Anderson said the latest drop was just part of the unpredictability of the market.

Kernel founder Dean Anderson. Supplied / Kernel

"The market is just being volatile at the moment on the back of trying to digest a lot of uncertainty and everyone is ultimately speculating on what moves a democratic House and Senate may make. So we actually have no visibility or clarity.

"These swings in the market are pure speculation as to what may come down the line. It's a great reminder for investors not to be trying to play that game. Overall, I think this is a real positive. I think actually it's kind of healthy to kind of just reset expectations and to dampen some of the euphoric sort of activity that was going on, not only with enlisted markets, but also what we've seen with, you know, some of the smaller AI-related companies in terms of the neocloud data centres."

He said a fall in share prices could help ensure businesses were operating with a focus on sustainability and quality.

"Thinking about our high growth…we've got a reasonable allocation on high growth, about 10 percent, to global infrastructure and global property. Both of those are actually up 7 percent in the past month. So that's actually a great reminder about why being diversified and not just say buying US only and actually having some of these more boring allocations helps in periods like this."

There has been significant dispersion in returns this year as those that have rode the technology wave have experienced much better results than those who hung back.

While those with more exposure may experience more losses, they would have to drop significantly to undo the returns banked so far.

"If we still keep an eye on what's coming down the line, a lot of these companies are still demonstrating and delivering strong earnings growth," Anderson said.

"And there's still a lot of potential for AI, right? And so I wouldn't be extrapolating the sort of sell-off as interpreting this as that's the end of AI, or that's the end of chemical growth stocks over the next five years."

World.title: Former England international Hughes to debut for Fiji in France test
World.content:
Former England international Nathan Hughes will make his return to international rugby in Fiji's Nations Championship clash against France in Lyon on Sunday morning.

New head coach Jake White has named the giant Racing club player in France's Top 14 competition in the starting lineup.

The 35-year-old Fiji-born number eight, who earned 22 caps for England between 2016 and 2019, is eligible to represent Fiji under revised World Rugby Regulation 8.

That allows players to switch international allegiance after a three-year stand-down period, provided they meet the birthright eligibility requirements.

Jake, who coached the Springboks to their Rugby World Cup win in 2007, said Hughes will complement their style of play.

"I think Nathan has done really well for Racing," he said.

"The talk here in France is that he's obviously played really well, and when he has played, you know, he's carried well.

"I think one thing that just from my experience, when you've had big number eights, all the number eights who played in World Cups have had that kind of similar skill set, and so I'm quite keen to see Nathan.

"I know it's his first cap for Fiji, but he has played for England and he has played Test rugby as well, so I think he'll he'll be fine. I think he'll fit in nicely. He complements the rest of the team."

Flyhalf selection

White has also made two other interesting selections in his starting lineup.

Young Isikeli Rabitu has been named at flyhalf ahead of Isaiah Washington-Ravula and Caleb Muntz, the regulars in the number 10.

In midfield White has gone for Vinaya Habosi at 12 and Iosefo Masi at 13.

White said the selections gives him and the team the chance to see new combinations and test them out.

"We are very fortunate in Fiji we got lots and lots of backline players," he told the media on Friday morning.

"I mean, I've given them this opportunity now, with some players being unavailable.

"They've got Habosi and Masi together and I'd like to see what they do together as a combination.

"I think also from a 10 point of view, if you look at Rabitu, I mean, he has played 10 before, and he's played 10 at school and he was a sevens player, so I mean, he understands space and time.

"I'd like to see just a different combination at 10."

White has been impressed with the players in his three weeks as coach and believes the team named will give France a good go this weekend.

"I'm blown away," he said of the talent in the team.

"I've coached many many good players in my time, and there's no reason why these Fijian players should take a step back.

"I mean, they're very talented. They've been together for a short space of time, but you know the energy they give, the ability to learn, the enthusiasm they show.

"I mean, I can't fault any of that, and that's why I think everyone, even in the group, are looking forward to Saturday night."

'A very different team'

White said the players know they have not reached the level they want to be playing at.

But he reckons things will be on the up, with the current squad in France made up of more Europe-based players, compared to the team that beat Japan in Tokyo two weeks ago.

"The team has been working hard, they get on well, they're spending a lot of time together, they're getting to know each other, they're getting to know the coaches, they're getting to understand the way we want to play, and yeah, I mean it is a very different team," White told the media.

"I really enjoyed the team that we took to Japan, but you can imagine this is a much bigger group physically, it's a much more experienced group because a lot of these guys have played overseas, and they've played against some of the best teams in the world.

"And as I look across here, a lot of these boys play in France as well. So, they know the opposition that they're playing against. They've played against them for their clubs and I know that if we just play as well as we can, that we can really make it difficult for France."

The Fiji vs France battle will kick off at 9am on Sunday NZT.

World.title: Mayors fear crumbling bridges could leave rural families stranded
World.content:
Councils fear hundreds of crumbling bridges around the country may leave rural families and businesses stranded, unless the NZ Transport Agency commits to helping fund replacements.

The Lower Kohuratahi Road Bridge in East Taranaki and Lower Valley Bridge in South Wairarapa are just two structures operating under weight restrictions, after recent surveys found they were beginning to fail.

Stratford District Council is responsible for about 150 bridges, some of which service just one or two properties at the end of rural roads.

Built in 1938, the historic Lower Kohuratahi Bridge is a 50-metre-long wooden suspension bridge. It was closed in September, after engineers found it at risk of structural failure.

Mayor Neil Volzke said its problems were symptomatic of a wider problem.

Audio player for " Councils fear crumbling bridges could leave people stranded " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/business/2388172%2Fmayors-fear-crumbling-bridges-could-leave-rural-families-stranded

Councils fear crumbling bridges could leave people stranded Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

"Across our district and across many rural districts in New Zealand, there are lots of bridges that are in that 100-year-old age bracket and some of them older. A lot of them are falling due for replacement."

One family lives beyond the Lower Kohuratahi Bridge and beekeepers use it for access to their hives. It had since been re-opened with a 400kg weight limit.

Volzke feared NZTA wouldn't contribute to a replacement likely to cost about $1 million.

"Normally, a bridge replacement would attract some subsidy or funding from NZTA, but they do have the ability to declare a bridge as uneconomic, in which case they can withdraw any funding that might have been there.

"If that happens, then of course the cost of replacement, if we choose to go ahead, falls entirely on the council."

South Wairarapa Mayor Fran Wilde. Getty Images / Hagen Hopkins

At the recent Local Government NZ conference, Stratford had a remit adopted, calling for NZTA to commit to co-funding uneconomic infrastructure, or for government to provide clearer guidance about downgrading or ceasing to service low-traffic areas.

South Wairarapa Mayor Fran Wilde was familiar with the looming problem.

"We've got about 140-odd bridges and large culverts, and frankly, we can't afford the maintenance on these.

"Some of them are significant in terms of getting heavy traffic in and out of the district, but some of the bridges might only go to one or two farms."

Wilde said issues had recently been identified with the about 100-year-old Lower Valley Bridge on Kahutrara Road, which was often used as a detour, when State Highway 53 floods.

"What has happened in the past is that, when the Waihenga Bridge has been closed, the traffic has been diverted through the Lower Valley Bridge, which is a little further away and a smaller bridge.

"We are now having all our bridges surveyed and we've just had a review of that [the Lower Valley Bridge]. They have said, 'Oops, it can't stand up to the heavy traffic it's getting', and we're having to now close it to some heavy traffic."

Now, every time the Waihenga Bridge is closed, the Lower Valley Bridge is also shut.

An engineer's report has suggested a range of options for the Lower Valley Bridge, from a band-aid repair costing about $370,000 to full replacement at $20 million.

Wilde said South Wairarapa could not afford a new bridge without NZTA assistance.

The Transport Agency acknowledged the financial burden councils currently faced and said it worked closely with all local authorities to best share that load.

"We appreciate the difficulty in funding uneconomic transport infrastructure in rural areas and we're aware of the remit that has been presented to Local Government NZ."

NZTA said current funding was guided by the Government Policy Statement on land transport, which identified value for money as a strategic priority.

It also had an Uneconomic Transport Infrastructure Policy, which involved a series of steps to help determine whether or not a proposed investment was efficient, and to identify what other sources of funding might be available.

"If the decision is to decline funding out of the National Land Transport Fund, a council can consider other funding sources for uneconomic transport infrastructure."

The Transport Agency said it applied a Funding Assistance Rate for regular investment in transport activities of councils and other approved organisations.

FARs, which could be applied to regular maintenance of bridges for example, were set out every three years and averaged about 53 percent currently.

"Where transport infrastructure was damaged due to an emergency event [like storms and earthquakes], there was a higher level of assistance for emergency works [normal Funding Assistance Rate, plus 20 percent]."

The Land Transport Management Act did not require emergency response work to be efficient.

World.title: Customary landowners welcome Kaiteretere name change as part of Nelson Tenths' case
World.content:
The spelling of the name of one of the most popular beaches at the top of the South Island has been changed to reflect its origins.

The name Kaiteriteri has been revoked by the New Zealand Geographic Board and replaced with the spelling Kaiteretere.

The change was part of legislation giving effect to the 'Nelson Tenths' settlement.

The Te Here ā Nuku (Nelson Tenths) Bill, which was passed in August, settled a historic land dispute that will see 3068 hectares, including the Kaiteriteri Recreation Reserve and part of the Abel Tasman Great Walk, returned to the original owners and a $420 million compensation payment.

Te Here ā Nuku Trust trustee Kerensa Johnston said Kaiteretere's corrected spelling was recognition of the customary landowners' language and tikanga, and an important step in a broader resolution process with the Crown.

She said place name misspellings were reasonably common, often happened by accident and became embedded in official documentation.

"The spelling as it was with the 'i' is incorrect," she said. "That's not a word that exists and so the significance really is just the correct spelling, the correct word.

"Now it will be about understanding the narrative that's behind that place and that coastline as a whole."

Johnstone said Kaiteretere and the area now known as the Abel Tasman National Park had been well occupied by whānau and hapū for centuries, and held cultural, spiritual and physical significance for Māori.

Archaeological evidence suggests there has been Maori occupation and use of the coastline for at least 500 years.

"It was there in 1841 that we first met with the representatives of the New Zealand Company and essentially agreed to the settlement of the Nelson area," Johnston said. "That's really the genesis of the Nelson Tenths."

In the 1830s, the Crown promised Māori at the top of the South Island that, if they sold 151,100 acres of land to the New Zealand Company, they would be able to keep one-tenth.

In 1845, a Crown grant stated that a tenth of all land used for the Nelson settlement - plus pā, wāhi tapu, urupā and cultivations owned by the whānau and hapū - would be reserved in a trust for the customary owners, but they instead received fewer than 3000 acres, which became known as the Nelson Tenths Reserves.

The New Zealand Geographic archives records that the spelling Kaiteriteri has been used on government records since 1859. Other documented spellings by government surveyors include Kaiteratera and Kaitiriteri.

Alexander Wyclif Reed's 1952 book The Story of New Zealand Place Names offered a description of the name Kaiteretere as 'kai: to eat' and 'teretere: to run or be spread about'.

"Some Māori were having a meal on the beach of an island in the bay, when they heard stones rolling through the bush behind them," the archive said. "Fearing an attack, they left in their canoes carrying their food with them and, on reaching Kaiteriteri Beach, returned hurriedly to their pā, eating their food as they went."

Johnston said there were different narratives about the history and meaning of Kaiteretere, and the trust had plans to share the stories with the wider community.

"Kaiteretere is actually just one part of that," she said. "There are other names of significant sites along that coastline that we want to bring back to life, so that's all part of the work that's ahead of us."

Johnstone said the overall response to the change had been positive, with people wanting to use the correct spelling and understand the origin of the name, although there had been some concerns raised from a commercial perspective about the impact of changes to branding and signage.

Johnston said the trust believed the changes could happen over time.

"This is certainly the first step, and we'll be making those changes ourselves in relation to the land and the businesses that we're operating over the next year," she said.

World.title: Aussie Calleja ready for winner-takes-all world championship weekend
World.content:
The biggest weekend in karting is here, with nearly 200 drivers descending on south-east Italy for the FIA Karting World Championship.

This weekend's event is the grand final of international karting, with drivers from around the world qualifying throughout the year for a chance to become world champion.

The OK (Original Kart) and OK-Junior world championships will be decided this weekend at the World Circuit La Conca in Muro Leccese, Italy.

F1 records broken by Kimi Antonelli in 2026 Kimi Antonelli sets numerous benchmarks that are likely to stand for some time.

There will be three Australians among the 194 competitors set to enter this weekend's racing.

William Calleja, Jenson Burns and Chris Lowe will all compete in the OK class, while Australian-born female racer Ava Jean Lawrence is in the OK-Junior event.

Calleja enters this weekend's world championship with a genuine chance of winning after a terrific season in the European Karting Championship.

The teenager from Victoria finished fourth in the championship, dominating the final round of the season in Kristiansand, Sweden, where he was fastest in qualifying and went on to win the final.

"It's great to have an FIA win under my belt, and I go into this very important race with winning experience in my hands," the Victorian said.

"The level of competition is the highest in the world in this category of motorsport, so winning any race at this level is a high achievement. I'm feeling good and looking forward to showing my best at La Conca."

The weekend's racing begins on Friday. Drivers go through qualifying sessions and heats in a bid to make it to Sunday's final race, which decides the world champion.

"It's a very mentally challenging race, and it will require proper preparation," Calleja said.

"I need to block out external noise and keep my eyes on the job ahead of me, not focusing too much on the end result but performing well in each stage throughout the weekend is what matters."

Burns, 16, from the Gold Coast in Queensland, placed 26th in the OK-N karting class at the FIA World Cup last month.

Lowe, from Melbourne, won a Victorian state title at his home track, Oakleigh, last year.

Meanwhile, Ava Jean Lawrence will compete in the junior class this weekend.

Despite racing under an Emirati licence, Lawrence is very much an Australian driver on the rise. She was signed to the Aston Martin F1 Academy program earlier this year.

World.title: Lynn's secret drugs ban revealed on BBL eve
World.content:
Big Bash League record-setter Chris Lynn's one-month suspension for a positive drugs test has been revealed, two months after he served the ban.

The revelation comes just days after the former Brisbane and Adelaide BBL big-hitter was linked with a move to the Melbourne Renegades for the season, which begins next month.

The 36-year-old was handed the suspension in August, after he tested positive on the day of England's T20 Blast finals in July, having helped Northamptonshire to the title.

After tests revealed an adverse analytical finding for cocaine's metabolite benzoylecgonine, Lynn admitted to using the drug days earlier.

The findings noted Lynn did not have a therapeutic use exemption for cocaine and that the cricketer had successfully argued his drug use amounted to an out-of-competition violation unrelated to sporting performance.

He was given a one-month ban, backdated to the period of between July 31 and August 30.

Lynn was set to play in Sri Lanka after the T20 Blast, but after one appearance he was ruled out with an unspecified leg injury on July 29.

Any further punishment would be at his BBL club's discretion, with Lynn available given he has served his penalty and is not on a Cricket Australia contract.

Lynn is the BBL's leading run-scorer and six-hitter, and has also played four one-day internationals and 18 T20 internationals for Australia.

He has also played for at least 25 different T20 franchises around the globe.

World.title: How a toy giraffe helped the AFLW Bulldogs rise back into finals
World.content:
Each week, Western Bulldogs fan-favourite Elaine Grigg looks forward to the side's player meetings.

It has been a good year for the Dogs, with eight wins from 12 games, finishing seventh on the ladder and back playing finals since 2022.

But reviewing the side's victories isn't the only reason Grigg likes getting together.

"This year, we've had a little mascot. Its name is Sawya, and it's a pet giraffe," Grigg told ABC Sport.

"Every week we spin a wheel, and someone has to take Sawya during the week … You have to make a video of what you do with it. So every Monday you present that, and it has been a really good laugh every week."

The "little mascot" a player takes home every week. (Supplied: Elaine Grigg)

Grigg, who joined the club as a high-profile draftee in 2023, said it has been a great way to get to know teammates and who they are off the field.

When she took Sawya, she said it was mostly work (as a student support officer at a school) and recovery, including a lot of time in the sauna. However, it has given away some teammates' hobbies, such as goalsneak Sarah Hartwig's creative side.

"That really surprised me," Grigg said. "How many different things she can do … She sews, she bakes, she does all these different things. I'm like, 'Twiggy, you need to start a business.' She makes all these different clothes as well."
