More than bonding for the fun of it, Grigg said it's part of the Bulldogs's focus on building team connection, which has helped them immensely on the field.

Elaine Grigg is quickly becoming one of the personalities of AFLW. (Getty: Quinn Rooney)

In 2023, the club hit rock bottom with a last-place finish, resulting in a review of its program and the appointment of a new coach, Tamara Hyett.

From there, it was a slow and steady climb back up the ladder. In both 2024 and 2025, the Dogs finished 12th.

This year, however, they fired back with a 26-point win over fellow finals team Gold Coast.

The Bulldogs' great AFLW turnaround The team's turnaround from rock bottom to the AFLW finals seems rapid but has been many years in the making. This is how they did it.

Many AFLW pundits and commentators have remarked on the side's new feel, particularly the excitement and "fun" factor.

"We know we need to lock in when we're at the club (and) when we're out on the footy field. But then it's the balance of having fun and also when it's time to be serious, to be serious as well," Grigg said.

"The connections that we have with everyone, it actually helps on the footy field."

The Western Bulldogs with their "little mascot" in Sawya. (Supplied: Elaine Grigg)

The side also dances before every game, with a new player picked each week to lead.

"That came about in our off-season trip. We were having a pool party and that dance, we did it, and that's carried on to our pre-game," she said, citing teammate Ellie Blackburn as the main instigator.

"It just shows how much fun we can have as a group, even before a game, to just let loose and be really connected with each other … It's something you look forward to and brings us closer as a group."

There was a lot of excitement around Elaine Grigg when she was drafted to the Bulldogs in 2023. (Getty: Quinn Rooney)

On the field, Grigg said one of her favourite moments this year was Emma McDonald kicking a fourth-quarter haul against Sydney in round four, handing the Swans their first loss of the season.

"She went on a rampage to kick her three goals and to get us up and about," Grigg said.

"But it was her first one (liked the most). It was a team goal."

Grigg will hope for a similar finish this Sunday, when the Bulldogs face the Swans in an elimination final at Henson Park.

World.title: The anthem mix-up that became an enduring myth in the Alan Jones legend
World.content:
The engines screamed in anticipation as the grid for the 1977 Austrian Grand Prix waited for the signal to burst into action.

On pole was the indomitable hometown hero Niki Lauda, almost exactly a year on from the horrific crash in Germany that would leave his face permanently scarred.

A spot behind him was the glamorous and charismatic Brit James Hunt, a man that Lauda described as the only person he ever envied.

Niki Lauda and James Hunt were the stars of the F1 circuit in the 1970s. (Getty Images: David Phipps/Sutton Images)

In third there was the American motorsport legend Mario Andretti, who ended his career with an incomparable resume that included an F1 championship, four IndyCar titles, and a Daytona 500 victory.

And 11 places back from there, waiting in a car that had never won a race, sat the understated and comparably unfashionable Alan Jones, the 30-year-old Victorian who had only joined the F1 season four months earlier to replace Welshman Tom Pryce after his horrific death at the South African Grand Prix.

Alan Jones (left) trains with Frank Williams, owner and founder of F1 team Williams. Jones's physique was often questioned through his career. (Getty Images: David Phipps/Sutton Images)

Jones, who died on Thursday aged 80, didn't have the glitz of Hunt or the unwavering focus of Lauda. He would variously be described as overweight, laconic and underprepared throughout his career.

But what he did have was raw talent.

On that overcast August day, the underdog Aussie who used to sell Holdens for his dad at a car dealership in suburban Melbourne would shock the Formula One world with his daring and deftness.

Niki Lauda chats with Alan Jones in the pit lane ahead of the 1977 Austrian Grand Prix. (Getty Images: LAT)

With rain clearing as the race started, the grid was split between those racing on wet weather tyres and those on slicks. Lauda fell behind quickly in his Ferrari as it struggled in the slippery conditions, as Andretti overtook both the Austrian and Hunt following a small collision between the two.

Fans and pundits kept one eye on the superstar American, and another on the Swedish driver Gunnar Nilsson, who had made a stunning run from 16th into second on the back of wet weather tyres.

Quietly, Jones had moved up from his 11th spot into fourth, weaving in and out of the pack on slicks in a daring decision that other drivers had battled with.

Alan Jones in action driving his Shadow car at the 1977 Austrian Grand Prix. (Getty Images: David Phipps/Sutton Images)

As the sun came out, Nilsson was forced to pit to replace his shredded rubber, while Andretti's Lotus engine exploded both his car and his chances of victory, leaving Hunt to take the lead with Jones hot on his tail.

Lauda, now on fresh tyres and with greater control, hammered through the field to sit in third.

Hunt and Lauda, the protagonists of the 2013 Hollywood blockbuster Rush, were split only by the chubby-cheeked Aussie who let his racing do the talking.

Then, in a moment that would change Jones's life forever, Hunt's McLaren blew up in a burst of sparks and flames, his car slowing to a stop on the side of the track as marshals enveloped the vehicle in the thick dust of their fire extinguishers.

Shadow team members run onto the track and jump in celebration as Alan Jones claimed their first, and only, F1 grand prix victory. (Getty Images: LAT)

From the cloud, Jones would emerge as the race leader, holding off Lauda to claim the first of his 12 grand prix victories, and the only race win his team, Shadow, would ever claim in its eight-year F1 history.

Jones's team would run out onto the road to celebrate as the track announcer told the crowd, with uncertainty, that it was Australia's first F1 victory in seven years.

"The first Grand Prix win for Alan Jones, and the first Grand Prix win for the hard-working Shadow team," he said over the PA system.

"And, we think, the first Grand Prix win for Australia in seven years."

Jones would be surrounded by well-wishers in pit lane. With then-wife Beverley in one arm, and a bottle of champagne in the other, he laid a big kiss on Bev before popping the champers at the encouragement of his better half.

Alan Jones smiles as he speaks with fellow driver Hans-Joachim Stuck after the 1977 Austrian Grand Prix. (Getty Images: David Phipps/Sutton Images)

Taking a big swig of booze before being ushered to the podium and draped in a golden wreath, the band played in the background, leading to one of the more enduring, and ultimately false, stories that Jones would tell of his win.

"[The win] was a bit of a surprise to everybody," Jones would later tell Wide World of Sports co-host Daryl Eastlake.

"In fact they had trouble finding the Australian national anthem, so some drunk played Happy Birthday on a trumpet.

"That'll give you an idea how prepared they were for me to win."

Australian racing icon and F1 world champion Alan Jones dies Alan Jones dies a few days after turning 80, after a short illness. He won the 1980 Formula 1 world championship and 12 grands prix.

Audio from the day shows the story is not entirely true.

Trumpeters were blasting away somewhere in the distance playing La Cucaracha, among other songs, before launching into Advance Australia Fair as Jones accepted his trophy.

The Australian national anthem of God Save the Queen, which had been reinstated as the country's tune in 1976 after Gough Whitlam had introduced Advance Australia Fair in 1974, was not played.

It's possible that in the excitement and colour of it all that Jones had mistaken Advance Australia Fair for Happy Birthday to You. It's possible that he had blanked out the anthem all together and could only remember the joyous refrains of various other trumpeted songs before he took his place on top of the podium. It's also possible that he didn't even recognise the new anthem, which had already become the old anthem, before becoming the new anthem again.

What is unequivocal though is that in the coming years, F1 organisers came to know our national anthem well as Jones left his indelible mark.

In the golden age of F1, Australia's contribution to it was a bloke who looked more like a bank teller than a movie star.

And it's that understated legacy that has, and always will, fill Australian motorsport fans with pride.

World.title: Socceroos still waiting for World Cup payment from FA
World.content:
Socceroos players who competed at this year's World Cup are yet to be paid their match fees, three months after the tournament's conclusion.

Just days after it was revealed that both male and female national team players were taking legal action against Football Australia (FA) in a dispute over their revenue-sharing agreement, members of the Socceroos World Cup squad in North America are also chasing match payments from the FA.

The payments were due within a fortnight of the players' departure from camp.

Socceroos, Matildas take FA to court The players' union is expected to argue the revenue share agreement between the governing body and national teams players is not being serviced properly.

Australia was knocked out of the tournament at the round-of-32 stage in a loss to Egypt on July 3.

FA, which recorded a $23 million loss over the last two financial years, said tax complications in the US were the cause of the delay.

The body said it was working with the players' union, Professional Footballers Australia (PFA), to "resolve the outstanding matters as quickly as possible".

"Football Australia is ready to make the match payments related to the FIFA World Cup," FA said in a statement.

"Before those payments can be processed, however, we require final specialist advice on the North American taxation obligations applicable to the payments, as well as some further player distribution information being provided through the PFA.

"Recognising the complexity of North American taxation requirements, FIFA facilitated access to specialist tax support for all participating member associations to help them understand and meet their respective obligations.

"We have been actively engaging with those specialist advisers since the World Cup to confirm the applicable tax and withholding treatment."

If a player sees game time or is an unused substitute for the national team, they earn about $6,000 in match fees.

The Socceroos played two friendlies against Mexico and Switzerland before three World Cup group games and the Egypt shootout defeat, meaning players named for all six games are heading into camp this week out of pocket to the tune of roughly $36,000.

There were no known payment issues for the four friendlies which took place in the US in the October and November windows last year.

Australia played Canada, the US, Venezuela and Colombia in North America in the back half of 2025 in the build-up towards the World Cup.

"It is clearly an unacceptable situation that three months after the conclusion of the World Cup the Socceroos match fees remain unpaid," PFA chief executive Beau Busch said.

"Any matter related to international tax was foreseeable and should have been addressed long before a ball was kicked at the tournament."

Members of the squad who faced Brazil in two friendlies in Queensland in September earlier this year are understood to have been paid in full.

The FA's delay in paying World Cup match fees has done little to quell discontent from Socceroos players heading into November's friendly window in the Middle East.

Some players have expressed concerns about travelling to the region — Australia will face Qatar in Doha and Jordan in Amman — in light of the wider conflict.

The purpose of those friendlies in the current climate has been brought into question since the Asian Football Confederation opted to delay the Asian Cup.

AAP

World.title: A Batmobile, Wharfie Time and an elephant — the footy gimmicks gone wrong
World.content:
Some blocked their ears while others dropped their jaws in disbelief, yet a surprising number cheered as if it didn't take them back to one of the worst moments in Fremantle Football Club's history.

During Freo's AFLW match against Sydney last weekend, the club reprised Wharfie Time, a home-ground gimmick that includes playing the opening bars of AC/DC's Hells Bells in a tight spot to spur the team on.

What is Wharfie Time? It was meant to be a celebration of Fremantle's moment in the grand final sun, but their viral Wharfie Time backfired spectacularly on Saturday.

That was despite the recent AFL Grand Final where Wharfie Time was activated with just four minutes to go and what was supposed to be a moment of celebration for Freo — up 17 points and looking strong — instead spurred the Lions into a ravenous frenzy to steal the match.

With many a Freo supporter still blinking in surprise that anyone would play it again so soon, CEO Simon Garlick has since stated that Hells Bells will be back for the 2027 AFL season.

Footy has a history of crowd gimmicks, and with Wharfie Time's future apparently set, it's only fair to take a look back at other stunts AFL and VFL clubs have pursued — for better or worse.

The Crows' power stance

The Adelaide Crows were the league's minor premiers in 2017 and were expected to fly through the grand final against Richmond.

But after a strong season that didn't need any gimmicks, they decided to introduce what became known as the power stance for the finals season.

During the national anthem, the team and coach Don Pyke stood in a rigid pose, arms down and facing the other team in an unwavering stare at the opposition that was probably supposed to be intimidating.

The Adelaide Crows maintained their pre-game power stance in September 2017. (Supplied: afl.com.au)

It was instead reminiscent, perhaps, of people freezing with horror as they realise they're about to pass an unexpected bowel movement.

And while the Crows thumped the Giants and the Cats in their first two finals, it was a different story against the Tigers.

A young team enjoying their first grand final appearance in 35 years, they were in no mood for gimmicks and ended up beating the flag favourites by 48 points, going on to win three premierships in four years.

The Crows' power stance was never seen again and it took the club nine years to win another final.

North Melbourne's elephant

In 1978, North Melbourne Football Club made the bizarre decision to field a circus elephant at Arden Street Oval before its round five match against Collingwood.

The club said it had organised what it called a "special surprise" as a promotion for a local circus that was owned by pennant member Jack Allan.

Handlers at Arden Street Oval try to slow a galloping elephant down. (Supplied: nmfc.com.au)

It started well and, in front of more than 31,000 people, the elephant was ridden by a member of the cheer squad and led around the oval.

But when Collingwood ran onto the field and drew a loud roar from the crowd, the elephant got spooked and started to gallop.

Afraid it could crush dozens of people, police started moving them from the area until the handler calmed the pachyderm and the crisis was over without injury to animal or human.

North Melbourne managed to win that game by nine points, but the idea of an elephant for crowd entertainment was retired.

Carlton's Betty Blue Hovercraft

In the 1990s, Carlton Football Club launched its own pre-game gimmick, a blue hovercraft ridden by Captain Carlton.

Captain Carlton rode a hovercraft dubbed Betty Blue onto the MCG in 2015. (Facebook: Carlton Football Club)

It came out onto the field during home games at Princes Park to rev up the crowd and was eventually retired in 1999.

But in 2015, Captain Carlton returned with a new hovercraft, dubbed Blue Betty, before the team's round one match against Richmond.

He rode the machine as it tore around the MCG leaving a rooster tail of fireworks.

Carlton ended up losing the match by 27 points.

Things took a turn for the worse later that year when Blue Betty reportedly wasn't allowed onto the Docklands stadium because of concerns for the turf, and Captain Carlton had to instead abseil from the roof.

Carlton lost that game to the Brisbane Lions, which had been winless until then.

The following day the hovercraft flipped over on the Yarra River and had to be dragged to dry land.

Angry Anderson in a Batmobile

The AFL itself decided that for the grand final's half-time entertainment in 1991, it would send singer Angry Anderson out onto the field with its own version of a Batmobile.

Angry Anderson and marathon runner Robert de Castella inside the AFL Batmobile. (YouTube: moto1986)

Sitting in the modified 1970 VG Valiant Coupe with champion marathon runner Robert de Castella, the now-late Anderson eventually belted out his hit song, Bound for Glory.

Unfortunately, it was an outing Anderson would probably rather forget.

He struggled to hear his backing track from the stands of Waverly Stadium, where the grand final was being played for the first and only time while renovations were underway at the MCG.

He also later said the straight-out exhaust of the Batmobile was so loud it was near-impossible to hear the music he was supposed to be singing along to.

History has not remembered the moment kindly, and the performance was mocked by an AFL sponsor in an advert nearly 20 years later.

A pig on the loose

Less of an official gimmick and instead a cheeky stunt, in 1993 a pig was let loose onto the goal square during the second quarter of the round 18 clash between St Kilda and Sydney at the SCG.

It had Plugga painted on one side and the number four on the other, and was rumoured to have been drafted by a Sydney Swans supporter who had earlier talked to players about getting in the head of legendary goal-kicker Tony "Plugger" Lockett, who was playing for The Saints at the time.

After running about the square to the delight of commentators while dodging attempts to catch it, the pig was eventually tackled to the ground by the Swans' Darren Holmes.

However, the stunt had little effect because Lockett wasn't even playing that day due to injury, and the Swans lost by 37 points.

But it may have impressed Plugger because he went on to play for Sydney, where he became club champion in 1995.

Crowd activations that work

Despite the disasters, some gimmicks have done wonders.

John Denver's Take Me Home, Country Roads continues to be sung by Brisbane Lions fans after every goal Charlie Cameron kicks at home, a moment that might induce cringe for the rest of us but clearly works for the Lions.

The club plays different songs for all its players after they kick a goal.

But considering the team is in the midst of a three-peat premiership dynasty, they have been kicking a lot of them, meaning those songs are probably off the playlist for everyone else.

The same could be said of Port Adelaide Football Club's use of Never Tear Us Apart by INXS.

INXS's Never Tear Us Apart is a much-loved pre-game anthem for Port Adelaide fans. (Supplied: portadelaidefc.com.au)

A reference to the club's chip on its shoulder towards the SANFL for insisting it enter the AFL in 1997 as a separate entity to its traditional Magpies team, fans sing it before every home game.

That separation ended last decade, but the song still invokes great passion among the faithful, even if, for the rest of us, Andrew Farriss's composition and Michael Hutchence's lyrics may be ruined forever.

Time will tell if AC/DC's Hells Bells will suffer the same fate, perhaps for Dockers fans most of all.

After all, the Lions' premiership coach Chris Fagan said after the grand final that they had talked about Wharfie Time the previous day and had agreed that, should it be activated, they would use it to "flip the switch ourselves, and turn it on them" instead.

Hells Bells indeed.

World.title: WA quick Lance 'Wild Thing' Morris hopes to be even faster after surgery
World.content:
It has been just over a year since Lance Morris had the surgery he hopes will save his cricket career.

For three years before going under the knife, the Western Australian fast bowler had struggled to string together games as he tried to manage a fracture in his spine.

"I was going under an MRI machine every six weeks and just checking up and it would occasionally get a bit worse after a bigger day," Morris said.

" Just having that in the back of your head, knowing that is there all the time and looming over you, that was really frustrating. "

Lance Morris regularly hit 150kph before surgery. He's confident he'll be back there again. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

Morris was first called into Australia's Test squad in late 2022 after a stunning start to the Sheffield Shield season, and it appeared just a matter of time until he pulled on the baggy green.

Since then, he has played just three one-day internationals, six Shield matches and 22 Big Bash games, as injury repeatedly left him sidelined.

Ahead of the 2025-26 domestic season, Morris decided enough was enough and elected to undergo pars stabilisation surgery, which involved bolts and wire being put into his lower back.

Bancroft reaches acceptance over Test recall chances after 'dejection' Cameron Bancroft says he no longer gets worked up over being ignored at the selection table despite scoring mountains of Shield runs.

"I was playing a game, missing a game and really trying to pick and choose which games to take on without overdoing the load," Morris said.

"I was pulling up with back soreness as I was trying to get ready for a series and I didn't want to carry that into the season.

"We had tried to go, I guess, the natural way about healing the back and giving it a good three-months stints to recover, doing absolutely nothing and then starting again, but we just weren't really having any luck.

" It got to the point where it was a bit of a line in the sand moment where it's like, 'Alright, let's really address this and get some certainty around my back.' "

No speed limit

State teammate Cameron Green, Indian quick Jasprit Bumrah and England spearhead Jofra Archer are among others who have travelled to New Zealand to see specialist Rowan Schouten for the surgery in recent years.

Their returns to cricket have left Morris optimistic he will be as quick as he was before injuries started taking their toll.

Jofra Archer is one of several high-profile players to undergo pars stabilisation surgery and make a successful return to international cricket. (AAP Image/Joel Carrett)

"That [a loss of pace] was a huge question for me leading into the surgery because I knew that was the asset that made me potentially selectable for red-ball cricket," he said.

"I had to look around at other guys that have had the surgery, the likes of Jofra, Jasprit Bumrah, the guys that have returned to Test cricket at the same speed if not better.

"I've got one eye on the speed gun at all times to see where things are at, but I'm pretty happy with where it's at."

Australia has an enormous Test summer on the horizon, with a visit by New Zealand, a tour of India and the 150th Anniversary Test in March, before the Ashes in England in the winter.

Lance Morris looked on the cusp of a Test debut after touring with Australian side in 2023. ((AAP Image/Darren England))

If last summer is anything to go by, there will be opportunities for the country's fast bowlers across the 18 Tests through to the end of the Ashes.

Josh Hazlewood missed last summer's Ashes with hamstring and ankle issues, while Pat Cummins only played once in that series, leaving Mitchell Starc as the only first-choice bowler available.

Morris, who lost his Cricket Australia (CA) contract because of his surgery, has an eye on a Test return.

"There's a heap of Test cricket there and red-ball cricket has always been a pretty big priority for me," he said.

"Basically, targeting Shield games where we see fit and prioritising them is how I got around the Test squad in the first place and how I think I'll put my name back up for a potential selection.

"There was also some pretty pretty positive conversations [with CA] that I'm still a player of interest, and it's just a matter of getting back and bowling fast in front of the group."

World.title: Aussie Hijikata backs up Djokovic triumph with another big win in Paris
World.content:
Rinky Hijikata has backed up his statement win over Novak Djokovic with another impressive victory in Paris, downing Alex de Minaur's conqueror, Tomas Martin Etcheverry, to reach his first ATP Masters quarterfinal.

The 25-year-old Australian came from behind to beat the Argentine world number 31 2-6, 6-3, 7-5.

Besides making the last eight, where he will face local favourite Luca Van Assche, he has climbed into the world's top 60 for the first time in his career.

Rinky Hijikata defeats Novak Djokovic at Paris Masters Rinky Hijikata has pulled off a stunning upset over 24-time grand slam champion Novak Djokovic, eliminating him from the Paris Masters and ending his hopes of qualifying for the end-of-year ATP Finals.

Beginning the event in qualifying, ranked at number 83, Hijikata has beaten five higher-ranked players so far and will climb to number 48 if he does it again.

Many a tennis underdog has pulled off a shock win but, drained by the feat and the attention, they rarely back it up.

It seemed as if this would be the case with Hijikata in the French capital on Thursday, local time, when he lost the first set in 26 minutes. The Sydneysider lost the first eight points, and while he then held to love to get into the tie, he was broken again in his third service game.

Hijikata survived a break point in the 12-minute opening game of the second set, then broke in the fourth game. He maintained that advantage to win the set in 43 minutes and force a decider.

That went with serve until 5-5. Hijikata had to save three break points at 1-2, but his other four service matches had all been serenely held to love. However, he had not forced a break point of his own.

Now, at the key moment, he did, and he took it. That left Hijikata serving for the match. He opened with an ace.

Etcheverry levelled to 15-all, but Hijikata won the next three points to take the game, set and match, ending with an emphatic forehand smash across court.

Hijikata celebrated joyously, prompting television pundit Ryan Harrison, the American former top-40 player, to comment: "He is a guy who is typically mild-mannered; he's as fired up as I've ever seen him before."

Next up is 47-ranked Van Assche, who beat Lorenzo Musetti 7-5 3-6 6-4 in a seesaw epic that had the crowd gripped after watching two French defeats.

Hijikata has never played Van Assche and will also have to deal with a home support that helped Van Assche come back from two break points down at 3-4 in the third. He won 12 of the next 13 points to seal the match.

That came after Ben Shelton and Tommy Paul overcame home hopes to set up an all-American quarterfinal. Twelfth-seed Paul saw off Quentin Halys 7-6 (7-3) 6-4, but Shelton was pushed hard by Arthur Rinderknech. The third seed eventually won 3-6, 6-4, 7-6 (7-5).

Earlier, Carlos Alcaraz received a walkover into the quarterfinals after ‌Matteo Berrettini withdrew from their third-round clash with an arm ‌injury.

The match had been ‌scheduled to headline the evening session, but the Italian world number 43 pulled out after experiencing pain in his arm.

Second ‌seed Alcaraz advanced directly to ‌the last eight, where he will face Taylor Fritz, who inflicted another American defeat on the hosts when he beat Arthur Fils 6-3, 6-4.

In the other quarterfinal, Portuguese lucky loser Nuno Borges, who beat Ignacio Buse 6-0, 6-2, will play Casper Ruud or Jan-Lennard Struff.

AAP

Tech.title: OpenAI is stepping back from NDAs for data center projects
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Following this week’s midterms where voters resoundingly voiced their opposition to data center expansion, OpenAI today announced new commitments to communities where it is working on data center projects, including that it won’t use non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with public officials.

Many data center projects have come under scrutiny for relying on NDAs to hide discussions between developers and local officials. However, OpenAI says it is now allowing “only narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.” In October, Amazon announced it would no longer use NDAs with government agencies it works with on data center projects.

Related Data centers lost the midterms

OpenAI’s additional commitments include paying “the full cost” of electricity it uses and the “infrastructure needed to serve us.” It will make opportunities for local communities by publishing the jobs it expects to create and by reporting on hiring. And every future “compute campus” (its rebranding phrase for data centers) the company owns and operates will have a “local compact” that includes the commitments and will reflect “local priorities,” OpenAI says.

Tech.title: Airbnb is working on an AI travel agent
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Airbnb plans to roll out an AI agent in the first half of 2027 that will help users plan and book travel, the company said in its Q3 2026 earnings shareholder letter released today.

“Today’s AI agents are good at simple, routine tasks, like making a restaurant reservation or scheduling an appointment,” Airbnb said. “But planning a trip on Airbnb is different.” The company argued that its experience matching hosts and guests, its current role in being part of reservations already, and a “new interface” built “specifically for travel” gives it an edge.

Here’s how Airbnb says that new interface will work:

We don’t think a traditional chatbot is the right way to plan a trip. We’re developing a custom-designed, AI-native experience that builds the interface around your question. Rather than a chat window, our agent draws on a library of hundreds of travel-specific interface elements—maps, photos, comparisons, calendars, itineraries—and composes them in real time to match what you’re looking for. Our agent will help guests explore options, make decisions with the people they’re traveling with, and take action directly in Airbnb.

Airbnb co-founder and CEO Brian Chesky has said before that the company plans to launch an agent in 2027, telling the Skift Global Forum that it would have an interface that’s “much richer than a chatbot.”

In its shareholder letter, Airbnb also said that AI is “the best thing to ever happen to Airbnb” and has changed how it develops products and operates.

Tech.title: The New York Times is in talks to buy Letterboxd for around $330 million
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The New York Times Company is in talks”exclusive negotations” to acquire Letterboxd, the social network for film lovers, for around $330 million, The New York Times reports. The Times Company, Sony Pictures Entertainment, and A24 were all recently rumored to be among those interested in buying Letterboxd.

The negotiations with the Times Company have included the potential for Letterboxd’s co-founders to stay in charge but report to a Times Company executive. Letterboxd would likely remain standalone for the “foreseeable future,” according to the NYT. The company would also integrate the Times Company’s ad tech.

NYT spokesperson Charlie Stadtlander declined to comment. Letterboxd and current parent company Tiny Ltd. didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment from The Verge.

Tech.title: T-Mobile owner on Elon Musk launching a wireless carrier: ‘Welcome to the party’
Tech.content:
He [Musk] has now bought 76 megahertz of spectrum. By the way, we have 400. So if you now say he can buy the spectrum prospectively, do your math. These are kind of triple-digit billions which are needed to gain the spectrum position. If he has the money, go for it. Then he has to build a network. I can tell you, we have 85,000 towers. No, he can rent towers, no question. But this is another $20 to $30 billion which are required.

Put antennas on it. You can buy antennas… and you can get [them] maybe even in a cheaper way, or you construct it in a new way, but you need money for that. So therefore, my assessment is that SpaceX at least — if they want to play in that industry — needs at least minimum $200 billion. But even beyond that, to play in an industry which we have, let’s say, professionalized over the last 20 years — okay, welcome to the party.

Tech.title: Perplexity launches its own take on AI agents for work
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Perplexity is taking on OpenAI and Anthropic with its own work-focused AI agents. The startup’s new always-on “Teammates” can take on multiple roles within a workspace, while pulling existing projects, skills, and memory from the Perplexity tools you already use.

Teammates integrate with Perplexity Computer, an AI system that can deploy agents on your device to complete tasks. But Perplexity says Teammates “build on top” of Computer by offering the ability to collaborate and complete “ongoing, large-scale work.” You can assign each Teammate different jobs that they can perform simultaneously — much like OpenAI’s Dots and Claude Duet. Perplexity’s take on the feature is much more expensive, however, as it requires a subscription to its $200 / month Max plan.

Each Teammate gets their own thread. Image: Perplexity

Perplexity notes that you can keep tabs on Teammates’ progress through individual threads in the Perplexity app, as well as interact with them in Slack. “Over time, we envision every org having hundreds of teammates working for each person,” Perplexity CEO Aravind Srinivas says on X.

Tech.title: Salon is shutting down after 31 years
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Salon launched 31 years ago as one of the first online-only news magazine outlets, and it announced today in an unsigned post that it’s ceasing publication.

The company said that the “business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years,” and it decided that its publishing model is “no longer sustainable.” It didn’t go into detail about why, but many websites are grappling with “Google Zero” and the impact of AI tools. When reached for comment, Salon general manager Amanda Wolfe pointed The Verge to today’s announcement post.

“Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them,” Salon said in its post. “Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.”

On Bluesky, Salon chief content officer Erin Keane says that the editorial archive will “stay live for now.”

Current Salon owner Find.co acquired Salon in 2023 and describes itself as a “Performance Marketing Ecosystem transforming crypto marketing with performance and precision.”

Tech.title: The midterms proved once and for all that X is not real life
Tech.content:
A week before the midterm elections, Vice President JD Vance hosted a town hall in Texas with Fox News host Jesse Watters. It was a friendly event with a friendly audience in what should have been a friendly state, and maybe that’s why Vance couldn’t help himself. When a college student earnestly asked how the right expected young people like her to settle down and have kids, given the ever-growing cost of living, Vance replied with a quip about Jon Husted’s ass.

The student, Kate White, introduced herself as the vice president of the Texas Christian University chapter of Turning Point USA, the conservative group started by Donald Trump ally Charlie Kirk. She was offering Vance an opportunity to explain how MAGA could work for young people, and he turned it into a joke. Vance did eventually answer the question, saying Republicans don’t pay enough attention to the issue of affordability and blaming rising housing costs on institutional investors and the “20 million illegal aliens” supposedly living in the United States. But the order of operations revealed the fatal flaw of Republicans’ 2026 strategy: Everything is a gag to them, and they’re way too online.

For the past decade, Republicans have adhered to Steve Bannon’s maxim that politics is downstream from culture. This fixation with liberals’ alleged capture of elite institutions has animated the right’s war against Big Tech and in particular social media platforms — which the right claims actively silenced conservative voices — and its crusade against diversity, equity, and inclusion. With his purchase of X, Elon Musk finally succeeded in building a conservative platform where right-wing voices not only had real influence but also a direct line to those in power. More recently, some people have claimed that Musk’s X is the only social media that really represents the people, unlike platforms like Bluesky, which have more left-leaning user bases.

Cocooned in their online echo chamber, MAGA figureheads convinced themselves the public was on their side, even when polling suggested otherwise. They ignored their base’s valid concerns about affordability and served them nonsensical memes instead. And they failed spectacularly in the realm where it actually mattered: politics. X, we can now declare once and for all, is not real life. Republicans not only lost historically red states like Texas, Kansas, and South Carolina, but barely managed to win Florida. The Senate race in Mississippi, of all places, is still too close to call.

Vance, especially, is a creature of X, where his following list includes such illustrious accounts as Raw Egg Nationalist, Bronze Age Pervert, Howling Mutant, and Captive Dreamer. But White House aides, department employees, and Hill staffers are stewing in the same ecosystem. Writer John Ganz has termed this phenomenon “groyperfication,” after followers of influencer Nick Fuentes, who call themselves groypers. This is a useful shorthand, though Fuentes’ fans are mostly too NEET-pilled to land jobs on the Hill. American Moment, a boot camp for young conservative up-and-comers, reportedly screens out groypers. There’s a real need for such protective measures. Kingsley Wilson, the hard-right press secretary for the Department of War (or per its legal name, Defense), has posted antisemitic conspiracy theories about Leo Frank, a Jewish man who was lynched in Georgia 1915 for allegedly raping a teenage girl. (Historians largely believe Frank was innocent.) The Department of Homeland Security regularly posts fascist fancams and wink-wink references to white supremacist memes.

Republicans saw their 2024 victory as a mandate. Having clawed the White House and Congress back from Democrats, they assumed the public was on board with MAGA’s cultural project when in fact people were largely mad about the price of eggs. And with two years of dominance under their belt, they decided to go even harder on culture, not realizing — or maybe just not caring — that people are still mad about gas prices and groceries.

Cocooned in their online echo chamber, MAGA figureheads convinced themselves the public was on their side, even when polling suggested otherwise.

In the run-up to the midterms, the Department of Education was posting about “Malfoid” — a gender-swapped version of Draco Malfoy from Harry Potter that far-right influencers claimed would save Western literature from the scourge of wokeness. The Department of Homeland Security was bragging about record lows in legal immigration, which outside white nationalist circles is typically not considered a negative thing. Pseudonymous shitposters like Howling Mutant were posting memes comparing themselves to noted child murderer Anakin Skywalker, the new avatar for the online right. Musk, a Republican megadonor, got in on the fun, as did Katie Miller, wife of ultranationalist White House adviser Stephen Miller, who dressed up as Anakin’s wife Padmé Amidala for Halloween. (Katie Miller’s last government role was advising Elon Musk’s failed Department of Government Efficiency; now she devotes her time to throwing lavish parties and hosting a podcast no one listens to.)

Most of the American public isn’t on X, but the conversations conservatives have there do bleed out into the mainstream — often with disastrous results. Bo French, the Republican candidate for Texas railroad commissioner, lost his election by a huge margin after posting anti-Indian memes on X. (Asian American voters, including Indian Americans, moved to the left in Texas elections down the ballot.) Musk did his part to drive turnout, spending nearly half a billion dollars on Republican candidates and PACs. But even Musk’s money failed to make up for voters’ dissatisfaction with Republicans’ performance, perhaps because the ads he funded focused largely on culture war issues that were out of step with voters’ concerns about the cost of living.

And Miller, it turns out, didn’t even vote, telling CBS Newsshe feared doing so would put her safety at risk, since Virginia law makes voters’ home addresses public. (The Millers, like other members of the Trump administration, live on a military installation with tight security; it’s unlikely intruders would be able to get to their home.) Republican myopia may have contributed to their poor performance across the board, including with groups that were touted as their new base. One poll found that a majority of young men of all races — including young white men — voted for Democrats in the midterms.

In a long postmortem on X — reportedly posted without input or permission from White House officials — Vance said he asked “the smartest data guy” he knows for insight on the electorate ahead of the midterms. Vance claims several pollsters told him that voters’ main concerns were the war against Iran, the cost of living, and America’s relationship to Israel. So why didn’t Republicans listen?

The answer lies in the algorithmic nature of social media, X especially. If you interact with even one post about a relatively niche topic — say, genderbent Harry Potter fanfiction — the algorithm will feed you post after post after post about the same thing. Just like Trump spent the early years of his first term obsessing over Fox News, the single mainstream network that would reflect his biases back to him, MAGA is now all in on X. And if you’re the kind of person who spends a lot of time scrolling, you may even delude yourself into thinking the issue clogging up your feed is something people just can’t stop talking about.

Tech.title: Blue Origin’s next launch now won’t happen until 2027
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Blue Origin plans to do its next New Glenn rocket launch in January 2027, according to CNBC and the Financial Times, which cite a memo from CEO Dave Limp sent to staff. The new timeline follows a May launchpad explosion that damaged Blue Origin’s New Glenn launchpad ahead of a flight that would have brought Amazon Leo satellites into space.

In October, Blue Origin founder Jeff Bezos told Fox News that the company was aiming for a December New Glenn launch, joking that it could be “probably December 31st.” The new, revised launch window is “about 10 days later than Blue Origin’s earlier launch target,” CNBC reports. Limp also reportedly cited bad weather as having an effect on the launchpad rebuilding process.

“This small adjustment doesn’t diminish what we’ve accomplished or the importance of the work still ahead,” Limp wrote in his memo, per CNBC and the FT. “Returning New Glenn to flight remains our top priority — it’s worth it.”

Tech.title: The New York Times reportedly in talks to buy Letterboxd for $330 million
Tech.content:
In Brief

The New York Times Company has reportedly “entered exclusive negotiations” to acquire Letterboxd for $330 million, according to a report from The New York Times itself.

Letterboxd, an online platform for movie lovers that could be compared to Goodreads for movies, has grown dramatically in recent years. Letterboxd reported 3 million users in January 2021, a figure that grew to 28 million by April of this year. More than half of its users are under 35.

Letterboxd was previously reported to be seeking a new owner. According to the Times, film studios A24 and Sony were interested in the acquisition, but A24 was priced out.

Letterboxd is free, but users can access advanced features with a paid subscription. Its projected earnings for this year are estimated at $15 million, which is only about 4.5% of what the Times is supposedly offering to buy the company for.

The New York Times Company declined to comment on the acquisition to its own paper (lol). Personally, we wouldn’t be surprised if these anonymous tips were coming from inside the house, so we’re inclined to take this report pretty seriously.

Tech.title: Meta, Google, and TikTok sue California AG over teen social media law
Tech.content:
Meta, Google, and TikTok have each filed lawsuits against California Attorney General Rob Bonta in an attempt to block a law that restricts social media features it deems addictive for users under 16.

California Governor Gavin Newsom signed the bill, known as AB 1709, into law in September, and it’s slated to take effect at the start of the new year.

The law prohibits social platforms from offering autoplay videos and personalized feeds to users under 16, and it requires the platforms to delete these users’ accounts if they don’t turn those features off. If platforms do not comply, they could be liable for fines of up to $50,000 per affected user under 16 years old.

Meta claims that AB 1709 violates the First Amendment by overriding its editorial decisions about how to display content, adding that Section 230 preempts the law. TikTok and Google made similar arguments.

“Meta currently organizes its feeds of content to include personalized content recommendations and to automatically play media, [so] the Act would make it unlawful for Meta to disseminate speech to minors altogether, and would require Meta to delete minors’ accounts, unless it changes these practices,” the company wrote in its lawsuit.

In an emailed statement, a TikTok spokesperson added, “AB 1709 is a blatantly unconstitutional restriction on free expression that erodes the long-standing and protected practice of curating content based on user preferences, which book stores, TV networks and streaming services all use.”

AB 1709 follows a trend of legislation around the world that seeks to curb teen social media use in an attempt to improve teen mental health outcomes. However, digital safety experts often caution against these laws because they can inadvertently compromise the privacy of all platform users, including adults, by requiring age verification checks that collect more user data.

“AB 1709 compels platforms to collect even more information from every user, invading everyone’s privacy and frustrating our ability to remain anonymous online,” EFF Associate Director of State Affairs Rindala Alajaji said in a press briefing. “Online surveillance by social media companies is harmful, and yet this bill requires even more of it, further concentrating power in the hands of tech companies rather than actually protecting users.”

Alajaji added that teenagers’ use of social media has been instrumental in enabling impactful digital activism, citing the Parkland shooting survivors’ March for Our Lives and climate activist Greta Thunberg’s global reach.

“As a functional ban on social media for youth under 16, AB 1709 cuts young people off from essential information and experiences, silencing the very voices it claims to protect,” Alajaji said.

These platforms are primed to fight this California law as they navigate similar legal battles in various countries. That’s especially true for Meta, which agreed to pay a settlement of up to $18 billion to resolve children’s safety claims brought by 29 U.S. states.

In December 2025, Australia became the first country to ban social media for users under 16 altogether. France passed a similar law, but its top court struck it down, citing concerns about violations of free expression rights.

These platforms also argue that the law would affect parents’ ability to make decisions about their teens’ internet use through parental controls.

A Google spokesperson noted that autoplay on YouTube is turned off for minors by default, and that parents have the ability to turn off their teens’ access to Shorts altogether.

“We believe parents are best positioned to make the right decisions for their families, which is why we offer a range of protections and tools that put parents in control,” a Google spokesperson said. “Overly broad laws like this actually break the systems we’ve built to help kids find high-quality, age-appropriate videos.”

A representative for Attorney General Bonta said that his office is reviewing the filings and is committed to “defending California’s commonsense laws to protect kids online.”

Tech.title: Airbnb says it’s launching an AI travel agent in the first half of 2027
Tech.content:
Airbnb has teased its plans to build its own AI travel agent before, but on Thursday the company announced that the new AI feature will launch in the first half of 2027. In the company’s Q3 shareholder letter on Thursday, Airbnb also provided more detail about how the agent will work, what it will actually do, and how it’s different from a typical AI chatbot.

In prior interviews, CEO Brian Chesky sketched out the travel company’s approach to AI, describing a plan to build an AI agent that has a richer interface than a conventional chatbot. He also expressed his opinions about how chatbots aren’t the right interface for travel, noting that people take pleasure in the planning process and in anticipating a trip. Any agent that it built, then, shouldn’t take away from the inspiration and the browsing, he told TechCrunch in an interview last month.

Chesky today reiterated that belief, telling analysts on the earnings call that people won’t use one AI agent for everything.

“Today’s AI agents like Muse and Instinct are good at simple routine tasks like making a restaurant reservation or scheduling an appointment. But planning a trip is different,” he said. “Travel is aspirational. Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience. In fact, 80% of travelers say they enjoy spending time researching trips. People want to look at photos. They want to compare homes. They want to make decisions with people they’re traveling with,” he continued. “And I don’t think the general-purpose agents are the best to do that. So that is why we are building our own AI agent,” Chesky said.

Airbnb described its agent as having a personalized interface that’s designed specifically for travel, where it will “build an interface” around a user’s question instead of simply responding as a chatbot would.

“What we are doing is developing a custom-designed AI-native experience that responds to what guests are looking for,” Chesky said. “So instead of relying on traditional chat alone, which is very text-heavy — which, again, is definitely not the way you should plan travel, our agent draws from a library of hundreds of travel-specific interface components — maps, photos, comparisons, calendars, itineraries — and composes them in real time to match what they’re looking for.”

The exec said the agent will feel “a little bit like generative UI” as it’s designed to offer up “the right interface at the right time” for someone’s specific travel needs.

In its shareholder letter, the company touted that its nearly 20 years of experience in bringing hosts and guests together is informing how the agent is built, as it incorporates insights about how people both book and host on its platform. The agent will also be able to help travelers beyond the booking itself.

“Our agent will be able to help guests throughout their trip — from changing a reservation or resolving a payment issue to getting help with refunds, rebooking, or 24-hour safety support. These are things an outside agent can’t easily do on its own,” the company wrote.

Over time, Airbnb expects the agent will be able to help travelers with other aspects of their trip, including not only homes and hotels, but also services and experiences. Services and experiences are two areas that have become a bigger focus for the company following its redesign last year.

While the company previously said to expect its AI agent sometime in the next year, it’s now more specifically committing to roll out the new technology to consumers in the first half of 2027.

The news of the agent’s release was delivered alongside strong third-quarter earnings, with revenue growing 19% to $4.87 billion, topping Wall Street estimates. It also raised its 2026 revenue growth forecast, which it now predicts will be in the high teens, instead of the mid-teens.

“Airbnb is back in growth mode,” Chesky told analysts on the Q3 earnings call on Thursday. “It’s rare for a marketplace of our size to reaccelerate growth, but that’s exactly what we’re doing. Q3 was our fastest revenue growth in more than three years,” he added.

Tech.title: Serve Robotics launches new business to become the AWS for robots
Tech.content:
Serve Robotics, a maker of self-driving sidewalk delivery robots, is expanding beyond its autonomous delivery operations in a bid to become a technology supplier to other companies building robots.

The company, which spun out of Uber’s acquisition of Postmates in 2021 and went public in 2024, said Thursday it will launch a new business line called Physical AI Services.

Specifically, Serve Robotics will offer customers its connectivity and data tools. Bedrock Robotics, a startup developing self-driving systems for construction equipment, is a customer, according to Serve. It’s also working with T-Mobile to bring AI computing power closer to robots, Serve announced alongside its third-quarter earnings on Thursday.

“We are solving the problem of robots in human spaces,” Serve Robotics CEO and co-founder Ali Kashani told TechCrunch.

Serve Robotics already makes two kinds of robots, the cute googly-eyed sidewalk delivery robot and one designed for hospitals that it got through its acquisition of Diligent Robotics.

Those businesses are not going away, Kashani emphasized in a recent interview. Instead, he said there is opportunity to sell the technology it developed for its own robots to other companies developing robots for farms, warehouses, and other uncontrolled environments.

“I kind of think of it as the AWS moment where we are taking the technology we’ve built for us, and we’re opening it up for more people to build on,” he said, adding this wouldn’t have been possible without developing its own robot fleet.

The expansion comes as Serve’s sidewalk delivery business expands, but is shifting away from Uber and toward other partners, including DoorDash and Wonder.

Its new Physical AI Services business line will offer three products. Serve Link helps connect robots in the field to AI systems running in data centers, which would allow companies to potentially tap into more powerful AI models without having to put all that computing power onboard.

“Any robotic application generally needs to connect the robots to some offline intelligence, whether it’s to collect data or do exception handling or whatever,” said Kashani. “It’s the connectivity piece that has to be really high performance. You need to be able to manage really unreliable networks and still reliably connect, and that’s what we solve.”

It’s also launching a data curator tool that helps companies find edge cases in the reams of real-world data a robot collects, which can then be fed back into a training model to improve performance. Its third product is a real-world, foundation-model data catalog built from Serve’s own sidewalk robots that can teach AI models how to understand complex human environments.

Kashani said he’s been thinking about this idea — a playbook he learned from Amazon — for years.

“When the technology is so nascent, you have got to build the end-to-end application because that’s the only way you know what to build, but then over time, as the technology gets more advanced, a lot more people are going to be wanting to build similar things,” he said. “And what you want to do is to open your technology so others build with you and on your platform.”

Tech.title: Meta says US users can now video chat with their Muse AI avatar
Tech.content:
Muse Voice, a feature that lets users call and video chat with Meta’s consumer AI agent, Muse, is now available to everyone in the U.S., the company announced on Thursday.

First introduced at Meta’s Connect developer conference in September, the video-chatting feature involves new AI models, Muse Realtime Avatar and Muse Realtime Voice technology, which help power the digital avatar that chats with the user.

While other AI competitors offer voice chat features, Meta’s Muse offers a cute, animated avatar (nicknamed Jolly), which users interact with as they ask questions or request tasks to be handled on their behalf. Users can also customize the avatar as they choose, changing it to something that looks more like a person, animal, or some other character.

The company believes that anthropomorphizing Muse in this way could make consumers feel more connected to their AI agent — a connection that could grow even stronger as they begin to engage in live conversations with it.

As the Muse avatar speaks, Meta says it will use “subtle expressions and gestures” that match the tone of the conversation. (Muse doesn’t actually “see” the user, but it hears them and reacts based on their conversations.)

The news of the rollout was announced via blog post and on X by Meta’s chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang, who shared a demo of his Muse in action. The video saw Wang joking around, referencing his love of posting memes on X, which he told his Muse may have gotten him in trouble with his boss. His Muse, a fluffy white dog, responds with a suggestion to add disclaimers to those memes that could be misinterpreted as Meta endorsing anything risqué. (Ha!)

The added support for video chats and calls comes just before Meta’s plan to launch a Tamagotchi-like wearable device for its Muse AI agent before year-end. When the device arrives, the digital avatar will appear on its small screen, letting users talk to the agent, which can then reply or carry out tasks for them.

Meta says the real-time conversations are supported on mobile, web, and Mac and will later come to its AI Glasses and the upcoming “Muse Charm” hardware device.

Tech.title: Meta warns that election backlash against data centers could make AI expansion harder
Tech.content:
Meta president Dina Powell McCormick said that the Democratic wins in the midterm elections are going to make it a lot harder for companies to build data centers, adding that the industry has “not done as good a job as we needed to explain the benefits of these investments.”

Speaking at the WSJ Tech conference on Wednesday, the Meta exec pointed out that the backlash against data centers — which was very much on the ballot during this election season — was also tied to people’s feelings about AI technology overall.

“The visible sort of manifestation of AI is a data center, and it’s something that people can say, ‘I don’t want this in my community,’” she explained. “I think there’s an underlying bigger issue, which is how people feel about AI in general.”

Meta believes it could turn around the negative consumer sentiment around AI if it’s able to demonstrate the value, not only of the data centers coming to local communities, but also in the technology itself.

“The stakes of who builds the technology that cures cancer, that gives access to education, that is also a very fundamental difference … Mark [Zuckerberg, Meta CEO] is very ‘long human,’ and he’s betting on humans more than machines,” Powell McCormick explained. “And that’s what we mean when we say the future is for everyone. That people should not be left behind. But the way to ensure that is that this technology is democratized, that people have access to it in a very fair and transparent way,” she said.

The exec also touted Meta’s experience in building data centers, saying that the company has been doing so for 20 years, as it takes a lot of compute power to offer the products it does in the social networking space. Today, the company has data centers in 23 states, she said, and five of them, including one in Texas, are planned as projects of 1 gigawatt or more.

But Meta is now worried that it could lose some of its investments after politicians ran on anti-data-center platforms during the midterms.

“I think it’s going to be harder,” Powell McCormick said, describing what the future of building data centers looks like. “It has been hard, I should say, but I also think that it’s becoming clear what models work, and the states want those models that work.”

Specifically, communities only want data centers when it benefits them in some way, she explained, laying out the approach that Meta today uses to close its data center deals in local communities.

Successful projects see Meta paying for its own electricity, directing any tax surpluses as a result of the data centers toward teachers and first responders, keeping the labor force local, and getting bipartisan support for the project, among other things.

Going forward, she expects data center projects to come under more review and be weighed against whether the constituents actually want them.

Meta has pinned its hopes on its AI investments, particularly its consumer AI agent Muse scaling far beyond the 10 million users it has today, to become a business that one day serves billions. But even if that’s not the case, it believes that its investments in data centers will not be for nothing, as the compute itself will be valuable.

“We’re getting calls every day to lease that compute [we’ve built], and so one way or another, we’re seeing a path to monetization,” Powell McCormick said.

Tech.title: OpenAI released a new cybersecurity model. Is that enough?
Tech.content:
Max Justicz, the chief technology officer and co-founder of the startup Charge Robotics, used an OpenAI model to find a severe vulnerability that — if exploited — could allow hackers to take control of servers running Ubuntu, a widely used open source Linux-based operating system.

Justicz, who has a hobbyist’s interest in cybersecurity and previously found a vulnerability in the same codebase, told TechCrunch that he found this issue using GPT 5.6 Sol, released in July, through the AI maker’s Daybreak Blue, a program that gives cybersecurity defenders access to powerful frontier models.

“I literally just aimed ChatGPT at the same body of code and said ‘I found this bug previously that was fixed several years ago, please find bugs as bad or worse,’ and it came back in two hours with this,” Justicz said. “It’s extremely convoluted and hard for a human to find, but it works!”

He reported the issue to the Debian Project, which maintains the software in question and issued a patch to fix the vulnerability. There has been no known evidence of exploitation. Still, the ease with which he found it suggests that we’ve only seen the tip of the iceberg when it comes to potential exploits that even novice hackers can utilize with the help of AI models.

“I can only imagine what one could do with more time and access to less neutered models. We should expect some extremely crazy bugs to be found and exploited over the next few months,” Justicz wrote in a social media thread discussing his finding. “This might be obvious to most folks here, but there is currently huge alpha in taking some code or binary someone has not audited yet and just aiming a powerful AI model at it.”

OpenAI appears to have noticed. Today, the AI giant announced a new model focused on cybersecurity, ChatGPT Cyber, would be made available to the highest tier of users in the cybersecurity program, Daybreak Red, which allows offensive cybersecurity researchers tools for vulnerability hunting and development. Yesterday, OpenAI said that the same model had been used to scan and prepare patches for vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel, finding 948 potential issues. OpenAI also found 81 “novel” vulnerabilities in Firefox, the web browser.

“Our goal is to dramatically expand Daybreak, bringing advanced security research to organizations of every size, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers,” the frontier lab said in a statement.

OpenAI has insisted that there is a narrow window of time for the people who safeguard digital infrastructure to take action before AI models become even better at hacking and easier to access. For cyber defenders, however, it can feel like the frontier labs have unleashed a mountain of new work that outstrips their resources. Justicz said that he personally spent about $5,000 on subscriptions and tokens to find several exploits.

Besides Daybreak’s model access, OpenAI has also announced a $1 billion initiative to support cybersecurity professionals in the program who work on critical infrastructure like the electrical grid or water systems.

The Daybreak program has its own critiques. Justicz notes that the frontier lab appears to have recently “nerfed” Daybreak Blue to make it less useful at finding vulnerabilities. On one hand, it may be good to limit access from potential bad actors — Justicz said he just uploaded a photo of his driver’s license to join the program. On the other, cybersecurity professionals say they have one hand tied if they can’t use frontier technology while bad actors can deploy open-weight models with abliterated guardrails.

Still, OpenAI says just “thousands” of cybersecurity professionals are participating in the Daybreak program, versus a far larger number of potential hackers.

It’s unclear if frontier labs are devoting enough of their resources to this issue. Eric Wallace, a researcher on OpenAI’s technical staff, said that “we are now allocating a significant amount of our frontier compute towards discovering and patching vulnerabilities in open source codebases, fully pro bono.”

But the Linux bug hunt cost $1.2 million, which is significantly less than the approximate $6 million token spend the company invested in finding a potential solution to a famous problem of fluid dynamics.

If there is a narrow window of time to patch the digital infrastructure the world depends on, more urgency may be required.

Tech.title: US government warns of ‘ongoing cyber threat’ amid mass hacks of industrial retail and military freezers
Tech.content:
The U.S. government is warning of an “ongoing cyber threat” facing industrial refrigeration units, after reports of cyberattacks targeting freezers and fridges in supermarkets around the world, U.S. military bases, and at least one blood bank.

U.S. cybersecurity agency CISA, the FBI, and several other federal government departments warned in a joint statement on Thursday that hackers are targeting and compromising internet-connected refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems in grocery stores and cold storage facilities. The statement said that the hacks are hitting critical infrastructure, such as the food, agriculture, transportation, and medicine-shipping industries.

“If successfully exploited, the actors could change the temperature and possibly cause physical impacts such as fire hazards, loss of inventory and changes to the service life of the system,” the agencies warn.

The warning comes after several waves of cyberattacks targeting industrial refrigeration units across the United Kingdom and Europe in recent weeks. Two separate waves of attacks allowed hackers to crank up the temperature on freezers and chilling units in at least a dozen countries, spoiling defrosted food and destroying produce. Some of the affected systems included remote-controlled refrigeration units made by Danish company Danfoss, which had stopped providing security updates to its customers’ freezers.

Hackers also targeted a blood bank in France, causing its refrigerated units to boost temperatures in its cold units containing donated blood supplies — but were stopped before the attack could compromise blood stores. The U.S. Department of Defense is investigating a spate of hacks targeting freezers run by the military, according to Reuters. The hacks were first reported by Signal and Silence.

The U.S. has not attributed the hacks to a particular group or government, but security researchers have broadly attributed the attacks to Iran; U.S. officials also reportedly suspect Iran is the likely culprit.

CISA, the FBI, and the Departments of Agriculture, Health and Human Services, and Transportation urged affected industries to remove remote control systems from the internet, change and strengthen passwords, apply patches where possible, and retire equipment that’s no longer supported by the vendor.

In a separate fact sheet, the departments said that hackers may attempt to “force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.”

“Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target,” said CISA’s acting cybersecurity chief Chris Butera.

Tech.title: 6 Best VPN Services (2026), Tested and Reviewed
Tech.content:
Top VPNs Compared

Number of Devices Number of Locations P2P Support Kill Switch Split Tunneling Double Hop Connection Ad/Tracker Blocker Packet Obfuscation WireGuard Support Proton VPN 10 127+ Yes Yes Yes Secure Core NetShield Yes Yes NordVPN 10 178+ Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes (NordLynx) Windscribe Unlimited 69+ Yes Yes Yes No Yes Yes Yes Bitdefender VPN 10 100+ Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Mullvad 5 50+ Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes (via Extension) Yes Yes ExpressVPN 14 170+ Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes No Yes (Lightway)

Other VPNs We’ve Tested

Surfshark: I've used Surfshark personally for a few years, and I'd still be using it if Proton didn't impress me so much. Surfshark is dead simple to use. It pops up and connects before swiftly getting out of my way so I can get on with my day. If you spring for a two-year plan, it's cheap. You can score over two years for around $54 with the Starter plan.

If you want to dig in deeper, you can. Surfshark is one of the most feature-rich VPNs I've used, sporting the basics like a double-hop connection and split tunneling, as well as an ad blocker and email masking. Like Proton, Surfshark offers other security tools like antivirus and dark web monitoring if you pick up a more expensive plan. Surfshark loses out just a bit when it comes to privacy, however. It has a no-logs policy, and it maintains a transparency report and a warrant canary, so it’s not bad in this regard. However, it doesn't have open-source applications, so you’ll need a bit more faith in Surfshark’s app security than with some other VPN services.

EventVPN: This is a free, ad-supported VPN from ExpressVPN. Ads and VPNs don't really mix, but EventVPN says it's able to offer a free service via Apple's App Tracking Transparency (ATT) and Identifier for Advertisers (IDFA), basically allowing it to serve ads without harvesting your personal data. The problem is the pervasiveness of ads. A banner lives at the top of the app at all times, and you'll need to sit through a 30-second ad each time you connect or disconnect; a big problem when some servers post unreasonably slow speeds. I'll admit EventVPN is a unique concept, but I see nothing better than ProtonVPN or Windscribe for a free VPN service. And when it comes to the inconvenience of sitting through ads, it's straight-up worse.

IVPN: This privacy-focused VPN provider is similar to Mullvad. It does not ask you to create an account with a username, password, and email, but instead generates a random ID, which you use to log in. That helps preserve your anonymity, since that information can’t be tied to your usage even if IVPN suffered a security incident. IVPN also accepts cryptocurrency payments (Bitcoin and Monero). Unlike Mullvad, IVPN offers one-year, two-year, and three-year plan options, as well as an unusual weekly option, which might be nice if you want a VPN while on vacation (IVPN standard is $2 per week). These can be more affordable than Mullvad’s monthly fee. However, IVPN lacks some privacy features you will find with Mullvad, such as RAM-less servers. IVPN scheduled a security audit for 2025, but as of January 2026, the results have not been posted. IVPN also has a tight two-device limit on the Standard plan. The Pro plan raises that to seven, but the Pro plan’s price is $10 per month, so it’s more expensive than Mullvad, which has a five-device limit. That remains true even if you go with a multi-year IVPN plan. Still, IVPN is a fine alternative if you want annual plan options. And while most VPN apps serve their purpose, I do think IVPN’s app is both more attractive and easier to use than Mullvad’s. —Matthew S. Smith

Private Internet Access (PIA): With its long history in the VPN space, PIA has maintained a track record of defending user privacy—even in the face of actual criminal activity. In 2016, a criminal complaint was filed in Florida against Preston Alexander McWaters for threats made online. McWaters was eventually convicted and sentenced to 42 months in prison. Investigators traced the online threats back to PIA's servers and subpoenaed the company. As the complaint reads, “A subpoena was sent to [Private Internet Access], and the only information they could provide is that the cluster of IP addresses being used was from the east coast of the United States.” According to the complaint, McWaters engaged in several other identifying activities, but PIA wasn't among them. Despite such a clear view of a VPN provider upholding its no-logging policy, PIA didn't impress me during my tests. It delivered the worst speeds out of any VPN I tested, with more than a 50 percent drop on the closest US server. (Windscribe, for context, only dropped 15.6 percent of my speed.)

MysteriumVPN: This is the go-to dVPN, or decentralized VPN, as far as I can tell. The concept of a decentralized VPN has existed for a while, but it's really gained traction over the last couple of years. The idea is to have a network of residential IP addresses that make up the network, routing your traffic through normal IP addresses to get around the increasingly common block lists for VPN servers. Mysterium accomplishes this network with MystNodes. It's a crypto node. People buy the node to earn crypto, and they're put into the Mysterium network. It's not inherently bad, but routing your traffic through a single residential IP is a little worrisome. Even without the decentralized kick, Mysterium was slow, and it doesn't maintain any sort of privacy materials, be it a third-party audit, warranty canary, or transparency report.

PrivadoVPN: A popular option to recommend as a free VPN, offering a decent free service, with a handful of full-speed servers and 10 GB of data per month. You'll have to suffer through four—yes, four—redirects begging you to pay for a subscription before signing up, but the free plan works. The problem is how new PrivadoVPN is. There's no transparency report or audit available, and although the speeds are decent, they aren't as good as Proton, Windscribe, or Surfshark. PrivadoVPN isn't bad, but it's hard to recommend when Proton and Windscribe exist with free plans that are equally as good.

VPNs to Avoid

You'll find dozens of free VPNs all claiming to protect your privacy. Most of them don't. There are plenty of VPNs I don’t recommend, but these are a few I've tested that are worth mentioning.

Hola is an infamous name in the VPN industry, but it's been close to a decade since its very public debacle. Hola is free, and it's able to stay free because it uses a peer-to-peer network. Hola also owns Bright Data (formerly Luminati), which is a data collection company. In 2015, Hola sold access to the network of its free users (via Luminati), which was used in a distributed denial-of-service attack on 8chan. It's been a decade since that incident, but Hola still operates in a similar way. If you don't pay, you could be used as an exit node in Bright Data's network, and the privacy policy makes it clear that Hola logs data about your usage, including your IP address, the pages you visit, and timestamps.

X-VPN is available on desktop, but it primarily shows up in results on the Apple App Store and Google Play, targeting mobile users with a free offering. X-VPN hasn't done anything explicitly wrong like Hola, but it has way too many inconsistencies to recommend. For starters, it uses a proprietary VPN protocol, which it obfuscates within the app. Proprietary protocols like NordVPN's NordLynx and ExpressVPN's Lightway are based on existing, open-source protocols. Further, X-VPN was highlighted in a Tech Transparency Project report about free VPNs with links to the Chinese government; X-VPN is based in Hong Kong. There's no smoking gun with X-VPN, but there doesn't need to be. The speeds aren't the best, the app lacks basic features like split tunneling, and the pricing for a paid plan is in line with top providers.

How We Test VPNs

Functionally, a VPN should do two things: keep your internet speed reasonably fast, and actually protect your browsing data. That's where I focused my testing. Extra features, a comfy UI, and customization settings are great, but they don't matter if the core service is broken.

Speed testing requires spot-checking, as the time of day, the network you're connected to, and the specific VPN server you're using can all influence speeds.
